The lawmakers also raised concerns about the CPSC’s intention to expand data collection under the NEISS-R program, “Historically, hospitals have been instructed to exclude reports on emergency department visits outside of the CPSC’s jurisdiction. Based on public reporting, the NEISS-R appears to be effectively eliminating that guidance and dramatically expanding data collection efforts to include more than 10,000 injury codes. This includes incidents with no relation to consumer products governed by the CPSC, including both suicide attempts and vaccines.”

The lawmakers continued, “Given President Donald Trump’s recent claims that widely used vaccines could be ‘quite lethal’, these actions raise concerns that yet another formerly nonpartisan arm of government has been conscripted into Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy’s relentless search for data to bolster his unsupported theories about the dangers of approved vaccines.”

The lawmakers called on CPSC to halt the implementation of NIESS-R in light of privacy concerns and a lack of transparency involving its implementation process “The use of AI has the potential to expose patient data to unnecessary security risks, including unintended data breaches and the improper use of individuals’ data to train current or future AI systems. Some of these concerns have already been echoed by former CPSC officials who explained the liability associated with collecting and storing massive amounts of data…Americans deserve the certainty that their personal health information is safe and that the CPSC is adequately managing the roll out of NEISS-R.”

The full text of today’s letter is available here and below.

Dear Acting Chair Feldman,

We are deeply troubled by the Consumer Product Safety Commission’s (CPSC) decision to continue with the expansion of the National Electronic Injury Surveillance System (NEISS) without providing detailed information about its rollout to the public or to Congress. The NEISS is an important tool that allows the CPSC to monitor product safety trends and issue product recalls or warnings to protect consumers. However, a review of the proposed NEISS-Remodel (NEISS-R) raises serious concerns about potential violations of agency process, changes to data collection that could impact agency rulemaking, and the use of artificial intelligence (AI).[1]

As you know, the NEISS allows hospitals across the country to voluntarily submit information on emergency department visits involving consumer products.[2] With this information, the CPSC is able to produce estimates of product-related injuries, monitor safety trends, and determine if a product recall or warning is necessary.[3] On July 22, 2026, the CPSC announced an update to the system that will dramatically increase the scope of its surveillance and the use of AI.[4] Under the Paperwork Reduction Act, the CPSC is obligated to submit a Federal Register notice and set up a public comment period along with publishing a System of Records notice before making this change.[5] Despite this legal requirement, the Commission has yet to initiate this process.[6] Based on the novel nature of AI and the plethora of concerns that have been raised by experts, including AI industry leaders,[7] it is essential that the CPSC seek appropriate input from relevant stakeholders – as required by law – before exposing patient data to undue risk. Therefore, we continue to strongly urge the CPSC to hold off on further action until the proper procedures are followed.

Not only is the CPSC disregarding federal law and risking patient privacy, it is also departing from established operating policies. Historically, hospitals have been instructed to exclude reports on emergency department visits outside of the CPSC’s jurisdiction.[8] Based on public reporting the NEISS-R appears to be effectively eliminating that guidance and dramatically expanding data collection efforts to include more than 10,000 injury codes. This includes incidents with no relation to consumer products governed by the CPSC, including both suicide attempts and vaccines.[9]

Recently, you told Nextgov/FCW that collecting medical records on vaccines was necessary because the CPSC regulates drug packaging under the Poison Prevention Packaging Act. This absurd justification is wrong on its face: PPPA was enacted to require the use of child-resistant packaging, primarily for household products.[10] While the law includes certain medications, such as common over the counter drugs, that could pose a hazard to children if they are not appropriately packaged, patients are not shopping for vaccines and taking them home, where they could be accidentally tampered with by a child. You also did not provide any evidence to back up your claim that there have been reported poisoning incidents involving vaccines that were not in child-resistant packaging.[11] Given President Donald Trump’s recent claims that widely used vaccines could be “quite lethal”, these actions raise concerns that yet another formerly nonpartisan arm of government has been conscripted into Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy’s relentless search for data to bolster his unsupported theories about the dangers of approved vaccines.[12]

Further, we are deeply concerned that these changes under NEISS-R could impact agency rulemaking procedures and outcomes. Major changes to the NEISS could fundamentally reshape how safety rules are prioritized, justified and litigated. NEISS is designed to represent a statistical sample of injury data from across U.S. that the CPSC has used to estimate national injuries and deaths, as well as support rulemakings. It is unclear how this new system will provide comparable nationally representative data and whether differences in methodology and data collection could hamper future rulemakings that require demonstrable risk over time. Consumer safety from hazardous products hinges on strong agency rules that hold industries accountable. It is critical that the agency provide honest and transparent information to the public regarding this matter.

The need for transparency is increasingly important given the use of AI in analyzing patients’ personal information and medical data. Konza Health, the CPSC’s contractor for this project, has claimed it will use “advanced analytic parsing and filtering capabilities” to automatically filter and transmit the massive amount of data collected from hospitals to the CPSC.”[13] Additionally, a spokesperson from the CPSC shared that after receiving the information from Konza Health, the CPSC would use AI to conduct data analysis and identify trends. Given the role that AI will play in the NEISS-R and the fact that Konza Health could be responsible for storing and securing large swaths of user medical data, it is imperative that the public receive a full account of what technologies and software they will use to comply with this initiative.[14] This is especially important because neither Konza Health nor the CPSC have confirmed if patients will be asked to consent to having their information shared. The use of AI has the potential to expose patient data to unnecessary security risks, including unintended data breaches and the improper use of individuals’ data to train current or future AI systems. Some of these concerns have already been echoed by former CPSC officials who explained the liability associated with collecting and storing massive amounts of data.[15]

Americans deserve the certainty that their personal health information is safe and that the CPSC is adequately managing the roll out of NEISS-R, including strong oversight of Konza Health. The CPSC has claimed that the final architecture of the NEISS-R has not yet been determined since the CPSC does not expect to finalize the NEISS-R until 2027. If that is indeed true, this means that hospitals have been solicited for participation and asked to consent to data sharing requirements before the CPSC can even answer basic questions about the new system. If the CPSC is committed to honesty and transparency, implementation of the NIESS-R must be publicly halted until the CPSC, Congress, and the public have an understanding of the full scope and impact of these updates. To achieve this, we request answers to the following questions by November 19th, 2026:

Will the CPSC require consent from patients prior to the use of their medical data for the NEISS-R system?

How will the CPSC use AI to analyze and sort the data collected from hospitals?

Konza Health has claimed that they are not using AI. Please describe how Konza Health will perform its obligations under its contract and whether it includes the use of AI.

Will any Personally Identifiable Information (PII) obtained through NEISS-R be used to train AI software?

If using a third-party AI product not hosted by the CPSC, will PII be used as an input or otherwise exposed to the model?

What restrictions, if any, does the CPSC plan to implement on transferal of PII to any third party?

Please provide a detailed description of any current or future plans to share NEISS-R data with the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).

Please specify what type of data analyses Konza Health will conduct that require the use of PII.

Please explain why the analyses cannot be done with data that has been anonymized and/or aggregated before Konza has access.

How will changes to data collection methodologies impact the CPSC’s ability to extrapolate trends or use the data for rulemaking?

How will the CPSC ensure the statistical validity of the system if hospitals select not to respond to the request for information?

As stated above, you recently defended the CPSC’s decision to collect vaccine information because of the CPSC’s oversight of the Poison Prevention Packaging Act. Please explain how the PPPA applies to vaccines administered in a health care setting.

Please provide a detailed list of incidents related to the “poisonings associated with… pharmaceutical packaging that doesn't meet specific child-resistant special packaging requirements” that you alluded to in your statement.

Please provide a detailed explanation of any staffing changes planned to accommodate NEISS-R and the expanded use of AI.

What support is the CPSC providing to hospitals to meet its request for information?

Does the CPSC plan to issue a System of Records Notice or to publish the proposal for public comment as required by the Paperwork Reduction Act? If so, when and if not, please explain why?

WASHINGTON — U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, released the following statement after the Senate advanced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), bipartisan legislation to lower energy bills, hold data centers accountable, reduce emissions, and create good-paying jobs.

U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee Ranking Member Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) and U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee Ranking Member U.S. Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) host press conference to urge Senate passage of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, November 9, 2026.

Watch the full video of Heinrich’s remarks here.

A transcript of Heinrich’s remarks as delivered is below:

Every once in a while, I don’t wear my Senate pin, even if it means I’m going to get stopped on the way in.

I wear this pin.

It’s my dad’s 60-year IBEW pin, and he spent those 60 years keeping people’s lights on and working to keep their electricity bills affordable.

A little over a month ago, Senator Whitehouse and myself announced, along with our Republican colleagues, our bipartisan permitting bill.

And today, just one week after Americans sent a pretty resounding message about their priorities, we are taking our first vote on that legislation.

And that message that the people sent was pretty clear: they want Congress focused on making their lives more affordable, and that’s precisely what this permitting reform bill will do.

BAAJA will save households billions of dollars in electricity costs, so that families can have money in their pockets for more than just keeping the lights on and their homes warm.

This bill directly holds data centers accountable, forcing big corporations to pay their full share instead of pushing costs on the consumers.

That one provision is worth $35 billion dollars to American households.

That’s pretty remarkable.

BAAJA will create over 100,000 trades and manufacturing jobs, good-paying jobs that workers can be certain will be around to support their families through a project’s completion.

And BAAJA will cut emissions up to 20% from the power sector over the next decade, meaning cleaner air, healthier communities, and fewer healthcare costs.

This bill’s not perfect.

We’ve never pretended it was.

It is, after all, bipartisan, and that means that neither side got everything they want.

We had to find common ground.

We had to make compromises, and we had to work through some very real disagreements.

But bipartisanship doesn’t mean we stop listening, and it doesn’t mean we stop working to make the legislation better.

I have worked hard to incorporate the feedback that we’ve heard from Tribes and New Mexicans into our Manager’s Amendment, and I want to walk you through a few of those changes because they’re pretty important.

First, on Tribal consultation, I’ve heard directly from Tribal leaders about the importance of having a meaningful voice in decisions that affect their communities and affect their ancestral lands.

We work to strengthen that dramatically in this Manager’s Amendment.

Tribes will now have an equal seat with states in transmission planning, and federal agencies will be required, and let me say that again: required “shall” consult, not “may” consult, “shall” consult early with Tribes on projects that will affect important cultural sites, including on what properties are affected, the impacts of the project, and ways to avoid, minimize, or mitigate potential harms, and basically that means that mandatory Tribal consultation is now built into every single step of the Section 106 process by law.

We’ve also extended the window for objections to agency reports.

We’ve strengthened opportunities for states to weigh in, and we’ve given states a way to ask FERC to investigate local utility projects that gouge consumers.

That, in my view, is particularly important as private equity and other outside investors seek to take a larger role in electric utilities.

States need the tools to protect their ratepayers.

Third, we’ve made sure that workers’ rights are protected.

The Manager’s Amendment preserves collective bargaining agreements for union employees of the power of bargaining administrations, so that those workers can continue to bargain collectively and stand up for workers’ rights.

And finally, we’ve added a new Department of Energy Data Center Community Assistance Program because when a community is considering whether or not to grant a permit to a major data center, it needs to understand what that project will mean for its electricity supply, costs, water resources, infrastructure, and local economy, in order for them to make a good decision.

This program will give state, local, and Tribal governments the technical assistance they need to make their own informed decisions.

These are meaningful improvements.

They reflect the feedback that we’ve heard and they make an important piece of legislation, in my view, even stronger.

And importantly, they don’t change what this bill was always about: lowering energy costs, building the infrastructure our country so desperately needs, creating good-paying jobs, protecting our communities, and making sure that data centers pay their fair share.

That’s what we set out to accomplish when we started this project, and that’s what we’re still working to deliver.

So I would urge all my colleagues: Let’s get this done.

Let’s make it possible for America to build big things in this country again.

The people sent us a very clear message on Tuesday that they expect us to lower the costs in their daily lives.

We don’t have to wait for the new Congress to start lowering costs.

We can do that today.

So let’s pass permitting reform.

WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Senators Mark R. Warner and Tim Kaine (both D-VA) and U.S. Rep. Jennifer McClellan (D-VA-04) raised concerns about the Social Security Administration’s (SSA) abrupt decision to halt funding for the Work Incentives Planning and Assistance (WIPA) program’s National Training and Data Center (NTDC) at Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU), threatening critical services that help Americans with disabilities navigate Social Security benefits while seeking employment.

The NTDC provides training, certification, and technical assistance to more than 900 benefits counselors serving individuals with disabilities across the country. On October 2, 2026, SSA abruptly declined to fund VCU’s contract for another year and ordered the university to immediately halt work, disrupting essential training and support services for 74 WIPA projects nationwide.

In a letter to SSA Commissioner Frank Bisignano, the lawmakers demanded an explanation for the decision and pressed the agency to clarify how it intends to restore these critical services and fulfill its statutory obligations.

The lawmakers wrote, “We write to inquire about the Social Security Administration’s (SSA) decision to defund the Work Incentives Planning and Assistance program’s (WIPA) National Training and Data Center (NTDC). We are aware that on Friday, October 2, 2026, the SSA exercised its option not to extend its contract with Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU) to administer the NTDC and ordered VCU to immediately halt all work providing Community Work Incentives Coordinators (CWICs) nationwide with training, certification, technical assistance, and other resource support.”

The WIPA program helps individuals who receive Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) or Supplemental Security Income (SSI) due to severe, long-term medical conditions understand how employment may affect their benefits. Benefits counselors provide free, individualized guidance to help Americans with disabilities pursue employment opportunities without inadvertently jeopardizing the benefits they rely on.

The lawmakers continued, “CWICs at WIPA projects help bridge the information gap for beneficiaries by looking at their individual circumstances and advising them on how to maintain their benefits while working. To ensure the efficacy of the WIPA programs, the law also required SSA to establish a corps of work incentives specialists and provide training and technical assistance for those specialists. CWICs provide information and resources to help beneficiaries make informed decisions on returning to work.”

Despite Congress appropriating $23 million for the WIPA program in Fiscal Year 2026, SSA’s decision has left benefits counselors nationwide without access to necessary training resources, certification services, performance data, and institutional knowledge. These resources are critical to training new counselors and ensuring that both new and existing counselors provide accurate, reliable guidance to Americans with disabilities. The sudden loss of these services raises serious concerns about SSA’s ability to meet its statutory obligations and ensure that beneficiaries continue receiving the support they need.

The lawmakers pressed SSA to explain the rationale and timing of its decision, identify what training and certification resources remain available to benefits counselors, address disruptions to required performance reporting, and clarify whether the agency intends to restore these services through VCU, bring them in-house, or award a new contract.

Read the full letter here and below.

Dear Commissioner Bisignano,

We write to inquire about the Social Security Administration’s (SSA) decision to defund the Work Incentives Planning and Assistance program’s (WIPA) National Training and Data Center (NTDC). We are aware that on Friday, October 2, 2026, the SSA exercised its option not to extend its contract with Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU) to administer the NTDC and ordered VCU to immediately halt all work providing Community Work Incentives Coordinators (CWICs) nationwide with training, certification, technical assistance, and other resource support.

Disabled beneficiaries who qualify for SSDI or SSI benefits are among the most vulnerable populations who suffer from severe, long-term medical conditions. To maintain compliance, beneficiaries must navigate a series of strict and complex requirements set out by the Social Security Act, including on earned income. For beneficiaries who need to earn extra income to support themselves or their families, incorrectly interpreting the rules can lead to a termination of benefits.

The Ticket to Work and Work Incentives Improvement Act of 1999 directed the Commissioner of Social Security to establish a program to provide information about work and benefits to people who receive Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) or Supplemental Security Income (SSI) because of a disability. Using that authority, SSA established 74 WIPA projects in all 50 states, the District of Columbia, and U.S. territories. WIPA projects and community organizations employ over 900 benefits counselors who provide free in-depth counseling to disabled beneficiaries on the effect of work on their SSDI or SSI benefits.

CWICs at WIPA projects help bridge the information gap for beneficiaries by looking at their individual circumstances and advising them on how to maintain their benefits while working. To ensure the efficacy of the WIPA programs, the law also required SSA to establish a corps of work incentives specialists and provide training and technical assistance for those specialists. CWICs provide information and resources to help beneficiaries make informed decisions on returning to work.

In Fiscal Year 2026 Congress appropriated $23 million to operate the WIPA program, 0.1 percent of SSA’s annual administrative budget. However, despite clear Congressional intent in support of the WIPA program, SSA has decided to unilaterally disband a vital component of the program. Without the NTDC, WIPA projects nationwide have lost access to valuable training resources and performance data to train new CWICs and ensure both new and existing Coordinators provide accurate and relevant information to beneficiaries. WIPA projects are also losing access to an invaluable source of institutional knowledge.

After this abrupt decision, it is unclear how SSA intends to comply with the statutory requirements of the Ticket to Work and Work Incentives Improvement Act of 1999 and Congressional intent set out in the Fiscal Year 2026 Consolidated Appropriations Act.

We request answers to the following questions by November 16, 2026:

Why was the decision made to defund NTDC? Please provide a full account of the facts that informed the decision to defund NTDC.

When was the final decision made to defund NTDC? When were NTDC staff and VCU staff informed of the decision?

What training resources, if any, do WIPA projects have access to following the closure of the NTDC?

WIPA projects are required to submit its quarterly performance data at the end of this month. The performance data WIPA projects submit to maintain grantee status was collected and tracked through the WIPA STAR system. Given the sudden cancellation of the WIPA STAR system, will the reporting deadline be extended?

To obtain/maintain certification, CWICs were required to receive training through VCU. How will CWICs now receive certification training? Will SSA waive certification requirements if CWICs are unable to access the training?

Will SSA bring the training and technical assistance previously performed by VCU in-house? If not, does SSA plan on issuing a recompete of the contract?

Letter Text (PDF)

Washington (November 9, 2026) - Senator Edward J. Markey (D-Mass.), a member of the Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee, today wrote to Sundar Pichai, CEO of Alphabet Inc. and Google, demanding the company reverse its policy to block access to Google Search on K-12 student accounts at schools that want to disable artificial intelligence (AI) services, including Gemini, Google’s AI chatbot. AI chatbots are often designed to encourage compulsive use and emotional attachment exposing children to risks of manipulation and, in some more serious cases, have resulted in chatbots encouraging children to die by suicide. Google should not use its dominant position in the education technology market to force schools to adopt potentially dangerous AI technologies or risk losing a critical research tool like Google Search.

In the letter, Senator Markey wrote, “Just this month, a girl and her family sued Google after Gemini allegedly ‘helped coach her through a plan to commit suicide.’ The girl accessed Gemini through Google Search on a school-issued Chromebook, even though the school had blocked access to Gemini’s standalone app and website. At a time when schools, parents, and policymakers are working hard to implement safeguards on AI chatbots for our children, Google is recklessly forcing AI on schools and treating kids like collateral damage. Schools deserve the right to block student access to AI chatbots without also forfeiting access to an important educational tool.”

Senator Markey continued, “Google’s dominant position in education technology makes this ultimatum particularly concerning. Although Google has a right to create and offer new educational tools, it should not use its dominant market position to force schools to adopt them.”

Senator Markey requested the following information by November 30, 2026:

Will Google commit to allowing schools to disable generative AI features and chatbots on K-12 student accounts, including AI Overviews, Gemini, and Guided Learning, while retaining access to Google Search?

Is it technically feasible for Google to provide K-12 student accounts with Google Search results that exclude AI Overviews, Guided Learning, and other generative AI features or chatbots?

Please provide any research, testing, or risk assessments that Google has conducted on the safety, mental health, and learning effects of AI Overviews, Gemini, and Guided Learning on K-12 students, including for children under age 13.

How many K-12 schools and districts that use Google’s products currently restrict or prohibit students’ access to generative AI features or AI chatbots outside Google Search?

Washington (November 9, 2026) - Senator Edward J. Markey (D-Mass.), a member of the Environment and Public Works Committee, released the following statement on the Senate’s vote to invoke cloture on the motion to proceed to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) of 2026.

“We need to stop the Trump administration’s weaponization of our government against clean, affordable, and ready-to-go energy sources, and we need to build an energy grid that works for Americans now and into the future—that means cutting emissions and cutting costs. But as currently drafted, this bill attempts to address these goals by asking communities to trade the benefits of interstate transmission and the ability to make data centers pay more for grid power for the sacrifices of weakened clean water protections, intrusion on sovereign Tribal rights, and limits on the ability to be heard and considered during federal approval of projects ranging from hyperscale data centers to petrochemical plants. Legal experts have also raised serious concerns about the potential unintended effects of provisions that are meant to prevent Trump’s misuse of the permitting process but could impair environmental protections into the future at taxpayers’ expense. And without a committee process and sufficient time to work through and resolve these tradeoffs and questions, we do not have the answers we need.

“Voters sent a clear message last week that they want better deals than the ones they’ve gotten under unified Republican leadership. I believe we owe it to them to fight to win a better deal that delivers clean energy megawatts and jobs, near- and long-term savings on energy bills, and real climate benefits without leaving so many important members of our community on the losing side of the ledger.

“Because of these issues on timing, transparency, and threats to our clean air, water, and Tribes, I will vote against the motion to invoke cloture on this legislation. I will continue to discuss all these issues with my colleagues, both in the coming days and into the next Congress, and hope to work toward a better deal in the future.”

Washington, DC – Today, Oregon’s Senator Jeff Merkley released the following statement on proposed legislation in the Senate to reform permitting:

“Transmission is much needed to move renewable energy from solar and wind farms to the places where there is a high demand for electricity.

“Data centers should pay their fair share for the resources they use.

“And having cleaner, cheaper renewable energy is important for reducing energy costs here at home, for our country’s competitive status in the world, and for our ability to tackle climate chaos.

“I strongly support the portions of this bill that seek these outcomes and praise the work of my colleagues – Senators Whitehouse and Heinrich – who have strived to accomplish these objectives.

“But at the demand of the fossil fuel titans, this bill also accelerates the extraction and burning of fossil fuels.

“Very simply: getting more renewable electrons where they are needed doesn’t tackle climate change if you simultaneously promote the burning of more fossil fuels. Unfortunately, this bill does exactly that.

“This bill could make it easier to build more data centers powered by ‘behind the meter’ natural gas plants.

“It makes it much easier to build natural gas pipelines that will transport incredible quantities of natural gas overseas as LNG.

“More pipelines and export terminals equal more American fracked gas burned at home and abroad.

“And while the models exclude American gas burned abroad from the climate impact of this bill, the Earth is affected the same no matter where the gas is burned.

“This bill has a number of other features that merit careful analysis. Yet, the bill has never had a public hearing. Not in the House. Not in the Senate.

“Robust consideration of the bill should be a priority in the new Congress.

“Here are some of the other issues that merit careful examination.

“The bill restricts states’ ability to raise and address clean water concerns on gas pipelines as well as transmission lines.

“It shortens timelines that make it hard-to-impossible for grassroots and community groups to raise concerns about projects.

“It eliminates tools that states and localities use to fight the development of new data centers and detention centers.

“And it impacts the sovereignty and rights of Tribes.

“Permitting reform for electrical transmission lines is essential.

“But the current bill raises too many serious issues that require more deliberation.

“I will vote against the bill before us today, but I look forward to working with my colleagues to get permitting reform right.”

WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator Brian Schatz (D-Hawai‘i) released the following statement on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026.

“The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is a historic bill that reflects years of bipartisan work to reform our outdated permitting processes while protecting the environment.

“Permitting delays drive up costs and stall projects, making electricity, housing, and public transportation more expensive. This legislation will help lower costs, build clean energy, modernize America’s grid, cut emissions, and hold data center developers accountable.

“This bill is a bipartisan compromise, and deals like this are tough. We heard from Native leaders and advocates and secured some key changes to improve the historic preservation title and ensure that federal agencies consult with Native Hawaiian organizations, Tribes, and others about historic and cultural resources. Washington, D.C. – Following U.S. Senator Schiff (D-Calif)’s recent inquiry to Meta and public backlash about the company’s updated Commercial Terms of Use to require all commercial accounts using Meta platforms to grant expansive authorization to the company to deploy automated crawlers and web scrapers, the company has announced it is reversing course.

Washington, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), member of the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works and Ranking Member of the Fisheries, Water, and Wildlife Subcommittee, issued the following statement after voting against the motion to proceed to the permitting reform legislation on the Senate floor:

“The need for a permitting reform package has only grown in the past decade, as bureaucracy has stymied the development of vital projects from clean energy to housing that could lower costs. And I appreciate the work done by Senators Whitehouse and Heinrich to negotiate a bipartisan agreement, as a lasting solution can only be reached by reaching across the aisle. In particular, the transmission and grid reform provisions are very positive. And the changes that they secured in the manager’s amendment make this a better bill. Nevertheless, the bill needs further improvement before I can support it.

“My top priorities in such an agreement are to bring down energy bills through new clean energy development, to lower emission rates, to support tribal sovereignty, and to stop the administration from attacking American clean energy projects. This includes restoring the billions of dollars in terminated energy projects in California, as well as the offshore wind projects the administration baselessly and illegally canceled. The president’s comments today, that notwithstanding any compromise in this bill, he intends to continue blocking wind projects, demonstrate a singular but telling lack of good faith. I have said from the start that we need to have confidence that any permitting reform legislation is not going to be weaponized by this or any future administration to single out states and provide giveaways to the oil and gas industries. In its current form, this bill does not satisfy those priorities and raises other serious concerns.

“This legislation would jeopardize tribal sovereignty through major changes to the National Historic Preservation Act, impact the State of California’s authorities under the Clean Water Act, and constrict federal agencies’ ability to protect vulnerable wildlife under the Endangered Species Act. While I support the provisions in this bill that require data center companies to cover the costs of grid infrastructure and protect American taxpayers from footing the bill — which mirror my legislation — the legislation overall contains too many giveaways to oil and gas with insufficient constraints on an energy policy that has prioritized corporate profit over the pocketbooks of hard-working Americans and public health. I believe Congress should work on stronger guardrail provisions to ensure that such provisions will not be used to improperly tilt the playing field in favor of fossil fuels by the Trump administration, which has failed to provide any assurance to Congress that it will follow the law if this bill is enacted.”

The Ticket to Work and Work Incentives Improvement Act of 1999 directed the Commissioner of Social Security to establish a program to provide information about work and benefits to people who receive Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) or Supplemental Security Income (SSI) because of a disability. Using that authority, SSA established 74 WIPA projects in all 50 states, the District of Columbia, and U.S. territories. WIPA projects and community organizations employ over 900 benefits counselors who provide free in-depth counseling to disabled beneficiaries on the effect of work on their SSDI or SSI benefits.

CWICs at WIPA projects help bridge the information gap for beneficiaries by looking at their individual circumstances and advising them on how to maintain their benefits while working. To ensure the efficacy of the WIPA programs, the law also required SSA to establish a corps of work incentives specialists and provide training and technical assistance for those specialists. CWICs provide information and resources to help beneficiaries make informed decisions on returning to work.

In Fiscal Year 2026 Congress appropriated $23 million to operate the WIPA program, 0.1 percent of SSA’s annual administrative budget. However, despite clear Congressional intent in support of the WIPA program, SSA has decided to unilaterally disband a vital component of the program. Without the NTDC, WIPA projects nationwide have lost access to valuable training resources and performance data to train new CWICs and ensure both new and existing Coordinators provide accurate and relevant information to beneficiaries. WIPA projects are also losing access to an invaluable source of institutional knowledge.

After this abrupt decision, it is unclear how SSA intends to comply with the statutory requirements of the Ticket to Work and Work Incentives Improvement Act of 1999 and Congressional intent set out in the Fiscal Year 2026 Consolidated Appropriations Act.

We request answers to the following questions by November 16, 2026:

Why was the decision made to defund NTDC? Please provide a full account of the facts that informed the decision to defund NTDC.

When was the final decision made to defund NTDC? When were NTDC staff and VCU staff informed of the decision?

What training resources, if any, do WIPA projects have access to following the closure of the NTDC?

WIPA projects are required to submit its quarterly performance data at the end of this month. The performance data WIPA projects submit to maintain grantee status was collected and tracked through the WIPA STAR system. Given the sudden cancellation of the WIPA STAR system, will the reporting deadline be extended?

To obtain/maintain certification, CWICs were required to receive training through VCU. How will CWICs now receive certification training? Will SSA waive certification requirements if CWICs are unable to access the training?

Will SSA bring the training and technical assistance previously performed by VCU in-house? If not, does SSA plan on issuing a recompete of the contract?

Washington, D.C. (11/10/2026): Today, Rep. Burchett introduced the Community Control of Data Centers Act. This legislation prevents federal funds from going towards the construction or operation of data centers before obtaining state and local approval. The recent boom in AI has made data centers a central component of infrastructure that may have major economic implications. Despite potential benefits, it is important that the decision to build them should be made by the Americans who live in those towns, not Washington bureaucrats and Big Tech CEOs.

“As the former Mayor of Knox County, I know how important local control is over projects that could have adverse effects on the municipality where they’re located,” said Rep. Tim Burchett. “This bill allows local governments to retake control over new data center construction, putting the power back in the hands of the folks who are most affected. People are sick and tired of federal overreach that harms their communities, businesses, and the places they call home.”

matches.text:
Washington, D.C. — In case you missed it, Congressman Rich McCormick (GA-07) recently wrote an op-ed in The Hill highlighting his newly introduced Common-Sense Cloud Security Act and the urgent need to modernize America's cybersecurity standards as threats to our critical infrastructure continue to evolve.

The legislation directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to update cloud security guidance, strengthen cyber risk assessments, and establish a voluntary certification program to help organizations better prevent, detect, and contain cyberattacks. In the op-ed, McCormick emphasized that protecting America's digital infrastructure requires more than keeping hackers out. It means limiting the damage they can cause once inside, ensuring a single breach cannot compromise an entire network.

“The key challenge is not simply keeping attackers out. It’s limiting what they can do when they get in,” McCormick wrote.

McCormick underscored the importance of practical, risk-based security standards that protect the hospitals, businesses, financial institutions, and government agencies Americans rely on every day without slowing American innovation.

You can read the full op-ed in The Hill or below.

Image

America has embraced cloud computing at a remarkable pace with nearly every aspect of life now running through the cloud. Businesses, hospitals, banks, and government agencies rely on cloud services to store data, run operations, and deliver critical services. As our reliance grows, so does our exposure to cyber threats. The very innovation that has transformed our economy has also created new vulnerabilities that demand our attention.

That’s why I introduced the Common-Sense Cloud Security Act. This bill directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology to develop updated guidance for securing cloud environments and assessing cyber risk in ways that reflect how modern systems actually operate.

The key challenge is not simply keeping attackers out. It’s limiting what they can do when they get in.

Think of a cloud network like a building. Strong locks, passwords, and identity checks keep intruders out. But security also depends on what happens inside. An intruder should not be able to walk into every room, access every file, or reach every critical system. The same principle applies in the cloud.

For far too long, cybersecurity has focused on preventing a breach without giving enough attention to containing one. In today’s increasingly interconnected environments, one compromised account or application should not put an entire network at risk.

Resilience matters just as much as prevention.

As a Marine Corps veteran and member of the House Armed Services Committee, I know firsthand that military and national security depend on the strength of the systems behind them. My work on the House Science, Space, and Technology Committee and the House AI Task Force have reinforced a critical lesson: American innovation and digital security must advance together. As technology evolves, so must our ability to protect it.

Security experts often use the term “blast radius” to describe how far an attack can spread and how much damage it can cause. A single compromised account, application or service should not become a gateway to an entire organization. Effective cybersecurity is not just about detecting threats. It is about containing them. Measuring and reducing that risk provides a more meaningful assessment of security than simply determining whether suspicious activity can be detected.

The rise of super intelligence (formerly, “artificial intelligence”) makes this challenge even more urgent. Modern SI systems increasingly interact with multiple applications, databases and services across an organization. While these capabilities can create tremendous productivity and efficiency gains, they can also expand the potential consequences of a compromise. The more authority a system has, the more important it becomes to establish clear limits on what it can access.

This is not about slowing innovation with another unnecessary layer of bureaucracy. It is about developing practical, risk-based security standards that reflect how modern cloud systems actually work and giving organizations meaningful ways to demonstrate that they are in compliance.

If effective cybersecurity means limiting the damage caused by a breach, then our standards must reflect that reality. That is why my Common-Sense Cloud Security Act directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology to develop updated guidance for modern cloud environments, including identity management, oversight of third-party connections, detection of suspicious activity, and ways to assess the potential impact of a compromise. The bill would also establish a voluntary certification program and help ensure federal cloud security requirements keep pace with evolving technology and threats.

No law or standard can eliminate every cyber threat. What we can do is make attacks harder, limit their impact, and improve our ability to recover when they occur.

I will continue working with cybersecurity experts and industry leaders to strengthen the security of the cloud infrastructure Americans rely on every day. In today's interconnected world, security is not measured by whether a breach occurs. It is measured by how well we contain it. Cyber threats will continue to evolve, but a single breach should never be allowed to become a systemic failure. That is the standard we should strive for as we secure America’s digital future.

Congressman Chris Pappas (NH-01) and Congressman Lloyd Doggett (TX-37), Ranking Member of the Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, led 23 members incalling on the Government Accountability Office (GAO) Acting Comptroller General to investigate the ways that the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for administrative purposes by hospitals and insurers impact cost and quality of patient care.

“AI has the potential to help develop drugs, diagnose patients more effectively, cut down on paperwork for physicians, and improve speed for insurer decision-making. But its largely federally unregulated use for administrative tasks within the health care field poses significant risks to patient care and costs. While these benefits are promising, we must determine how the use of AI is impacting patient care and affordability,” the members wrote.

Pappas and members highlighted the importance of ensuring that AI isn’t raising costs for patients, explaining that “Patient costs have continued to rise drastically in recent years. Many individuals and families saw their insurance premiums double or even triple after Congress failed to extend the Affordable Care Act (ACA) enhanced premium tax credits. More than one million people have lost health coverage this year because the Trump administration has allowed prices to skyrocket for ACA plans and cut Medicaid coverage for our most vulnerable families. Individuals are being forced to stretch their budgets thinner than ever to maintain their health insurance, some having to choose between affording medical care and putting food on the table or making rent. AI use by hospitals and insurers may only further burden patients if left unchecked.”

AI use by both hospitals and insurers in coding, billing, and making coverage determinations may be impacting the cost and quality of care. Citing pending lawsuits against UnitedHealth, Cigna, and Humana, the members raised the question, “Is the use of AI by insurers denying American families’ access to their covered benefits?... Strong evidence shows how delays and denial of benefits can result in patient harm, and we must determine if and how AI may be exacerbating such delays and denials.”

They continued, “Patients can benefit from AI assisting medical professionals in providing more holistic care and reducing coding errors. However, it is unclear if this is the case or if AI is simply identifying all possible ways the visit could be reimbursed, regardless of what treatment the patient received. More clarity is needed around AI’s impact on coding and billing and the implications for both patient care and premiums.”

The members push GAO to investigate and answer several questions on the use of AI by hospitals and insurers given the importance of providing appropriate and timely health care to all individuals and ensuring costs do not increase further for patients.

The text of the letter can be found here.

matches.text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Chairman of the Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) Committee, spoke on the Senate floor to highlight the urgency of passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), legislation to reform our nation’s permitting and environmental review processes and make life more affordable for American families. Following Chairman Capito’s remarks, the Senate advanced BAAJA by a vote of 73-25.

Below are the floor remarks of Chairman Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) as prepared for delivery.

“Madam President, for far too long, critical investments in our nation’s infrastructure, energy production, and economy have been forced to sit on the sidelines due to endless red tape, duplicative reviews, and regulatory uncertainty.

“Businesses large and small, looking to invest meaningfully in our country, lack the certainty they need to make decisions. Communities nationwide have waited in regulatory limbo for roads, bridges, energy infrastructure, manufacturing facilities, and other investments that create jobs and strengthen local economies. All this has led to lost jobs, missed economic opportunities, and higher prices across America.

“Data from the National Association of Manufacturers shows that permitting delays are costing America’s manufacturers $12.1 billion every year, including $87 million in additional costs in West Virginia alone. According to new data from McKinsey, $1.8 trillion of investments are locked up in the federal permitting system right now, including $22.3 billion of sidelined investments in my home state of West Virginia.

“These are projects that could provide good-paying jobs, improve mobility, increase access to clean drinking water, deploy broadband in rural areas, and so much more. The environmental permitting and review processes should be tools for informed decision-making, not reasons that decisions can’t be made. This is not a sustainable way for the United States to compete with the rest of the world, and it is certainly not a sustainable way to address the energy and affordability issues we are facing today.

“It’s no secret that America’s energy demand is growing rapidly to meet the needs of a modern economy. To meet these needs, we must modernize our grid, increase our energy production, and build the infrastructure that will keep America competitive and secure for decades to come.

“It is time for Congress to act. It is, actually, well past time.

“As Chairman of the Environment and Public Works Committee, I worked with my Ranking Member, Senator Whitehouse, as well as Chairman Lee of the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and Ranking Member Heinrich, to introduce a comprehensive permitting reform solution: the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, or BAAJA. This bill will unlock economic opportunity, infrastructure development, and energy production across the United States.

“The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act consists of two parts. The first part of the bill is in the EPW Committee’s jurisdiction, and it consists of reforms to the laws that set the framework for our environmental review and permitting processes, including the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the Clean Water Act, and the Endangered Species Act. The EPWsection also provides certainty that permitted projects will retain their permits if they remain in compliance with the law.

“The second part of the bill captures reforms to statutes in the ENR Committee’s jurisdiction, including the National Historic Preservation Act and the Federal Power Act. This section also includes the Ratepayer Protection Act, legislation that will make potential data centers pay their own way instead of American consumers facing increased costs through rising utility bills.

“Together, the package that our committees put together fulfills key policy priorities from members of both sides of the aisle and a diverse set of stakeholders. I believe these comprehensive permitting reforms will generate benefits for our country for years to come for three reasons.

“First, this bill is bipartisan. Senators Lee, Whitehouse, Heinrich, and I have worked together throughout this Congress to craft a solution that both Republicans and Democrats can support. That is the only way we can achieve durable and implementable reforms to our environmental review and permitting processes. There is something in this bill for everyone, because it is fair to everyone, and we owe it to the American people to come together as a body and pass this legislation in the weeks ahead.

“Second, this bill will help all types of projects. We cannot adjust the processes for some types of projects, but not others. Projects like coal mines, windmills, gas pipelines, solar farms, and steel mills will all benefit from this legislation.

“Third, the package addresses critical stages of the permitting process. This will create predictability, consistency, and finality in securing a permit. It will allow our laws to balance public health, the environment, and the needs of our economy. Finally, our legislation will prevent unnecessary delays and endless litigation that blocks growth.

“In West Virginia, investments have collapsed under the weight of legal challenges, denying potential benefits to areas that need support the most. When a project sits in the environmental review and permitting processes for years, jobs are not created, critical infrastructure is not built, energy is not brought onto the grid, and ultimately, American families and businesses face higher costs and fewer opportunities.

“The White House Council of Economic Advisers (CEA) released a report analyzing the ways that the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would benefit families and businesses, and the results are clear. According to their analysis, the reforms made under BAAJA would result in $82 billion to $164 billion in additional economic output every year. Families would feel these economic benefits directly, as CEA estimates that for the average American household, real wages will increase, electricity bills will fall, and everyday expenses will be reduced. We cannot continue to let the costs of permitting delays fall onto American families.

“I am no stranger to the challenge of addressing permitting reform in Congress. Throughout my career, I have introduced multiple bills to improve this process. While Congress has passed some very limited reforms through various legislative packages, we have not passed significant reforms to NEPA in several decades.

Republicans and Democrats alike recognize the need for reforms to unlock investment to build projects that are important to our states. On both sides of the aisle, we understand that our constituents need lower costs and good jobs, communities need economic investment, businesses need certainty, and America needs to build. These are not partisan ideals. They are American principles.

“The Trump administration has also rallied behind this deal, supporting our efforts in the Senate to pass durable reforms so we can unleash our nation’s full potential. Additionally, we have made it a priority to have a robust manager’s amendment to this legislation that makes targeted changes based on feedback from our members and stakeholders to further build support.

“I am thankful for my colleagues’ efforts to strengthen BAAJA, and the contributions from members of the House of Representatives as well. This legislation reflects a vast amount of perspectives and priorities, and I’m proud of the product we are voting on today.

“We have received letters of support from over one thousand stakeholder organizations, representing a broad swath of groups across our country, including oil and gas producers and solar energy groups, labor unions, and business associations. They all recognize the urgent need for permitting reform, and the benefits that BAAJA would have on affordability, energy reliability, and economic growth across our country.

“In a statement from the American Petroleum Institute, President and CEO Mike Sommers said, 'Washington has a generational opportunity to fundamentally transform a broken permitting system and help address the affordability challenges facing American consumers. Congress should seize this moment and finish the job.'

“In another statement from the Solar Energy Industries Association, CEO Tim Pawlenty said, 'This is the kind of bipartisan action America needs to meet growing energy demand, put downward pressure on energy prices, and deploy more affordable, exactly reliable solar and storage for American families and businesses.'

“Xan Fishman, Executive Vice President of the Energy Program at the Bipartisan Policy Center, said, '[The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act] would fix our permitting processes so that we can review and build efficiently, reducing costs, improving quality of life, growing our economy, and improving economic outcomes.'

“From my home state, the Gas and Oil Association of West Virginia’s President, Rebecca McPhail, said the following, 'GO-WV supports the [Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act]’s stated goals of modernizing federal environmental review, providing certainty for holders of federal permits and authorizations, and supporting an all-of-the-above energy strategy.'

“From the business community, Rodney Davis, Senior Vice President and Head of Government Affairs at the U.S. Chamber, said, 'The Senate's progress toward a comprehensive, bipartisan permitting reform deal brings us one step closer to streamlining the outdated process that is holding up critical projects of all kinds, from energy and water infrastructure to roads, broadband, and manufacturing.’

“Demonstrating the breadth of support this bill has received, the Laborers’ International Union of North America General President, Brent Booker, gave the following statement of support, 'For more than a decade LIUNA has testified before Congress, submitted comments, participated in roundtables, and endorsed numerous iterations of permitting bills…We urge lawmakers in both parties to seize this moment, pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, and finally deliver meaningful permitting reform.'

“And finally, representing a broad coalition of labor groups, in a letter from Sean McGarvey, President of North America’s Building Trades Unions, he said, 'This legislation represents a significant step toward a more efficient permitting system that supports job creation, strengthens America’s energy and infrastructure capabilities, and helps reduce costs for working families.'

“I could not agree more. This is an unprecedented opportunity, and a legislative breakthrough we can accomplish in this unique moment. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is a win for America, and we cannot let this moment pass us by.

“The reality is this: over the next several years, we will have no choice but to increase our national energy production and manufacturing capacity to meet increasing demand, and that means making sure our infrastructure projects can be built quickly, efficiently, and responsibly.

“The House has already passed several key pieces of legislation on this matter, including the SPEED Act and the PERMIT Act. Now, it’s our turn in the Senate to act on the opportunity in front of us. I encourage my colleagues to rise to the importance of this moment, and to vote in favor of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.

“American growth, competitiveness, and security are at stake. With that, I yield the floor.”

# # #

WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator Bill Cassidy, M.D. (R-LA) today recommended Brad Kelley to the Senate Judiciary Committee for consideration as a United States District Judge for the Eastern District of Louisiana. Cassidy highlighted Kelley’s distinguished military service, extensive legal experience, and record of public service.

Remarks as prepared below:

Mr. Chairman and Ranking Member,

It is my privilege to recommend Brad Kelley to the Committee to be a United States District Judge for the Eastern District of Louisiana.

Brad’s record reflects academic excellence, distinguished military service, significant public service, and sophisticated legal practice. Brad is a proud double-graduate of LSU, where he graduated, summa cum laude, with degrees in Political Science, History, and International Studies. In recognition of his academic achievement, he was inducted into Phi Beta Kappa.

Brad later attended LSU’s Paul M. Hebert Law Center, where he was an editor of both the Louisiana Law Review and the Journal of Civil Law Studies. Brad received his law degree, magna cum laude, and was inducted into the Order of the Coif.

Following law school, Brad clerked for the Honorable Donald E. Walter of the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Louisiana, where he gained a rare view into the inner workings of a federal court.

If confirmed, Brad will take an Oath to uphold the Constitution. He knows something about that firsthand. Between college and law school, he served our country honorably as a captain in the United States Army. Brad served as an infantry platoon leader and as a lead intelligence officer for a unit of nearly one thousand soldiers. During the Iraq War, he also advised senior command leadership on combat missions.

Brad’s commitment to those who serve did not end when he left the Army. As an attorney, he provides regular legal assistance and counsel to Gold Star Families––those special Americans who have suffered the grievous loss of immediate family killed in the line of duty. In addition to helping the families of those who have fallen, Brad has aided those who live on with the wounds of their service. In recognition of his extensive pro bono work on behalf of our veterans, Brad received a commendation.

Brad also brings substantial experience in public service. After a stint in private practice, Brad returned to government service, where he served as a senior official during both Republican and Democrat administrations, including as a Senior Policy Advisor at the U.S. Department of Labor and as Chief Counsel to a Commissioner of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC). Those positions gave him firsthand experience with federal law, administrative agencies, and the practical consequences of government decision-making.

Brad then returned to private practice, where he became an equity partner at one of the world’s largest labor and employment law firms. He now co-chairs the firm’s artificial intelligence and technology practice group and has served as lead counsel in complex litigation across the country.

That breadth of experience matters. Our federal district courts benefit from exposure to how difficult legal issues have been settled in other circuits, in addition to their own. Brad’s cross-jurisdictional experience makes him apt for this task. He is admitted to the practice of law in Louisiana, Virginia, and the District of Columbia. He is also admitted to the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the Third, Fourth, Fifth, and D.C. Circuits.

And Brad is no stranger to the court on which he has been nominated to serve. He has litigated several matters in the Eastern District of Louisiana, including matters as recently as this year.

Mr. Chairman and Ranking Member, I am confident that Brad Kelley has the credentials, experience, rigor, and patriotism that mark exceptional nominees to the federal bench. I support his nomination without question.

With that, I yield.

Today, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) held a press conference to lay out her legislative priorities for a Democratic Senate majority.

The press conference follows historic Democratic gains she fought for as chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) in the midterm elections, during which both the House and the Senate flipped from Republican to Democratic control. With this new majority, Senator Gillibrand is focused on lowering costs and bringing relief to working Americans who have struggled to make ends meet under the Republican trifecta.

“Last week, voters across the country made clear that they are ready for change. But the real work is just beginning,” said Senator Gillibrand. “With a Democratic Senate majority, I am laser-focused on lowering costs to bring much-needed relief to working Americans who have struggled to make ends meet under the Republican trifecta. That starts with ending the war with Iran, halting President Trump’s tariffs, making healthcare more affordable, protecting Social Security, developing commonsense guardrails for artificial intelligence, and combating Trump administration corruption.”

Gillibrand’s top priorities for the Democratic majority include:

Ending the war with Iran: Gas prices in New York are over 40 percent higher today than they were at the start of the war more than eight months ago. Ending the war with Iran is critical to get these prices under control. Gillibrand has voted 14 times on War Powers Resolutions to end the war with Iran.

Halting President Trump’s tariffs: Gillibrand’s Banning Antiquated Duties and Delivering Equitable American Levies (BAD DEAL) Act would repeal all tariffs levied under Section 338 of the Tariff Act and refund Americans for all duties paid under this authority. This includes President Trump’s 50% tariffs on Canada, which are driving up costs in New York.

Restoring access to healthcare and bringing down healthcare costs: Gillibrand cosponsors myriad legislation to restore access to healthcare and lower healthcare costs, including the Health Care Affordability Act, which would restore and permanently extend the enhanced premium tax credits offered for Affordable Care Act marketplace plans. She also supports legislation to reverse Republicans’ Medicaid cuts made through President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, restore coverage under New York’s Essential Plan, expand Medicare eligibility to individuals under 65, and cap prescription drug costs.

Developing commonsense guardrails for artificial intelligence: Gillibrand introduced the Secure and Accountable Military AI Act, which would impose strong restrictions on certain uses of AI by the Department of Defense, including by banning the use of AI to launch nuclear weapons.

Protecting Social Security: If Congress does not act, seniors could see their Social Security benefits cut by about 20% in just six years. Gillibrand’s Social Security Expansion Act would extend the solvency of Social Security for 75 years by requiring the wealthiest American households to pay their fair share of payroll taxes.

Combating Trump administration corruption: Gillibrand’s No Stock Act would ban senior government officials, including members of Congress, the president, the vice president, Supreme Court justices, and their spouses and dependents, from holding or trading covered financial assets.

“A Democratic Congress means pressing to put an end to Trump’s stupid tariffs and trade wars. Nobody in America wants to pay more for groceries just so Trump can pick a fight with Canada.

[ACCOUNTABILITY FOR ICE]

“A Democratic Congress means real accountability for ICE. Republicans wrote ICE a blank check. We are going to be writing them subpoenas.

[CRACKING DOWN ON CORRUPTION]

“A Democratic Congress means cracking down on corruption: insider trading, selling pardons and access, crypto scams, no-bid contracts, war profiteering—all of it.

“If you thought Trump was your ticket to get rich quick by breaking laws, abusing power, and defrauding the American people, you thought wrong. When the gavels change hands, the days of rampant, consequence-free grifting will come to an end. Bet on that.

[ACCESSIBLE AND AFFORDABLE HEALTH CARE]

“And of course, when it comes to health care, a Democratic Congress means reversing health care cuts—just for a start. Every time Republicans take power, they make a mess out of health care.

“We have got to reverse the Medicaid cuts that are shutting down our hospitals. We have got to restore the ACA tax credits that make health care far more affordable for families. And we need to stop Trump’s plan to use AI to cut seniors off from their Medicare benefits.

“But we can’t stop there—because if Republicans’ health care strategy is ‘death by a thousand cuts,’ Democrats have to be more than the party of a thousand band-aids.

“We need a robust public option, and universal coverage. And we are going to have that conversation in the next Congress.

[PUBLIC HEALTH]

“We are also going to have a conversation about undoing all the damage RFK Jr. has done to our health in this country.

“A Democratic Congress means putting science back in public health.

“Right now, measles cases are at record levels. Instead of solving the problem, our nation’s highest health official is covering it up. Instead of championing vaccines, RFK Jr. has been championing conspiracies. He should be fighting viruses, not vaccines.

“Americans don’t want viruses that we eliminated roaring back and killing babies. Americans don’t want lettuce to give them diarrhea. They don’t want promising clinical trials cut off, or respected researchers sacked. They don’t want FDA’s gold standard overruled by Secretary Kennedy’s wildest conspiracies or Trump’s biggest donors.

“Chaos and corruption may have spread like a plague under Trump and RFK Jr, but you know what they say: sunlight is the best disinfectant. Accountability is coming. And RFK Jr. is far from the only person we will be holding accountable.

[HOLDING VOUGHT ACCOUNTABLE]

“A Democratic Congress means Russ Vought’s days of breaking our laws and extorting our communities without consequence are coming to an end. As incoming Chair of the Appropriations Committee, you better believe I am going to be demanding answers and accountability for the brazen robbery and illegality we have seen from Trump’s OMB director.

“I’m going to have hearings, and I’m going to use our funding bills to rein in the abuses and corruption of this administration while we invest in our American families. I will expose this administration’s corruption and the games Russ Vought and OMB have been playing with our American tax dollars.

“I am going to drag this Administrations’ crooked schemes into the light of day for every American to see—and you better believe I am going to stamp this president’s very ugly and very un-American brand of politics and corruption into the dust.

[MAKING CHILD CARE AFFORDABLE]

“Now let me just say: I am going to make certain a Democratic Congress means getting serious about the child care crisis. Child care is too hard for parents to find. It’s too expensive for families to afford. It is too tough for providers to keep their daycare facilities open. And this all is crushing our families and our economy.

“I have been fighting for child care since my first day in politics—and you can bet that next Congress I am going to be loud about beating the drum, pounding the pavement, and charting a course towards a future where every family in this country can get quality, affordable child care. And with so many new colleagues now coming who have young kids joining us, I know we are going to make progress.

[DEFENDING PUBLIC EDUCATION]

“That doesn’t just go for child care though—it also goes for defending public education.

“A Democratic Congress means Trump’s plan to demolish the Department of Education is dead in the water. We’ve been fighting these efforts since Trump’s first day in office—but with gavels in hand, we are going to have even more power to put an end to this nonsense once and for all.

“There is no world where this former Pre-K teacher will let Trump bulldoze the programs that support our kids, because every student deserves to be able to get a great education—and afford college—no matter their zip code, or the size of their parent’s bank account.

[INVESTING IN INFRASTRUCTURE]

“And a Democratic Congress means building infrastructure for all Americans—instead of letting Trump build monuments to himself. Republicans have voted to cut off vital investments to create great jobs and rebuild America’s infrastructure. Well guess what? Democrats are going to fight to keep investing in the roads, and bridges, and ports, and airports that people use every day.

[FIGHTING FOR REPRODUCTIVE FREEDOM]

“We are also going to be pushing hard to fight back on abortion. A Democratic Congress means countering Republican attacks on abortion and clawing back the rights they have chipped away.

“Make no mistake, Republicans spent decades on their crusade to overturn Roe and rip away women’s rights. So I will spend every day of this majority fighting to win them back. Democrats will be relentless and tenacious.

“And that means putting abortion rights to a vote on the floor and making every senator say where they stand. It means protecting Title X, Planned Parenthood, and contraception access from this administration’s attacks. It means elevating the voices of women across the country about being investigated for miscarriages, or forced to death’s door before a doctor could treat them.

“I do not expect quick, easy victories—but I am in this fight for as long as it takes. We will claw back every inch we can at every opportunity we can. I will keep pushing until we have the trifecta we need to restore abortion rights in all 50 states.

[KILLING TRUMP’S BLANK CHECK FOR WAR]

“Now, when it comes to Trump’s wars, let’s be clear: a Democratic Congress means Donald Trump is absolutely not getting his $1.5 trillion war budget, or the nearly $70 billion he wants to bankroll the Iran war.

“There is no way on God’s green earth that I am going to let Republicans jam through a funding bill that blows war spending through the roof and at the same time cutting family priorities like child care, housing, and health care.

“This war with Iran should never have started. It is putting our service members in harms’ way. It is blowing gas prices through the roof. It is undermining our credibility on the world stage—not to mention weakening our position on other fronts. This administration is responsible for the deaths of nearly 200 Iranian school children, for God’s sake.

“Trump’s war has been a disaster from top to bottom. We are going to push to end this war as responsibly as we can, and we are going to hold Trump and Hegseth accountable for starting it in the first place.

[LOOKING FORWARD]

“Now, there’s going to be a lot more to say on these issues—and many other challenges where Republicans are going to have to accept reality and come to the table to work with us. Like: how do we develop a responsible framework for AI regulation that makes sure regular people are the ones reaping the benefits of this technology, not the ones bearing the burdens of it?

“The clock is ticking to get our arms around this. We cannot let this powerful technology—and the companies developing it—run amok.

“Or, how do we preserve Social Security in a way that keeps our promise to seniors, and prevents painful cuts to benefits? Social Security is projected to run dry in 2032—meaning every Senator just elected is going to have a say in how we solve this. Those conversations need to start now.

“Or, for anyone wondering if I can find common ground with Trump: Let’s pass the Sunshine Protection Act. Let’s give people a bit more sunshine. Let’s finally end the tyranny of changing the clock back and forth just to see the sun set before you leave work.

“There is no question we have got our work cut out for us in the Congress ahead. I think we all know this is not going to be easy. I’d like to say the overwhelming results sent an undeniable message to the White House, but we all know this President has no problem denying election results, or spitting in the face of Congress, or flouting our laws.

“Republicans forgot Congress is not a rubber stamp. Our challenge is to remember it is not a magic wand. We are a co-equal branch of government. We can check this President, but we still have to contend with his veto power, and we still have to face a conservative Supreme Court.

“We can bring down prices, but not with a wave of our hands. We can fight corruption, but not with a strong press statement. And we can end Trump’s war with Iran, but not with a snap of our fingers.

“We are fighting a deeply entrenched and lawless Administration. So, it is not going to be easy or quick. The only way to accomplish our goals is the hard way. We are going to have to roll up our sleeves, and grind it out. It’s going to take hard work, sustained pressure, and sharp political strategy. Building something is always going to be harder, slower work than burning it down.

“But I want to end with the good news. The American people turned out in a very big way last week. They sent a message as loud and clear as I have ever heard in politics. And as a result, next year Democrats will have more hands to take on that work than at any time in the Trump era.

“And we are—every single one of us—ready to meet this moment.”
