matches.text:
Today, U.S. Senator Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), along with more than ten of his colleagues, is pressing Senate and House leadership to exclude provisions in the FY2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) that would require the President to expand and enhance defense cooperation and intelligence sharing with the Government of Israel. These provisions would undermine the United States’ ability to act independently and in line with U.S. national security interests at a time when the Government of Israel’s actions are increasingly not aligned with those interests. This effort follows a Dear Colleague letter sent by Senator Van Hollen in July urging Senators to oppose any motion to proceed on the NDAA vote until these provisions were addressed.

Senator Van Hollen was joined in sending this letter by Senators Patty Murray (D-Wash.), Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), Elizabeth Warren, (D-Mass.), Ed Markey (D-Mass.), Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), Tina Smith (D-Minn.), Peter Welch (D-Vt.), and Andy Kim (D-N.J.). The letter was sent to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, House Speaker Mike Johnson, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Senate Armed Services Committee (SASC) Chair Roger Wicker, SASC Ranking Member Jack Reed, House Armed Services Committee Chair (HASC) Mike Rogers, and HASC Ranking Member Adam Smith.

The Senators begin, “As you prepare to conference the Fiscal Year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), we respectfully urge you to exclude three provisions from the final bill that would further entrench concerning aspects of the U.S.-Israel defense and intelligence relationship at a time when the Israeli government’s actions are increasingly undermining U.S. interests and values. These provisions would constrain the Administration’s ability to independently determine how best to protect U.S. national security and would lock in long-term commitments despite our serious concerns with the Israeli government’s actions in Gaza, the West Bank, and other parts of the region.”

On the threats to U.S. national security, the lawmakers note, “The agreements and projects these provisions envision threaten U.S. national security interests by handing Israel leverage over American weapons systems and military technology. This is not hypothetical. The Netanyahu government has already leveraged its existing coproduction agreement with the United States on missile defense to block American Iron Dome batteries from reaching Ukraine, in direct opposition to U.S. national security interests. Should these provisions be enacted, it would further increase Israel’s leverage over the United States through some of the most sensitive technologies in warfare. That is not in the U.S. interest. If enacted, these agreements would create long-term dependencies by embedding Israeli technology into the U.S. defense industrial base that could make future policy changes costly or difficult to implement. President Trump, at his own discretion, could choose to enter new agreements with Israel under existing law. The executive branch does not need a congressional mandate to more deeply entrench U.S.-Israel defense cooperation.”

“Moreover, we do not share, let alone co-produce, many of these sensitive technologies even with our closest partners, including NATO or other treaty allies. To do so in this instance would be unwise, especially as the Government of Israel continues to pursue policies in Gaza, the West Bank and other parts of the region that are inconsistent with U.S. interests and values,” the lawmakers write.

“Prime Minister Netanyahu has openly stated that such an initiative was his idea. In a letter to Representative Stutzman, who led a resolution calling for an effort similar to these provisions, Prime Minister Netanyahu states, ‘I was glad to receive your proposed Congressional resolution endorsing my plan to shift the framework of the US-Israel defense cooperation from aid to partnership.’ The intention behind this is clear: to move U.S. security assistance governed through more traditional pathways, like Foreign Military Financing and arm sales, to more opaque, less discernible avenues through defense acquisitions and programs of record that reduce transparency, as well as increase Israel’s leverage over the United States and our dependency on Israeli technology. This is particularly problematic after Prime Minister Netanyahu boasted that he has been trying to start a war with Iran for 40 years. That war has proven to be a strategic disaster for the United States and against U.S. interests,” the Senators continue.

“For all these reasons, we should not legally mandate an expansion in defense co-production or a requirement to increase intelligence sharing with the Government of Israel. We therefore urge you to exclude Section 1217, Section 219, and Section 618 from the NDAA final conference report,” they conclude.

The full text of the letter is available here and below.

Dear Majority Leader Thune, Minority Leader Schumer, Speaker Johnson, Minority Leader Jeffries, Chairman Wicker, Ranking Member Reed, Chairman Rogers, and Ranking Member Smith:

As you prepare to conference the Fiscal Year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), we respectfully urge you to exclude three provisions from the final bill that would further entrench concerning aspects of the U.S.-Israel defense and intelligence relationship at a time when the Israeli government’s actions are increasingly undermining U.S. interests and values. These provisions would constrain the Administration’s ability to independently determine how best to protect U.S. national security and would lock in long-term commitments despite our serious concerns with the Israeli government’s actions in Gaza, the West Bank, and other parts of the region.

Both Section 1217 from the Senate Armed Services Committee-reported bill and Section 219 of the House-passed bill mandate the creation of a “United States-Israel Defense Technology Cooperation Initiative” to expand and accelerate the U.S.-Israel defense relationship, including technology sharing, co-production of weapons systems, and bilateral research and development across multiple domains of warfare such as biotechnology, quantum, autonomous systems, artificial intelligence, cyberwarfare, and others.

The agreements and projects these provisions envision threaten U.S. national security interests by handing Israel leverage over American weapons systems and military technology. This is not hypothetical. The Netanyahu government has already leveraged its existing coproduction agreement with the United States on missile defense to block American Iron Dome batteries from reaching Ukraine, in direct opposition to U.S. national security interests. Should these provisions be enacted, it would further increase Israel’s leverage over the United States through some of the most sensitive technologies in warfare. That is not in the U.S. interest.

If enacted, these agreements would create long-term dependencies by embedding Israeli technology into the U.S. defense industrial base that could make future policy changes costly or difficult to implement. President Trump, at his own discretion, could choose to enter new agreements with Israel under existing law. The executive branch does not need a congressional mandate to more deeply entrench U.S.-Israel defense cooperation.

Moreover, we do not share, let alone co-produce, many of these sensitive technologies even with our closest partners, including NATO or other treaty allies. To do so in this instance would be unwise, especially as the Government of Israel continues to pursue policies in Gaza, the West Bank and other parts of the region that are inconsistent with U.S. interests and values.

Prime Minister Netanyahu has openly stated that such an initiative was his idea. In a letter to Representative Stutzman, who led a resolution calling for an effort similar to these provisions, Prime Minister Netanyahu states, “I was glad to receive your proposed Congressional resolution endorsing my plan to shift the framework of the US-Israel defense cooperation from aid to partnership.” The intention behind this is clear: to move U.S. security assistance governed through more traditional pathways, like Foreign Military Financing and arm sales, to more opaque, less discernible avenues through defense acquisitions and programs of record that reduce transparency, as well as increase Israel’s leverage over the United States and our dependency on Israeli technology. This is particularly problematic after Prime Minister Netanyahu boasted that he has been trying to start a war with Iran for 40 years. That war has proven to be a strategic disaster for the United States and against U.S. interests.

In addition to the provisions discussed above in the Senate and House NDAAs, the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence (SSCI) FY27 Intelligence Authorization Act, which is typically incorporated in the final NDAA, includes a provision (Sec. 618) that mandates the executive branch “expand and enhance intelligence sharing with the Government of Israel,” and also states that intelligence sharing with Israel “shall not be suspended, reduced, or otherwise materially limited.” The provision would tie the President’s hands from limiting intelligence sharing with Israel, even when doing so may be necessary to protect U.S. national security. That would be irresponsible and especially troubling given public reports that the Defense Intelligence Agency recently raised the counterintelligence threat from Israel to its highest level.

For all these reasons, we should not legally mandate an expansion in defense co-production or a requirement to increase intelligence sharing with the Government of Israel. We therefore urge you to exclude Section 1217, Section 219, and Section 618 from the NDAA final conference report.

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Congresswoman Maxine Dexter, M.D. (OR-03) introduced the Protecting Our Public Lands from Data Centers Act to ban the construction of new data centers and related infrastructure on federal public lands managed by the U.S. Forest Service and the Department of the Interior.

“Public lands belong in public hands and Oregonians must have a say before the federal government hands over millions of acres of public land managed by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) for data centers,” said Congresswoman Dexter. “These treasured lands are where people hunt, fish, hike and graze livestock. They are where wildlife habitat and our critical watersheds are protected. My bill keeps these lands safe from data centers now, and for the generations who come after us.”

The Trump administration is opening federal public lands to data center development as demand for computing power grows. Large data centers will put pressure on local water supplies and electric grids. Some proposed campuses include their own gas-fired power plants which can have devastating impacts on air quality, noise pollution can be extreme, and fencing off these sites restricts public access and disrupts wildlife habitat.

“Data centers have no place on public lands,” Randi Spivak, Public Lands Policy Director, Center for Biological Diversity. “They’re water-guzzling, pollution-spewing facilities that turn lands meant for wildlife and recreation into corporate industrial sites. Once a data center goes up, hundreds to thousands of acres of wildlife habitat will be stripped bare and closed to the public for good. We’re deeply grateful to Rep. Dexter for standing up to keep public lands public.”

The Congresswoman’s bill would prohibit the development, sale or transfer of covered federal lands nationwide for new data centers and related infrastructure. It would also require covered lands that are sold or transferred to return to public ownership if used for a data center without congressional approval.

“Our national forests and other public lands should be protected for future generations, not sold off or paved over to make way for massive commercial data centers,” said Athan Manuel, Director of Lands Protection Program, Sierra Club. “Representative Dexter’s legislation draws a clear line by keeping these industrial facilities and their associated infrastructure off lands managed by the Forest Service and Department of the Interior. The Sierra Club applauds Representative Dexter and Senator Wyden for standing up for our public lands and ensuring they remain protected for the people, wildlife, and communities that depend on them.”

“America's public lands are national treasures, and they should be managed as a legacy for future generations, not sacrificed to make way for corporate data centers,” said Steve Pedery, Conservation Director, Oregon Wild. “We strongly support Representative Maxine Dexter's legislation to protect our lands, wildlife, and clean water from data center development.”

“Mt. Hood National Forest supplies drinking and irrigation water to one-third of Oregonians,” said Jordan Latter, Forest Watch Program Manager, Bark. “Its protected headwaters keep our water clean, shelter endangered species, and anchor our shared identity as Oregonians. Data centers have no place here.”

The Center for Biological Diversity, Sierra Club, Earthjustice Action, Save Our Wild Salmon, WaterWatch of Oregon, Bark, Oregon Wild, Columbia Riverkeeper and the Oregon Data Center Defiance Coalition endorse the bill.

matches.text:
Washington, D.C. — Colorado U.S. Senator Michael Bennet, a member of the Senate Intelligence Committee, sent a letter to Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, Attorney General Todd Blanche, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton demanding an update on the U.S. government’s investigation into Megaspeed, a Singapore-based firm that reportedly acts as a major conduit for transfers of restricted U.S. technology to China, including Nvidia’s advanced AI chips.

The letter also requests U.S. engagement with Southeast Asian governments to address potential violations of U.S. export controls; punitive U.S. action against Megaspeed, such as putting the firm on the Entity List; and far stronger approaches to export controls and enforcement. Additionally, the letter requests an explanation of the Intelligence Community (IC)’s analysis of the threat Megaspeed poses, as well as an explanation of the IC’s sharing of that information with the Departments of Commerce, Justice, State, and the White House. These efforts are crucial given reports that the IC concluded a Megaspeed executive was a Chinese intelligence asset with close ties to Nvidia’s CEO.

“I request an update on the U.S. government’s investigation into the Singapore-based firm Megaspeed International Pte. Ltd. (“Megaspeed”) for potentially circumventing U.S. export controls and exploiting gray areas in the U.S. export control regime to divert advanced American semiconductor capabilities to China, including advanced Nvidia semiconductors. The Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security initially led this investigation but New York Times reporting indicates that the Department of Justice is now leading this effort. Additionally, we request that you engage countries hosting Megaspeed infrastructure – such as Singapore, Malaysia, and Indonesia – to address potential violations of U.S. export controls. I also request your consideration of specific punitive measures against Megaspeed, as well as stronger approaches to export controls and enforcement,” Bennet wrote.

“This flow of advanced AI chips to China and China’s access to restricted cloud computing capabilities risk enabling Beijing’s development of autonomous weapon systems, advanced cyber-warfare capabilities, and more powerful surveillance tools – which could eventually pose significant challenges to U.S. capabilities. China’s military could one day use these technologies against American servicemembers. Large-scale diversion also creates a gray market that penalizes law-abiding companies and devalues the intellectual property that sustains U.S. global economic leadership,” he continued.

The letter concluded by requesting that Secretary Lutnick, Attorney General Blanche, Secretary Rubio, and Director Clayton provide the following information by November 24, 2026:

An update on the Department of Justice’s continuation of the Department of Commerce investigation into Megaspeed;

A detailed description of any Department of Commerce efforts to prevent Megaspeed, whose top executive is reportedly a Chinese intelligence asset, from purchasing Nvidia chips, such as by sending an “Is Informed” letter to Nvidia blocking certain semiconductor shipments to Megaspeed and potentially placing Megaspeed on the Entity List;

A detailed accounting of:

The Department of Commerce and Department of State’s efforts to coordinate a rigorous response with partners including Singapore, Malaysia, and Indonesia;

The Department of Commerce’s efforts to close loopholes in U.S. export controls that allow Chinese companies to access restricted U.S. technology, such as semiconductors and cloud computing, through Southeast Asia; and

The Department of Commerce’s efforts to close loopholes in U.S. export controls that allow subsidiaries of China-headquartered firms, including those on whom the United States has already sanctioned, to buy export-controlled AI chips in the United States.

A detailed explanation of the IC’s analysis of Alice Huang’s reported service as a Chinese intelligence asset and the broader threat Megaspeed poses to U.S. national security.

A detailed explanation of the IC’s sharing of such information, on Ms. Huang; and Megaspeed, with the Department of Commerce, the Department of Justice, the Department of State, and the White House.

Bennet has led efforts to ensure U.S. competitiveness and national security by preventing the transfer of advanced U.S. technologies to China. He helped pass legislation to bar American investments in certain advanced technologies with military uses, such as AI and semiconductors, in China and other countries of concern. He secured language in the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence-passed Fiscal Year 2027 Intelligence Authorization Act requiring an intelligence assessment before the U.S. government approves AI technologies for export or signs an AI agreement with a foreign government. That assessment would evaluate the recipient country’s export control regime, its ties to adversaries like China and Russia, the risk of onward proliferation, and the likely end-uses of the technology. Bennet has blasted the Trump administration’s decision to allow the sale of Nvidia H200 AI chips to China and President Trump’s decision to pause U.S. export controls restricting the sale of critical technology to China.

The text of the letter is available HERE and below.

Secretary Lutnick, Attorney General Blanche, Secretary Rubio, and Director Clayton:

I request an update on the U.S. government’s investigation into the Singapore-based firm Megaspeed International Pte. Ltd. (“Megaspeed”) for potentially circumventing U.S. export controls and exploiting gray areas in the U.S. export control regime to divert advanced American semiconductor capabilities to China, including advanced Nvidia semiconductors. The Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) initially led this investigation, but New York Times reporting indicates that the Department of Justice is now leading this effort. Additionally, I request that you engage countries hosting Megaspeed infrastructure – such as Singapore, Malaysia, and Indonesia – to address potential violations of U.S. export controls. I also request your consideration of specific punitive measures against Megaspeed, as well as stronger approaches to export controls and enforcement.

These efforts are crucial and time-sensitive given New York Times reporting that the U.S. intelligence community found Megaspeed executive Alice Huang to be a Chinese intelligence asset who passed critical information to the Chinese government. Ensuring the integrity of our export controls is central to advancing America’s national security and our long-term economic prosperity, including by preventing China – our only near-peer competitor – from obtaining advanced U.S. technologies with military applications, such as cutting-edge artificial intelligence (AI) chips. Our export control regime must be able to identify and curtail entities actively seeking to evade those controls.

Extensive public reporting suggests that Megaspeed acts as a high-volume conduit for China-bound transfers of advanced American technology through the following activities:

Intelligence Operations: According to The New York Times, U.S. intelligence agencies concluded that a top executive at Megaspeed, Alice Huang (also known as Huang Le), acted as a Chinese intelligence asset to gather information for Beijing. Per this report, electronic surveillance revealed that Ms. Huang cultivated a close relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The report also indicated that Ms. Huang likely funneled information not only about Nvidia to the Chinese government, but also about President Trump’s plans and intentions. The report indicates that Megaspeed continues to trumpet its close connections to Nvidia.

Exploitation of Sanctioned Intermediaries: Reports indicate that Megaspeed operated as a middle man, using Aivres – a U.S.-registered subsidiary of Chinese technology giant Inspur, on which the United States imposed sanctions for supporting China’s military – to source restricted hardware, such as advanced Nvidia AI chips. Aivres was able to purchase this hardware (1) because Aivres was not subject to the sanctions imposed on its parent company Inspur; (2) because the Department of Commerce has rolled back steps that restrict the subsidiaries of Chinese-headquartered firms from buying export-controlled AI chips from U.S. firms; and (3) because the Department of Commerce halted enforcement of licensing requirements for Chinese-headquartered subsidiaries in Malaysia from May 2025, creating more loopholes that have enabled the illicit diversion of sensitive U.S. technology. Aivres thus continued purchasing advanced Nvidia chips, which a Malaysia-based Megaspeed subsidiary then bought. BIS officials who visited Megaspeed’s Malaysia data center suspected that Megaspeed may have sent some of these chips to China. Meanwhile, Aivres currently advertises access to Nvidia’s most advanced and recently released Vera Rubin chips.

Physical Smuggling and Diversion: Reports indicate that since 2023, Megaspeed’s Malaysian and Indonesian subsidiaries have purchased advanced Nvidia chips worth at least $4.6 billion, including the advanced Blackwell processors that the United States has not approved for export to China. A late 2024 BIS inspection of a Megaspeed site in Malaysia discovered advanced hardware in boxes rather than installed and in use, an unusual practice that BIS officials considered a potential indicator of diversion to China.

Backdoor Remote Access: Reports indicate that Megaspeed operates AI data centers in Southeast Asia, potentially with Nvidia Blackwell processors, and may have used them to provide Chinese clients with remote cloud computing power from restricted U.S. hardware. As of October 29, 2026, Nvidia continued to list Megaspeed on its website as a cloud partner. This highlights another gap in current U.S. export control regulations, since the administration has not imposed restrictions to prevent companies headquartered in countries outside of China, like Megaspeed, from providing Chinese clients remote access to export-controlled chips.

Opaque Ownership: Reports indicate that Megaspeed is a spin-off of 7ROAD, a Chinese firm with state-backed ties – raising concerns of corporate restructuring obscuring Beijing’s control in order to evade U.S. oversight. Recent probes underscore the severity of these allegations. The Singapore Police Force has investigated Megaspeed for potential legal violations. Major infrastructure partners like Bridge Data Centres, backed by Bain Capital, have terminated their ties with Megaspeed. That Megaspeed reportedly ceased new orders amid these probes raises serious questions warranting an American response. These facts raise serious concerns about Chinese companies using opaque corporate structures to circumvent U.S. export controls.

This flow of advanced AI chips to China and China’s access to restricted cloud computing capabilities risk enabling Beijing’s development of autonomous weapon systems, advanced cyber-warfare capabilities, and more powerful surveillance tools – which could eventually pose significant challenges to U.S. capabilities. China’s military could one day use these technologies against American servicemembers. Large-scale diversion also creates a gray market that penalizes law-abiding companies and devalues the intellectual property that sustains U.S. global economic leadership.

Accordingly, I respectfully request that you provide the following information to my office in writing by November 24, 2026:

An update on the Department of Justice’s continuation of the Department of Commerce investigation into Megaspeed;

A detailed description of any Department of Commerce efforts to prevent Megaspeed, whose top executive is reportedly a Chinese intelligence asset, from purchasing Nvidia chips, such as by sending an “Is Informed” letter to Nvidia blocking certain semiconductor shipments to Megaspeed and potentially placing Megaspeed on the Entity List;

A detailed accounting of:

The Department of Commerce and Department of State’s efforts to coordinate a rigorous response with partners including Singapore, Malaysia, and Indonesia;

The Department of Commerce’s efforts to close loopholes in U.S. export controls that allow Chinese companies to access restricted U.S. technology, such as semiconductors and cloud computing, through Southeast Asia; and

The Department of Commerce’s efforts to close loopholes in U.S. export controls that allow subsidiaries of China-headquartered firms, including those on whom the United States has already imposed sanctions, to buy export-controlled AI chips in the United States.

A detailed explanation of the Intelligence Community’s analysis of Alice Huang’s reported service as a Chinese intelligence asset and the broader threat Megaspeed poses to U.S. national security; and

A detailed explanation of the Intelligence Community’s sharing of such information, on Ms. Huang and Megaspeed, with the Department of Commerce, the Department of Justice, the Department of State, and the White House.

Thank you for your attention.

###

matches.text:
Cantwell-Led Bipartisan Legislation to Modernize Weather Forecasting & Research Unanimously Passes Senate

Act would improve wildfire forecasts and deploy new tools to fight fires, establish an atmospheric river forecast improvement program, strengthen landslide preparedness, and deploy new tech and tools to forecast droughts and heat waves that harm crops; Extreme weather is driving local impacts: August’s wind-fueled fires burned hundreds of thousands of acres and destroyed hundreds of Spokane homes, December’s atmospheric rivers dumped 5 trillion gallons of rain on WA, and 73 landslides were recor

WASHINGTON, D.C. – The U.S. Senate passed the bipartisan Weather Research and Forecasting Innovation Reauthorization Act of 2026 (the Weather Act) which authorizes programs at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) that will strengthen weather research and forecasting to save lives and better prepare our nation against dangerous weather disasters. The legislation is led by U.S. Senator Maria Cantwell (D-WA), ranking member of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation and senior member of the Senate Finance Committee.

“Americans are facing increasingly dangerous and costly weather disasters, and better forecasts give communities more time to prepare and get out of harm’s way,” said Sen. Cantwell. “The Weather Act will advance next-generation weather radar, modernize lifesaving warning systems, and improve forecasts for atmospheric rivers and wildfires, like the devastating fires that forced thousands to evacuate in Spokane last month. Senate passage brings us one step closer to giving forecasters, emergency managers, and communities the tools they need to save lives and protect property.”

Improves Fire Weather Forecasting:

The bill would establish an official Fire Weather Services Program within NOAA and fund the research and acquisition of new technology to improve forecasts of wildfire conditions. It would also create a Fire Weather Testbed to deploy new tools to fight fires, including a pilot program for unmanned aircraft to gather data such as chemical information and survey damage. It would ensure that meteorologists in the field receive fair compensation for longer-term deployments.

Wildfires burn thousands of acres in the state of Washington every year. More than 900,000 acres have burned during the 2026 fire season. Wind-fueled fires destroyed more than 800 homes in Spokane, forced tens of thousands of residents to evacuate, and is estimated to cost over $1 billion to rebuild.

The bill would also establish a NOAA program to coordinate agencies’ activities and ensure a united Federal approach to reducing risks to human health from heat and improve the delivery of data, forecasts, and warnings, related to extreme heat to help protect communities.

READ MORE: The Spokesman-Review: Spokane fire damages will exceed $1 billion

Improves Atmospheric River Forecasting:

The Weather Act would establish an atmospheric river forecast improvement program to advance accurate, effective, and actionable forecasts and warnings for atmospheric rivers. It also enables NOAA to improve atmospheric river hazard communication.

The bill would require NOAA to maintain and improve how the National Weather Service and other federal partners like the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) support emergency managers and communicate potential hazardous weather or water events to the public. It also directs NOAA to upgrade outdated weather radio technology to provide reliable and continuous weather and emergency alerts, expanding coverage to 98-99% of the United States. Despite the State of Washington having 17 National Weather Radio transmitters, large gaps in coverage remain.

December’s atmospheric rivers dumped five trillion gallons of rain across the state and caused devastating floods. In the western United States, atmospheric rivers account for 84% of flood damages costing approximately $1.1 billion a year, and in King County, atmospheric rivers are responsible for 97% of flood damages.

READ MORE: The Cascadia Daily News: Flooded Whatcom businesses face ‘long road’ to recovery

Improves Landslide Preparedness:

The bill would require the United States Geological Survey (USGS) and NOAA to incorporate risks from atmospheric rivers into landslide preparedness and response planning. It would expand the National Landslide Hazards Database to cover areas needing additional landslide risk assessments due to factors such as hydrological changes and atmospheric river flooding. It includes funding for the purchase and deployment of landslide early warning systems in high-risk area.

In December 2025 at least 73 landslides were reported after the atmospheric river event and there were likely many more that went undocumented. Some of these blocked critical transportation corridors for days on end. A section of U.S. 2 near Leavenworth was closed for weeks due to flood damage. North Cascades Lodge at Stehekin was forced to close for the summer of 2026 due to the flood damage. This week, following soaking rains and with the National Weather Service forecasting more heavy rain starting Friday, emergency management officials have warned Washingtonians about increased landslide risks.

READ MORE: National Park Service: Services limited at Stehekin Landing following winter flood damage

Improves Drought Monitoring:

The bill directs the National Integrated Drought Information System to advance and deploy next generation drought monitoring technologies and use observations from state or regional hydrological monitoring projects. The bill reauthorizes the National Weather Service’s work to provide agricultural and silvicultural weather and climate information and directs NOAA to establish at least two pilot projects to support improved extended range precipitation forecasts for agriculture and water management.

READ MORE: Yakima Herald-Republic: Washington state facing third-worst snowpack year on record, researchers say

Large portions of the State of Washington remain in moderate to severe drought, primarily due to snowpack deficits. Low precipitation and snowpack threaten irrigation water supplies, agriculture, and summer stream flows, which depend heavily on gradual snowmelt.

“We are tremendously appreciative of Sen. Cantwell’s continued leadership in protecting our natural resources, including our ocean,” said Jan Newton, Director of the Northwest Association of Networked Ocean Observing Systems (NANOOS) and affiliate professor with the University of Washington Collee of the Environment. “NANOOS is grateful that our policymakers understand the importance of the ocean to our weather, which is created and driven by many inter-related systems. We are excited that the Integrated Ocean Observing Systems (IOOS) network, of which NANOOS is a key component, is reauthorized as a part of the larger Weather Act reauthorization legislation. We thank the bipartisan group of Senators engaged in this effort.”

"Accurate weather forecasts are among the most direct ways science serves the public, and the stakes have never been higher as extreme weather grows more frequent and costly. The Weather Act Reauthorization Act would move research breakthroughs into operational forecasts faster, strengthening the nation's ability to prepare for, respond to, and recover from severe weather. AGU applauds Congress's bipartisan commitment to science-informed decision-making that safeguards communities across the country.” – Janice Lachance, Executive Director/CEO, American Geophysical Union

“Weather impacts everyone, every day, and the ability to provide timely, accurate weather information depends on a strong weather enterprise. The bipartisan Weather Act recognizes the importance of investing in the observations, science, technology, and forecasting capabilities that help us save lives, protect property, and support our economy. Strengthening those capabilities is an investment in the nation’s future." – Alan Sealls, President, American Meteorological Society

“Passage of the Weather Act Reauthorization is a giant step forward for the Weather Enterprise and its delivery of forecasts that save lives, protect communities, support businesses, and bolster our national economy. This bill strengthens public-private partnerships by augmenting critical government systems with increased use of innovative commercial data, paving the way for needed advances in observations, modeling, and information delivery. The American people will benefit every day from this legislation – from improved aviation and agricultural operations to earlier warnings for extreme weather such as tornadoes and flash flooding.” – Douglas Hilderbrand, Executive Director, American Weather Enterprise Association

Complete Highlights of the Legislation Include:

Enhancing Federal Weather Forecasting and Innovation

Addresses NOAA’s aging radar network by directing the agency to design and deploy the next generation of weather radar technology by 2037. It also authorizes NOAA to manage existing gaps in the current radar network by supplementing weather radar coverage with data, services, and technologies from third parties.

Establishes an atmospheric river forecast improvement program to develop tools and improved forecast models to address the increasingly frequent and powerful atmospheric rivers impacting the US, especially across the West coast.

Directs the National Weather Service to include turbulence events and icing conditions in their forecasting capabilities and establishes an airborne observation program to acquire atmospheric data from commercial aircraft.

Directs NOAA to improve accuracy and timeliness of weather, water, and space weather forecasts and effective dissemination of critical information using artificial intelligence.

Creates a project to improve forecasts of coastal marine fog with the goal of enhancing vessel safety and reducing the economic impact of coastal marine fog events.

Strengthening Emergency Preparedness by Improving Communication

Requires NOAA to maintain and improve the system that communicates potential hazardous weather or water events to the public.

Requires upgrades to outdated weather radio technology to provide reliable and continuous weather and emergency alerts and expands radio coverage to rural areas that do not currently have access to the National Weather Radio alert system.

Modernizing Critical Research Programs

Updates the Tsunami Forecasting and Warning Program to evaluate tsunami alert levels, maintain fail-safe warning capabilities, and align the analytic techniques and methodologies of the two existing tsunami warning centers in Hawaii and Alaska.

Builds on the progress of the Hurricane Forecast Improvement Project by establishing it as a long-term program that will incorporate social, behavioral, risk, and communication science into modeling, forecasting, and response guidance.

Expands the goals of the Tornado Warning Improvement and Extension Program to improve the effectiveness and timeliness of tornado forecasts, predictions, and warnings by increasing lead times, improving forecasting, and updating the system to rate the severity of tornadoes in collaboration with local communities and emergency managers.

Provides funding for weather laboratories; tornado, severe storm, and next generation radar research; and transitioning the latest scientific and technological advances into operations.

Supporting Farmers and Ranchers with Better Tools for Agriculture and Water Management

Directs the National Integrated Drought Information System to advance and deploy next-generation drought monitoring technologies and transition existing drought products to probabilistic forecasts, as well as use observations from state or regional hydrological monitoring projects.

Reauthorizes the National Weather Service’s work to provide agricultural and silvicultural weather and climate information and directs NOAA to establish at least two pilot projects to support improved sub-seasonal to seasonal extended range precipitation forecasts for agriculture and water management.

Codifies and authorizes the National Mesonet Program, a network of automated weather stations that are used to monitor and observe weather events and microclimates. The program is directed to obtain observations to improve understanding of and forecast capabilities for atmospheric, drought, fire, and water events and increase the quantity and density of environmental observations.

Expanding Commercial Data Partnerships

Increases NOAA’s access to critical forecasting data by expanding its authority to contract with the private sector to acquire commercial weather data.

Codifies the Commercial Data Program to coordinate and acquire a variety of weather and environmental data and services from the private sector for operational use.

Modifies the existing commercial data pilot program to be a testing program within the Commercial Data Program, and authorizes the program to test and evaluate all sources and types of observation services, imagery, products, and data from private sector entities.

Preparing for Disasters

Establishes within NOAA an interagency committee to coordinate agencies’ activities and ensure a united federal approach to reducing health risks from heat, as well as a NOAA system to improve the delivery of data, information, forecasts, warnings, prediction, and projections related to temperature and extreme heat.

Improves the monitoring, forecasting, prevention, and mitigation of harmful algal blooms and hypoxia that threaten aquatic ecosystems, hurt local economies, and endanger public health by reauthorizing and amending the National Harmful Algal Bloom and Hypoxia Program. Establishes a national harmful algal bloom observing network and a national incubator program and increases the avenues of assistance NOAA can provide to affected communities.

Requires the national landslide strategy to include an assessment of risks from atmospheric river flooding and extreme precipitation events and expands the National Landslide Hazards Database to cover areas needing further risk assessment due to factors such as hydrological changes and atmospheric river flooding

Read the bill text HERE.

Sen. Cantwell continues to insist on deploying the best technology to help our weather forecasters. Last year, Senator Cantwell called out the Administration’s decision to cancel its plan to launch a large-scale test of a new advanced weather radar technology, called Phased Array Radar.

Senate passage of the bill is another important next step to Sen. Cantwell’s 5 Point Plan to bolster the United States’ weather readiness, which she outlined in a letter to President Donald Trump in July of last year.

###

“The thing I hear most from communities in Arizona where these proposed data centers are built is ‘how can we have our voices heard?’”

Today, during a Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) Committee hearing, Arizona Senator Mark Kelly pressed Justin Schwab, President Trump’s nominee to lead the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) Office of Air and Radiation, on the agency’s proposal to eliminate longstanding public comment requirements for certain air pollution permits, including for data centers building their own power plants. Kelly also secured a commitment from Schwab to prioritize final approval of a Maricopa County air quality rule aimed at reducing air pollution from off-road equipment.

Kelly raised concerns that EPA’s proposal to eliminate the 30-day public comment period for certain air pollution permits could leave communities without a say in new data center projects: “As you know, there’s a massive boom in data center development across the country. The thing I hear most from communities in Arizona where these proposed data centers are built is, ‘how can we have our voices heard?’ That’s especially true if a data center is proposing to build what’s called behind-the-meter generation. Or in other words, they’re going to build their own power plant. For decades, EPA has required at least 30 days for the public to review and comment on proposed permits. Seems rather reasonable.”

Kelly questioned who pushed for the rollback after seven major data center developers responded to an October inquiry from Kelly, and none indicated they had requested the change: “Earlier this year, EPA proposed a new rule that would allow states to eliminate the public comment opportunity for any minor source facility that emits less than 100 tons of pollution per year. I think that’s unacceptable, and what I can’t understand is who asked for this.”

Last month, Kelly and Whitehouse urged EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin to withdraw the proposal, arguing that faster permitting should not come at the expense of transparency or communities’ ability to shape decisions that affect them. During the hearing, Schwab committed to looking into the senators’ letter after Kelly pressed him to ensure EPA provides a response.

Kelly also secured a commitment from Schwab to advance Maricopa County’s efforts to improve air quality: “Just last week, EPA formally approved the county’s Rule 205, which allows businesses to generate emissions credits by replacing older, higher-polluting vehicles with cleaner ones. I appreciate that progress, but Rule 204, which would establish a similar program for off-road equipment, still needs final approval.”

When Kelly asked whether Schwab would prioritize EPA’s ongoing work with Maricopa County to move Rule 204 toward final approval as quickly as possible, Schwab responded, “Yes. If confirmed, I do commit to prioritize in that regard.”

Sen. Kelly questions EPA nominees in EPW hearing.

Click here to download a video of Kelly’s remarks. See the transcript below:

Sen. Mark Kelly: Thank you, Madam Chair and thank you, Mr. Schwab, for being here today. I’d like to first ask you about Maricopa County’s efforts to improve air quality, which has spanned multiple administrations. Just last week, EPA formally approved the county’s rule 205, which allows businesses to generate emissions credits by replacing older, higher polluting vehicles with cleaner ones.

I appreciate that progress, but rule 204, which would establish a similar program for off road equipment, still needs final approval. Mr. Schwab, if confirmed, will you commit to prioritizing EPA’s ongoing work with Maricopa County to move rule 204 toward final approval as quickly as possible?

Justin Schwab, Nominee, Assistant Administrator for the Office of Air and Radiation: Thank you for the question, Senator. Yes. If confirmed, I do commit to prioritize in that regard.

Kelly: Well, thank you. Mr. Schwab, next, I want to talk about data centers. As you know, there’s a massive boom in data center development across the country. The thing I hear most from communities in Arizona where these proposed data centers are built, is how can we have our voices heard? That’s especially true of a data center is proposing to build what’s called behind the meter generation.

Or in other words, they’re going to build their own power plant. Right now, those facilities would need to get a minor new source review permit. And for decades, EPA has required at least 30 days for the public to review and comment on proposed permits. Seems rather reasonable. 30 days. It basically says to a developer, if you want to admit up to 100 tons of nitrous oxide or soot a year, you need to give the surrounding community opportunity to understand the impacts of a project and voice their concerns before construction begins.

Mr. Schwab, let me ask you a question. So, would you be comfortable with a data center that admitted just less than the 100 tons of NOx or PPM 2.5 near your home, without a guaranteed opportunity to give your input?

Schwab: Thank you for the question, senator. Matters of permitting are in the first instance, the responsibility of state or local governments.

The Clean Air Act does provide certain minimum requirements. The Clean Air Act does expressly require state permitting programs in order to be approved by EPA to provide for public engagement when it comes to major new source, review sources, but does not contain any such requirement with respect to minor news source review sources and in that regard.

Kelly: Well, that’s what I’m asking but from your personal life, would you be comfortable with a data center that admitted just less than, the cutoff is 100 tons, just less than the 100 tons of NOx or PPM 2.5 near your home without a guaranteed opportunity to give your own input. That’s the question.

Schwab: Thank you for the question, senator. It would depend on the particular circumstances of the facility.

Kelly: The circumstance is a data center is being built, and it’s going to admit, let’s say, a just under 100 tons of night nitrous oxide of NOx. Would you be comfortable with that without having an opportunity to give your own input on the issue?

Schwab: Thank you for the question, senator. As I said, matters of permitting are appropriately where consistent with federal law, the prerogative of state and local governments. And those are the ones that know their communities best.

Kelly: Yes, so you don’t think homeowners, people in the region of where the data center is being built should get a say if it’s just less than the 100 tons or you don’t think it’s up to them at all.

Schwab: Senator, the Congress Enacting the Clean Air Act, has provided those areas in which federal law does require all state permitting process to engage, to include a public participation phase. And there are other areas in which federal law does not have that express requirement. And there is a pending proposal in that regard from.

Kelly: Well, it sounds like your answer is no. I’m trying to understand where are you on this? If it’s less than 100 tons, you don’t think people should get an input. You keep coming back to the law, but I’m just asking you your opinion.

Schwab: My opinion is that, as a general principle, state and local governments and agencies understand their communities and their concerns best.

Kelly: Well, earlier this year, EPA proposed a new rule that would allow states to eliminate the public comment opportunity for any minor source facility that emits less than 100 tons of pollution per year.

I think that’s unacceptable and what I can’t understand is who asked for this. So, I worked with Ranking Member Whitehouse to ask nine of the leading data center developers said seven of them responded, and none of them said they asked EPA to make this rule. So, Mr. Schwab, you’ve been at EPA since these rules were proposed and you’ve been in the Trump administration since the president took office.

So maybe, you know, like who asked the EPA to roll back these common-sense protections?

Schwab: Thank you for the question, senator. The proposal is not specific to data centers. The proposal addresses generally requirements for minor —

Kelly: Who asked to roll them back? Because it wasn’t the data centers. So must have been somebody, unless it was just decided internally that you don’t think the community should have an input.

Schwab: Senator, the policies of the United States is articulated by the president’s executive orders are where consistent with law, to reform permitting processes to ensure that they do not include non-statutory non legally required provisions that may hinder development.

Having said that, it is the prerogative of state and local governments in the first instance where federal law is silent on a question to determine what level of public participation may be appropriate under their own —

Kelly: It sounds like you’re saying it came from the White House. Well, what I’m going to ask you here is, will you commit to speaking with Administrator Zeldin and his team about the letter we sent to make sure we get an answer to our letter.

Schwab: Thank you for the question, senator. I’m not familiar with this letter, but, yes, I do confirm the looking into the letter.

WASHINGTON, DC — US Senator James Lankford (R-OK) today announced he intends to seek the position of Ranking Member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee (HSGAC) in the 120th Congress:

“In the days ahead, I intend to ask my Republican colleagues on HSGAC for their support for me to be selected as Ranking Member next Congress. There is important work ahead on FEMA reform, the federal workforce, and making government operate more effectively and efficiently for the American people.

“In many areas of government operation, HSGAC can operate in a bipartisan manner. Waste and inefficiency should not be a Republican or Democratic issue. Over the last decade on the Homeland Security Committee, I have worked across the aisle to improve emergency communications in federal buildings, strengthen the United States Postal Service, increase federal cybersecurity preparedness, government transparency, and the use of artificial intelligence. This Committee has a broad responsibility to make sure the federal government does its job well.

“As the only Committee with broad oversight and subpoena authority across the federal government, we have an important responsibility to ask hard questions, get answers, and make sure government is working as it should. However, the job of any Ranking Member is to also push back on a majority that goes too far. There is important work done at the Department of Homeland Security by brave men and women and their efforts should not be hampered simply because of partisan politics. Oversight is responsible, but obstruction is unacceptable.

“I look forward to serving with Senator Maggie Hassan in our new roles. We have worked together very productively on numerous occasions, most recently on our Prevent Government Shutdowns Act. Years ago, Dr. Tom Coburn of Oklahoma and Senator Tom Carper of Delaware worked together on this same Committee to do essential oversight and non-partisan work for the American people. I plan to work together when we can agree and be a fierce opposition if there is an attempt to undercut our nation’s security.

“The Department of Homeland Security is the third-largest federal department, and its work touches the lives of Americans every day. From TSA and CISA to Border Patrol and the United States Coast Guard, the men and women of DHS work to keep America safe on our borders, at sea, and in our skies. I look forward to highlighting their work and making sure the Department is fulfilling its mission.”

Background

Lankford has served on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee since 2015 and has spent more than a decade working on issues within its jurisdiction. He has served as Chairman of the Subcommittee on Regulatory Affairs and Federal Management and currently chairs the Subcommittee on Border Management, Federal Workforce, and Regulatory Affairs, where he has led oversight hearings on border security, federal workforce readiness, government operations, and regulatory accountability.

Lankford has worked to make the federal government more accountable to the people it serves. He authored the Taxpayers Right-to-Know Act, which became law in 2021, and has worked on issues ranging from federal hiring and regulatory reform to cybersecurity and artificial intelligence.

As Subcommittee Chairman, Lankford has also led oversight of border security and federal preparedness, including a 2025 hearing examining federal readiness ahead of the 2026 FIFA World Cup, 2028 Olympics, and America’s 250th anniversary.

Former Oklahoma Senator Tom Coburn served as Ranking Member of HSGAC from 2013 to January 2015.

Washington, DC – TODAY, Congressman Gabe Amo (D-RI) issued the following statement on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation:

“This week I led colleagues in calling for a full investigation into Jensen Huang’s actions by Trump's Department of Commerce because they put us all at risk. No CEO or government official should be allowed to put America’s technological edge in jeopardy.

Now, Trump must crack down on advanced chip exports before he hands our AI advantage to an adversary.

And we still need answers: What did this administration know, when did it know it, and who signed off on these exports?

Stop the shipments. Enforce the law. Give Congress and the American people the answers they deserve. Our security is not for sale.”

Background

Earlier this week, Amo, Ranking Member Gregory Meeks (D-NY), and Ranking Member of the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on South and Central Asia Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-CA) sent a letter demanding answers from Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick about the Trump Administration’s approval of advanced AI chip exports, including to companies with concerning links to China and amid alarming reports of potential Chinese intelligence ties to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

In January 2026, Meeks and Amo challenged Secretary Lutnick over President Trump’s dangerous decision to loosen export controls and approve the sale of advanced AI chips to China.

U.S. Representatives Don Beyer, Jennifer McClellan, Suhas Subramanyam, Eugene Vindman, and James Walkinshaw, Democrats from Virginia, today urged the Virginia State Corporation Commission (SCC) to reject the proposed acquisition of Dominion Energy by Florida-based NextEra. The letter further raises concerns about NextEra’s corporate governance, including its history of political spending and interference, warning these practices could undermine regulatory oversight, create conflicts with Virginia’s Clean Economy Act requirements, and expose ratepayers to additional financial risks.

Dear Commissioners:

We write to express our opposition to the current proposed merger whereby NextEra Energy, Inc. ("NextEra") would acquire control of Dominion Energy, Inc. ("Dominion"). Under the Utility Transfers Act, the State Corporation Commission ("Commission") may approve an acquisition of control if it finds that "adequate service to the public at just and reasonable rates will not be impaired or jeopardized. “Applicants must prove that the transaction causes no harm to captive customers. We believe the joint petition fails this statutory test.

We respectfully urge the Commission to reject the proposed NextEra Dominion merger in its current form, as recommended by Commission staff.

Rate Base Inflation and Misaligned Incentives

NextEra’s investor disclosures emphasize that Dominion's territory offers immense multi-decade capital deployment opportunities, driven in large part by the extraordinary concentration of AI data centers in Northern Virginia and future planned load. Given that this projected future energy demand in the Commonwealth will be reliant on massive bulk transmission lines, which are still socialized across residential rate classes, much of that potential infrastructure will be paid for by ratepayers. And as NextEra’s growth strategy is dependent on maximizing capital deployment, its potential acquisition of Dominion risks creating a sustained, multi-decade upward pressure on ratepayers’ bills. Captive residential and small business ratepayers will be locked into paying decades of capital carrying charges, depreciation, and an authorized Return on Equity (ROE) on this expanded rate base.

We are concerned that much of NextEra’s growth strategy is heavily dependent on data center customers. This increases vulnerabilities that exist due to overbuilding and the ramifications that could materialize for ratepayers if projected revenue from large-load customers fails to cover the full cost of the transmission buildout and necessary upgrades to the grid that increased data center presence would require. While Dominion has started work to hedge against this stranded asset risk, there is insufficient protection in the case for bankruptcy, differing time horizons for service contracts and infrastructure lifespans, as well as the burden of broader grid upgrades required by data centers (rather than just point-to-point infrastructure) where every day ratepayers foot the bill.

There have also been documented concerns about how this merger affects market competition within the broader grid that Dominion is a part of, particularly with respect to transmission and energy generation and how the new merger could create “self-preferencing” or foreclose potential competition, and how those ripple effects could then increase wholesale prices and therefore raise costs for ratepayers in Virginia.

Despite those long-term upward financial pressures, the merger sweeteners of customer bill credits and added funds for the EnergyShare program are both inadequate and only short-term. Once the sweeteners expire, the Virginia-based Dominion workforce would be at risk of significant job cuts, Virginia households and small businesses would be locked into paying those multi-decade elevated rates, with the joint petition providing for no base rate increase moratorium, no cap on escalating rate adjustment clauses (riders), and no binding mechanism to track and pass fuel or operational synergies to captive customers. Additionally, the proposed bill credit for consumers barely covers the impact that increased fuel costs are having on electric bills. Dominion already petitioned the Commission for a $10 per month increase for fuel-related costs this year.

For these reasons, the Independent Market Monitor stated, the “scale, financial strength, and operational breadth all enhance market power and any economic gains are more likely to accrue to investors rather than customers.” Thus, we must look past the near-term sweeteners and toward robust binding, structural protections that prevent long-term negative impacts on Virginia ratepayers.

We believe the primary benefits of the merger should be designed to benefit our constituents, the ratepayers, and we believe the current merger design will raise rates. To that extent, we urge the Commission to, at a bare minimum, require long-term rate protections for consumers as recommended by Commission staff and require substantially larger bill credits as recommended by the Governor’s Office before any potential merger can proceed. The Commission must ensure that any acquiring entity submits to complete regulatory transparency and that captive ratepayers do not cross-subsidize non-utility operations, political spending, or parent-company agendas.

NextEra’s operational history and recent testimony demonstrates documented resistance to transparent regulatory scrutiny. NextEra recently entered into a $150 million settlement to resolve widespread political interference and dark money schemes, which included funding “ghost candidates” against state legislators and covert surveillance of an investigative journalist. This Commission’s Hearing Examiner properly recognized the relevance of these governance practices to regulatory integrity by ordering the production of the internal "Robo memo" into the evidentiary record. We share the position that this memo should be available for review to the Commission and intervenors.

At a time when regulatory scrutiny is at an all-time high, NextEra’s top leadership has aligned itself financially with federal agendas that raise rates and undermine Virginia’s statutory obligations. NextEra’s participation in high-level, opaque federal lobbying networks heightens the risk that Virginia ratepayers could be improperly forced to subsidize national political advocacy that runs counter to their own interests. In this case, aligning with a federal agenda that rolls back renewable energy incentives, curtails offshore wind development, and props up uneconomic generation. Engaging in that advocacy, including through means designed to obscure its involvement, puts NextEra in direct conflict with Virginia’s statutory mandates under the Virginia Clean Economy Act, and introduces an acute risk of asset stranding, resource inadequacy, and costly non-compliance penalties that will inevitably fall upon Virginia consumers.

Conclusion

The Commission’s statutory mission is to safeguard captive consumers and ensure the long-term reliability and affordability of utility service. As proposed, we do not believe the merger is in the public interest. We believe the proposed transaction fails to satisfy the statutory requirements and because the joint petition lacks the structural protections necessary to prevent material harm, the Commission should deny the merger petition in its current form.

We appreciate the Commission’s careful scrutiny of this proceeding and submit these comments on behalf of our constituents.

matches.text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Congresswoman Kat Cammack (FL-03) this week voted on legislation that would end a decades-old penalty on combat-wounded veterans and protect the benefits of Gold Star spouses.

On Veterans Day, the House passed what House Veterans’ Affairs Committee Chairman Mike Bost calls the most comprehensive veterans package in a decade: more than 60 veterans-focused measures to expand health care access for rural veterans, cut red tape at VA, and ensure surviving spouses aren’t penalized for finding love again.

Right now, a surviving spouse who remarries before age 55 forfeits survivor benefits. The Love Lives On Act ends that penalty, letting them keep those benefits and restoring TRICARE coverage if a later marriage ends.

“We owe veterans, active duty servicemembers, and their families a debt we will never be able to fully repay,” said Congresswoman Cammack. “For too long, we’ve walked back our promises to these brave men and women even after they’ve kept theirs. If you lost your husband or wife in service to our country, you shouldn’t have to choose between finding love again and keeping the benefits your family earned, and if you’re wounded in combat and medically retired, Washington shouldn’t dock your pay. It is fitting the House is acting on these important bills as we observe Veterans Day, and I will keep fighting every single day for veterans in North Central Florida and around the country.”

Beyond the Star Act and the Love Lives On Act, highlights of the package include:

Benefits for veterans and survivors

Raises monthly pay for veterans with the most severe service-connected disabilities, the first significant increase in decades

Boosts survivor payments an extra 1% a year for three years

Guarantees surviving spouses of veterans lost to ALS the full survivor benefit, no matter how long the illness lasted

Health care

Expands suicide and overdose treatment and speeds up admission to VA residential treatment programs

Extends VA’s community suicide prevention grants for three more years

Locks in community care access standards for eight years, so veterans far from a VA hospital keep their options

Puts a lactation space in every VA medical center

Claims and accountability

Stops VA from denying a claim because a veteran missed a single exam

Lets the Board of Veterans’ Appeals decide appeals that raise the same issue together, under a three-year pilot

Sends military sexual trauma claims to a specialized team

Gives veterans one VA phone number to call, with call centers in every time zone

Families and caregivers

Extends health coverage for family caregivers six months after the veteran passes away or leaves the program, with help getting back to work

Lets spouses and dependent children receive a VA headstone, whatever the date of death

Jobs and education

Raises GI Bill housing pay for student veterans studying online or training in apprenticeships

Expands VET TEC tech training to fields like artificial intelligence and semiconductors

These reforms are backed by more than 30 veterans and military family organizations, including the Military Order of the Purple Heart, the Military Officers Association of America, TAPS and Gold Star Spouses of America.

Earlier this week, the House also passed the Veterans’ Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act (H.R. 8552), which raises VA disability compensation and survivor benefits on December 1 to keep pace with the cost of living.

Cammack also voted in favor of the Major Richard Star Act (H.R. 2102).

This bill allows veterans with combat-related disabilities who were medically retired before 20 years of service to collect their military retirement pay and their VA disability compensation in full. The Congressional Budget Office counts about 58,000 retirees who would qualify. Cammack has cosponsored the bill in every Congress she has served.

North Central Florida is home to about 57,000 veterans, and Florida has about 1.4 million, the third most of any state. The district anchors the nation’s largest VA health care system, from the Malcom Randall VA Medical Center in Gainesville to the Lake City VA Medical Center.

“I wanted to serve twenty years, and I would have, except for what happened to me in the war. We have so many young veterans who served two or three years before they were blown up by an IED in Iraq or Afghanistan, and they still get their retirement cut. It’s just not fair. Every veteran wants the other veteran to be treated fairly, especially those who gave of themselves in combat, and we appreciate and support Congresswoman Cammack’s efforts to get these veterans what they earned,” said Captain Stephen Petty, U.S. Army (Ret.), a Vietnam helicopter pilot from Ocala, FL.

“We support the effort to pass the Star Act, and we appreciate Congresswoman Cammack standing up for our veterans,” said Charles Calhoun, President of the On Top of the World Veterans Club and Chairman of the Marion County Veterans Advisory Council.

WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, Congressmen Vince Fong (CA-20) and Suhas Subramanyam (VA-10) introduced the Promoting High-skilled Doctoral Talent (PHD Talent) Act of 2026, bipartisan legislation to build accelerated pathways that take students from a bachelor’s degree to a Ph.D. in critical and emerging technology fields. This legislation will propel more American scientists and engineers into the domestic workforce, ensuring China does not surpass the United States as the global technological leader.

The bill creates a five-year Department of Energy (DOE) pilot program that brings universities, National Laboratories, and private industry together. Students in these programs would get hands-on research experience, mentorship, and workforce training while earning an advanced degree in less time.

“America’s economy and national security depends on us having a deep bench of skilled, capable, and credentialed American workers,” said Congressman Fong. “Whether it’s cybersecurity, advanced manufacturing, defense research, advanced energy systems, medical innovations, or other emerging technologies, we need more homegrown talent. The PHD Talent Act gives students in the Central Valley and across the country a faster, clearer path to the advanced degrees these fields demand.”

"Our country faces a critical shortage of scientists, engineers, and mathematicians,” said Congressman Subramanyam. “This bill shores up and strengthens our pipeline of researchers. This will in turn help the next generation of students make breakthrough discoveries in science, health, and technology, solidifying our country's leadership in these fields."

Specifically, the bill:

Establishes a five-year DOE pilot program, with Ph.D. fellowships, for accelerated bachelor’s-to-Ph.D. pathways in critical and emerging technology fields, including artificial intelligence, quantum science, semiconductors, cybersecurity, and advanced manufacturing, among others.

Supports partnerships among universities, National Laboratories, and industry for accelerated hands-on research and training.

Shortens the time it takes to earn a STEM Ph.D. while maintaining robust academic standards.

Directs funding to fields where DOE identifies a need for more domestic doctoral talent.

Ensures taxpayer-funded student support is reserved for U.S. citizens, U.S. nationals, and lawful permanent residents.

Background

The bill builds on the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy’s July 2026 report, Science: A New Golden Age, which calls for investing directly in American researchers and strengthening the domestic pipeline of advanced STEM talent. It was developed in coordination with DOE as part of The Genesis Mission, an initiative to unite industry, academia, and National Labs to harness artificial intelligence and emerging technologies.

Congressman Fong is a Member of the Subcommittee on Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Protection in the House Homeland Security Committee, and the Subcommittee on Research and Technology in the House Science, Space, and Technology Committee. He has made workforce development a priority, including with his NSF AI Education Act, which builds AI and technology pipelines through community colleges and regional universities.

Senators Todd Young (R-IN) and Mark Warner (D-VA) are leading the Senate companion bill of the PHD Talent Act. Text of the legislation can be found here.

matches.text:
In DC, majority and minority parties impact the art of legislating.

The majority party in office controls the daily legislative agenda, wields greater representation on committees and sets the chamber rules.

As a result, the minority party has less say in contributing to the legislative process.

However, as a matter of governance, there are many opportunities for the majority and minority to engage on policy in a bipartisan manner.

One such opportunity is the Faster Clinical Trials Act. Massachusetts Democratic Congressman Jake Auchincloss came to me shortly after I became Chair of the Health Subcommittee with an idea to modernize clinical trials and reform some aspects related to medication and treatment approval at the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

As Chairman, I asked Auchincloss to work with my health care team to develop actual language to facilitate what I believe to be a great idea. After a year of us working together, we agreed on an expansive bill which not only benefits patients doing clinical trials, but specifically includes opportunities for rural patients to participate in such trials.

I recently co-introduced this bill along with Auchincloss.

Clinical trials serve patients like those with rare diseases. Medical researchers lead the trials to help test potential new treatments and medical breakthroughs for these patients.

While participation in these trials is open to the public, certain patient groups are underrepresented, particularly those in rural communities.

Depending on the type of clinical trial and where you are in Virginia’s Ninth District, the closest clinical trial may be in Charlottesville, Bethesda or Cincinnati.

This places patients in a difficult situation where they question if it is worth the time, the effort and the attention to seek care for their rare illness.

The Faster Clinical Trials Act supports a new and more inclusive landscape where patients can stay closer to home and participate through local health care settings. Our bill creates clinical trial opportunities in community health centers, rural facilities and other underserved settings.

Accordingly, researchers will be able to integrate clinical trials into routine health care delivery.

With this solution, rural communities including those in Virginia will be better represented in our clinical studies!

When it comes to patient and researcher representation, the U.S. needs greater data.

That is why the proposed model in our bill pushes for an increase in U.S. patient representation in clinical trials as well as strengthening oversight of foreign clinical research.

Moreover, the oversight of clinical research moves one step further as the Faster Clinical Trials Act establishes a National Biobank Program.

The National Biobank Program would collect, store and generate molecular data and analyze biological specimens and clinical data. Program participation requires representation from every U.S. State and territory, including urban and rural populations.

By expanding the pool of patient participants, particularly in rural communities, our researchers will be able to more effectively and thoroughly study rare diseases.

As a result, rural patients’ access to care and treatment discovery will improve!

In addition to these provisions, our bill updates cancer drug development. And it authorizes the use of artificial intelligence in lieu of testing on animals.

Taken together, these ideas constitute a substantive proposal that revamps the U.S. clinical trials process, advances American medical research and accelerates the development of new treatments for patients.

The limited calendar for this Congress means that action on the Faster Clinical Trials Act is unlikely by the end of the year. However, Congressman Auchincloss and I remain committed to working with each other in the next Congress to gather widespread support for our bill.

This joint legislative effort proves that it is possible to get things done for the American people.

Notwithstanding the bipartisan collaboration discussed above, there will be areas where working together is not possible.

As someone who previously served in the minority party in both the Virginia House of Delegates and Congress, I recognize there will also be times that require me to stand up and defend the conservative values of Virginia’s Ninth District. That means stopping radical Democratic proposals to take your guns, open our borders and raise your taxes.

Accordingly, I am committed to using whatever resources available to stop radical Democrat ideas.

While governance in the minority for the 120th Congress will look different from the Republican majority in the 119thCongress, I will continue to work with my colleagues on issues that serve the interests of Virginia’s Ninth District.

If you have questions, concerns, or comments, feel free to contact my office. You can call my Abingdon office at 276-525-1405 or my Christiansburg office at 540-381-5671. To reach my office via email, please visit my website at https://morgangriffith.house.gov/. Also on my website is the latest material from my office, including information on votes recently taken on the floor of the House of Representatives.
