Washington D.C. – Today, Congressman James Walkinshaw (VA-11) joined Congressmen Don Beyer (VA-08), Congresswoman Jennifer McClellan (VA-04), Suhas Subramanyam (VA-10), and Eugene Vindman (VA-07), Democrats from Virginia, to urge the Virginia State Corporation Commission (SCC) to reject the proposed acquisition of Dominion Energy by Florida-based NextEra. In a letter submitted ahead of the SCC’s November 12 public comment deadline, the Members warned that the merger, as currently structured, threatens to increase electricity costs for Virginia families and small businesses for decades to come.

They wrote:

“As proposed, we do not believe the merger is in the public interest. We believe the proposed transaction fails to satisfy the statutory requirements and because the joint petition lacks the structural protections necessary to prevent material harm, the Commission should deny the merger petition in its current form.”

The Members noted that while NextEra stands to benefit from the expanded investment opportunities created by the rapid expansion of data centers across Northern Virginia, residential customers and small businesses could be left footing the bill. The Members also cautioned that the merger could consolidate market power across the regional electricity grid, stifling competition and ultimately increasing electricity costs for Virginia consumers.

They argued that the proposed merger’s temporary incentives fail to offset the merger’s potential long-term costs. They also pointed to the absence of a moratorium on base rate increases, a cap on escalating rate adjustment clauses, and a binding requirement to pass operational savings on to customers.

The letter further raises concerns about NextEra’s corporate governance, including its history of political spending and interference, warning these practices could undermine regulatory oversight, create conflicts with Virginia’s Clean Economy Act requirements, and expose ratepayers to additional financial risks.

Emphasizing the SCC’s statutory responsibility to safeguard consumers and ensure the long-term reliability and affordability of utility service, the Members stated that approving the merger without adequate, enforceable protections would undermine that responsibility.

Full text of the letter follows below, and a signed copy is available here.

***

Dear Commissioners:

We write to express our opposition to the current proposed merger whereby NextEra Energy, Inc. (“NextEra”) would acquire control of Dominion Energy, Inc. (“Dominion”). Under the Utility Transfers Act, the State Corporation Commission (“Commission”) may approve an acquisition of control if it finds that “adequate service to the public at just and reasonable rates will not be impaired or jeopardized. “Applicants must prove that the transaction causes no harm to captive customers. We believe the joint petition fails this statutory test.

We respectfully urge the Commission to reject the proposed NextEra Dominion merger in its current form, as recommended by Commission staff.

Rate Base Inflation and Misaligned Incentives

NextEra’s investor disclosures emphasize that Dominion’s territory offers immense multi-decade capital deployment opportunities, driven in large part by the extraordinary concentration of AI data centers in Northern Virginia and future planned load. Given that this projected future energy demand in the Commonwealth will be reliant on massive bulk transmission lines, which are still socialized across residential rate classes, much of that potential infrastructure will be paid for by ratepayers. And as NextEra’s growth strategy is dependent on maximizing capital deployment, its potential acquisition of Dominion risks creating a sustained, multi-decade upward pressure on ratepayers’ bills. Captive residential and small business ratepayers will be locked into paying decades of capital carrying charges, depreciation, and an authorized Return on Equity (ROE) on this expanded rate base.

We are concerned that much of NextEra’s growth strategy is heavily dependent on data center customers. This increases vulnerabilities that exist due to overbuilding and the ramifications that could materialize for ratepayers if projected revenue from large-load customers fails to cover the full cost of the transmission buildout and necessary upgrades to the grid that increased data center presence would require. While Dominion has started work to hedge against this stranded asset risk, there is insufficient protection in the case for bankruptcy, differing time horizons for service contracts and infrastructure lifespans, as well as the burden of broader grid upgrades required by data centers (rather than just point-to-point infrastructure) where every day ratepayers foot the bill.

There have also been documented concerns about how this merger affects market competition within the broader grid that Dominion is a part of, particularly with respect to transmission and energy generation and how the new merger could create “self-preferencing” or foreclose potential competition, and how those ripple effects could then increase wholesale prices and therefore raise costs for ratepayers in Virginia.

Despite those long-term upward financial pressures, the merger sweeteners of customer bill credits and added funds for the EnergyShare program are both inadequate and only short-term. Once the sweeteners expire, the Virginia-based Dominion workforce would be at risk of significant job cuts, Virginia households and small businesses would be locked into paying those multi-decade elevated rates, with the joint petition providing for no base rate increase moratorium, no cap on escalating rate adjustment clauses (riders), and no binding mechanism to track and pass fuel or operational synergies to captive customers. Additionally, the proposed bill credit for consumers barely covers the impact that increased fuel costs are having on electric bills. Dominion already petitioned the Commission for a $10 per month increase for fuel-related costs this year.

For these reasons, the Independent Market Monitor stated, the “scale, financial strength, and operational breadth all enhance market power and any economic gains are more likely to accrue to investors rather than customers.” Thus, we must look past the near-term sweeteners and toward robust binding, structural protections that prevent long-term negative impacts on Virginia ratepayers.

We believe the primary benefits of the merger should be designed to benefit our constituents, the ratepayers, and we believe the current merger design will raise rates. To that extent, we urge the Commission to, at a bare minimum, require long-term rate protections for consumers as recommended by Commission staff and require substantially larger bill credits as recommended by the Governor’s Office before any potential merger can proceed. As energy prices have considerably increased, and this merger threatens to exacerbate market conditions that could further increase prices for ratepayers it is paramount that the Commission use its authority to protect consumers who are already struggling to afford to keep the lights on.

Corporate Governance Deficits Threaten Rate Case Prudency

A utility’s corporate culture directly governs accounting integrity, affiliate transactions, and ratemaking prudency. The Commission must ensure that any acquiring entity submits to complete regulatory transparency and that captive ratepayers do not cross-subsidize non-utility operations, political spending, or parent-company agendas.

NextEra’s operational history and recent testimony demonstrates documented resistance to transparent regulatory scrutiny. NextEra recently entered into a $150 million settlement to resolve widespread political interference and dark money schemes, which included funding “ghost candidates” against state legislators and covert surveillance of an investigative journalist. This Commission’s Hearing Examiner properly recognized the relevance of these governance practices to regulatory integrity by ordering the production of the internal “Robo memo” into the evidentiary record. We share the position that this memo should be available for review to the Commission and intervenors.

At a time when regulatory scrutiny is at an all-time high, NextEra’s top leadership has aligned itself financially with federal agendas that raise rates and undermine Virginia’s statutory obligations.NextEra’s participation in high-level, opaque federal lobbying networks heightens the risk that Virginia ratepayers could be improperly forced to subsidize national political advocacy that runs counter to their own interests. In this case, aligning with a federal agenda that rolls back renewable energy incentives, curtails offshore wind development, and props up uneconomic generation. Engaging in that advocacy, including through means designed to obscure its involvement, puts NextEra in direct conflict with Virginia’s statutory mandates under the Virginia Clean Economy Act, and introduces an acute risk of asset stranding, resource inadequacy, and costly non-compliance penalties that will inevitably fall upon Virginia consumers.

It is unacceptably risky to transfer Virginia’s premier electric utility to an acquiring entity that displays such a pattern of routine spending, through opaque affiliate channels, to influence regulatory and political outcomes. Such practices, if expanded into Virginia, would directly threaten the Commission’s ability to police affiliate transactions, enforce cross-subsidization prohibitions, and verify the prudency of test-year operating expenses. Captive ratepayers bear the cost when compliance breaks down, transactions lack transparent auditing, or management priorities subordinate the public interest to unregulated political agendas.

Conclusion

The Commission’s statutory mission is to safeguard captive consumers and ensure the long-term reliability and affordability of utility service. As proposed, we do not believe the merger is in the public interest. We believe the proposed transaction fails to satisfy the statutory requirements and because the joint petition lacks the structural protections necessary to prevent material harm, the Commission should deny the merger petition in its current form.

We appreciate the Commission’s careful scrutiny of this proceeding and submit these comments on behalf of our constituents.

Sincerely,

WASHINGTON, D.C. – This afternoon, Senator Jim Banks (R-Ind.) joined America Reports on Fox News Channel to discuss the growing controversy surrounding former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and advanced AI chips export control.

Click the image above for the full discussion.

Key Excerpts on the AI Export Controls:

Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.): “This news is as concerning as it gets. I served in a war; I served in Afghanistan. When you’re at war with another country, you don’t give them your best technology, and that’s why lawmakers for the past two years have been pushing hard to stop our high-end computer chips from being exported to China. And that’s why my AI Overwatch Act is more important than ever. Last year I had the GAIN AI Act, which would have blocked our chips from being sold to China if American customers wanted to buy them first. Nvidia opposed my legislation a year ago; they have opposed other export control laws. And now we know that the Department of Commerce, Secretary Lutnick, appears to have used loopholes to allow some of these chip sales to occur even though President Trump has directed his administration and the Department of Commerce not to allow that to happen. Not only do I hope for Jensen Huang to come and testify, but I would like for Secretary Lutnick to testify ASAP in front of the Senate Banking Committee. We have a lot of bipartisan questions and concerns over what has happened over the last year that would allow these issues to occur.”

“We’ve had concerns about Nvidia and Jensen Huang and their relationship with China for a very long time. I’ve been calling out those concerns for the last couple of years. Nvidia has employed several lobbying firms and spent millions of dollars in Washington, D.C., to lobby against my legislation because I have been trying to crack down on these chip sales to China and how they compromise our national security. The right thing to do is to pass my bill that protects our high-end Blackwell chips that go to China. We are in an AI race with China, and we shouldn’t be helping them win the race on their end; we should be strengthening our hand.”

“We need to protect our chips; we need to protect American national security and prevent these companies that largely profit from selling chips to China against our own interest. Pass these export control laws that will prevent this from happening in the future.”

Medicare At 50 Act Would Give More Than 58 Million Americans Ages 50 To 64 Another Option For Affordable Healthcare

Today, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) joined nine of her Senate colleagues to introduce the Medicare at 50 Act, legislation to lower the Medicare eligibility age to 50 and allow Americans ages 50 to 64 to buy into Medicare. As Americans list the cost of healthcare as a top concern, the bill would expand access to affordable healthcare and give more than 58 million Americans more coverage options.

“Under President Trump, Americans nearing retirement are being forced to choose between paying for lifesaving care and simply being able to afford a life,” said Senator Gillibrand. “The Medicare at 50 Act would provide the security and support of Medicare years earlier to millions of aging Americans, lowering their healthcare costs and helping them save for retirement. As the top Democrat on the Senate Aging Committee, I am proud to support this important legislation, and I will continue fighting to expand access to quality and affordable care for older Americans.”

More than 60 million Americans are between the ages of 50 and 64, a population that faces significant challenges accessing affordable, comprehensive health insurance. While the Affordable Care Act (ACA) expanded access to coverage, millions of older Americans continue to face high premiums, out-of-pocket costs, and limited coverage options. Today, 11.5% of Americans between the ages of 55 and 64 remain uninsured.

President Trump and Republicans have made matters worse with sweeping healthcare cuts in their Big Ugly Bill and their refusal to extend the ACA’s enhanced premium tax credits, driving up costs for older Americans who purchase insurance through the ACA Marketplace.

The Medicare at 50 Act would help close this gap and give Americans between the ages of 50 and 64 the option to buy into Medicare before reaching the traditional eligibility age of 65. Individuals who choose to enroll would receive the same benefits and protections available under Medicare Parts A, B, and D, including the option to enroll in a Medicare Advantage plan. The legislation would also allow eligible individuals to receive the same premium tax credits and cost-sharing subsidies they would qualify for through the ACA Marketplace, helping make coverage more affordable.

Senator Gillibrand has long fought to lower healthcare costs for older Americans and to protect Medicare access. This year, she introduced the Medicare Cost Cap Act to cap out-of-pocket costs for seniors with Medicare, and she demanded an end to the Trump administration’s WISeR program that allows for AI-driven Medicare denials. Last year, she pressed Republicans to extend the enhanced ACA premium tax credits that helped millions of Americans afford coverage.

In addition to Senator Gillibrand, the bill is co-sponsored by Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Jeff Merkley (D-OR), Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), Jack Reed (D-RI), Tammy Duckworth (D-IL), Andy Kim (D-NJ), Cory Booker (D-NJ), Ed Markey (D-MA) and Tammy Baldwin (D-WI).

Full text of the bill is availablehere.

matches.text:
Broad coalition of national and local labor organizations representing hundreds of thousands of skilled workers supports legislation projected to create up to 105,600 trades and manufacturing jobs

WASHINGTON — The AFL-CIO has endorsed U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich’s (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), joining a broad coalition of national and local labor organizations representing the skilled workers who build, operate, and maintain America’s energy infrastructure.

The AFL-CIO’s endorsement adds to growing support from across organized labor, including the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW), International Association of Iron Workers, International Association of Sheet Metal, Air, Rail, and Transportation Workers (SMART), International Brotherhood of Boilermakers, International Brotherhood of Teamsters,International Union of Operating Engineers (IUOE), Laborers’ International Union of North America (LIUNA), North America’s Building Trades Unions (NABTU), United Association of Plumbers and Pipefitters, Pipeliners Local 798, and the New Mexico Building and Construction Trades Council. These organizations represent the electricians, ironworkers, sheet metal workers, boilermakers, Teamsters, operating engineers, laborers, plumbers, pipefitters, and other skilled tradespeople who will build the next generation of America's energy infrastructure.

The labor support comes as an independent analysis from Employ America estimates that BAAJA will create up to 105,600 trades and manufacturing jobs through 2040 by making it easier to build and maintain new energy infrastructure, including wind, solar, battery storage, and transmission projects.

BAAJA will lower energy costs for working families, provide greater certainty for energy infrastructure projects, and help ensure American workers are on the job building the infrastructure our country needs.

Independent analyses find that BAAJA will:

Create up to 105,600 trades and manufacturing jobs through 2040;

Require data centers to pay for increased grid and energy costs they create, estimated at $55 billion over the next 10 years;

Save $19 billion in residential electricity bills over the next 14 years;

Nearly double the amount of solar and wind that can connect to the grid; and

Avoid 1.5 gigatons of CO2 emissions, the equivalent of taking 39 coal plants offline for a decade.

BAAJA will lower energy costs for working families, provide greater certainty for energy infrastructure projects, and help ensure American workers are on the job building the infrastructure our country needs.

A fact sheet on BAAJA is here.

The full text of the bill is here.

Washington, D.C. — U.S. Senator Patty Murray (D-WA), Vice Chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, joined Senator Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) and colleagues in pressing Senate and House leadership to exclude provisions in the FY2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) that would require the President to expand and enhance defense cooperation and intelligence sharing with the Government of Israel. These provisions would undermine the United States’ ability to act independently and in line with U.S. national security interests at a time when the Government of Israel’s actions are increasingly not aligned with those interests.

The Senators begin, “As you prepare to conference the Fiscal Year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), we respectfully urge you to exclude three provisions from the final bill that would further entrench concerning aspects of the U.S.-Israel defense and intelligence relationship at a time when the Israeli government’s actions are increasingly undermining U.S. interests and values. These provisions would constrain the Administration’s ability to independently determine how best to protect U.S. national security and would lock in long-term commitments despite our serious concerns with the Israeli government’s actions in Gaza, the West Bank, and other parts of the region.”

On the threats to U.S. national security, the lawmakers note, “The agreements and projects these provisions envision threaten U.S. national security interests by handing Israel leverage over American weapons systems and military technology. This is not hypothetical. The Netanyahu government has already leveraged its existing coproduction agreement with the United States on missile defense to block American Iron Dome batteries from reaching Ukraine, in direct opposition to U.S. national security interests. Should these provisions be enacted, it would further increase Israel’s leverage over the United States through some of the most sensitive technologies in warfare. That is not in the U.S. interest. If enacted, these agreements would create long-term dependencies by embedding Israeli technology into the U.S. defense industrial base that could make future policy changes costly or difficult to implement. President Trump, at his own discretion, could choose to enter new agreements with Israel under existing law. The executive branch does not need a congressional mandate to more deeply entrench U.S.-Israel defense cooperation.”

“Moreover, we do not share, let alone co-produce, many of these sensitive technologies even with our closest partners, including NATO or other treaty allies. To do so in this instance would be unwise, especially as the Government of Israel continues to pursue policies in Gaza, the West Bank and other parts of the region that are inconsistent with U.S. interests and values,” the lawmakers write.

“Prime Minister Netanyahu has openly stated that such an initiative was his idea. In a letter to Representative Stutzman, who led a resolution calling for an effort similar to these provisions, Prime Minister Netanyahu states, ‘I was glad to receive your proposed Congressional resolution endorsing my plan to shift the framework of the US-Israel defense cooperation from aid to partnership.’ The intention behind this is clear: to move U.S. security assistance governed through more traditional pathways, like Foreign Military Financing and arm sales, to more opaque, less discernible avenues through defense acquisitions and programs of record that reduce transparency, as well as increase Israel’s leverage over the United States and our dependency on Israeli technology. This is particularly problematic after Prime Minister Netanyahu boasted that he has been trying to start a war with Iran for 40 years. That war has proven to be a strategic disaster for the United States and against U.S. interests,” the Senators continue.

“For all these reasons, we should not legally mandate an expansion in defense co-production or a requirement to increase intelligence sharing with the Government of Israel. We therefore urge you to exclude Section 1217, Section 219, and Section 618 from the NDAA final conference report,” they conclude.

In addition to Senators Murray and Van Hollen the letter was cosigned by Senators Ron Wyden (D-OR), Bernie Sanders (I-VT), Jeff Merkley (D-OR), Brian Schatz (D-HI), Elizabeth Warren, (D-MA), Ed Markey (D-MA), Tammy Duckworth (D-IL), Tina Smith (D-MN), Peter Welch (D-VT), and Andy Kim (D-NJ). The letter was sent to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, House Speaker Mike Johnson, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Senate Armed Services Committee (SASC) Chair Roger Wicker, SASC Ranking Member Jack Reed, House Armed Services Committee Chair (HASC) Mike Rogers, and HASC Ranking Member Adam Smith.

The full text of the letter is available HERE and below.

Dear Majority Leader Thune, Minority Leader Schumer, Speaker Johnson, Minority Leader Jeffries, Chairman Wicker, Ranking Member Reed, Chairman Rogers, and Ranking Member Smith:

As you prepare to conference the Fiscal Year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), we respectfully urge you to exclude three provisions from the final bill that would further entrench concerning aspects of the U.S.-Israel defense and intelligence relationship at a time when the Israeli government’s actions are increasingly undermining U.S. interests and values. These provisions would constrain the Administration’s ability to independently determine how best to protect U.S. national security and would lock in long-term commitments despite our serious concerns with the Israeli government’s actions in Gaza, the West Bank, and other parts of the region.

Both Section 1217 from the Senate Armed Services Committee-reported bill and Section 219 of the House-passed bill mandate the creation of a “United States-Israel Defense Technology Cooperation Initiative” to expand and accelerate the U.S.-Israel defense relationship, including technology sharing, co-production of weapons systems, and bilateral research and development across multiple domains of warfare such as biotechnology, quantum, autonomous systems, artificial intelligence, cyberwarfare, and others.

The agreements and projects these provisions envision threaten U.S. national security interests by handing Israel leverage over American weapons systems and military technology. This is not hypothetical. The Netanyahu government has already leveraged its existing coproduction agreement with the United States on missile defense to block American Iron Dome batteries from reaching Ukraine, in direct opposition to U.S. national security interests. Should these provisions be enacted, it would further increase Israel’s leverage over the United States through some of the most sensitive technologies in warfare. That is not in the U.S. interest.

If enacted, these agreements would create long-term dependencies by embedding Israeli technology into the U.S. defense industrial base that could make future policy changes costly or difficult to implement. President Trump, at his own discretion, could choose to enter new agreements with Israel under existing law. The executive branch does not need a congressional mandate to more deeply entrench U.S.-Israel defense cooperation.

Moreover, we do not share, let alone co-produce, many of these sensitive technologies even with our closest partners, including NATO or other treaty allies. To do so in this instance would be unwise, especially as the Government of Israel continues to pursue policies in Gaza, the West Bank and other parts of the region that are inconsistent with U.S. interests and values.

Prime Minister Netanyahu has openly stated that such an initiative was his idea. In a letter to Representative Stutzman, who led a resolution calling for an effort similar to these provisions, Prime Minister Netanyahu states, “I was glad to receive your proposed Congressional resolution endorsing my plan to shift the framework of the US-Israel defense cooperation from aid to partnership.” The intention behind this is clear: to move U.S. security assistance governed through more traditional pathways, like Foreign Military Financing and arm sales, to more opaque, less discernible avenues through defense acquisitions and programs of record that reduce transparency, as well as increase Israel’s leverage over the United States and our dependency on Israeli technology. This is particularly problematic after Prime Minister Netanyahu boasted that he has been trying to start a war with Iran for 40 years. That war has proven to be a strategic disaster for the United States and against U.S. interests.

In addition to the provisions discussed above in the Senate and House NDAAs, the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence (SSCI) FY27 Intelligence Authorization Act, which is typically incorporated in the final NDAA, includes a provision (Sec. 618) that mandates the executive branch “expand and enhance intelligence sharing with the Government of Israel,” and also states that intelligence sharing with Israel “shall not be suspended, reduced, or otherwise materially limited.” The provision would tie the President’s hands from limiting intelligence sharing with Israel, even when doing so may be necessary to protect U.S. national security. That would be irresponsible and especially troubling given public reports that the Defense Intelligence Agency recently raised the counterintelligence threat from Israel to its highest level.

For all these reasons, we should not legally mandate an expansion in defense co-production or a requirement to increase intelligence sharing with the Government of Israel. We therefore urge you to exclude Section 1217, Section 219, and Section 618 from the NDAA final conference report.

###

WASHINGTON, DC – Today, after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of NVIDIA, U.S. Senator Jack Reed (D-RI), the Ranking Member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, issued the following statement:

“Jensen Huang’s resignation does not excuse his recklessness or dispel the alarming questions surrounding NVIDIA and the Trump Administration’s failure to protect American national security from Chinese espionage.

“American semiconductor technology is essential to our military capabilities and our technological advantage over China. Yet the Trump Administration reversed course on critical export restrictions, allowing NVIDIA to sell advanced AI chips to China despite clear national security risks. I am aware of reports that these chips were diverted through intermediaries with ties to Chinese intelligence. This crisis raises alarming questions about the security of our technology and the integrity of our military supply chains under the Trump Administration.

“Indeed, the Commander of U.S. Pacific Command testified to Congress this year that the transfer of advanced semiconductors to China would ‘undoubtedly’ come at the expense of American servicemembers in the event of a conflict.

“Even more disturbing are reports that President Trump was briefed on intelligence linking a suspected Chinese operative to Huang and chose not to act. BURLINGTON, Vt., Nov. 12 – Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) has launched his 17th annual State of the Union Essay Contest for Vermont students.

Each year, the president of the United States delivers an address to a joint session of Congress, which outlines priorities for the coming year. Sanders knows that great ideas can come from everyone — not just those in power — which is why he created the State of the Union Essay Contest to encourage young people to engage in the political process. The contest is an opportunity for Vermont high school students to describe a major issue facing our country and propose what they would do to solve it.

“The purpose of this contest is to get young people to start thinking about the many important issues that we deal with every day,” said Sanders. “As proven by the recent midterm elections, all people have the right to express their views and help shape the direction in which our country goes — and that includes young people. I want to see our students be actively engaged, no matter where they stand on the issues.”

The 250-to-500-word essays can be on any issue of national importance. A volunteer panel of Vermont educators will judge the essays on the students’ ability to articulate an issue and propose a solution, without regard to the students’ political views. Following the contest, Sanders will invite the finalists to a roundtable discussion at the Vermont State House and will enter their essays into the Congressional Record — the official archive of the U.S. Congress.

More than 7,000 students from high schools across Vermont have written essays in the past 16 years about critically important issues, including climate change, racial justice, corporate power, immigration reform, artificial intelligence, political polarization and much, much more. Last year, Saralynn Anderson from Essex High School was selected as the winner from 417 submissions for her essay on mental health care for students.

The deadline for student essay submission is January 11, 2027. More information can be found on Sanders’ Senate website HERE or by calling (800) 339-9834.

WASHINGTON — U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) today delivered the following remarks on the Senate floor:

Thune’s remarks below (as delivered):

“Mr. President, in January of 2026, part of a key sewer line serving customers in the Washington, D.C., area collapsed.

“The resulting sewage spill was, the Washington Post reported, and I quote, ‘one of the largest spills of untreated wastewater in U.S. history. Enough raw sewage to fill 364 Olympic-size swimming pools flushed into the Potomac River north of the nation’s capital, exacting an ecological toll that scientists are still trying to calculate.’

“Why do I bring this up, Mr. President?

“Well, I’ll tell you.

“Because D.C. Water had first identified weaknesses in the pipe and proposed repairs a full seven years earlier – seven years earlier – but had been prevented from starting them by a federal permitting process that dragged on. And on. And on. Until the pipe suffered a catastrophic failure.

“It’s an excellent illustration of the need for permitting reform in this country.

“Too often, everything from critical repairs to important new energy projects get bogged down in federal bureaucracy, and are delayed for not months, but years at a time.

“And the Washington, D.C., sewage spill is an outstanding example of the potential consequences.

“Now, Mr. President, it’s important to ensure that serious environmental concerns are addressed before projects are undertaken.

“And it is essential to ensure that the concerns of local stakeholders – in particular local landowners – are listened to and that they have a voice in the approval process.

“But the federal permitting process has gone way beyond that to include years of senseless delays, often caused by endless litigation from environmental groups or from agencies who are set on studying a project literally to death.

“We’ve seen those delays happen to projects for everything from drinking water and irrigation to building affordable energy sources and better roads and bridges.

“And like in the case of the D.C. sewage spill, these delays can even apply to projects where we’re simply replacing something that’s been there for many years.

“These delays all add costs, and those costs are ultimately paid by families through things like higher energy costs, higher gas and diesel prices, and higher taxes.

“The legislation that we are considering today would address that.

“The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would streamline and reform the permitting process to ensure that projects are approved or rejected in a timely fashion.

“This is particularly good news on the energy front.

“Needless to say, Americans have been dealing with an elevated cost-of-living since the early days of the Biden administration.

“And when it comes to affordability, energy prices affect pretty much everything. We all know that.

“High energy costs don’t just mean higher gas and electric bills, they mean higher costs for almost everything.

“And one of the best ways to keep prices of all kinds down is to expand domestic energy production – everything from oil and gas to solar and wind to hydropower.

“Too often, however, as I said, new energy projects get bogged down in federal government bureaucracy and end up in limbo for years.

“Streamlining bureaucracy, by contrast, like the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will do, will speed up key projects and bring more jobs and more affordable prices along with it.

“Mr. President, we’ve talked about what this bill would do for energy projects.

“But there’s another kind of project on a lot of Americans’ minds right now – and that is data center construction.

“Communities in my state of South Dakota and around our country are concerned about the movement of data centers into their communities – in particular about what their construction can mean for energy prices.

“And I am pleased to report that the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would enact new protections for local communities.

“For starters, it would require that data centers shoulder the energy costs associated with their operation and construction – whether that’s day-to-day running costs or the cost of additional infrastructure.

“But Mr. President, the legislation doesn’t stop there.

“It would also provide technical assistance to communities to help them understand and explore the impact a proposed data center would have on their locality – everything from the economic impact to the energy costs and infrastructure requirements that would be associated with the project.

“Mr. President, there are a number of other good elements in this bill.

“I’m always particularly invested in what legislation can do to help farmers and ranchers – which is the livelihood of our economy in South Dakota.

“And I’m very pleased that this bill will extend Clean Water Act permits for farmers from five to 10 years, significantly reducing the frequency with which farmers have to engage with government bureaucracy through that process.

“This legislation will also provide for faster grazing-related reviews, which will make a real difference to ranchers.

“Mr. President, if there’s one thing Americans across our country said in the election last week, it’s that they are hurting economically.

“This bill is one important way that we can help.

“Reforming the permitting process will help advance the kind of projects that will create new jobs, grow our economy, and increase wages.

“And more American energy development means a more reliable and affordable energy supply for American families.

“I want to thank Chairmen … Shelley Moore Capito and Mike Lee for their tremendous work on this legislation.

“This is a bipartisan bill, and President Trump strongly endorsed this legislation on Truth Social earlier this week.

“Mr. President, I look forward to swift Senate passage.

“And I hope the House will follow suit and get this legislation to the president’s desk in the very near future.”

Above: Gottheimer Announces Federal Actions to Expand VA Disability Benefits.

BOGOTA, N.J. — Today, Friday, November 13, 2026, Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5) hosted a roundtable with North Jersey veterans and representatives from veteran service organizations at the Bogota VFW Post 5561 in honor of Veterans Day. Gottheimer also introduced three new pieces of bipartisan legislation to expand disability benefits for veterans with his colleague Congressman Mike Lawler (NY-17).

“Nothing is more important in this job than my responsibility to always have the backs of those who have stepped forward to protect us — to bravely get our backs. That’s why I’m proud to have worked across the aisle to improve veterans’ benefits and care, and to continue that work to find common ground to ensure you receive the benefits you deserve,” said Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5).

Watch Gottheimer’s full remarks here.

New Jersey is home to nearly 300,000 veterans, including about 38,400 across Bergen, Passaic, and Sussex counties: 22,085 in Bergen, 10,616 in Passaic, and 5,683 in Sussex. More than 65,000 New Jersey veterans receive VA disability compensation. More than 65,000 New Jersey residents receive VA disability compensation, and nearly 74,000 turned to the VA for care in 2023.

Following the roundtable, Gottheimer announced new bipartisan federal legislation to make it easier for veterans to qualify for VA disability benefits:

The SARC Act (Sarcoidosis After Service Recognition and Coverage Act) will allow veterans who develop sarcoidosis more than a year after leaving the military to qualify for VA disability benefits. Under current VA rules, sarcoidosis is presumed to be service-connected only if it becomes at least 10 percent disabling within one year of separation or if the veteran qualifies under the PACT Act. The SARC Act would remove the one-year cutoff so eligible veterans whose sarcoidosis becomes at least 10 percent disabling at any point after service could qualify for disability benefits..

The LINK Act (Linking Identified Neurological Conditions to Known PTSD Act) will allow eligible veterans with service-connected PTSD who later develop dementia or Parkinson’s disease to qualify for VA disability benefits by presuming the condition is linked to their PTSD.

The Protecting Vets From Chronic Illness Act will require the VA to review its list of 41 chronic diseases presumed to be connected to military service, which hasn’t been updated since 1988. The bill would require the VA to recommend updates to its chronic disease list, including diseases to add and deadlines to extend for conditions that become disabling after veterans leave the military.

“We are immensely grateful to Representative Josh Gottheimer for introducing this bill on behalf of the as many as 32,000 veterans who have been diagnosed with sarcoidosis or are still navigating their path to their sarcoidosis diagnosis. The Foundation for Sarcoidosis Research (FSR) enthusiastically endorses this bill,” said FSR’s President and CEO, Mary McGowan. “For far too long veterans with sarcoidosis have struggled to be seen, understood, and treated – the introduction of this bill ushers in a new era that acknowledges these veterans’ sacrifice and provides them hope for the future.”

“Sarcoidosis is one of the most difficult diseases to diagnose. Patients often visit four or more physicians and wait three to five years from their first symptoms to a diagnosis, long after the VA’s one-year window has closed. Veterans who served our country should never lose the benefits they earned because their disease took longer to diagnose. The Life & Breath Foundation for Sarcoidosis proudly endorses Congressman Gottheimer’s bill and thanks him for standing up for veterans living with sarcoidosis,” said Saul Kuciauskas, Vice President of the Life & Breath Foundation.

Gottheimer also highlighted that the House overwhelmingly passed the bipartisan Major Richard Star Act this week. This bill will ensure that combat-injured veterans who were medically retired can receive both their retirement pay and their VA disability compensation, so that about 59,000 veterans can receive both payments in full.

Gottheimer’s new legislation builds on his record to improve care and expand access to benefits for veterans. Gottheimer’s first piece of legislation signed into law helps the VA hire post-9/11 veterans. Gottheimer also helped author and secure provisions in the PACT Act to address the mental health impacts of toxic exposure for veterans. In July, the House passed Gottheimer’s bipartisan bill to rename the Newton VA clinic in Sussex County to the Anthony “Tony” J. Gallopo VA Clinic, honoring the local veteran who fought to open it. He has also introduced bipartisan legislation, including the Data-Driven Suicide Prevention and Outreach Act to use AI to identify suicide risk factors among veterans, the Veterans STAND Act to expand access to assistive technology for veterans with spinal cord injuries, the VETS Act to make sure VA residential facilities and state veterans’ homes have resident advocates, among others.

Gottheimer was joined by Senator Gordon Johnson; Mayor Danielle Fede of Bogota; Councilwoman Diana Vergara of Bogota; Councilman John Mitchell of Bogota; Mayor John Glidden, Closter; Howard Burrell, Former Mayor of Vernon Township; Mary McGowan, Foundation for Sarcoidosis Research; Marsha Henderson, Sarcoidosis Veteran; Bradley Christensen, VSO from the NJ Department of Veterans Affairs; Shaun Hutchinson, Director of the Bergen County Department of Human Services Division of Veterans Services; Gloria Derteano, Deputy Director of Veterans Services at the Bergen County Administrative Departments; Alexander Hernandez, Bogota VFW Commander; Members of VFW Post 5561, Bogota; Members of Service Academy Board 2026; Jeremy Baratta, Benefits Protection Team Leader, DAV – Department of New Jersey; Joseph Fricker, First Vice Commander for American Legion of NJ.

Below: Gottheimer Announces Federal Actions to Expand VA Disability Benefits.

U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren has big plans when she and her fellow Democrats fully retake control of Capitol Hill next year.

Mostly, that means delivering on the populist economic agenda that Democrats pitched on the campaign trail and that voters chose when they propelled a historic blue wave on Election Day.

“Some people have said it is wasted energy to send strong policy changes to the Trump White House. I disagree,” Warren, D-Mass., said in a post-election video posted to YouTube.

“(President Donald Trump) says he welcomes the nickname ‘Mr. Veto.’ Well, let’s test him out on that. That means passing legislation to make life more affordable for Americans and to make our government less corrupt,” the Cambridge lawmaker said.

First, Warren says she wants to end the administration’s war in Iran, which she has denounced as illegal. Second, she wants to cut costs. She’s spent months castigating Trump for failing to do that during the first two years of his second term.

“Trump may still be president, but Democrats have the power on spending bills. And we should use it,” she said.

If all goes to plan, Warren could be uniquely positioned to put those plans into action next year. She’d also have plenty of company.

Three more Massachusetts women lawmakers — U.S. Reps. Katherine Clark, D-5th District, Lori Trahan, D-3rd District, and Ayanna Pressley, D-7th District — will see their clout and prestige increase in the new Congress.

“It reflects the great bench that Massachusetts has in the House of Representatives,” Tatishe Nteta, a pollster and political science professor at UMass Amherst, said. “The number of capable women who have distinguished records and will continue to build (them) up.”

They are part of a larger contingent of women lawmakers who will change the way the next Congress will operate.

At least 116 Democratic women will serve in Congress next year, up from the previous record of 111 set in 2025, according to the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University’s Eagleton Institute of Politics.

Of them, 100 Democratic women are expected to serve in the 435-member House, according to the center’s research. That’s up from the 2025 record of 95 Democratic women.

Democratic women were responsible for flipping at least 10 formerly Republican seats nationwide.

Meanwhile, the number of Republican women in Congress — both the U.S. House and Senate — as well as statewide elected executive offices will drop as a result of the midterms, the center’s research found.

“This was an impressive result for women in American politics, with women setting records and breaking significant barriers around the nation,” the center’s executive director, Debbie Walsh, said.

“But it also shows how closely women’s fortunes are bound to the fortunes of the Democratic Party. The Republican Party consistently runs fewer women candidates than Democrats. Women are nearing parity across levels of office among Democrats,” Walsh said. “Political parity in America can’t be achieved if only one party is intentionally recruiting and supporting women candidates.”

In Massachusetts, Warren is poised to take the reins of the Senate Banking Committee, which would give her a big say over financial policy. She’s currently its ranking Democrat.

She’s also believed to be eyeing the No. 3 leadership position in the Senate Democratic Conference.

That’s Steering and Policy chair, a post U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., is vacating after winning her home state’s gubernatorial race on Election Day.

The job would put Warren in charge of shaping the Democrats’ strategic and legislative priorities. On a more mechanical level, she’d also be in charge of doling out committee assignments.

One of the upper chamber’s most high-profile and vocal progressives, Warren also will serve as a “bridge” to the party’s moderates, Nteta said.

Warren donated hundreds of thousands of dollars to Democratic candidates during the midterms. And she crisscrossed the country to campaign for the party’s candidates.

That work matters. And her voice could speak loudly if, as expected, current Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., faces a bumpy road in his quest to become majority leader.

Warren “understands how to wield influence and clout,” Nteta said.

Clark, of Melrose, is set to become the first woman to serve as U.S. House majority leader when, as expected, current Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., steps into the role of House speaker.

In a Nov. 5 speech before the left-leaning Center for American Progress, Clark reflected on the election and the message voters had sent by electing Democrats.

“And in every corner of this country, people who feel angry, exhausted, cheated by their own government summoned what hope they had left and turned out to vote,” she said.

“And these are people who are voting to survive, whether it’s under the brutality and terror or the crushing weight of a broken and rigged economy, cuts to their health care, hikes in their bills, whether they live in the cities or the suburbs or across rural America, whether the media deem them red or blue voters, people fighting to survive the uncertainty of tomorrow and what that may bring to their families,” Clark said. “They found faith in this 250-year-old promise and experiment that they made it work and they forced it to work by voting for something better.”

She’s positioned to become the highest-ranking lawmaker from the Bay State since the late Democratic U.S. House Speaker Thomas P. “Tip” O’Neill of Cambridge.

In her years on Capitol Hill, Clark has been an “invisible powerhouse,” rising steadily through the ranks, Nteta said. He’ll be watching to see if the suburban Boston lawmaker emerges as a “household name” like Jeffries and other prominent Democrats next year.

Pressley, of Boston, will serve on an energized U.S. House Oversight Committee, which is expected to launch investigations of Trump and the Republican White House. A fellow Bostonian, U.S. Rep. Stephen Lynch, D-8th District, also serves on the panel.

“We fully intend … to use the full weight of our subpoena power. And let me just say this, Jacob,” Pressley told MS Now in a recent interview. “We might not win every fight, but we have a responsibility to the electorate, to the communities and the people that we serve, at least to go after it. We may not win every fight, but we have to fight. And that’s exactly what I expect this committee to do.”

The media-savvy Pressley is likely to become a public face as House Democrats launch their White House probes, Nteta said.

“She definitely knows how to speak in quotable phrases, which will be a benefit as the committee makes its case.” he said. “This is something the American people wanted — for Congress to root out possible corruption.”

Trahan, of Westford, has emerged as the Democrats’ point-person on artificial intelligence policy.

She’s reportedly revamping an AI safety bill she introduced in August with U.S. Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., to reduce efforts to preempt state laws that seek to regulate the industry, Politico reported.

In October, she also unveiled legislation that would hold AI developers liable for the rogue actions of their agents.

“When someone breaks the law and hurts you, you can take them to court. That shouldn’t change just because the wrongdoer is an AI agent,” Trahan said in a statement.

“Developers have already built systems capable of acting on their own and causing real damage. The CLAIM Act makes sure they answer for what their systems do.”

Two more Bay Staters, U.S. Reps. Richard Neal, D-1st District, and Jim McGovern, also are set to occupy important leadership perches.

McGovern, of Worcester, will take the gavel on the powerful House Rules Committee, the chamber’s “traffic cop” controlling the flow of legislation to the House floor.

Neal, of Springfield, will chair the budget-writing House Ways and Means Committee, putting him in a position to bring home federal money to Massachusetts.

“We’re in line for a lot of influence,” Nteta said.

WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Representatives and Virginia Democrats Eugene Vindman, Don Beyer, Jennifer McClellan, Suhas Subramanyam, and James Walkinshaw urged the Virginia State Corporation Commission (SCC) to reject the proposed acquisition of Dominion Energy by Florida-based NextEra.

In a letter submitted ahead of the SCC’s November 12 public comment deadline, the Members warned that the merger, as currently structured, threatens to increase electricity costs for Virginia families and small businesses for decades to come.

In the letter, Vindman and his colleagues wrote, “As proposed, we do not believe the merger is in the public interest. We believe the proposed transaction fails to satisfy the statutory requirements and because the joint petition lacks the structural protections necessary to prevent material harm, the Commission should deny the merger petition in its current form.”

The Members noted that while NextEra stands to benefit from the expanded investment opportunities created by the rapid expansion of data centers across Northern Virginia, residential customers and small businesses could be left footing the bill. The Members also cautioned that the merger could consolidate market power across the regional electricity grid, stifling competition and ultimately increasing electricity costs for Virginia consumers.

They argued that the proposed merger’s temporary incentives fail to offset the merger’s potential long-term costs. They also pointed to the absence of a moratorium on base rate increases, a cap on escalating rate adjustment clauses, and a binding requirement to pass operational savings on to customers.

The letter further raises concerns about NextEra’s corporate governance, including its history of political spending and interference, warning these practices could undermine regulatory oversight, create conflicts with Virginia’s Clean Economy Act requirements, and expose ratepayers to additional financial risks.

Emphasizing the SCC’s statutory responsibility to safeguard consumers and ensure the long-term reliability and affordability of utility service, the Members stated that approving the merger without adequate, enforceable protections would undermine that responsibility.

Full text of the letter can be found here.

–

Dear Commissioners:

We write to express our opposition to the current proposed merger whereby NextEra Energy, Inc. (“NextEra”) would acquire control of Dominion Energy, Inc. (“Dominion”). Under the Utility Transfers Act, the State Corporation Commission (“Commission”) may approve an acquisition of control if it finds that “adequate service to the public at just and reasonable rates will not be impaired or jeopardized. “Applicants must prove that the transaction causes no harm to captive customers. We believe the joint petition fails this statutory test.

We respectfully urge the Commission to reject the proposed NextEra Dominion merger in its current form, as recommended by Commission staff.

Rate Base Inflation and Misaligned Incentives

NextEra’s investor disclosures emphasize that Dominion’s territory offers immense multi-decade capital deployment opportunities, driven in large part by the extraordinary concentration of AI data centers in Northern Virginia and future planned load. Given that this projected future energy demand in the Commonwealth will be reliant on massive bulk transmission lines, which are still socialized across residential rate classes, much of that potential infrastructure will be paid for by ratepayers. And as NextEra’s growth strategy is dependent on maximizing capital deployment, its potential acquisition of Dominion risks creating a sustained, multi-decade upward pressure on ratepayers’ bills. Captive residential and small business ratepayers will be locked into paying decades of capital carrying charges, depreciation, and an authorized Return on Equity (ROE) on this expanded rate base.

We are concerned that much of NextEra’s growth strategy is heavily dependent on data center customers. This increases vulnerabilities that exist due to overbuilding and the ramifications that could materialize for ratepayers if projected revenue from large-load customers fails to cover the full cost of the transmission buildout and necessary upgrades to the grid that increased data center presence would require. While Dominion has started work to hedge against this stranded asset risk, there is insufficient protection in the case for bankruptcy, differing time horizons for service contracts and infrastructure lifespans, as well as the burden of broader grid upgrades required by data centers (rather than just point-to-point infrastructure) where every day ratepayers foot the bill.

There have also been documented concerns about how this merger affects market competition within the broader grid that Dominion is a part of, particularly with respect to transmission and energy generation and how the new merger could create “self-preferencing” or foreclose potential competition, and how those ripple effects could then increase wholesale prices and therefore raise costs for ratepayers in Virginia.

Despite those long-term upward financial pressures, the merger sweeteners of customer bill credits and added funds for the EnergyShare program are both inadequate and only short-term. Once the sweeteners expire, the Virginia-based Dominion workforce would be at risk of significant job cuts, Virginia households and small businesses would be locked into paying those multi-decade elevated rates, with the joint petition providing for no base rate increase moratorium, no cap on escalating rate adjustment clauses (riders), and no binding mechanism to track and pass fuel or operational synergies to captive customers. Additionally, the proposed bill credit for consumers barely covers the impact that increased fuel costs are having on electric bills. Dominion already petitioned the Commission for a $10 per month increase for fuel-related costs this year.

For these reasons, the Independent Market Monitor stated, the “scale, financial strength, and operational breadth all enhance market power and any economic gains are more likely to accrue to investors rather than customers.” Thus, we must look past the near-term sweeteners and toward robust binding, structural protections that prevent long-term negative impacts on Virginia ratepayers.

We believe the primary benefits of the merger should be designed to benefit our constituents, the ratepayers, and we believe the current merger design will raise rates. To that extent, we urge the Commission to, at a bare minimum, require long-term rate protections for consumers as recommended by Commission staff and require substantially larger bill credits as recommended by the Governor’s Office before any potential merger can proceed. As energy prices have considerably increased, and this merger threatens to exacerbate market conditions that could further increase prices for ratepayers it is paramount that the Commission use its authority to protect consumers who are already struggling to afford to keep the lights on.

Corporate Governance Deficits Threaten Rate Case Prudency

A utility’s corporate culture directly governs accounting integrity, affiliate transactions, and ratemaking prudency. The Commission must ensure that any acquiring entity submits to complete regulatory transparency and that captive ratepayers do not cross-subsidize non-utility operations, political spending, or parent-company agendas.

NextEra’s operational history and recent testimony demonstrates documented resistance to transparent regulatory scrutiny. NextEra recently entered into a $150 million settlement to resolve widespread political interference and dark money schemes, which included funding “ghost candidates” against state legislators and covert surveillance of an investigative journalist. This Commission’s Hearing Examiner properly recognized the relevance of these governance practices to regulatory integrity by ordering the production of the internal “Robo memo” into the evidentiary record. We share the position that this memo should be available for review to the Commission and intervenors.

At a time when regulatory scrutiny is at an all-time high, NextEra’s top leadership has aligned itself financially with federal agendas that raise rates and undermine Virginia’s statutory obligations. NextEra’s participation in high-level, opaque federal lobbying networks heightens the risk that Virginia ratepayers could be improperly forced to subsidize national political advocacy that runs counter to their own interests. In this case, aligning with a federal agenda that rolls back renewable energy incentives, curtails offshore wind development, and props up uneconomic generation. Engaging in that advocacy, including through means designed to obscure its involvement, puts NextEra in direct conflict with Virginia’s statutory mandates under the Virginia Clean Economy Act, and introduces an acute risk of asset stranding, resource inadequacy, and costly non-compliance penalties that will inevitably fall upon Virginia consumers.

It is unacceptably risky to transfer Virginia’s premier electric utility to an acquiring entity that displays such a pattern of routine spending, through opaque affiliate channels, to influence regulatory and political outcomes. Such practices, if expanded into Virginia, would directly threaten the Commission’s ability to police affiliate transactions, enforce cross-subsidization prohibitions, and verify the prudency of test-year operating expenses. Captive ratepayers bear the cost when compliance breaks down, transactions lack transparent auditing, or management priorities subordinate the public interest to unregulated political agendas.

Conclusion

The Commission’s statutory mission is to safeguard captive consumers and ensure the long-term reliability and affordability of utility service. As proposed, we do not believe the merger is in the public interest. We believe the proposed transaction fails to satisfy the statutory requirements and because the joint petition lacks the structural protections necessary to prevent material harm, the Commission should deny the merger petition in its current form.

We appreciate the Commission’s careful scrutiny of this proceeding and submit these comments on behalf of our constituents.

BACKGROUND

Vindman was the first member of Virginia’s congressional delegation to publicly oppose the proposed merger between NextEra and Dominion Energy, raising concerns about its potential impact on electricity rates and Virginia consumers.

Most recently, he delivered remarks at a Virginia State Corporation Commission (SCC) public hearing on the proposed merger, urging regulators to reject the proposal and put the interests of ratepayers ahead of corporate profits.

WASHINGTON, D.C. –Today, Congressman James R. Walkinshaw (VA-11), founder and co-chair of the Federal Workforce Caucus, introduced the Keep Federal Tech Talent Act, legislation that would let technologists and scientists in temporary federal roles, such as fellowships, move into permanent government careers. As agencies struggle to recruit and keep technical talent, the bill gives these public servants a clear pathway and real incentives to stay and keep serving their country.

Over the past two years, the Trump administration’s DOGE policies have forced out experienced federal employees and created a culture of fear inside federal agencies. This has exacerbated the long-term challenge that federal agencies have faced in recruiting and retaining the next generation of technical talent.

The administration launched the U.S. Tech Force, which places early-career technologists in federal agencies for two-year terms. The government needs this kind of talent, but two years is rarely long enough for a new hire to gain the experience needed to modernize complex federal systems or improve the services Americans depend on. And as the program stands, fellows who want to keep serving their country have no clear pathway or incentive to do so.

“Americans who want to serve their country deserve every opportunity to do so,” said Congressman Walkinshaw. “These professionals are writing code that delivers services to Americans, securing networks that keep our data safe, and supporting research that saves lives. If they want to keep serving, we should open the door to a long-term career in federal service.”

“For the federal government to deliver essential public services to the American people, we must hire and retain qualified personnel, including technology experts with specialized skill sets,” said NFFE National President Randy Erwin. “NFFE endorses the Keep Federal Tech Talent Act, which would help temporary federal workers in the tech sector build permanent careers in the civil service while expanding access to training and student loan assistance. These investments are critical to ensuring the government can recruit and retain the skilled personnel it needs. Thank you to Representative Walkinshaw for leading on this issue and his unwavering commitment to the federal workforce.”

“At a time when the federal workforce has just endured a massive loss of personnel and expertise in STEM and highly skilled roles, we look to Congress to find urgent solutions that strengthen the federal talent pipeline,” said Matt Biggs, International Federation of Professional and Technical Engineers (IFPTE) President. “That’s why IFPTE supports the Keep Federal Tech Talent Act, legislation that seeks to ensure that temporary federal employees are given opportunities to continue their careers in the civil service. We thank Rep. Walkinshaw for introducing this necessary bill that will bolster the federal government’s research and technology workforce and provide federal agencies with talented and dedicated innovators who serve the American public."

The Keep Federal Tech Talent Act would:

Create a pathway for federal agencies to hire limited term employees in specialized technology and science roles, including software engineering, cybersecurity, AI, data science, and scientific research, into permanent federal careers when they meet the qualifications for an open role.

Require agencies to help those who stay with student loan repayment or additional skills training.

Require agencies to report each year to the Office of Personnel Management on how many workers convert and which positions they fill.

As Walkinshaw fights to recruit technical talent into the federal workforce, he also continues to fight President Trump’s proposed federal pay freeze. “A pay freeze is a pay cut, and it’s one more barrier to attracting top talent,” said Walkinshaw. “We can’t ask these professionals to consider a career in government and then tell them their work isn’t worth fair pay.”

The full text of the Keep Federal Tech Talent Act is available here.

Consensus Grows for Permitting Reform

WHY LEADING EDITORIAL BOARDS AND POLICY VOICES ARE FINDING COMMON GROUND ON PERMITTING REFORM

When the New York Times and Wall Street Journal find common ground on energy legislation, Washington should pay attention.

NATIONAL EDITORIAL BOARDS FIND COMMON GROUND

The New York Times editorial board endorsed BAAJA, urging Democrats to advance their affordability agenda and warning that they “should not pass up a chance to start delivering immediately.” The Washington Post editorial board called the agreement “a major step toward historic permitting reform,” emphasizing the opportunity to build energy infrastructure faster.

The Wall Street Journal editorial board warned that permitting delays “may be America’s biggest economic Achilles’ heel,” while Bloomberg Opinion described Congress as being “on the cusp of a major bipartisan victory” and urged lawmakers to complete the agreement.

BEYOND THE EDITORIAL PAGES: POLICY LEADERS MAKE THE CASE

Policy commentators have also examined the deal through the lenses of affordability, investment, and governing consistency. Wall Street Journal chief economics commentator Greg Ip examined the economic costs of delayed approvals. Jane Flegal and Pavan Venkatakrishnan of the Searchlight Institute explicitly argued for passage to accelerate clean-energy construction. Republican strategists Chris Johnson and Liam Donovan argued that predictable permitting rules must apply consistently, regardless of which projects political leaders favor.

Climate and center-left voices have made different arguments for accepting the compromise. Writing in the New York Times, Ezra Klein assessed the tradeoffs of accepting an imperfect deal, while former Energy Secretary Jennifer Granholm called for passage. Climate investor Tom Steyer appealed to fellow progressives: “this is a bill we should support, and I’m asking you to join me.” Third Way’s Josh Freed criticized groups “more interested in obstructing imperfect solutions than working to improve them,” while Columbia University’s Jason Bordoff argued against rejecting the clean-energy and affordability opportunities solely because the agreement also benefits fossil fuels. Arnab Datta and Skanda Amarnath examined the relationship between affordable, reliable electricity and climate goals, while Colin Mortimer of the Progressive Policy Institute linked the agreement to a broader center-left permitting-reform agenda.

Former economic and national security officials offered a direct bipartisan endorsement. In an October 20 letter organized by the Institute for Progress, 19 former officials—including Treasury Secretaries Janet Yellen, Steven Mnuchin, Timothy Geithner, Henry Paulson, and Robert Rubin; former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo; and former National Security Advisor Jake Sullivan—urged Congress to pass BAAJA, citing the importance of infrastructure development to U.S. competitiveness in semiconductors, critical minerals, artificial intelligence, and energy.

Policy institutions have contributed both explicit endorsements and analysis of the agreement’s practical effects. Sarah Ladislaw of the New Energy Industrial Strategy Center argued that permitting reform is essential to delivering semiconductor, energy, and defense projects. Alex Mechanick and Baillee Brown of Inclusive Abundance examined how the bill could improve government capacity and remove infrastructure supply constraints. Thomas Hochman examined transmission reform, enforceable timelines, and durable approvals, while Rachel Levine of the Niskanen Center stressed the urgency of transmission development in western states. The Institute for Progress, led by co-CEO Alec Stapp, endorsed BAAJA as “the most ambitious bipartisan permitting bill in decades.” Timothy Male of the Environmental Policy Innovation Center discussed ways to accelerate infrastructure and environmental projects while maintaining safeguards.

Consensus this broad is rare. Congress needs to meet this moment.
