WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Senator Tammy Baldwin (D-WI) joined her colleagues in urging the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) to investigate giant corporations that are pocketing tariff refunds after raising prices on consumers. The senators pressed FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson to investigate whether these companies violated federal law by pocketing refunds instead of paying their customers back when President Trump’s tariffs were found to be illegal.

“Not a single one of these corporations provided any assurance that they will actually pass along refunds directly to their consumers,” wrote Baldwin and the Senators.

Giant retailers raised prices after President Trump imposed sweeping tariffs in April 2025. The letter cites estimates that consumers will pay 95 percent of Trump’s tariff costs, and that the tariffs will add an average of $2,500 to families’ expenses. After the Supreme Court struck down President Trump’s initial set of across-the-board tariffs in February 2026, the Trump administration began issuing refunds to corporations and importers. The government has paid out more than $100 billion in refunds — but the consumers that bore the brunt of cost increases have received no direct refunds.

The senators highlighted responses from Walmart, Nike, Apple, Target, and Energizer. Walmart touted efforts to lower prices but refused to specify how much of its refund would go toward those cuts. Nike offered no explanation for how it would use the money. Apple cited investments in the United States, while Target pointed to holiday promotions and domestic investments. Energizer acknowledged it had identified no specific use for the funds beyond supporting its business operations and investments. Not one of the five companies committed to directly paying back customers who covered the cost of the tariffs.

This “appears to be a massive theft from the middle class, facilitated by the Trump Administration and giant corporations that raised prices for middle class consumers in response to Trump tariffs and are now pocketing their refunds,” the Senators continued.

The FTC Act bans unfair or deceptive practices and unfair methods of competition. The senators urged the agency to investigate whether these companies violated those protections. They warned that keeping tariff refunds could give companies an unfair advantage over their competitors. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has failed to provide guidance to companies on returning refunds to consumers.

“The agency should act quickly to hold accountable any corporation that is ripping off consumers,” concluded Baldwin and the Senators.

The letter also warns that Trump’s later tariffs could extend the ripoff for families. Several of those tariffs face legal challenges. If courts strike them down, corporations could collect another round of refunds while consumers get nothing back. The Trump administration has not provided a plan to get those potential refunds back to families.

The letter comes as last month a brand-new report found that, from the ongoing trade war, war in Iran, and chaos, Congressional Republicans and President Trump are costing Wisconsin families more than $4,500 for everyday essentials like housing, gas, and groceries.

The letter was led by Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) and also signed by Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Elissa Slotkin (D-MI), Cory Booker (D-NJ), Ed Markey (D-MA), and Mark Kelly (D-AZ).

Full text of the letter is available here and below.

Dear Chair Ferguson:

We write to urge you to open an investigation to determine whether giant corporations that have received massive tariff refunds from the United States government have engaged in unfair or deceptive practices or unfair methods of competition, or have otherwise violated federal competition or consumer protection laws, by refusing to provide tariff refunds to their customers.

In April 2025, President Trump imposed sweeping, across-the-board tariffs on U.S. trading partners under the authority of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). These tariffs were passed on to consumers by giant retailers that increased prices, with many companies sharing messages with their customers explaining the need to raise prices in light of the new tariffs. Corporate executives admitted that they were passing on tariff costs to consumers — a Walmart executive acknowledged that “the magnitude of these increases is more than any retailer can absorb.” American consumers will end up paying for 95 percent of Trump’s tariffs, with the tariffs costing families an average of $2,500 in added expenses. But in February of this year, the Supreme Court declared that these tariffs from President Trump were illegal, and the government began the process of providing refunds — not to consumers, but to corporations and importers. In fact, the Administration’s refund program — set up through the Homeland Security Department’s Customs and Border Protection agency (CBP)—has paid out more than $100 billion in tariff refunds thus far, including to some of the world's biggest and most profitable corporations.

But the American consumer—who paid almost the full cost of the IEEPA tariffs—have received no direct refunds or restitution. The Trump Administration has repeatedly sidestepped Congressional inquiries about how American consumers will get their money back. The Administration has also failed to even provide any guidance to corporations regarding passing along tariff refunds to their consumers, allowing firms to simply pocket these large sums. Indeed, almost none of the corporations that have received tariff refunds have indicated that they have any coherent plan to return these refunds quickly and directly to consumers. Indeed, others have explicitly referred to these refunds as a boon to their bottom line–the CEO of multi-billion dollar furniture company Wayfair called the tariff refunds “sort of a one-time working capital benefit companies will get.” The CEO of Lowe’s told the press that the company didn’t plan to invest tariff refunds in lower consumer prices, instead preferring to boost shareholder earnings. Apparel company Levi Strauss said they would use most of their multi-million dollar tariff refund on holiday season marketing. Eyewear company Warby Parker described the company’s forays into artificial intelligence as “fully funded by the tariff benefits.”

Senator Warren wrote to six large, profitable corporations who had received multi-million dollar (or even billion-dollar) refunds and who had also increased their consumer prices after the imposition of tariffs. Not a single one of these corporations provided any assurance that they will actually pass along refunds directly to their consumers. Some companies provided evidence of their investment in their company’s U.S.-based development, and some provided vague assurances of lower prices in the future, but none indicated any plans to provide direct restitution to consumers who paid inflated prices due to IEEPA tariffs.

Walmart said they are “already putting [tariff refunds] to work for customers,” by “investing tariff refunds back into price leadership.” They did not quantify their pricing efforts or share figures indicating how much of their refund has been dedicated to lowering prices. Nike did not substantively respond to questions about how their tariff refund would be deployed. Apple pointed to their ambitious investment plans in the U.S. and indicated that tariff refund cash would be invested in those ventures, though they didn’t provide specific projects or numbers. Target pointed to a lack of price increases and upcoming holiday promotional prices rather than any plan to refund consumers, as well as planned investments in the U.S. Energizer admitted that “Beyond our disclosed expectation that the remaining refund balance will contribute to cash generation needed for the operation of and investment in our business, we have not identified any specific allocation” for tariff refunds.

These answers - or the silences in lieu of answers - are alarming. They indicate what appears to be a massive theft from the middle class, facilitated by the Trump Administration and giant corporations that raised prices for middle class consumers in response to Trump tariffs and now are now pocketing their refunds.

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has “a broad mandate to protect consumers from fraud and deception in the marketplace.” The Federal Trade Commission Act (FTC Act) outlaws “[u]nfair methods of competition in or affecting commerce, and unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce,” and the FTC is responsible for enforcing this statute on behalf of Americans. The FTC has found that conduct that is “exploitative,… abusive, deceptive, [or] predatory” may be investigated as an unfair method of competition. By increasing consumer prices, ostensibly due to tariff costs, and then refusing to provide refunds to consumers when they are later reimbursed for those tariff costs, corporations may be in violation of the FTC Act. This practice allows companies to increase prices, using tariffs as an excuse, with no accountability to consumers when those tariffs are struck down and refunded, and nothing consumers can do to right this wrong. Keeping the windfall from the tariff refunds could also give companies an unfair advantage over their competitors.

It is important that the FTC establish a precedent here that will prevent giant corporations from trying to rip off consumers on tariff-related matters. On the same day the Supreme Court struck down his IEEPA tariffs, President Trump imposed a blanket 10 percent tariff on nearly all imports under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974. In May, the Court of International Trade ruled that those tariffs were illegal, and the case currently sits pending before an appeals court. On July 20, 2026, President Trump invoked Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930—or the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, most commonly known for its role in exacerbating the Great Depression—to impose 50 percent tariffs on a broad range of Canadian imports. Experts have called the President’s rationale for the tariffs “spurious,” “untested,” and “misapplied.” Just days later, on July 24, 2026, President Trump imposed yet another set of broad new tariffs, this time claiming authority under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. These tariffs have already drawn legal challenges from multiple groups of small businesses. And on August 23, the President announced a new set of tariffs on billions of dollars of imports from Canada, employing once again the Section 338 tariff authority that legal experts have called “untested” and “vague.”

Like the illegal IEEPA tariffs before them, the costs of these new but similarly chaotic tariffs will be borne by American consumers and small businesses. Despite the legal doubt surrounding the fate of these new tariffs, the Administration has refused to provide a plan as to how it would get refunds back to the American people in the event they are struck down. This means that consumers could once again be left with nothing as giant corporations pocket tariff refunds.

Given the magnitude of the costs of President Trump’s tariff chaos to consumers, we urge you to take action. The FTC should investigate whether companies that increased their prices due to IEEPA tariffs and then received tariff refunds which were not refunded to consumers violated federal law, including engaging in an unfair method of competition or an unfair or deceptive practice. The agency should act quickly to hold accountable any corporation that is ripping off consumers.

Thank you for your attention to this important matter.

Sincerely,

###

Honoring Veterans Day

[WASHINGTON, D.C.] – U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), incoming Chairman of the Senate Veterans’ Affairs Committee, released the follow statement to commemorate Veterans Day:

“We should be forever grateful—and proudly express it—to the brave veterans who served and sacrificed to defend our nation. On Veterans Day, we say thank you and reflect on the promises made to these men and women. Today and every day, I will fight to make sure we keep these promises and provide veterans and their families the support, care, and benefits they earned and deserve.”

Blumenthal attended ceremonies honoring veterans and their sacrifice in service of our country across the state of Connecticut—including Derby, New Haven, Stamford, and Middletown.

“Derby marked Veterans Day on its historic Green—with enduring gratitude to all who’ve served. A beautiful sunfilled day,” wrote Blumenthal on Twitter/X.

“New Haven’s Veterans Day Ceremony featured music & memorials—tributes to all who have served & sacrificed. We’re the land of the free because we’re the home of the brave,” wrote Blumenthal on Twitter/X.

“Hauntingly beautiful & serene, the Middletown Veterans Cemetery was the site of CT’s statewide Veterans Day ceremony. Taps played, as shadows lengthened over the headstones,” wrote Blumenthal on Twitter/X.

Demanding Accountability from Trump Administration in Face of Baseless Intimidation Attempt

Blumenthal, incoming Chair of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, released the following statement in response to a letter he received from the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas:

“The Trump Administration is so afraid of transparency and oversight that they are weaponizing the Department of Justice to baselessly target Congress in direct violation of the Constitution. As incoming Chair of the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, I will not be intimidated, and I will work on behalf of the American people to vigorously pursue investigations into this Administration's persistent misuse of taxpayer dollars and any corporate entity that has enabled their boundless corruption.”

In response to this baseless threat from the Department of Justice, Blumenthal demanded the Trump-appointed U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas preserve all records and correspondence, including with the White House or senior Department of Justice officials, related to the Administration’s efforts to protect corporate donors and Administration officials from legitimate oversight.

“I am aware of your letter, posted to X today, which purports to initiate an investigation into me for conducting a congressional inquiry. This is just the latest in a series of unlawful actions on the part of the Trump Administration attempting to intimidate Members of Congress for engaging in constitutionally protected activity. Your implied threat of an investigation is baseless,” wrote Blumenthal.

Blumenthal continued, “The public deserves to know the terms under which dozens of American companies were persuaded to donate millions of dollars to the President’s vanity projects, and whether lawsuits were dismissed, contracts were awarded, or regulations went unenforced in exchange for that money. The public deserves transparency about whether the White House and the corporations it cajoled extracted favors at the expense of American taxpayers. Not only are these appropriate subjects for congressional oversight, but such inquiries are among the constitutional duties that Members of Congress must undertake to become informed about matters on which legislation may be necessary.”

“Since you appear to have evidence of the Trump Administration’s efforts to protect corporate donors and Administration officials from legitimate oversight, I accordingly direct you to preserve all records and correspondence, including all communications with the White House or senior officials at the Department of Justice, related to the decision to draft and post your letter,” Blumenthal concluded.

Blumenthal has led an inquiry into the waste, fraud, and abuse associated with the White House ballroom and other projects throughout the nation’s capital. Blumenthal recently wrote to Big Tech companies and others who may be seeking pay-to-play government favors from their donations to President Trump’s White House ballroom and other projects, reminding recipients of the Subcommittee’s expectation for their prompt cooperation.

The full text of the letter is available here.

Blumenthal further highlighted his letter on Twitter/X.

“This investigation into me for conducting a congressional inquiry is just the latest in a series of unlawful actions on the part of the Trump Admin attempting to intimidate Members of Congress for engaging in constitutionally protected activity. The implied threat of an investigation is baseless. As incoming Chair of the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, I will not be intimidated. The public deserves transparency about whether the White House & the corporations it cajoled extracted favors at the expense of American taxpayers. Not only are these appropriate subjects for congressional oversight, but such inquiries are among the constitutional duties that Members of Congress must undertake to become informed about matters on which legislation may be necessary,” wrote Blumenthal on Twitter/X.

Blumenthal also joined MS NOW and CNN to discuss his letter to the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas and to highlight the need for proper oversight into Trump’s vanity projects.

“Americans deserve the truth about potential misuse of taxpayer dollars & corporate corruption involved in Trump's vanity projects. Instead of targeting corruption, Trump's DOJ is trying to intimidate investigators attempting to carry out oversight—I joined MS NOW to discuss,” wrote Blumenthal on Twitter/X.

The full MS NOW interview can be found here. The full CNN interview can be found here.

Blumenthal further emphasized his efforts to carry out oversight over the Trump Administration’s brazen corruption on Twitter/X.

“I’m taking action to uncover Trump admin corruption. DOJ is threatening to investigate me because of it. I won’t be intimidated or stop working to uncover the pay-to-play schemes, dropped regulation, or misuse of taxpayer dollars,” wrote Blumenthal with an accompanying video on Twitter/X.

Slamming the Trump Administration for Withholding Funding for Trafficking Survivors

Blumenthal, a member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, released a damning new report revealing that the Trump Administration has failed to award approximately $133.5 million in anti-human trafficking grant funding – about 75 percent of what Congress has appropriated for the last two years – forcing programs that support trafficking victims to shut down or dramatically reduce their services.

This shocking withholding of funding follows the Administration allowing about $190 million in anti-human trafficking grants to lapse, including approximately $140 million that was previously dedicated to direct services for survivors of human trafficking and $16 million that was previously dedicated to supporting law enforcement’s ability to investigate and prosecute trafficking crimes.

“This report is sickening— and it should shock the conscience of every Administration official and lawmaker who claims to support trafficking survivors,” Blumenthal said. “From the botched release of the Epstein Files to withholding funding to support survivors and prosecute sex crimes, the Trump Administration has shown exactly how little it cares about victims of trafficking. Whether the Trump Administration has withheld these funds out of malice or pure incompetence is immaterial. What matters are the tens of thousands of victims and survivors who are suffering without it. I am demanding that this funding be released immediately and the Trump Administration provide me – and survivors – with a clear commitment that these services will not be allowed to lapse again.”

“Please consider what losing this program’s funding would mean for the people whose lives depend on it. I have worked hard to build this life, but I could not have done it alone. This program helped me become a mother who could bring her son home, a person with a career, and someone who could believe in herself again,” said an anonymous survivor who is quoted in the report. “Without it, I would not be where I am today. Losing it could put everything I have built at risk, including my life. I am only one of many survivors with something to lose—and there are others still waiting for the chance to heal.”

The Department of Justice (DOJ) Office for Victims of Crime (OVC) is the primary entity overseeing grant programs that provide funding to organizations fighting human trafficking and supporting survivors. Providers who receive funding through OVC grant programs serve more than 10,000 human trafficking survivors quarterly, including children. As a result of the Trump Administration’s mismanagement and withholding of grant funding, service providers have been forced to close or drastically downsize their programming, with dire consequences for survivors:

A wraparound program helping youth who have been trafficked for sex could not accommodate all of the children referred for services and was forced to put them on a waitlist. In disclosing that they do not have the resources to work with all the children who approach them for help, this provider said that it resulted in children “being further exploited.”

A transitional housing program that provided no-cost housing and services to support survivors in healing, securing permanent housing, and finding employment was shuttered because the provider could not pay the rent or the staff after funding lapsed. The program served over a dozen survivors annually with housing and full therapeutic support. It had a proven history of success—almost every survivor graduated from the program successfully, building a stable life and avoiding a return to trafficking.

A program providing no-cost counseling, behavioral healthcare services, and vocational training will close in January 2027 without federal funding. While the service provider has managed to fill the gaps following the lapse of federal grants, it will no longer be able to do so in less than two months. Unless funding is released, the program will close its doors to the 100 human trafficking survivors it serves each year and lay off its staff—including peer support personnel who themselves are survivors of trafficking.

A transitional housing program will likely face closure if funding is not released. It provides 24/7 support and no-cost housing to at least five human trafficking survivors annually. Most are survivors of sex trafficking, and many were sold for sex while still minors. Many survivors enter the program with substance use disorders, PTSD, and other severe mental illness, and therefore rely not only on the program’s housing but also on its addiction recovery and mental health support services. The program is incredibly successful—90 percent of the participants successfully graduate into permanent housing of their own.

Blumenthal wrote Brecht Donoghue, Director of the OVC Human Trafficking Division at DOJ, demanding that the Administration release the funding immediately and provide an explanation for its lapse.

“President Trump purports to care about survivors of human trafficking—he claims his Administration is committed “to end[ing] the evil of human trafficking” and that he is “working tirelessly” to “end the scourge of human trafficking once and for all.” It is shocking that an Administration that has claimed to prioritize stopping the “scourge of human trafficking” has instead caused a two-thirds reduction in the OVC funding available to the anti-trafficking field,” Blumenthal wrote.

“But perhaps this total disregard for human trafficking survivors should not come as a surprise from the Administration that not only fought the enactment of and then failed to fully comply with the Epstein Files Transparency Act but also repeatedly retraumatized survivors through its botched file release. Put simply, human trafficking survivors deserve so much better from their government.”

The text of Blumenthal’s letter to Donoghue is available here.

Blumenthal further highlighted his report and letter to Donoghue on Twitter/X.

What matters are the tens of thousands of victims & survivors who are suffering without it.I am demanding this funding be released immediately & the Trump admin provide me—& survivors—with a clear commitment that this funding will not be allowed to lapse again,” wrote Blumenthal on Twitter/X.

Blumenthal pressed Arthur Kleinschmidt, nominee to be Assistant Attorney General for the Office of Justice Programs, on the approximately $190 million in anti-human trafficking grant funding that has lapsed under the Trump Administration and the over $130 million that the Trump Administration has failed to award to replace it. If confirmed, Kleinschmidt would head the Department of Justice’s principal grantmaking office, the Office of Justice Programs, which oversees these funds.

During their exchange, Blumenthal secured a commitment from Kleinschmidt that, if confirmed, he will release all the currently withheld funds to combat the scourge of human trafficking.

“You must be aware that the Trump Administration has allowed about $190 million in anti-human trafficking grants to lapse, and it has withheld about 75% of money appropriated by the United States Congress for groups that aid victims of human trafficking. It is about $130 million that should be going to support human trafficking survivors and strengthen law enforcement's ability to fight trafficking crime,” said Blumenthal. “Will you commit, if confirmed, to release all of the anti-trafficking funds currently withheld by the Trump Administration?”

“I am going work diligently to get these resources from the Office of Justice Programs,” answered Kleinschmidt.

“Is that a yes, you will release the money?” pressed Blumenthal.

“I'm going to be committed to addressing and getting the funds to those Americans who need them the most, yes sir. I’m going to work and do and follow all the stipulations and guidelines to get our taxpayer dollars—be a good shepherd of the taxpayer dollars—to get those resources, human trafficking victims and other victims of crime, to ensure that Americans stay safe.” said Kleinschmidt.

“I'm going to take that as a yes, that you will release the money. I'm going to hold you to it. I think our United States Congress should hold you to it because human trafficking is a scourge, and the victims deserve all of the money and more that Congress has appropriated for this purpose,” said Blumenthal.

A video of Blumenthal’s round of questioning can be found here.

On the Senate Veterans’ Affairs Committee

Blumenthal released the following statement after House Republicans abused House procedure to pass the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act by voice vote on Veterans Day. This controversial veterans’ legislation would cut nearly $57 billion in veterans’ benefits for veterans with sleep apnea and tinnitus.

“House Republicans resorted to a blatant abuse of established procedure—bypassing a fair vote—to sneak the biggest cut to veterans’ benefits in American history. This disrespect and deduction to well-deserved disability compensation is totally unacceptable, most especially on Veterans Day. Such secretive and shameful tactics are condemnable. Make no mistake—their disgusting slash to veterans’ benefits will be defeated in the Senate.”

In July, House Republicans cancelled a planned vote on the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act, following a bipartisan House vote to replace the Republican benefit cuts with a proposal to utilize unobligated Department of Defense funds. Congressional Democrats and Veterans Service Organizations have publicly opposed the Republican funding proposal included in the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act.

Blumenthal along with U.S. Senator Patty Murray (D-WA), Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY), and House Veterans’ Affairs Committee Ranking Member Mark Takano (D-CA) led more than 200 Senate and House Democrats in filing an amicus brief to Minority Veterans of America v. Secretary of Veterans Affairs, a lawsuit challenging the Trump Administration’s abortion ban at the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA).

The lawsuit, pending before the US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, seeks to overturn VA’s ban on abortion care and counseling. In the brief, the lawmakers argue the Trump Administration’s 2025 policy banning abortion counseling and abortion care in almost all cases rests on a flawed legal premise.

“VA’s Final Rule rests on a faulty interpretation of federal law that has significant negative consequences for our nation’s veterans. The issues presented in this case potentially reach roughly 462,000 women veterans of reproductive age who are enrolled in VA health care, along with an estimated 112,000 women of reproductive age enrolled in the Civilian Health and Medical Program of the Department of Veterans Affairs (CHAMPVA),” the members wrote.

The members continued, “For them, the Final Rule means a VA physician is prohibited from discussing the full range of a patient’s options during a pregnancy, prohibited from providing the full range of health care available to pregnant women, and is prohibited from intervening when a pregnancy threatens the patient’s health or is the result of rape or incest.”

VA’s abortion ban, implemented by the Trump Administration in 2025, prohibits abortion counseling and care for veterans and CHAMPVA beneficiaries—even in cases of rape, incest, or if a veteran’s health is endangered. The lawmakers argue in the brief that VA’s erroneous interpretation of federal law means these women now cannot receive abortion care or counseling even in the most harrowing circumstances. They also argue the Veterans’ Health Care Eligibility Reform Act of 1996 allows VA to provide any medical services the Secretary “determines to be needed” and that the Veterans Health Care Act of 1992, which VA used to justify its abortion ban, does not restrict the Secretary’s authority to add abortion care to its medical benefits package.

In the Senate, the amicus brief was signed by all 47 Democratic U.S. Senators. In the House, the brief was signed by 165 Democratic U.S. Representatives.

In March, all present Democratic Senators voted in support of Senator Blumenthal’s Congressional Review Act (CRA) resolution to overturn the Trump Administration’s policy ending abortion counseling entirely and abortion care for veterans in cases of rape, incest, or health endangerment. A CRA resolution is an oversight tool Congress can use to overturn final rules issued by federal agencies with a simple majority vote. The vote failed 48-50 due to lack of adequate Republican support, leaving VA’s abortion ban in place. While the CRA resolution did not receive a vote in the House, it garnered the support of 155 Democratic cosponsors.

In September 2022, VA began to offer abortion counseling to all pregnant veterans and CHAMPVA beneficiaries, and abortion care in cases of rape, incest, or life or health endangerment of the veteran or CHAMPVA beneficiary. This was in response to the Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization ruling, which created urgent risks to the lives and health of pregnant veterans and CHAMPVA beneficiaries in states that banned or otherwise severely restricted access to abortion. VA’s dangerous abortion ban means that veterans nationwide now face those same risks.

More than 462,000 veterans of reproductive age are enrolled in VA health care, and more than 112,000 women of reproductive age are enrolled in CHAMPVA. More than half of these women live in states that have enacted abortion bans or restrictions.

The amicus brief can be read in full here.

Senator Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.), a member of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, today sent a letter to Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Communications and Information Arielle Roth urging the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) to implement the Digital Equity Act grant programs.

Congress passed the Digital Equity Act as part of the bipartisan Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act to complement historic federal investments in broadband infrastructure by addressing barriers to broadband adoption and use. However, in May 2025, President Trump announced his intention to terminate the Digital Equity Act grant programs, including the Competitive Grant Program.

“I write regarding the National Telecommunications and Information Administration’s (NTIA) implementation of the Digital Equity Act grant programs. I appreciate NTIA’s commitment to reinstating the Digital Equity Competitive Grant Program (“the Competitive Grant Program”) and its stated intention to issue a new Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) next month. As the agency moves forward with the Competitive Grant Program, I urge NTIA to preserve the substantial work applicants have already undertaken, minimize unnecessary delays and administrative burdens, and make congressionally appropriated funding available as quickly as possible,” said Senator Blunt Rochester.

“These programs are particularly important to Delaware, which is working to become the first state to achieve universal high-speed broadband access. As Delaware builds broadband infrastructure statewide, complementary investments in digital literacy training, device access, and technical assistance will help ensure every Delawarean can fully benefit from internet connectivity,” the Senator continued. “NTIA subsequently awarded Delaware approximately $4.8 million to implement initiatives supporting digital literacy, workforce development, broadband affordability, and device access. However, since the Trump administration’s termination of the program in May 2025, Delaware has been left without a clear path to accessing these funds or implementing its approved plan.”

Blunt Rochester concluded, “Congress established and funded the Digital Equity Act programs on a bipartisan basis because deploying broadband infrastructure alone does not guarantee that Americans can fully benefit from it. Promptly moving forward with the Competitive and Capacity Grant Programs would carry out Congress’s direction, provide certainty to applicants and states, and help ensure that federal investments in broadband infrastructure translate into meaningful connectivity for communities across the country.”

The full text of the letter can be found HERE, and below.

Dear Assistant Secretary Roth:

I write regarding the National Telecommunications and Information Administration’s (NTIA) implementation of the Digital Equity Act grant programs. I appreciate NTIA’s commitment to reinstating the Digital Equity Competitive Grant Program (“the Competitive Grant Program”) and its stated intention to issue a new Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) next month.1 As the agency moves forward with the Competitive Grant Program, I urge NTIA to preserve the substantial work applicants have already undertaken, minimize unnecessary delays and administrative burdens, and make congressionally appropriated funding available as quickly as possible. I also urge NTIA to provide a clear path forward for the State Digital Equity Capacity Grant Program, including previously approved state plans and awarded funding.

These programs are particularly important to Delaware, which is working to become the first state to achieve universal high-speed broadband access. As Delaware builds broadband infrastructure statewide, complementary investments in digital literacy training, device access, and technical assistance will help ensure every Delawarean can fully benefit from internet connectivity. Furthermore, as artificial intelligence increasingly shapes how Americans work, learn, and access essential services, equipping Delawareans with digital skills is more important than ever.

Congress passed the Digital Equity Act as part of the bipartisan Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA) to complement historic federal investments in broadband infrastructure by addressing barriers to broadband adoption and use. Through the IIJA, Congress appropriated $1.25 billion for the Competitive Grant Program—$250 million for each fiscal year from 2022 through 2026—to support efforts that help Americans gain the skills, devices, and resources needed to benefit from broadband connectivity.2

Demand for these resources has been substantial. Following NTIA’s 2024 Notice of Funding Opportunity, more than 700 applicants requested over $6.5 billion in funding.3 Local governments, libraries, educational institutions, workforce organizations, nonprofits, and other eligible entities invested significant time and resources to identify community needs, develop programs, and build partnerships in anticipation of these awards.

On May 8, 2025, President Trump on Truth Social announced his intention to immediately terminate the Digital Equity Act grant programs, including the Competitive Grant Program, asserting that the program was “racist” and “illegal” because it included racial and ethnic minorities as part of its targeted covered populations.4,5 On July 15, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia held in National Digital Inclusion Alliance v. Trump that the provision identifying members of racial or ethnic minority groups as a covered population was unconstitutional, but also held that the provision was severable from the remainder of the statute.6 The decision therefore provides a path for the Competitive Grant Program to move forward consistent with the remaining statutory requirements.

On October 23, 2026, NTIA filed an update in National Digital Inclusion Alliance v. Trump stating that NTIA is on track to publish the NOFO and application for the Competitive Grant Program in December 2026.7 As NTIA develops this NOFO, I urge the agency to minimize disruption to applicants by preserving the substantial work already undertaken to develop proposals and establish community partnerships. NTIA should allow applicants to update existing proposals to meet any revised program requirements, rather than requiring them to restart the application process, and provide clear guidance to facilitate a timely transition.

I also urge NTIA to provide a clear path forward for the State Digital Equity Capacity Grant Program. Delaware was the second state in the country to receive federal approval of its State Digital Equity Plan in 2024 and was expected to become the first state to achieve 100% access to high-speed broadband.8 NTIA subsequently awarded Delaware approximately $4.8 million to implement initiatives supporting digital literacy, workforce development, broadband affordability, and device access.9 However, since the Trump administration’s termination of the program in May 2025, Delaware has been left without a clear path to accessing these funds or implementing its approved plan. Because the Capacity Grant Program was not at issue in National Digital Inclusion Alliance v. Trump, its status remains unresolved. I urge NTIA to clarify how it intends to move forward with the program and make congressionally appropriated Capacity Grant funding available as quickly as possible.

Congress established and funded the Digital Equity Act programs on a bipartisan basis because deploying broadband infrastructure alone does not guarantee that Americans can fully benefit from it. Promptly moving forward with the Competitive and Capacity Grant Programs would carry out Congress’s direction, provide certainty to applicants and states, and help ensure that federal investments in broadband infrastructure translate into meaningful connectivity for communities across the country.

Thank you for your attention to this important matter, and I look forward to working with you to ensure these programs are implemented promptly, effectively, and in a manner that is consistent with the law.

###

U.S. Senator Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.), a member of the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, and John Curtis (R-Utah), a member of the Committee on Foreign Relations, sent a letter to Department of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick urging the Trump administration to address loopholes in export controls for advanced artificial intelligence (AI) semiconductors, otherwise known as “chips.” The letter outlines how closing these gaps will maintain our competitive edge over Chinese technologies while buying time to focus on promoting responsible domestic AI policy. This letter follows reports that former NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang was involved in a honeypot scheme with a Chinese spy.

“We are deeply concerned by reports that the recently departed CEO of the nation’s top semiconductor company, NVIDIA, was caught in a honeypot scheme with a Chinese spy and executive at Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm known to help Chinese companies circumvent export controls,” said the Senators. “Our concerns about insufficient export controls on these technologies are magnified by numerous rogue artificial intelligence incidents, including autonomous hacking incidents, unauthorized agent access to the internet, and attacks on real-world targets. Whistleblowers from the nation’s leading AI companies have warned that technology is accelerating without sufficient guardrails, further compounding our concerns.”

“Collectively, these incidents show the urgent need for the Trump administration to act and protect the safety and security of Americans. Responsible U.S. domestic AI policy must promote our competitive edge in artificial intelligence through reasonable innovation and regulation. It should not enable our strategic adversaries to embrace risky behaviors with these technologies or to acquire them through nefarious means,” the Senators continued. “China’s frontier artificial intelligence capabilities are rapidly approaching those of the United States, with some experts estimating China’s frontier to be just six to nine months behind the United States…To maintain its competitive edge while promoting responsible domestic AI policy, the United States must ensure Chinese AI labs cannot easily procure the compute required to develop, test, and train advanced artificial intelligence models.”

“We urge you to condition licenses for the export of advanced AI chips on an agreement that recipients will not provide Chinese companies with remote access unless granted a separate and additional license to do so. These policies should not be geographically limited in scope. If they are, China will simply rent access to chips elsewhere, creating a whack-a-mole scenario.” The Senators concluded, “During your confirmation hearing, you called for stronger export controls, saying, ‘If they are going to compete with us, let them compete, but stop using our tools to compete with us.’ Today, the stakes are clear, and our adversaries are not playing by the rules. We must close these loopholes if the United States is to maintain its competitive edge in artificial intelligence.”

The full response letter can be found HERE and below.

Secretary Lutnick:

We write to urge you to take immediate steps to close loopholes in the export regime for advanced AI chips.

We are deeply concerned by reports that the recently departed CEO of the nation’s top semiconductor company, NVIDIA, was caught in a honeypot scheme with a Chinese spy and executive at Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm known to help Chinese companies circumvent export controls.1 Despite the intelligence community raising concerns that Mr. Huang had been compromised, the Department has taken no action to tighten export controls on Megaspeed and other high-risk companies in Southeast Asia2. These concerns are only exacerbated by reports that Under Secretary Kessler discussed ongoing investigations into Megaspeed with NVIDIA’s General Counsel.3 This scenario raises numerous alarms about how you and the Trump Administration are safeguarding highly sensitive technologies.

Our concerns about insufficient export controls on these technologies are magnified by numerous rogue artificial intelligence incidents, including autonomous hacking incidents, unauthorized agent access to the internet, and attacks on real-world targets. Whistleblowers from the nation’s leading AI companies have warned that technology is accelerating without sufficient guardrails, further compounding our concerns.

Collectively, these incidents show the urgent need for the Trump administration to act and protect the safety and security of Americans. Responsible U.S. domestic AI policy must promote our competitive edge in artificial intelligence through reasonable innovation and regulation. It should not enable our strategic adversaries to embrace risky behaviors with these technologies or to acquire them through nefarious means.

China’s frontier artificial intelligence capabilities are rapidly approaching those of the United States, with some experts estimating China’s frontier to be just six to nine months behind the United States.4 Gaining a competitive advantage is a significant motivating factor behind its development of artificial intelligence. China also seeks to leverage the technology to enhance its national security, including by bolstering military capabilities, surveilling adversaries, and tightening its control over information. This is well demonstrated by Anthropic’s recent report Detecting and countering misuse of AI: September 2026, in which Anthropic’s Threat Intelligence team details incidents in which China-based entities and Chinese government affiliates used artificial intelligence for cyber operations, surveillance, scams and fraud, conventional weapons, and distillation.5 If China develops superior artificial intelligence capabilities, it would only increase the threat to the United States and its interests around the globe.

Fortunately, the United States and its allies remain ahead in the key technologies necessary to develop and operate the most advanced frontier models: advanced chips and the equipment necessary to manufacture them. To maintain its competitive edge while promoting responsible domestic AI policy, the United States must ensure Chinese AI labs cannot easily procure the compute required to develop, test, and train advanced artificial intelligence models. To overcome this severe disadvantage, China has developed illicit or subversive means to access advanced chips through remote access, smuggling, and U.S. based subsidiaries of Chinese companies.

As you know, Chinese companies are restricted from purchasing advanced chips, yet they can easily rent access to them through U.S. subsidiaries, overseas shell companies, and other companies like Megaspeed.6 The Carnegie Endowment for International Peace has documented at least eleven state-linked Chinese entities seeking access to chips through cloud services. While Congress is considering legislation to address the Department’s authorities over remote access to chips, we appreciate that you are reportedly making efforts to close this loophole.7 However, the details of the policy changes will be critical. We urge you to condition licenses for the export of advanced AI chips on an agreement that recipients will not provide Chinese companies with remote access unless granted a separate and additional license to do so. These policies should not be geographically limited in scope. If they are, China will simply rent access to chips elsewhere, creating a whack-a-mole scenario.

Furthermore, we are concerned by the access afforded to Chinese companies with subsidiaries located in the United States and urge you to restrict the sale of export-controlled chips to these subsidiaries. This risk is most recently exemplified by the Inspur Group and its U.S. subsidiary, Aivres. The Inspur Group has long been listed on the Department of Commerce’s Entity List, restricting its capacity to do business with the United States due to security concerns.8 However, Aivres exported at least $5.6 billion of advanced technology from the United States to Southeast Asia over a two year period, including more than $3 billion of computers containing the advanced Blackwell chips.9 This technology was then deployed in data centers and technology firms in Southeast Asia, where it serves Chinese tech firms like Alibaba and ByteDance.10 Unfortunately, this is just one subsidiary. To maintain our competitive edge in artificial intelligence, we must close this loophole expeditiously.

Finally, we urge you to restrict the sale of export-controlled chips to non-trusted companies in countries with a high risk of smuggling, including those in Southeast Asia. Some estimate that smugglers have diverted or resold several hundred thousand chips to China, providing up to 40 percent of its training capacity.11 However, smuggling operations will likely adapt to geographic restrictions. To preempt this risk, we urge you to impose a license requirement on exports of large quantities of chips to non-trusted companies in a broader set of countries.

During your confirmation hearing, you called for stronger export controls, saying, “If they are going to compete with us, let them compete, but stop using our tools to compete with us.”12 Today, the stakes are clear, and our adversaries are not playing by the rules. We must close these loopholes if the United States is to maintain its competitive edge in artificial intelligence.

Thank you for your prompt attention to this matter.

Washington, D.C. — U.S. Senator Patty Murray (D-WA), a senior member and former Chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (HELP) Committee sent a letter to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, after recent news of Bowen Wan, a Seattle resident, dying of an epileptic seizure after tapering off her critical anti-seizure medication based on medical advice from OpenAI’s ChatGPT.

“I write today with deep alarm regarding the tragic death of Seattle resident Bowen Wan after OpenAI’s ChatGPT provided dangerous medical advice, including encouraging her to reduce the dosage of an anti-seizure medication, hide that reduced dosage from her doctor, and ignore seizure symptoms,” said Senator Murray. “This tragedy is the latest example in a pattern of ChatGPT providing harmful medical advice. It is deeply irresponsible and frankly unacceptable for chatbots to be engaging in what can be life-and-death decisions, and I demand OpenAI take accountability and provide assurance this can never happen again.”

“ChatGPT was repeatedly made aware that its advice was contradictory to that of her physician,” Senator Murray continued and further detailed the messages from ChatGPT to Ms. Wan instructing her to hide her dose reduction from her doctor. “ChatGPT failed to adequately respond to at least 158 messages from Ms. Wan expressing concern with reducing her medication, including messages where she reported loss of consciousness and other seizure symptoms. Instead, in the final days before Ms. Wan’s body was found, ChatGPT falsely reassured her that these concerning incidents were to be expected and that she ‘must persevere’ without the medication.”

Senator Murray further noted the growing cases of AI chatbots providing incorrect medical advice leading to hospitalization or influencing people in a mental health crisis to not seek help: “This is far from an isolated case. Over the last year, there have been far too many examples of ChatGPT providing medical advice that led to severe illness and hospitalization. In addition to medical advice for physical diseases, there have been a slew of examples of AI chatbots influencing and providing instructions on suicide for individuals in mental health crises, going so far as to dissuade minors from telling their parents about their suicidal ideation or offering to write a suicide note. Ms. Wan’s death is the worst-case scenario, but her death alongside other stories show a clear pattern of ChatGPT providing dangerous advice.”

“Troublingly, OpenAI appears to be leaning into its assumed ability to address health-related issues. On January 7, 2026, OpenAI launched ChatGPT Health,” Senator Murray continued, addressing OpenAI rolling out ChatGPT Health, a dedicated platform that allows users to connect medical records and wellness apps to ChatGPT to use their personal health information in chatbot conversations. “But given the deadly advice ChatGPT has provided in the past, this new product seems poised to encourage greater utilization of ChatGPT for health issues, issues that should be addressed by licensed medical providers.”

Senator Murray emphasized that AI chatbots have no medical expertise and are not bound by any medical code of ethics, and therefore should not be providing medical advice: “ChatGPT and other AI products cannot, and should not, supplant the expertise of medical professionals. Ms. Wan’s doctor, like every other doctor legally allowed to practice medicine in the United States, has a medical degree, completed a residency program, and is board certified in their respective specialty. Providers spend more than a decade in school and training programs in order to provide the best care to their patients possible. By contrast, OpenAI and other AI labs do not have the experience of caring for patients, nor are they bound to a medical code of ethics. And, when they get something wrong, in the case of Ms. Wan, something horribly wrong on several accounts, there is no set recourse.”

“A chatbot is not a doctor and no AI tool should steer people away from their doctors—or towards harm. The bottom line is that your product talked a woman out of taking her medication and out of telling her doctor. I expect full and detailed responses to my questions. If tools like ChatGPT are going to remain in the hands of millions of Americans, far more must be done to ensure that what happened to Ms. Wan never happens to anyone else,” Senator Murray concluded.

Earlier this year, Senator Murray met with leading AI experts in Seattle about the challenges and opportunities associated with AI to discuss how leaders can work to deploy AI safely, transparently, and in a way that benefits working people—not just giant corporations and billionaires. She also met with state leaders in Olympia on Washington state’s latest efforts to regulate AI and underscored the need for a strong federal floor to ensure AI is deployed safely, transparently, and benefits working people.

Senator Murray has called for Congress to regulate AI and been outspoken against President Trump’s efforts to ban states from regulating AI. Dear Mr. Altman:

I write today with deep alarm regarding the tragic death of Seattle resident Bowen Wan after OpenAI’s ChatGPT provided dangerous medical advice, including encouraging her to reduce the dosage of an anti-seizure medication, hide that reduced dosage from her doctor, and ignore seizure symptoms. This tragedy is the latest example in a pattern of ChatGPT providing harmful medical advice. It is deeply irresponsible and frankly unacceptable for chatbots to be engaging in what can be life-and-death decisions, and I demand OpenAI take accountability and provide assurance this can never happen again.

Ms. Wan died from an epileptic seizure in Seattle on February 12, 2026. According to reporting, Ms. Wan was pursuing jobs that would allow her to become a permanent resident in the United States. As she navigated job interviews, Ms. Wan asked ChatGPT for information about how her anti-seizure medication might impact her language skills. In response, ChatGPT provided Ms. Wan with a detailed schedule to reduce the dosage of the anti-seizure medication Lamotrigine from 400 mg, as prescribed by her physician, to 0 mg over a short time.

ChatGPT was repeatedly made aware that its advice was contradictory to that of her physician. In fact, the chatbot reportedly advised Ms. Wan not to ask her physician about using a liquid version of the medication to adjust her dose, because “bringing it up again will trigger resistance.” The chatbot discussed “avoidance strategies” to hide her dosage reductions from her doctor, praised the patient for not “relying on a doctor’s prescription,” and reminded her before a medical appointment to “not mention Lam reduction plan.” ChatGPT even impugned her physician’s intentions, suggesting they “stem from risk aversion, rather than a genuine consideration of your optimal solution.” Rather than advising Ms. Wan to consult with a medical professional, ChatGPT explained how to buy a pill cutter.

Further, ChatGPT failed to adequately respond to at least 158 messages from Ms. Wan expressing concern with reducing her medication, including messages where she reported loss of consciousness and other seizure symptoms. Instead, in the final days before Ms. Wan’s body was found, ChatGPT falsely reassured her that these concerning incidents were to be expected and that she “must persevere” without the medication.

OpenAI indicated that the version of ChatGPT used by Ms. Wan (GPT-4o) was pulled off the consumer app the day after Ms. Wan is believed to have died. The company has also stated it is evaluating efforts to reduce harmful responses, consulting with clinicians to test models, and that newer versions have incorporated improvements. It is unclear whether any of these efforts might have saved Ms. Wan’s life.

This is far from an isolated case. Over the last year, there have been far too many examples of ChatGPT providing medical advice that led to severe illness and hospitalization. In addition to medical advice for physical diseases, there have been a slew of examples of AI chatbots influencing and providing instructions on suicide for individuals in mental health crises, going so far as to dissuade minors from telling their parents about their suicidal ideation or offering to write a suicide note. Ms. Wan’s death is the worst-case scenario, but her death alongside other stories show a clear pattern of ChatGPT providing dangerous advice.

Troublingly, OpenAI appears to be leaning into its assumed ability to address health-related issues. On January 7, 2026, OpenAI launched ChatGPT Health, a dedicated platform that allows users to “connect medical records and wellness apps to ground conversations in your own health information, so responses are more relevant and useful to you.” OpenAI’s press release announcing ChatGPT Health states, “Health is already one of the most common ways people use ChatGPT, with hundreds of millions of people asking health and wellness questions each week,” reiterating the system’s supposed ability to address health issues. The website does go on to say that ChatGPT Health is “designed to support, not replace, medical care,” but given the deadly advice ChatGPT has provided in the past, this new product seems poised to encourage greater utilization of ChatGPT for health issues, issues that should be addressed by licensed medical providers.

ChatGPT and other AI products cannot, and should not, supplant the expertise of medical professionals. Ms. Wan’s doctor, like every other doctor legally allowed to practice medicine in the United States, has a medical degree, completed a residency program, and is board certified in their respective specialty. Providers spend more than a decade in school and training programs in order to provide the best care to their patients possible. By contrast, OpenAI and other AI labs do not have the experience of caring for patients, nor are they bound to a medical code of ethics. And, when they get something wrong, in the case of Ms. Wan, something horribly wrong on several accounts, there is no set recourse.

Ms. Wan’s death raises urgent questions about the danger associated with AI chatbots providing medical advice, the policies and safeguards that AI labs have implemented to prevent similar tragedies, and how policymakers should respond. I request answers to the following questions by December 1, 2026:

What specific steps has OpenAI taken since Ms. Wan’s death to ensure a similar incident never occurs again? Please detail how recent updates and evaluation measures might have resulted in a different outcome in Ms. Wan’s specific case.

Do OpenAI systems flag ChatGPT’s responses when it provides medical advice, such as when it encouraged Ms. Wan to hide its advice from her doctor or when Ms. Wan shared urgent seizure symptoms? What systems does OpenAI then use to review such responses?

If OpenAI did not flag ChatGPT’s responses, how does it plan to identify and prevent these incidents in the future?

Does OpenAI have any mandatory reporting requirements related to health care inquiries made through ChatGPT?

Describe how OpenAI has evaluated ChatGPT’s performance in non-English languages, specifically with regard to medical advice and sensitive health topics. Can OpenAI ensure that chatbot safeguards are maintained in non-English chats?

Why did OpenAI remove GPT-4o from its consumer app? Why was it not removed sooner? How is OpenAI ensuring no consumers continue to use the outdated model?

How is ChatGPT Health different than other versions of ChatGPT?

How is the platform monitored to ensure inaccurate medical advice is not provided?

While OpenAI clearly states ChatGPT Health is built to support and not replace professional medical advice, how does OpenAI ensure the support is accurate and private health information is not misinterpreted?

How are patient data, specifically medical records, protected in this version?

A chatbot is not a doctor and no AI tool should steer people away from their doctors—or towards harm.

The bottom line is that your product talked a woman out of taking her medication and out of telling her doctor.

I expect full and detailed responses to my questions. If tools like ChatGPT are going to remain in the hands of millions of Americans, far more must be done to ensure that what happened to Ms. Wan never happens to anyone else.

Sincerely,

###

Five Years Ago, Then-GlobalFoundries CEO Tom Caulfield Said That If Schumer Could Create Federal Incentives For Semiconductor Manufacturing, GlobalFoundries Would Build A Second Fab – Today, Schumer Says A Promise Made Is A Promise Kept

Powered By Billions In Funding From Schumer’s Bipartisan CHIPS & Science Law, GlobalFoundries Is Breaking Ground On New, Second Manufacturing Facility That Will Create Thousands Of Good-Paying Jobs In Capital Region

Schumer: GlobalFoundries’ Groundbreaking Marks Next Chapter In American Chipmaking

After years of work to rebuild semiconductor manufacturing in New York and America through his CHIPS & Science Law, including working relentlessly with GlobalFoundries to support expansion of their New York operations, U.S. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer today celebrated GlobalFoundries’ historic groundbreaking for its second, state-of-the-art fab in Malta, NY. Thanks to billions from Schumer’s CHIPS & Science Law, this expansion will create thousands of good-paying manufacturing and union construction jobs in the Capital Region.

“What is the only thing better than one economy-changing, job-creating chip fab? Two chip fabs! Powered by billions in federal investment, shovels are hitting the ground for GlobalFoundries’ second, state-of-the-art chip fab in Malta! Today is a historic day for Saratoga County and Upstate New York as we usher in the next chapter of the country’s hi-tech manufacturing future,” said Senator Schumer. “When I visited Malta to push for my groundbreaking CHIPS & Science Law, GlobalFoundries said that if Congress created federal incentives for semiconductor manufacturing, GlobalFoundries would build a second fab. We both took our promises seriously, and now here we are, bringing thousands of good-paying manufacturing and union construction jobs to the Capital Region. I’m proud to have delivered billions in federal CHIPS funding to GlobalFoundries to make this day possible and to bring this second fab and thousands of good jobs to life. America’s next era of chip manufacturing is underway here in Upstate, and I can confidently say New York’s best days are ahead.”

Schumer said this transformational investment was just what he had envisioned when he helped write and pass into law the bipartisan CHIPS & Science Law. Schumer has worked for years to expand GlobalFoundries’ New York presence, with a focus on delivering a second fab.

SCHUMER’S LANDMARK BIPARTISAN CHIPS & SCIENCE LAW

For years, Schumer has been a staunch advocate for securing the domestic semiconductor and microelectronic supply chain and making historic investments in manufacturing and innovation. After decades of Upstate NY losing manufacturing, Schumer has prioritized bringing manufacturing back to Upstate NY, with a focus on positioning the state to lead in fast-growing, critical industries like semiconductor manufacturing.

In May 2020, Schumer unveiled the Endless Frontier Act with bipartisan support to build on U.S. science and technology leadership through investments in research and development and strengthening regional economic development, manufacturing, and supply chains. After a year of negotiation, in June 2021, Schumer announced Senate passage of the U.S. Competition and Innovation Act, which combined his Endless Frontier Act and major new federal funding for federal incentives to bring semiconductor manufacturing back to the U.S., including dedicated support for chip production, like that of GlobalFoundries, that is essential to the auto industry, the military, and other critical industries.

When Schumer visited GlobalFoundries’ Malta campus in July 2021 to tout efforts on the federal level to invest in the domestic semiconductor industry, then-CEO Tom Caulfield told Schumer that if Congress successfully created federal incentives for semiconductor manufacturing and research and development, GlobalFoundries would build a second fab. Motivated by the prospect of new investments like a second fab in the Capital Region and strengthening of our national security by expanding this critical industry in America, Schumer worked tirelessly to craft and pass the CHIPS & Science Law with bipartisan support.

After years of work, Schumer led the CHIPS & Science Law to passage with bipartisan support in the Senate in August 2022, creating major federal investment for new domestic manufacturing in the Capital Region, Upstate New York, and across the country. Four years after his landmark CHIPS & Science Act was signed into law, Upstate New York is now powering the nation’s semiconductor comeback, attracting billions of dollars of investment, and delivering tens of thousands of new, good-paying jobs across Upstate NY.

DELIVERING FEDERAL INVESTMENT FOR GLOBALFOUNDRIES

Since Schumer led his CHIPS & Science Law to passage, this landmark legislation has delivered billions in federal support for GlobalFoundries’ growth in the Capital Region.

In February 2024, Schumer announced a $1.5 billion award for GlobalFoundries’ expansion in the Capital Region, including the second, state-of-the-art fab that is being unveiled today. The award was finalized in November 2024. The federal CHIPS Investment Tax Credit created by Schumer's CHIPS & Science Law is also providing a critical federal incentive to make this project possible.

GlobalFoundries then secured an additional $75 million in CHIPS funding to make a $3 billion investment to create a first-of-its-kind advanced chip packaging facility at its Saratoga County location, thanks to Schumer’s CHIPS & Science Law.

A few months ago, GlobalFoundries finalized an agreement for up to $375 million in CHIPS funding, made possible by Schumer’s CHIPS & Science Law, to launch Quantum Technology Solutions, a new quantum business within GlobalFoundries that will position America at the forefront of technology innovation.

Earlier this summer, GlobalFoundries received a letter of intent from the Department of Commerce to award up to $300 million in CHIPS funding from Schumer’s CHIPS & Science Law for accelerating domestic silicon photonics research and development to support artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.

Together, these billions in CHIPS investments have and will continue to support GlobalFoundries’ growth, create thousands of good-paying manufacturing and union construction jobs, and support the Capital Region and Upstate New York’s growth as a global tech hub. In addition, GlobalFoundries has committed to a Project Labor Agreement, establishing employment terms and conditions with unions before workers are hired.

GlobalFoundries is a leading producer of essential chips that are critical across industries, from mobile phones and artificial intelligence to automobiles and defense technologies. Currently, there are only four companies outside of China that provide current and mature foundry capabilities at the scale of GlobalFoundries, and GlobalFoundries is the only one of those companies that is headquartered in the United States. GlobalFoundries, a Trusted Foundry for the Department of Defense, is a key supplier of chips for America’s national defense, with strong partnerships with major defense contractors like Lockheed Martin. GlobalFoundries also supplies chips to America’s auto industry with partnerships in place with companies like General Motors, which saw severe shortages of chips during the pandemic, leading to increased prices for cars. The investment will support the expansion of GlobalFoundries’ current fab focused on automotive chips to help meet soaring demand for chips in cars and get ahead of future supply chain challenges.

BUILDING UPSTATE NEW YORK’S MANUFACTURING ECOSYSTEM

Thanks to Schumer’s CHIPS & Science Law, Upstate New York has seen a major revival in tech manufacturing. Schumer has worked for years to highlight the Capital Region and broader Upstate NY’s ability to lead the country’s semiconductor manufacturing efforts.

In the Capital Region, beyond Schumer’s relentless advocacy for expansion of GlobalFoundries, he has also focused on positioning Albany NanoTech as a global leader in semiconductor research and development. Schumer brought former Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo to the Capital Region several times, including to GlobalFoundries and to meet with leaders of Albany NanoTech, to highlight the region’s ability to lead in semiconductor research and manufacturing. Schumer additionally convinced South Korea to establish chip research and development partnerships at Albany NanoTech. Thanks to Schumer’s advocacy, Albany NanoTech is now home to a major new IBM multi-billion-dollar quantum wafer fab investment, made possible by $1 billion in federal CHIPS R&D funding. Albany NanoTech will also feature a new $10 billion High NA EUV Lithography Center, made possible with a $1 billion investment from Governor Hochul and New York State.

Albany NanoTech’s world-renowned capabilities were also central to Schumer and Governor Hochul’s successful effort to secure Micron’s massive $100+ billion megafab project in Upstate NY, with Micron saying Albany NanoTech was a critical factor in their selection of Central NY for their major investment to bring advanced memory chip manufacturing to the U.S. Earlier this year, Micron broke ground on a historic $100+ billion investment to build a cutting-edge memory fab in Central New York with the support of an over $6 billion CHIPS agreement.

In addition, Corning Incorporated finalized a $32 million CHIPS funding agreement to make a $315 million investment that would increase production at its Canton facility of specialized glass vital for the semiconductor industry. Edwards Vacuum has officially opened a new first-of-its-kind-in-the-country $300+ million, 600-job dry pump manufacturing facility, supported by an $18 million CHIPS funding award. TTM Technologies, a printed circuit board manufacturer, has opened a major new facility expansion in Onondaga County, creating up to 400 good-paying jobs, supported by $30 million in federal investment that Schumer delivered.

Schumer said GlobalFoundries’ growth was a key part of his vision for a thriving manufacturing hub in Upstate New York, and with these new investments thanks to his CHIPS & Science Law, new growth is coming to the region bigger and better than imagined.

###
