matches.text:
WASHINGTON — U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), a member of the U.S. Senate Appropriations Committee and Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on the Legislative Branch, announced that he was able to get $338 million for New Mexico included in the newly released Fiscal Year 2027 (FY27) Military Construction and Veterans Affairs (VA); Commerce, Justice, Science, and Related Agencies (CJS); Agriculture, Rural Development, and Food and Drug Administration (FDA); Interior and Environment; Homeland Security; Energy and Water Development; and Legislative Branch Appropriations Bills, including Congressionally Directed Spending for 42 local projects.

“I’ve spent months fighting to secure federal funding to help New Mexico families put food on the table and afford housing, give local law enforcement the tools they need to keep our communities safe, support our veterans and military installations, and invest in critical water infrastructure, including $63 million for the Navajo-Gallup Water Supply Project. I’m proud to have secured $338 million for New Mexico in the released bills. But I remain frustrated by Senate Republicans refusal to include the critical funding needed for rural communities, necessary reforms to rein in an out-of-control ICE, and oversight tools to hold this administration accountable,” said Heinrich, a member of the U.S. Senate Appropriations Committee.

Heinrich continued, “Together, we got a lot into these bills. But New Mexicans deserve better than the totality of what Senate Republicans included, and my vote will reflect that. In this and future appropriations cycles, I will continue working to bring home investments that lower costs for working families, create more good-paying jobs, strengthen our communities, and honor the service of those who keep us safe.”

FY27 Military Construction, Veterans Affairs, and Related Agencies Key Points and Highlights

Military Construction

Heinrich successfully included $206 million for the following two projects:

$185,000,000 for a new operational facility that will support the intelligence needs of the Defense Intelligence Enterprise and the U.S. Space Force.

$21,000,000, combined with the $90,000,000 Heinrich secured in FY26, to build a new 192-bed dorm for the Air Force Special Operations Command at Cannon Air Force Base.

Heinrich and U.S. Senator Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) also successfully included $32.75 million for the following two projects:

$25,000,000 for the construction of a Deployment Processing Center at Cannon Air Force Base.

$7,750,000 for the construction of an Explosive Operations Building at Kirtland Air Force Base.

Veteran Healthcare

Toxic Exposure: This bill includes $54.6 billion to implement the PACT Act, which expands and extends eligibility for VA healthcare for veterans of the Vietnam War, Gulf Wars, and post-9/11 era who were exposed to dangerous toxins while serving our country. Heinrich championed the PACT Act into law in 2022.

Home Healthcare: Heinrich secured language that requires the VA to study the impacts of the 19% cut to reimbursement rates for home health aides serving veterans in New Mexico. If the VA finds that these cuts negatively affected veterans’ access to care, the VA is required to issue waivers to allow home healthcare providers to receive higher reimbursement, reversing the cuts and protecting veteran access to home healthcare.

Earlier this year, Heinrich led New Mexico and Texas congressional Democrats in introducing the Protecting Home-Based Care for Rural Veterans Act, legislation to reverse the Trump administration’s cuts to reimbursement rates for essential homecare services for veterans in New Mexico and Texas.

Rural Health: This bill provides $349 million to help veterans living in rural communities access health care, including the Highly Rural Transportation Grant, which provides free transportation services to help veterans in rural areas travel to VA health appointments at no cost.

An estimated 2.7 million rural and highly rural veterans are enrolled in the Veterans Health Administration (VHA). Many rural veterans enrolled in the VA healthcare system are at an advanced age, with approximately 54 percent aged 65 or older. With the aging veteran population growing increasingly medically complex and more likely to be diagnosed with chronic conditions like diabetes, obesity, high blood pressure, and heart disease, each requiring more frequent, ongoing, and costly care, these funds would help close the gap and get highly rural veterans the care they need.

Telehealth: The bill includes $6.7 billion to sustain and expand telehealth services at the VA, helping more veterans access care.

Mental Health: The bill includes nearly $3.7 billion for suicide prevention efforts at the VA. This includes a program to identify at-risk veterans established under the Commander John Scott Hannon Veterans Mental Health Care Improvement Act of 2019, which Heinrich helped pass into law.

Education

GI Bill: The bill asks the VA to study and report how much it would cost to adjust for inflation the books and supplies stipend GI Bill recipients receive. The current stipend has not been adjusted since 2008. This builds on Heinrich’s Veteran Education Assistance Adjustment Act, bipartisan legislation that will increase veterans’ yearly books and supply stipend to $1,500 to keep up with inflation. The bill also increases the supply stipend for veterans enrolled in apprenticeships and pursuing careers in the trades.

Housing

Reducing Veteran Homelessness: The bill includes $3.8 billion to help connect veterans with stable, secure housing with the goal of putting 45,000 veterans experiencing homelessness into long term housing by 2027.

FY27 Commerce, Justice, Science, and Related Agencies Key Points and Highlights

Congressionally Directed Spending

Heinrich successfully included $5 million for the following seven local projects:

$1,082,000 for Navajo United Methodist Center to expand support services for their Helping Hand Program, which helps domestic violence survivors secure housing and employment.

$931,000 for the Domestic Violence Resource Center to expand survivor access and response capacity.

$751,000 for Catholic Charities of Albuquerque to expand community-based legal navigation and accredited services for underserved individuals facing legal barriers.

$750,000 for Families and Youth, Inc. to expand their youth mental health intervention services across Doña Ana County communities.

$750,000 for the City of Portales to acquire a regional mobile command center.

$533,000 for Central New Mexico Community College to add campus lighting and security cameras to improve campus safety.

$350,000 for the Children’s Safehouse at All Faiths Children’s Advocacy Center to expand their capacity to conduct forensic interviews.

Heinrich and Luján also successfully included $6.5 million for the following seven projects:

$1,605,000 for Albuquerque Police Department to purchase forensic and investigative technology.

$1,320,000 for the Bernalillo County Sheriff’s Office to purchase four Crime Scene Investigation vans and ten patrol vehicles.

$1,000,000 for Chaves County Court Appointed Special Advocates Program to provide services and resources to child crime survivors, foster families, and trauma-response teams.

$1,000,000 for Albuquerque Police Department to replace their law enforcement training range and equipment.

$720,000 for the University of New Mexico to create trustworthy AI research, education, and infrastructure.

$500,000 for the Second Judicial District Attorney’s Office to expand its cold case investigation.

$368,000 for Albuquerque Community Safety to expand their youth violence intervention services.

Keeping New Mexico Communities Safe and Combating Crime

Combatting Crimes on Tribal Lands: Heinrich successfully included language directing the Department of Justice (DOJ) to continue allocating additional resources to address the crisis of Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons, including providing sufficient funding to investigate, respond to, and prevent crimes in Tribal communities.

Fentanyl Tracking System: Heinrich successfully included language directing the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) to develop a comprehensive fentanyl tracking system. That tracking system would include documentation of seizure location, chemical composition, probable or known manufacturing location, and probable or known point of entry into the United States. Currently, fentanyl interdiction is compiled at land ports of entry by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), but the DEA does not have readily accessible tracking data on the movement of illicit drugs within the U.S. or their point of origin. Requiring the compilation and organization of that data will complement DHS’ work and improve our country’s work to effectively combat the fentanyl crisis.

Firearm Straw Purchases Prevention: Heinrich successfully included language calling on the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) to continue its public awareness campaign to reduce firearm straw purchases at the retail level and to educate would-be straw purchasers of the penalties associated with knowingly participating in an illegal firearm purchase. This language builds on Heinrich’s work to negotiate and author the provision in the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act that increased criminal penalties for straw purchases and made it illegal to traffic firearms out of the United States. To date, more than 1,000 defendants have been charged by the Department of Justice because of those provisions, removing hundreds of firearms from the streets.

Removing Barriers to Lifesaving Medication: Heinrich successfully included language directing the DEA to take further action to remove barriers to access for opioid use disorder medications such as buprenorphine. The data clearly shows that prescriptions of medications for opioid use disorder significantly reduce the risk of overdose death, but despite their demonstrated effectiveness, approximately 87% of those suffering from opioid use disorder do not have a prescription for these lifesaving medications. The inclusion of this language will assist local medical and mental health providers and make medications, including buprenorphine, more accessible to New Mexicans.

FY27 Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and Related Agencies Key Points and Highlights

Congressionally Directed Spending

Heinrich successfully included $6 million for the following seven local projects:

$2,000,000 for New Mexico State University to rehabilitate and update the Farmington Agricultural Science Center Site.

$1,650,000 for Pueblo of Zuni Fire Department to purchase a ladder truck and equipment for the ladder truck.

$750,000 for Pueblo of Zia to purchase heavy equipment to maintain roads.

$550,000 for BEN Initiative to equip and expand the CHIYAAN Community Food and Nutrition hub to help support the aggregation and distribution of locally grown and culturally appropriate foods.

$500,000 for the City of Belén to update the Old City Hall building.

$500,000 for San Cristobal Mutual Domestic Water Consumers Association to upgrade the San Cristobal Community Center.

$75,000 for Guadalupe County Clerk’s Office to purchase a new election vehicle to ensure secure, reliable, and timely transportation of election equipment and staff to polling locations.

Heinrich and Luján successfully included $1.4 million for the following two projects:

$938,000 for Sandoval County to purchase and equip a wildland fire truck.

$500,000 for the Village of Mosquero to construct a new fire station.

Nutrition Assistance

WIC: The bill fully funds the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC), which serves nearly 7 million women and children nationwide, including over 45,000 in New Mexico — by providing $8.5 billion for the program, a $300 million increase over FY26. This increase will ensure that all eligible participants can continue to rely on the essential nutrition assistance and support provided by WIC.

SNAP: The bill fully funds the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), which serves an estimated 36 million people each month, including roughly 440,000 New Mexicans, without imposing new restrictive policy riders. While fully funding SNAP is critically important, it does not undo the cuts enacted through Trump and Republicans’ Big, Bad Bill. Those cuts have saddled New Mexico with hundreds of millions of dollars in new, unfunded mandates and contributed to a sharp decline in SNAP enrollment nationwide, including more than 20,000 New Mexicans who have lost their benefits.

Child Nutrition: The bill fully funds Child Nutrition Programs — like the School Lunch program, school breakfast program, and Summer EBT program — to ensure schools can continue to serve healthy meals to all eligible children. In 2027, this funding will help serve an estimated 5.3 billion lunches and 2.7 billion breakfasts to kids across the country.

Commodity Supplemental Food Program: The bill rejects the Trump administration's budget proposal to eliminate this program’s funding and provides $495 million, a $70 million increase over FY26, so that the program can continue to provide supplemental food to low-income Senior citizens.

Supporting New Mexico Rural Communities, Agriculture, and Food Security

Rental Assistance: The bill provides $1.7 billion for rental assistance to help ensure Americans living in rural communities have access to safe and affordable housing. The bill also includes $1 billion in Single Family Direct Loans to help more low-income families and first-time home buyers get mortgages.

Tribal Communities: The bill provides $271 million for the Food Distribution on Indian Reservation Program (FDPIR), a $36 million increase over FY26. The bill also provides $700,000 for processing and federal inspection of Tribal bison, which will help support Tribal food sovereignty by enabling Tribes to include bison raised on their own lands to be included in federal nutrition programs like school meals.

Additionally, the bill provides $5.1 million for the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s (USDA) Office of Tribal Relations, which is responsible for government-to-government relations between USDA and Tribal governments.

Economic Development: The bill includes a $3 million investment in the Southwest Border Commission (SBRC), a $500,000 increase over FY26, which supports economic and community development in southern New Mexico. Previously, Heinrich successfully secured the first-ever congressional investments to finally allow the SBRC to jump-start and expand its operations. The SBRC is one of eight authorized federal regional commissions and authorities.

Conservation and Wildlife: The bill rejects the administration’s proposal to eliminate all discretionary funding for the Natural Resources Conservation Service’s Conservation Technical Assistance program, which helps farmers and ranchers protect their land, improve soil health, and conserve water. Instead, the bill provides $748 million for conservation programs, $50 million more than FY26. This includes $51.6 million to help communities prevent flooding and protect watersheds and $10 million to help ranchers maintain healthy grazing lands.

The bill further provides $5.5 million to support non-lethal strategies to reduce wildlife-livestock conflict and includes direction to expand the Migratory Big Game and Working Lands for Wildlife Initiatives, a long-time Heinrich priority. Finally, the bill includes $22.5 million in funding for research and management of Chronic Wasting Disease, which funds the program created by Heinrich’s Chronic Wasting Disease Research and Management Act, passed into law in 2023.

Agriculture Research: The bill fully funds agricultural research, including a $39 million increase over FY26 for the Agricultural Research Service (ARS), which conducts research to help farmers and ranchers improve their operations and protect their land. The bill also continues funding for Climate Hubs, which help farmers and ranchers prepare for drought and extreme weather, and the Long-term Agroecosystems Research (LTAR) Network, which studies how to keep farmland and grazing lands healthy and productive for years to come. This includes research conducted jointly by New Mexico State University (NMSU) and ARS Experimental Station in Las Cruces. The bill also provides $1.5 million for agrivoltaics research by ARS and NMSU, which explores how farmers can use the same land to grow crops and produce solar energy.

Small Farms and Local Food Systems: The bill provides $5 million for the Office of Urban Agriculture, which helps people grow food in urban communities by providing training, resources, and tools to manage risks. Albuquerque is home to one of the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s (USDA) Urban Service Centers, which helps local farmers and growers access these resources. The bill also provides $16.3 million for the Local Agriculture Market Program (LAMP), which helps farmers and ranchers sell their products directly to customers, expand local food markets, and create new products from the crops and livestock they raise.

Food Safety: The bill provides $1.226 billion for the Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS), an increase of $11 million over FY26. This funding will help ensure FSIS can perform its vital work protecting America’s food supply without being forced to reduce its staffing levels, which would jeopardize food safety and exacerbate supply chain delays. The bill also includes $1.176 billion for the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, including $10 million, in additional funding for efforts to address the New World Screwworm infestation, a $5 million increase over FY26. This funding is in addition to over $1 billion the USDA has already spent using Commodity Credit Corporation funding and emergency funding.

Promoting Competition: The bill provides nearly $33 million for enforcement of the Packers and Stockyards Act to promote competition and prevent unfair or deceptive practices and monopolies.

International Food Aid: The bill provides $1.38 billion for the Food for Peace Program and $240 million for the McGovern-Dole International Food for Education and Child Nutrition Program. This funding is necessary to save lives around the world and reduce conflict.

Food and Drug Administration (FDA): The bill provides $7.265 billion for the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), including $3.5 billion in annual funding, a $196 million increase over FY26. This includes $2.6 billion for the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, which helps ensure prescription drugs are safe and effective; $627 million for the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research, which oversees vaccines, blood products, and other medical treatments; and $71 million for the National Center for Toxicological Research, which studies the safety of drugs, chemicals, and other products. The bill also provides $19 million for the Orphan Products Grants Program, which supports research into treatments for rare diseases, including $5 million for the FDA Rare Neurodegenerative Disease Grants Program, which funds research into rare diseases that damage the brain and nervous system.

The bill also provides at least $200 million for FDA enforcement efforts, including working with other federal agencies to crack down on illegal e-cigarettes and nicotine pouches, remove these products from the market, and hold companies that illegally import or sell them accountable.

FY27 Interior and Environment Key Points and Highlights

Congressionally Directed Spending

Heinrich successfully included $5.65 million for the following 10 projects:

$1,000,000 for the New Mexico Environment Department to address hexavalent chromium water contamination at San Ildefonso Pueblo.

$900,000 for the Pueblo of Cochiti to plan, design, and construct a new solid waste transfer station.

$750,000 for the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center to purchase climate-controlled equipment for the preservation and public display of their collection of cultural artifacts.

$700,000 for the University of New Mexico to conduct aerial waterfowl surveys.

$550,000 for Santa Fe County to purchase and install reverse-osmosis water filters.

$530,000 for the New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology to conduct magnetotelluric geothermal resource screening activities.

$500,000 for Taos Pueblo to conduct rehabilitation and renovation projects for the historic village.

$500,000 for the Bureau of Land Management to conduct trail maintenance within the Rio Grande del Norte National Monument.

$125,000 for the Forest Stewards Guild to conduct statewide home hazard risk assessment training.

$70,000 for the Pueblo of Zia to install new advanced water meter technology.

Heinrich and Luján included $1.87 million for the following 2 projects:

$1,200,000 for the New Mexico Department of Forestry to conduct forest and watershed health activities in the Rio Chama watershed.

$675,000 for the Village of Jemez Springs to rehabilitate its wastewater treatment and collection system.

Supporting Tribes, Investing in Education, and Conserving New Mexico’s Lands and Wildlife

Safeguard Tribal Objects of Patrimony (STOP) Act Implementation: Heinrich successfully included $500,000 to implement the Safeguard Tribal Objects of Patrimony (STOP) Act, a bipartisan law that Heinrich championed and passed in 2022 to prohibit the exporting of sacred Native American items and increase penalties for stealing and illegally trafficking Tribal cultural patrimony. Representing only the second year that this program has received dedicated funding, it will be used to halt the trade of culturally significant items and repatriate stolen pieces to the Tribal communities where they belong. Heinrich first introduced the STOP Act in 2016 after he helped halt the auction of a shield, stolen from the Pueblo of Acoma. Heinrich played a role in the effort to bring the shield home to Acoma by working with Governors Kurt Riley and Brian Vallo to call for its return.

Tribal Education: Heinrich fought for and successfully included $13,482,000 for the Institute of American Indian and Alaska Native Culture and Arts Development (IAIA). After the administration threatened to withhold FY25 funding from the IAIA, Heinrich secured the release of the funds and secured FY26 funding for the IAIA. This appropriations bill will ensure continued investment for the IAIA through FY27, supporting its mission to advance Indigenous arts, culture, and education for future generations. Heinrich also included language directing the U.S. Department of the Interior to continue to address the deferred maintenance backlog at Bureau of Indian Education (BIE) schools.

Historic Preservation: Heinrich successfully secured level funding for the Tribal Historic Preservation Offices, totaling $23,750,000 after the Trump Administration proposed zeroing out the program.

Abandoned Hardrock Mine Reclamation Program: Heinrich successfully included continued funding for the Abandoned Hardrock Mine Reclamation Program, after championing the creation of the program in the 2022 Infrastructure Law. Hardrock mines and mining features are related to the extraction of metals like copper, gold, silver, and uranium. When not reclaimed, many hardrock mines pose a hazard to public health and the environment. This funding will be used to clean up federal, state, Tribal, and private land and water resources affected by abandoned hardrock mines.

Southwest Ecological Research Institutes: Heinrich fought for and successfully maintained funding for the Southwest Ecological Research Institutes (SWERIs) after the Trump Administration proposed cutting the funding. SWERIs offer unique opportunities for dedicated research in forest science and watershed health and represent the future of science in forest management. New Mexico Highlands University houses one center along with Colorado State University and Northern Arizona University. This funding would ensure the continuation of valuable research in southwestern forest and fire management.

Conservation: Heinrich successfully protected funding for the North American Wetlands Conservation Fund, which leverages private dollars to restore waterfowl habitat across the country. Heinrich led the reauthorization of this fund last Congress. He also protected core wildlife management and science capabilities at the Fish and Wildlife Service and the U.S. Geological Survey from the steep cuts proposed by the Trump administration.

FY27 Homeland Security Key Points and Highlights

Heinrich successfully included $1.7 million for the following two projects:

$1,150,000 for the New Mexico Environment Department to complete two large-scale river and floodplain restoration projects in watersheds severely affected by the Hermit’s Peak/Calf Canyon Fire.

$550,000 for the City of Roswell to conduct a city-wide study of its drainage system and guide future investment in order to mitigate against future disasters.

Strengthening Public Safety, Election Security, and Emergency Preparedness

Election Security: Heinrich helped secure $39,610,000 for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s (CISA) Election Security Program, which the Trump administration proposed eliminating in its FY27 budget request. The Election Security Program provides state and local election officers with intelligence, resources, and tools to help secure critical election infrastructure.

Fentanyl Analogues: Heinrich helped secure language directing U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to identify the specific types of fentanyl analogues and fentanyl-related substances that it encounters at ports of entry, rapidly deploy technology to detect, interdict, and deter the flow of illicit drugs, and provide a briefing on how the agency tracks fentanyl with the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). Currently, interdiction data is compiled at ports of entry by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), and the DEA does not have readily accessible tracking data on the movement of illicit drugs within the U.S. or their point of origin when it is seized within the U.S.

E-Cigarettes: Heinrich fought for and secured a $5,000,000 allocation from CBP to improve the Office of Field Operations (OFO) and the Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) work on stopping the flow of illegal e-cigarettes into the U.S. The allocation will fund increased random inspections at ports of entry, increase the number of field examinations at ports of entry with high import volumes, and improve screening systems for field staff to better detect illegal e-cigarette imports.

Next Generation Warning System: Heinrich helped secure $56,000,00o for the Next Generation Warning System (NGWS). The NGWS supports the continuity, reliability, and resiliency of public broadcasting infrastructure, which is used across the country to provide alerts, warnings, and interoperable communications during emergencies.

FY27 Energy and Water Development Key Points and Highlights

Heinrich successfully included $2 million for the following two projects:

$1,782,000 for the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to monitor water operations in the Upper Rio Grande.

$500,000 for the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to perform construction activities to support wildfire prevention and restoration in the Middle Rio Grande Bosque in and around the City of Albuquerque.

Additionally, Heinrich and Luján successfully included $63,333,000 for the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation to design and construct the Navajo-Gallup Water Supply Project.

Heinrich and Luján have long supported efforts to fund and complete the Navajo-Gallup Water Supply Project. For more information, click here.

Investing in New Mexico Water Infrastructure, Sandia and Los Alamos National Laboratories, and the Southwest Border Regional Commission

Oversight of Federal Water Infrastructure: Heinrich successfully included report language that provides key oversight on federal water infrastructure throughout New Mexico, including the El Vado Dam and the San Juan-Chama Project.

Water Conservation and Natural Infrastructure: Heinrich secured level funding and significant increases for key Bureau of Reclamation WaterSMART programs that provide water savings and ecosystem benefits for New Mexico and across the West.

Southwest Border Regional Commission: Heinrich successfully included $5.5 million for the Southwest Border Regional Commission (SBRC). Since joining the Senate Appropriations Committee, Heinrich successfully secured the first-ever congressional investments to finally allow the SBRC to start its operations.

National Labs: Heinrich helped include $8.4 billion for the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Office of Science, which supports both Sandia National Laboratories (Sandia) and Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL). Over the course of his tenure in Congress, Heinrich has helped double the total budgets for Sandia and LANL, significantly increasing the total employees and local economic impact of both labs.

Hexavalent Chromium Plume: Heinrich secured $20 million for addressing groundwater contamination by hexavalent chromium in the area surrounding LANL. Heinrich has consistently pushed the DOE’s Office of Environmental Management to clean up its legacy waste. Within that funding, $2 million would support the San Ildefonso Pueblo to remediate its drinking water, and $5 million would be provided to Los Alamos County to build a new water well in another location away from the chromium plume.

FY27 Legislative Branch Key Points and Highlights

At a time when maintaining checks and balances is more important than ever, this bill falls short of ensuring Congress can effectively serve the American people and hold the executive branch accountable. As Ranking Member of the Legislative Branch Subcommittee, Senator Heinrich does not support this bill, which fails to provide robust funding for the Government Accountability Office (GAO) and the Congressional Research Service (CRS), both of which are crucial to Congress’s oversight functions.

Safety and Security: The bill includes $965 million to support security operations for members, staff, and visitors to the Capitol campus. This funding allows continued recruitment and retention of sworn and civilian personnel.

The bill also provides authority to continue mutual aid reimbursements for state and local law enforcement, which helps cover costs incurred by state and local police departments when protecting lawmakers and congressionally sponsored events. And the bill responds to increasing safety threats by providing $75 million for enhanced member security for both the Senate and the House.

Government Accountability Office (GAO): The bill rejects House Republicans’ efforts to cut the GAO by over $200 million but falls short of providing adequate resources to support aggressive oversight of the executive branch. Funding for the GAO is crucial for protecting taxpayer dollars, promoting government efficiency, and providing rigorous, nonpartisan oversight that builds public trust. Additional funding is necessary to support audits of federal programs, review of expenditures, and analysis of federal resource utilization.

Library of Congress: This bill includes $878.5 million for the Library of Congress, including $19.8 million for programs including Teaching with Primary Sources, the Surplus Books Program, Veteran History Project, and the Lewis Houghton Civics and Democracy Initiative. This is a rejection of House Republicans’ efforts to rewrite American history and hide the truth.

matches.text:
Rep. Katherine Clark, the House Minority Whip who has represented Massachusetts’s fifth district since 2013, is poised to become the first woman to serve as House Majority Leader after the blue wave election propelled Democrats to control of the chamber in the next Congress.

“It is beyond exciting,” she told WCVB’s On The Record. “It is historic in that, as you said, the first woman in the 250 years of our country to hold this position, which is the second in seniority in the House of Representatives.”

Clark pointed out that the 120th Congress will also have a record-breaking 120 women in the House Democratic Caucus.

Leadership questions

The current House Minority Leader, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York’s 8th district, is also expected to make history as the first Black Speaker of the House when Democrats take control. While Democrats in the U.S. Senate are not sure about their future majority leader, Clark said the decision in the House is clear.

“Hakeem has been a steady leader for us through the four years of minority, not afraid to take on this administration or anybody who is cheating the American people, and he has delivered a huge victory,” Clark said. “Hakeem played a huge role in making sure that Democrats were poised to win this House by what is a landslide.”

When asked if Clark was aware of a groundswell of support pushing Massachusetts Rep. Ayanna Pressley to run for Speaker of the House, she praised the Boston Congresswoman’s work and said she will likely be an influential voice in the caucus.

“To my knowledge, she is not running for Speaker. But listen, I think Ayana is an incredible voice, and I think that, you know, we want to have robust debates about all of the agenda and how we can best meet this moment,” she said.

Clark told OTR that she, Jeffries and the party are working to set priorities for the next two years. She said that effort includes considering priorities from the progressive wing of the party.

“With a 260-person Democratic majority, we are going to have the ability to really focus on the American people, put them back on the agenda,” Clark said.

Clark said the American people can expect “quick action” from the Democrats to reverse cuts to programs that were made during the first two years of President Donald Trump’s term.

“That is what this election was about, making sure that they are not paying the price for corruption,” she said.

Impeaching Hegseth?

OTR also asked Clark about the 11 Democrats who missed a recent vote on articles of impeachment for Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. Republicans were able to shift the issue to committee, effectively blocking the effort.

“Did Democrats screw this up?” OTR’s Sharman Scachetti asked.

“Yes. You know, we have to take accountability for that,” Clark responded.

Clark went on to say that if he’s not “long gone by January,” the Democrats could try again.

“We have a huge job to do, and part of it is holding Pete Hegseth and the President responsible for this reckless war, and that is the work we are going to do in January,” she said.

Investigating former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang

Clark said that her party will “absolutely” lead an investigation into former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s reported affairs, including a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

Huang resigned from the company he co-founded this week.

“AI is on the minds of Americans and to have this kind of potential national security breach, where the Chinese are able to access these chips, is very, very serious,” Clark said. “So we will be bringing in Jensen Huang. We will be investigating this fully.”

Clark said the investigation would also extend to what Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick may have known about the case.

“Did they know about this, and did they try to cover it up?” Clark said.

Assessing the next Congress

Political analysts Mary Anne Marsh and Ginny Buckingham assess the path forward for Democrats in Congress and Clark’s expected new roles.

Marsh, a Democratic strategist, said she expects Clark and Jeffries to make history.

“It is very clear from the interview you guys did with her that affordability and accountability are No. 1 issues right there, and they’re prepared to go after it,” Marsh said.

While offering “kudos” for Clark’s accomplishments, Buckingham offered some words of caution from the Republican perspective.

“I also think this verbal gymnastics of saying, ‘Accountability and affordability are the same thing,’ People aren’t going to be fooled by that,” Buckingham said. “Voters aren’t stupid. Go for accountability, but own it.”

Marsh and Buckingham also discussed the political fallout following the conviction of former police officer Matthew Farwell in connection with the death of Sandra Birchmore.

This week’s political wins

Buckingham and Marsh shared their nominees for the most impactful political wins of the week.

—

matches.title: Congresswoman Escobar Leads Over 20 Democrats in Urging DHS Inspector General to Investigate Big Bend Border Wall Contracts
snippets:
duces Bill to Improve Port Staffing, Infrastructure Needs

October 21, 2026 | Posted in Press Releases

Congresswoman Escobar Statement on Fort Bliss Data Center Project Update

October 5, 2026 | Posted in Press Releases
matches.text:
Today, Congresswoman Veronica Escobar (TX-16) led a group of 22 other Democrats in a letter to U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Office of Inspector General (OIG) Joseph Cuffari urging him to investigate the nearly $7.5 billion in taxpayer funds for border infrastructure projects in the Big Bend Border Patrol Sector.

Joining Congresswoman Escobar (in alphabetical order) are Representatives Greg Casar (TX-35), Joaquin Castro (TX-20), Jasmine Crockett (TX-30), Lloyd Doggett (TX-37), Lizzie Fletcher (TX-7), Sylvia Garcia (TX-29), Dan Goldman (NY-10), Vicente Gonzalez (TX-34), Al Green (TX-9), Jared Huffman (CA-2), Julie Johnson (TX-32), Raja Krishnamoorthi (IL-8), Stephen Lynch (MA-8), Seth Magaziner (RI-2), Christian Menefee (TX-18), Dave Min (CA-47), Brittany Petterson (CO-7), Emily Randall (WA-6), Rashida Tlaib (MI-12), Paul Tonko (NY-20), Gabe Vazquez (NM-2), and Nydia Velazquez (NY-7).

The full letter can be found here or below:

Inspector General Cuffari:

We write to urgently request that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Office of Inspector General (OIG) investigate the contracting process, potential political influence, and award of $7.5 billion in taxpayer funds for massive border infrastructure projects in and around the Big Bend Border Patrol Sector in Texas, including Big Bend National Park.

On October 15, 2025, former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem waived virtually every provision of federal law “with respect to all contracting actions necessary for the construction of physical barriers and roads” in the Big Bend Sector of Texas. This was followed by additional waivers of environmental, historic preservation, and other laws that would ordinarily provide independent review of federal actions affecting more than 500 miles of borderlands. In addition to Big Bend National Park, one of the nation’s most treasured landscapes, these waivers also impact Big Bend Ranch State Park, Texas’ largest state park, and hundreds of miles of privately owned land.

Publicly available information raises serious questions about how these contracts were awarded, whether political relationships played any role in contractor selection, whether the circumvention of normal contracting and oversight safeguards was in the public interest, and whether the enormous expenditures are justified by an operational need.

The Big Bend Sector, and especially Big Bend National Park, encompasses some of the most remote, rugged, and waterless terrain along the southern border. Local law enforcement officials and elected leaders from across the political spectrum, as well as former National Park Service officials, have questioned the need for extensive physical barriers or other major border security infrastructure in this region.

The available data further raises questions about the justification for the waivers or these massive contracts. The Big Bend Sector includes 26% of the southern border, but CBP’s published data shows that in the 5 years that DHS used to justify these actions, it accounted for less than 1% of the apprehensions of migrants across that same border. The national park accounted for only 0.016% of apprehensions in the same period despite spanning 6% of the southern border. DHS’ own press releases cites that apprehensions in the sector have fallen sharply in recent years.

Nevertheless, DHS designated the region an "area of high illegal entry" with an "acute and immediate need" for border infrastructure. “High illegal entry” is a legal necessity established by the Congress under Section 102(a) of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act (IIRIRA) to allow the Department to waive legal requirements and expedite construction.

We believe the DHS Office of the Inspector General has a responsibility to scrutinize how the Department has made the decisions, and the impact of those decisions, regarding whether the area in question is truly an area of high illegal entry, whether the subsequently awarded contracts were properly issued (even in light of the waivers), and whether the resulting expenditures are in the public interest. The scale of the expenditures is enormous. Five contracts, totaling $7.5 billion, have been awarded in the Sector.

These contracts include:

$1.0 billion to Barnard Construction (BB1 Project)

$1.2 billion to Fisher Sand & Gravel (BB2 Project)

$960.4 million to Barnard Construction (BB3 Project)

$1.7 billion to Southwest Valley Constructors for work associated with Big Bend National Park. (BB4 project)

$2.6 billion to Fisher Sand & Gravel for work in the Lower Canyons region downstream of the national park (BB5 project)

These expenditures warrant scrutiny because of the contracting practices and political relationships surrounding some of the companies receiving them. Public reporting has documented substantial political connections involving contractors that have received significant border construction awards.

Barnard Construction Chairman Tim Barnard and his wife donated approximately $1 million to a Trump campaign fundraising committee during the 2024 election cycle. Barnard Construction has subsequently received billions of dollars in border construction contracts, including a $1.6 billion contract for approximately 112 miles of border wall in New Mexico that was awarded without competitive bidding based on an asserted need for urgency.

Fisher Sand & Gravel has also been the subject of previous scrutiny over political influence in federal contracting. During President Trump's first term, the company received a $400 million border wall contract after President Trump personally and repeatedly urged federal officials to consider Fisher for the work. Those circumstances prompted a Department of Defense Inspector General review. Public reporting has also connected Fisher to a consulting firm formerly associated with White House Border Czar Tom Homan. Fisher reportedly paid Homan's consulting firm as much as $186,000 while seeking border wall work. The administration has stated that Mr. Homan does not participate in the actual awarding of contracts.

These facts do not by themselves establish that contracts were improperly awarded. They do, however, create a strong public interest in an independent review of whether political relationships, communications, or influence played any role in DHS contracting decisions.

The processes CBP used to award these contracts lacked any transparency, and there has been no opportunity for public oversight of the contracts, or even for the public to understand the scope of the contracts.

A lawsuit brought by a competing contractor – that was subsequently withdrawn -

- alleged that solicitations for broader Texas border work were not genuine competitive opportunities and that winningbidders were subsequently required to perform work outside the scope originally advertised. When discovery was sought in that litigation, DHS moved to seal materials including depositions and affidavits.

At the same time, DHS and CBP have repeatedly changed their public descriptions of what is being built in the Big Bend Sector.

CBP materials initially showed a border wall through the region. The wall later disappeared from public maps, then reappeared. In May, CBP publicly stated that there would be no wall in Big Bend National Park. Approximately one week later, DHS awarded a $1.7 billion contract whose contracting records described work associated with a border wall in the national park. More recently, CBP has described construction inside the park as involving roads, technology, and vehicle barriers.

Taken together, these circumstances warrant an independent investigation. We therefore request that the DHS Office of Inspector General examine:

Whether political relationships, communications, campaign contributions, or other political considerations played any role in the selection of contractors or award of contracts for border infrastructure in the Big Bend Sector;

Whether contracts awarded for work in the Big Bend Sector were awarded through full and open competition and, where they were not, whether DHS properly justified the use of noncompetitive or expedited procurement procedures;

Whether DHS adequately evaluated the operational need, cost effectiveness, and alternatives before committing billions of taxpayer dollars to border infrastructure in a region with comparatively low and declining levels of unlawful crossings;

Whether the scope of work ultimately assigned to contractors materially differed from the work described during the solicitation and bidding process, and whether any such changes disadvantaged competing bidders or increased costs to taxpayers;

Whether any current or former administration officials participated in, attempted to influence, or communicated with DHS or CBP officials concerning the selection of particular contractors;

Whether DHS's waiver of environmental and other statutory requirements, together with limitations on public access to contracting information, diminished safeguards against waste, fraud, abuse, or mismanagement; and

Whether the contracts and expenditures associated with these projects comply with applicable ethics, appropriations, and other federal requirements.

Big Bend National Park is an irreplaceable public resource. Taxpayers deserve confidence that decisions affecting it and the surrounding region— and billions of dollars in federal spending — are based on legitimate public needs rather than political influence or private advantage.

We expect a written response to this letter with an associated timeline for an OIG investigation no later than November 27, 2026. We further expect that the findings of such an investigation be made public.

[WASHINGTON, D.C.] – U.S. Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Katie Britt (R-AL), and Cory Booker (D-NJ) today introduced legislation to ensure families whose children have been killed, sexually assaulted or exploited, or otherwise hurt by Big Tech’s online platforms can seek public accountability through the civil justice system. The Ending Forced Arbitration of Children Online Act would re-establish Americans’ Seventh Amendment right to seek justice and stop Big Tech companies from strong-arming families out of court and into closed-door forced arbitration proceedings.

“Our initiative addresses a monstrous failure in current law: Big Tech companies routinely force grief-stricken families into closed-door contests where they write the rules and evade responsibility for endangering kids online,” said Blumenthal. “Our measure ensures that parents and survivors seeking Big Tech accountability can go to court and seek justice.”

“When a child is harmed online, that family deserves their day in court should they choose, not a closed-door process dictated by an online platform and private arbitrators,” said Britt. “For too long, Big Tech has weaponized forced arbitration to shield themselves from accountability and keep the harm done to children out of public view. The results of this bipartisan bill will shine a much-needed light on the predatory practices of Big Tech and take meaningful steps to protect America’s next generation by ensuring that when a platform fails our children, families get to decide how they seek justice.”

“I’m proud to partner with Senators Blumenthal and Britt to introduce this legislation which would ensure that the families of children harmed online can hold mega platforms accountable in court,” said Booker. “Our children are vulnerable to serious harms online, from sexual exploitation, unsafe content, and manipulation by AI chatbots. Their families should not lose the right to seek justice in a courtroom just because companies inserted fine print in their terms of service forcing them into arbitration. We must hold companies that harm children online accountable.”

There are currently upwards of 180 lawsuits from across the country pending in federal court, and over 30 in state court, against gaming platform Roblox alleging harms that children have suffered including self-harm, abduction, sexual exploitation, rape, sextortion, grooming, and physical abuse. Roblox is systematically trying to force these children and their families into forced arbitration in an effort to evade legal accountability, arguing that a child who clicks “I Agree” to the terms and conditions on the gaming platform means that that child and their family should be forced out of court and into arbitration.

Another company, Character.AI (C.AI), tried to argue that the mother of a 15-year-old boy, who alleges her son died by suicide after C.AI bots repeatedly encouraged him to take his own life, was bound to the platform’s terms which required forced arbitration and included a maximum liability of $100, because her son “agreed” to the terms and conditions. The Ending Forced Arbitration of Children Online Act would render forced arbitration agreements like those used by Roblox and C.AI unenforceable.

The Ending Forced Arbitration of Children Online Act is endorsed by the National Center on Sexual Exploitation (NCOSE) and ParentsTogether Action.

“Digital platforms try to avoid legal responsibility by incorporating forced arbitration language into the terms and conditions that users – even children – agree to when they create accounts. Roblox and Discord are prime examples, and both of those platforms are being sued for causing harm to children. Families should be able to sue a digital platform for causing harm, not be forced into arbitration,” said Richie Hamm, President of NCOSE.

“Parents are already up against the most powerful tech companies in the world as they try to keep their kids safe online. When a child gets hurt, families should not also have to face those companies’ lawyers in a forced arbitration process. The bipartisan Ending Forced Arbitration of Children Online Act from Senators Blumenthal and Britt would protect families in this unfair fight by ensuring their access to the courts, which is a necessary step in holding these companies accountable,” said Alien Arreaza, Executive Director of ParentsTogether Action.

Bill text is available here.

WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Senators Katie Britt (R-Ala.), Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), and Cory Booker (D-N.J.) today introduced the Ending Forced Arbitration of Children Online Act, bipartisan legislation that would give families the right to take online platforms to court when a child is harmed, rather than being forced into private arbitration by terms of service agreements.

“When a child is harmed online, that family deserves their day in court should they choose, not a closed-door process dictated by an online platform and private arbitrators,” said Senator Britt. “For too long, Big Tech has weaponized forced arbitration to shield themselves from accountability and keep the harm done to children out of public view. The results of this bipartisan bill will shine a much-needed light on the predatory practices of Big Tech and take meaningful steps to protect America’s next generation by ensuring that when a platform fails our children, families get to decide how they seek justice.”

“Our initiative addresses a monstrous failure in current law: Big Tech companies routinely force grief-stricken families into closed-door contests where they write the rules and evade responsibility for endangering kids online,” said Senator Blumenthal. “Our measure ensures that parents and survivors seeking Big Tech accountability can go to court and seek justice.”

“I’m proud to partner with Senators Blumenthal and Britt to introduce this legislation which would ensure that the families of children harmed online can hold mega platforms accountable in court,” said Senator Booker. “Our children are vulnerable to serious harms online, from sexual exploitation, unsafe content, and manipulation by AI chatbots. Their families should not lose the right to seek justice in a courtroom just because companies inserted fine print in their terms of service forcing them into arbitration. We must hold companies that harm children online accountable.”

Many online platforms require users to accept arbitration clauses and class-action waivers as a condition of signing up. Those provisions can force families into private arbitration, even when the user is a child, and the claim involves serious harm.

The Ending Forced Arbitration of Children Online Act would give families the choice to go to court. At the election of the person bringing the claim, no pre-dispute arbitration agreement or pre-dispute joint-action waiver would be valid or enforceable in a case where the alleged harm relates to a minor’s use of a covered platform. The bill applies to cases alleging physical injury, mental or psychological harm, or a violation of privacy or misuse of personal data, whether brought individually or on behalf of a class.

The legislation applies broadly to the platforms children use. Covered platforms include any online platform, video game, messaging application, video streaming service, or artificial intelligence system that connects to the internet and is used, or is reasonably likely to be used, by a minor. This includes popular gaming platforms, such as Roblox.

Under the bill, whether the law applies to a dispute would be determined under federal law. A court, rather than an arbitrator, would decide whether the law applies to an arbitration agreement and whether that agreement is valid and enforceable. The bill would take effect on the date of enactment.

The Ending Forced Arbitration of Children Online Act is endorsed by the National Center on Sexual Exploitation (NCOSE).

“Digital platforms try to avoid legal responsibility by incorporating forced arbitration language into the terms and conditions that users – even children – agree to when they create accounts. Roblox and Discord are prime examples, and both of those platforms are being sued for causing harm to children. Families should be able to sue a digital platform for causing harm, not be forced into arbitration,” said Richie Hamm, President of NCOSE.

Senator Britt has made protecting children online a top priority since taking office. She leads the Stop the Scroll Act with Senator John Fetterman (D-Pa.), which would require a mental health warning label on social media platforms, and joined Senators Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) and Blumenthal in introducing the GUARD Act. She is also a cosponsor of the Children and Teens’ Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA 2.0), which passed the Senate unanimously in March, and the Kids Off Social Media Act.

The full text of the bill can be found here.

WASHINGTON – In an op-ed published by The Economist, U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, highlighted the need for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), explaining how the legislation will speed up the federal approval process for energy projects to get more power onto the grid, lowering electricity bills for Americans and creating more jobs – while codifying into law Tribal consultation, maintaining key environmental protections, and holding data centers accountable for their costs.

“In June, the largest clean-energy-infrastructure project in the western hemisphere came online in New Mexico. “The[SunZia] project took 17 years to permit and build—and SunZia isn’t alone. Across America, energy-infrastructure projects take far too long to permit… Indeed, permitting might be the economy’s most expensive bottleneck,” began Heinrich.

“America’s ability to meet the energy demands of the 21st century depends on its ability to build a modern, clean energy economy… That process is now standing in the way of getting new clean energy online and unlocking important economic investment,” continued Heinrich. “The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act—which the Senate voted to advance on November 9th and which I co-sponsor with another Democrat and two Republicans—does not remove environmental considerations, the ability to litigate projects or the ability for local communities to comment… But it does make these reviews a standardized part of a predictable process.”

“Modelling by Resources For the Future suggests that BAAJA could cause a decline in cumulative CO2 of about 1.8 gigatons—more than if the entire light-duty vehicle fleet was taken off America’s roads for a year—between now and 2041. Similarly, the Solar Energy Industries Association, a trade body, estimates that BAAJA’s adoption would mean solar and wind would provide 37.4% of America’s electricity generation in 2035, against 19.6% if the current permitting regime remains in place. These forecasts starkly illustrate the heavy drag America’s permitting regime places on the economy. For the nation’s future prosperity and security, it must be reformed,” concluded Heinrich.

Heinrich’s full op-ed is here and below:

A plan to end America’s most expensive bottleneck

By: U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee

In June, the largest clean-energy-infrastructure project in the western hemisphere came online in New Mexico. The SunZia Wind and Transmission Project’s 916 wind turbines now power over 1m homes. It’s a momentous accomplishment I was proud to help deliver, but it’s one that should have come a dozen years sooner. The project took 17 years to permit and build—and SunZia isn’t alone. Across America, energy-infrastructure projects take far too long to permit. The approval process can stretch on a decade or more, before a single digger has moved in. Indeed, permitting might be the economy’s most expensive bottleneck.

America’s ability to meet the energy demands of the 21st century depends on its ability to build a modern, clean energy economy. Its permitting regime tells companies what they can build and how: projects like transmission lines, pipelines, energy-generation facilities, manufacturing plants and transport infrastructure require multiple approvals from multiple federal agencies across several environmental and permitting statutes. That process is now standing in theway of getting new clean energy online and unlocking important economic investment. McKinsey estimates that more than $3trn in American economic activity is tied to infrastructure projects awaiting federal permits.

At the same time, America’s electricity needs are expected to grow dramatically over the next decade, threatening grid reliability, energy affordability and economic competitiveness. I see the effects of this growing strain on my constituents every day.

Fortunately, there is a plan for tackling these problems head-on, and it goes by the acronym BAAJA. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act—which the Senate voted to advance on November 9th and which I co-sponsor with another Democrat and two Republicans—does not remove environmental considerations, the ability to litigate projects or the ability for local communities to comment. Those are necessary. But it does make these reviews a standardized part of a predictable process.

First, BAAJA creates standardized timelines for these processes, from authorization decisions to public comment periods to litigation windows. BAAJA takes reviews that drag on and on—because there is no legally mandated timeline—and creates a predictable workflow. Legitimate environmental considerations, legal challenges and community input are protected, but those processes would be efficient. For both project developers and consumers, this means getting electrons on the grid faster, more cheaply and more predictably. A study by Columbia University estimates that BAAJA would save eight years for transmission projects, three years for solar projects, two and a half years for geothermal projects and about two years for offshore and onshore wind projects.

BAAJA also creates new policies that would benefit energy production. It codifies federal transmission planning so that different regions all plan together instead of separately. It bans right-of-refusal rules, which currently give incumbent utilities the first chance to build new regional lines—creating a more competitive marketplace. It opens wholesale markets and requires grid operators to allow aggregators to energize the grid, which would allow small-scale power sources like solar panels to connect to the grid in times of high usage. And BAAJA would make it financially costly and virtually impossible for an administration to block or undo permits on a whim, so worthwhile renewables projects couldn’t be shut down by a president overnight simply because he is skeptical of clean energy.

BAAJA is also the first federal legislation to meaningfully hold data centers accountable for their costs. The bill requires them to pay the costs of connecting to the grid, a burden American citizens are currently shouldering. By requiring electric utilities to charge data centers for transmission services, we can drive down transmission charges to other customers. Grid Strategies, an energy consultancy, estimates that $55bn in transmission costs could be collected from data centers over ten years under BAAJA.

Now, this is a bipartisan bill that demanded compromise. While there are strict timelines under BAAJA, deadlines should not be mistaken for lack of review. The requirement that infrastructure projects consider the environments and communities they affect remains. Environmental Impact Statements—detailed documents on a project’s potential environmental consequences— are given two years with BAAJA, still substantial time for consideration. The bill mandates consultation with Native American tribes and other communities that may worry about the impact of cutting “red tape” for a clean-energy transition; the current administration, by contrast, has threatened to eliminate those requirements.

And although it is true that BAAJA will make it easier to permit any kind of project, clean or not, the reality is that a huge share of the energy waiting to connect to the grid is renewable energy and storage. Modelling by Resources For theFuture suggests that BAAJA could cause a decline in cumulative CO2 of about 1.8 gigatons—more than if the entire light-duty vehicle fleet was taken off America’s roads for a year—between now and 2041. Similarly, the Solar Energy Industries Association, a trade body, estimates that BAAJA’s adoption would mean solar and wind would provide 37.4% of America’s electricity generation in 2035, against 19.6% if the current permitting regime remains in place.

These forecasts starkly illustrate the heavy drag America’s permitting regime places on the economy. For the nation’s future prosperity and security, it must be reformed.

WASHINGTON — U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, released the following statement in response to the Department of the Interior’s (DOI) new plan to sell off public lands:

“The Interior Department says it’s going to sell off lands that aren’t of ‘national interest.’ But anyone who lives in the West knows that some of our most beloved public lands don’t meet that definition. They’re the places where our kids have their favorite picnic spot, where we go fishing on the weekends, or where we hike with our dogs.

“There is nothing in our public lands laws that says a place needs to be of ‘national interest’ to remain in public hands. These lands belong to the American people — not private interests or corporations looking to cash in.

“I’ve fought before to stop efforts to sell off millions of acres of public lands, and I’ll do it again. I will keep fighting to protect all of our public lands — from Yosemite to the Organ Mountains to all the places with no line around them on a map that mean so much to the communities who know and love them.”

Background:

The Federal Land Policy and Management Act (FLPMA) authorizes the sale of BLM-managed public land only if the land is difficult or uneconomic to manage as public land and can’t be used be another Federal agency; if the land was acquired for a specific purpose and is no longer needed for that or any other Federal purpose; or if the sale will serve important public objectives that can’t be achieved “prudently or feasibly” on other land, and which outweigh other public objectives like recreation or scenic values. There is no authority to sell land based on whether they are “nationally significant.”

In addition, the proceeds from the sale of BLM land cannot be transferred back to the purchasing entities, as proposed in DOI’s strategic plan. The Federal Land Transaction Facilitation Act requires proceeds from BLM land sales to be used to acquire new public land for conservation and recreation.

The Department of the Interior does not have the authority to sell land managed by agencies other than the Bureau of Land Management without explicit Congressional direction.

As Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, Heinrich is leading the fight in Congress to protect our public lands, expand access to national parks, and hold the Trump administration accountable for its attacks on our treasured places — from efforts to erase history in our national parks to diverting funding to Trump’s vanity projects.

This month, Heinrich demanded answers from Bureau of Land Management Director Steve Pearce about the Trump administration’s push to develop AI data centers on public lands. Heinrich raised concerns about the administration’s consideration of at least 15 proposals spanning more than 17,000 acres across six Western states, emphasizing that public lands must be managed in the best interests of the American people and the communities directly impacted by development. Heinrich called on BLM to provide transparency about the authorities it is using to approve data center development, the projects under consideration, and the public lands identified as eligible for development.

In October, Heinrich successfully pressured Major League Baseball to abandon its proposal to host a professional baseball game in Grand Teton National Park. After Heinrich sent a letter to MLB Commissioner Robert Manfred urging the league to withdraw its proposal, MLB confirmed it would no longer consider Grand Teton as a potential site. Heinrich emphasized that national parks are no place for commercial sporting events and warned that allowing such development would set a dangerous precedent for future uses of public lands.

In September, Heinrich joined a bipartisan group of 153 lawmakers in urging the DOI to abandon a proposed transfer of federally managed public land within Yosemite National Park that would facilitate private access to and development of an 83-acre parcel adjacent to the park known as Hazel Green Ranch. During a U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee hearing, Heinrich criticized the Trump administration for its plan to exchange public land in Yosemite National Park for private development.

In September, Heinrich led his Senate colleagues in sending a letter to DOI Secretary Doug Burgum demanding that the Trump administration stop work on President Trump’s commemorative arch on federal property, which federal officials have admitted will harm historic sites on public lands, including Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial.

In September, Heinrich spoke in support of the Roadless Rule at a New Mexico Wild community event, encouraging New Mexicans to submit public comment in support of preserving the Roadless Rule. The public had until October 6, 2026 to submit comments on the Trump administration’s repeal of the Roadless Rule. You can read more about Heinrich’s actions to protect the Roadless Rule here.

In August, Heinrich led his colleagues in opposing the Bureau of Land Management’s (BLM) proposal to overturn the 2024 Waste Prevention, Production Subject to Royalties, and Resource Conservation rule (the 2024 Waste Prevention Rule). The move will increase pollution on public lands, reduce domestic energy supply, expose nearby communities to avoidable health risks, and waste publicly owned natural gas, costing Americans tens of millions in foregone revenue.

In August, Heinrich joined top Senate Democrats in sending a letter to the Government Accountability Office (GAO) Acting Comptroller General Orice Williams Brown to audit and assess the full scope and cost of the White House ballroom project.

In August, Heinrich sent a letter requesting that the DOI Deputy Inspector General Caryl Brzymialkiewicz investigate what Department officials knew – and when they knew it – about engineering failures at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and whether Department employees withheld evidence from federal prosecutors.

In July, Heinrich criticized legislation that removes protections for public lands, emphasizing the need for bipartisan collaboration within the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee. Heinrich additionally fact-checked Trump administration actions that undo protections for the Chaco Canyon Cultural Protection Zone. You can read about Heinrich’s actions to protect Chaco Canyon here and here.

In July, Heinrich sent a letter to DOI Secretary Doug Burgum and U.S Park Chief of Police Scott Brecht demanding answers and transparency about the U.S. Park Police’s new vehicle pursuit policy following news reports that an innocent bystander, Nolberto Armando Sanabria Meza, a 46-year-old food delivery driver, was hit and tragically killed in D.C. by a driver being chased by U.S. Park Police.

In June, Heinrich helped advance the America the Beautiful Act, bipartisan legislation introduced by U.S. Senators Steve Daines (R-Mont.) and Angus King (I-Maine) to reauthorize the National Parks and Public Land Legacy Restoration Fund, out of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee.

In June, Heinrich sent a letter demanding answers from DOI Secretary Doug Burgum about the Trump administration redirecting tens of millions of dollars from fees paid to the NPS to fund President Trump’s vanity projects in Washington, D.C. – including redirecting funds collected at New Mexico sites such as Carlsbad Caverns National Park and Bandelier National Monument.

In April, during a U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee hearing to examine the Trump administration’s Budget Request for the DOI Fiscal Year 2027 (FY27), Heinrich grilled DOI Secretary Doug Burgum about the Department’s draconian staff cuts at the NPS.

In March, Heinrich joined lawmakers in filing an amicus brief that would put a stop to President Trump’s plan to construct a commemorative arch on federal property. The amicus brief argues that the President’s plan is illegal unless Congress authorizes it.

In March, Heinrich led his colleagues in delivering remarks on the Senate floor in condemning and drawing attention to the Trump administration’s efforts to erase American history from public lands.

In March, Heinrich sent a letter to DOI demanding answers from the NPS following reports that NPS staff across the country are removing signage from national parks about slavery, Tribal history, and climate change.

In February, Heinrich led his colleagues in calling on DOI Secretary Doug Burgum to halt efforts to create the Department’s new U.S. Wildland Fire Service (USWFS), citing potential life-or-death consequences that could come as a result of decoupling wildfire management from land management agencies, and emphasizing concerns related to recent reductions in staffing, combined with improperly severing wildfire management from land stewardship.

Last December, during a U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Subcommittee on National Parks hearing to consider 26 pending bills, Heinrich criticized the Trump administration for removing fee-free admission on Juneteenth and Martin Luther King, Jr. Day.

Last October, Heinrich delivered remarks on the Senate floor, criticizing Republicans for pushing forward Congressional Review Act (CRA) resolutions of disapproval targeting BLM Resource Management Plans (RMPs) that would undo protections for national parks, including the Gates of the Arctic National Park and Preserve.

Last October, during the government shutdown, Heinrich urged the DOI Secretary Doug Burgum to classify the Department’s staff as essential during the Republican government shutdown to maintain the health and safety of Americans who visit public lands, wildlife refuges, and national park sites.

In June of 2025, Heinrich successfully fought Senate Republican provisions to sell off public lands in the Big Bad Bill, lead an amendment to prevent the privatization of our public lands, hosted a roundtable and sounded the alarm about New Mexico public lands that were at risk of being sold off by Republicans, continuously uplifted New Mexicans’ voices who called his office to raise their concern with Republicans’ plan to sell off these lands, and released a statement immediately criticizing Senate Republicans’ plan to sell off public lands following the release of the reconciliation text.

In June 2025, Heinrich blasted the Trump administration for its plans to transfer national park units to state control, criticizing the administration for “cutting off our access to public lands and devastating state economies in the process, overwhelming state budgets and dismantling the systems that keep public lands running.”

In June 2025, Heinrich grilled the DOI Secretary Doug Burgum over the Trump administration’s Fiscal Year 2026 (FY26) budget request for the Department, which slashes funding for national parks and guts staffing for the agency.

In May of 2025, Heinrich sent a letter to DOI Secretary Doug Burgum, demanding answers from the Trump administration regarding its plans to transfer National Park System units from federal management. The letter followed Heinrich’s questioning of Secretary Burgum during a Senate Interior, Environment, and Related Agencies Appropriations Subcommittee hearing, where Burgum failed to provide sufficient answers on the Trump administration’s plan to transfer hundreds of sites managed by the NPS to the states.

In January 2025, Heinrich’s Simplifying Outdoor Access for Recreation (SOAR) Act and Every Kid Outdoors Extension Act, which extends free access to national parks and other public lands to all American fourth grade students and their families through 2031, were signed into law as part of the Expanding Public Lands Outdoor Recreation Experiences (EXPLORE) Act. The broader bipartisan package bolsters outdoor recreation and promotes public lands in New Mexico and across the United States.

WASHINGTON –U.S. Senator Dave McCormick (R-PA) is fighting for bipartisan legislative efforts to strengthen export controls, protect sensitive U.S. technology, and safeguard critical infrastructure from foreign adversaries.

“America must win the AI race, and that means keeping our most advanced technology out of the hands of China and other adversaries,” said U.S. Senator McCormick. “I’ve been working with colleagues on both sides of the aisle to close loopholes in our export controls, protect sensitive American technology, and strengthen our cybersecurity. I recognized these threats early on, and we need to stay ahead of them to protect our national security and technological edge.”

[Watch a clip of Senator McCormick talking about the threat here.]

Senator McCormick has introduced bipartisan legislation to protect America’s technological leadership, strengthen cybersecurity, and safeguard critical infrastructure from foreign adversaries:

• Remote Access Security Act (December 2025): Introduced with U.S. Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR), the bill would extend U.S. export controls to remote access of sensitive American technology through cloud services, preventing foreign adversaries from circumventing restrictions on advanced AI chips.

• Rural and Municipal Utility Cybersecurity Act (August 2026): Introduced with U.S. Senators John Hickenlooper (D-CO), John Hoeven (R-ND), John Curtis (R-UT), and Catherine Cortez Masto (D-NV), the bill would strengthen cybersecurity protections for rural electric cooperatives and municipal utilities, including those serving communities across Pennsylvania.

• Securing National Security Systems from Chinese Optical Transceivers Act (October 2026): Introduced with U.S. Senators Ruben Gallego (D-AZ), John Cornyn (R-TX), and John Fetterman (D-PA), the bill would help prevent potentially vulnerable Chinese-made optical transceivers from being used in sensitive U.S. national security systems.

• AI Overwatch Act (April 2026): Introduced by U.S. Senator Jim Banks (R-IN) and cosponsored by Senator Dave McCormick. This bipartisan bill would strengthen oversight of advanced AI chip exports to prevent critical American technology from falling into the hands of adversaries like China.

[Watch a clip of Senator McCormick talking about the threat here.]
