PITTSBURGH — U.S. Senators Dave McCormick (R-PA) and John Fetterman (D-PA) joined Governor Josh Shapiro, Penn State University, and regional partners in announcing Pennsylvania’s formal proposal to establish the United States Space Academy (USSA) near Pittsburgh International Airport (PIT). The proposed academy would prepare the next generation of American scientists, engineers, and space leaders while building on Pennsylvania’s growing aerospace industry and advanced manufacturing capabilities.

“Pennsylvania has the talent, technology, and industrial strength to help America win the race for space dominance,” said U.S. Senator Dave McCormick. “Bringing the U.S. Space Academy to Pittsburgh would build on those strengths, create new opportunities for Pennsylvanians, and train the next generation of leaders who will ensure America remains the world’s leader in space.”

“As a proud member of the Senate Commerce Committee, I’m deeply committed to investing in NASA and its workforce, our national security, and making sure Pennsylvania is part of those important conversations,” said U.S. Senator John Fetterman. “Our Commonwealth has contributed significantly to the nation’s military readiness, space exploration, and preparing the next generation of leaders in those areas and more. I join my colleagues in supporting the continuation of that legacy as we push for Pennsylvania to host the U.S. Space Academy.”

“The Commonwealth of Pennsylvania powered the first industrial revolution nearly 200 years ago and made the arsenal of democracy the most powerful manufacturing base in the world. Pennsylvania is now uniquely positioned to welcome the United States Space Academy – building off our robust space industry and world-class research universities – to launch the next generation of America’s scientists, engineers, astronauts, and servicemembers and ensure America remains the global leader in space,” said Governor Josh Shapiro. “Pennsylvania’s application provides the federal government with an opportunity to strengthen and diversify America’s space industry. My Administration is all in and we’ve assembled a bipartisan team of Pennsylvania leaders who are committed to the Space Academy’s success here in our Commonwealth.”

The proposal calls for a new campus on 300 acres near Pittsburgh International Airport, with construction beginning in 2027 and the academy opening to 1,200 students by fall 2031. The campus could eventually accommodate up to 4,000 students, attract billions of dollars in public and private investment, and support thousands of jobs across the region.

Pennsylvania is already a major contributor to America’s space industry, with more than 550 businesses generating approximately $8.6 billion in economic impact over the past four fiscal years. The proposed academy would build on this foundation, drawing on the Commonwealth’s strengths in robotics, artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing, and aerospace technology.

Under the proposal, Penn State University and six other Pennsylvania research universities would help develop the academy’s curriculum. An interim campus at the former Pittsburgh Technical College would welcome the first 300 students in 2028, ahead of the permanent campus opening.

The bipartisan proposal was submitted in response to President Trump’s August 2026 executive order and a NASA request for information. If selected, Pennsylvania would become home to the nation’s first new federal service academy since 1955.

WASHINGTON, D.C. — Congresswoman Kat Cammack (FL-03), Chairwoman of the Republican Women’s Caucus, hosted child safety advocate Paris Hilton and members of the Republican and Democratic Women’s Caucuses today at the U.S. Capitol to push for House passage of the DEFIANCE Act. The bipartisan bill would give survivors of nonconsensual, sexually explicit deepfakes a federal right to sue the people who create and spread them.

After the conversation, Cammack, Hilton and House members from both parties walked down the Capitol steps together and held a press conference at the House Triangle.

“Anyone can become a target. It takes one ordinary photo to make a fake, explicit image that spreads faster than it can be taken down,” said Congresswoman Cammack. “The DEFIANCE Act lets survivors take the people who did it to court. The Senate passed it without a single objection, and it’s sitting at the House desk right now. Let’s get it done before this Congress ends.”

The DEFIANCE Act (H.R. 3562) is led in the House by Reps. Laurel Lee (FL-13) and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (NY-13), with more than 50 cosponsors from both parties, including Congresswoman Cammack. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-IL) and the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-SC) introduced the Senate companion, S. 1837, which passed by unanimous consent on January 13, 2026.

Cammack voted for the TAKE IT DOWN Act, which passed the House 409-2 and became law in May 2025. That law makes it a federal crime to publish nonconsensual intimate images, including AI-generated ones, and requires platforms to remove them within 48 hours of a victim’s request. The DEFIANCE Act would add a civil path for survivors to sue for damages in federal court.

Hilton helped drive passage of the Stop Institutional Child Abuse Act, which cleared the Senate unanimously and the House 373-33 before it was signed into law in December 2024. In January, she joined Reps. Lee and Ocasio-Cortez at the Capitol to call for House action on the DEFIANCE Act.

“Paris has spent years fighting for survivors, and she’s brought that same heart to this bill,” Cammack added. “We’re grateful to have her with us, and we’ll keep showing up alongside her until the DEFIANCE Act becomes law.”

“When I make a promise to survivors, I keep it,” said Hilton. “So I will come back to these halls as many times as it takes until the DEFIANCE Act is signed. Because the abuse hasn’t stopped, and neither will I.”

“The images may be fake, but the victims are real,” said Rep. Lee. “Their suffering is real, and their right to seek justice should be real, too.”

“To Representatives Sykes and Cammack and the Democratic and Republican Women’s Caucuses, thank you both so much for working together to ensure that Congress does not overlook an issue so personal to so many women and girls across the country,” said Rep. Ocasio-Cortez.

What the DEFIANCE Act does:

Lets survivors sue anyone who knowingly makes or shares a nonconsensual, sexually explicit deepfake, solicits and receives one, or holds one intending to share it.

Sets liquidated damages at $150,000, or $250,000 when the deepfake is tied to actual or attempted sexual assault, stalking or harassment, so survivors don’t have to prove a dollar loss. Survivors can instead seek actual damages, including the defendant’s profits.

Allows courts to order the images deleted or destroyed and to block further spread. Survivors who win recover attorney’s fees and costs.

Protects survivors’ privacy in court, including the option to file under a pseudonym.

Gives survivors 10 years to sue, counted from when they discover the violation or turn 18, whichever is later.

Works alongside existing state and tribal laws.

November 17, 2026
Press Release
WASHINGTON, D.C.
– On November 13, 2026, Congressman Chris Deluzio (D-PA-17) joined with the entire Pennsylvania congressional delegation to send a bipartisan letter to NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman supporting the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania’s proposal to host the U.S. Space Academy. The congressmembers write, “
The proposed site in Southwestern Pennsylvania, adjacent to Pittsburgh International Airport, offers 1,000 acres of publicly owned land for the permanent campus. Additionally, an interim nearby campus at the former Pittsburgh Technical College in North Fayette Township would allow instruction to begin as early as 2028.”
They continue,
“Pennsylvania offers an exceptional combination of industrial heritage, technological capacity, world-class academic institutions, and a growing commercial space ecosystem. Our Commonwealth is home to seven R1 research universities, alongside robust manufacturing, energy, robotics, artificial intelligence, and advanced computing industries.”
In closing, the Pennsylvania delegation writes,
“Together, these assets provide an unparalleled foundation for an academic model that connects rigorous education and world-class research with real-world technology and industry… Establishing the Academy in Pennsylvania would complement existing NASA and defense installations, broaden the geographic footprint of federal space activity, and bring additional industrial and academic capabilities to the national space enterprise.”

Above: Gottheimer Hosts Congressional App Challenge Showcase

HACKENSACK, NJ — Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5) hosted his Congressional App Challenge Showcase in Hackensack, celebrating the talent and creativity of local middle and high school students who designed and built original apps.

matches.text:
Washington, D.C. –Congressman Jerrold Nadler, Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on the Administrative State, Regulatory Reform, and Antitrust, argued the need to regulate artificial intelligence (AI) to protect authors, artists, and creators from intellectual property (IP) theft in his latest op-ed published by Billboard.

Earlier this month, Congressmen Jerrold Nadler, Jamie Raskin, and Hank Johnson submitted an amicus brief opposing the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) dangerous argument in favor of allowing AI companies to train their models on copyrighted work, including New York Times journalism, without compensation. The brief, filed in the Southern District of New York in In re OpenAI, Inc. Copyright Infringement Litigation, reminds the court that the arguments in DOJ’s brief violate the plain text of the Copyright Act, which does not contain any national security exception to allow private companies free and unfettered use of copyrighted materials.

Read Congressman Nadler's op-ed here and below:

Stolen (Not Super) Intelligence: Why Congress Must Stop Big AI From Ripping Off Creators

For over 30 years, I’ve had the privilege of sitting on the House Judiciary Committee, and one of my priorities has been to ensure that the most powerful companies are held to account for ripping off Americans. As we grapple with fast-moving technological change, lawmakers must be vigilant that new technologies do not create new socio-economic harms. Sadly, some of the largest and wealthiest AI companies are running roughshod over intellectual property (IP) rights. Far from being “super intelligence” — as President Trump calls it — when you look at how these models are trained, they can more fittingly be described as “stolen intelligence.”

There are currently dozens of lawsuits in the U.S. and around the world alleging that AI companies have violated copyright by training their models on millions of articles, songs, books, voice recordings, videos and other creative content without permission and without payment.

The outcome of these lawsuits will have far-reaching ramifications. Worryingly, Trump’s Department of Justice is trying to put its finger on the scale, siding with billionaires in Silicon Valley against the creative and cultural beating heart of America, made up of thousands of journalists, authors, artists, actors, songwriters and musicians.

Last month, the DOJ filed a brief in the New York Times v. Microsoft and OpenAI in support of Microsoft and OpenAI. The Times alleges that Microsoft and OpenAI copied millions of its articles to train ChatGPT. Recently unsealed court filings show that a senior Microsoft scientist privately described the practice as “an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions,” yet Donald Trump and his hand-picked lawyers argue that the clear evidence of market harm isn’t theft, but “fair use.”

While just one filing, AI developers everywhere may try to use the Trump Administration’s argument to defend the practice of mass intellectual property theft.

It’s not just the free press that’s under attack. Just look at the music industry. Suno, the most widely used AI music generator, is being sued by major record labels for training its model on their recordings without permission. Like OpenAI, Suno claims this is “fair use,” despite admitting in court that it trained on essentially all music files of reasonable quality accessible on the open internet. If the DOJ’s argument takes hold, Suno will have every reason to keep doing it.

We’re already seeing widespread market harm from Stolen Intelligence across the creative sector. Anyone streaming music has almost certainly listened to an AI-generated track without even knowing it. Most platforms are drowning in AI-generated slop, and AI makes it easier than ever for bad actors to perpetrate streaming fraud — which costs artists and rightsholders hundreds of millions, or even billions, each year, according to experts.

This causes real and disproportionate harm to artists and consumers. Every listen on an AI-generated track dilutes the share of streaming proceeds that go to human artists, from global artists to independent musicians hoping a viral song will turn a passion into a career.

Consumers are served an imitation without even knowing it, with one label, Sony Music, recently stating they have requested over 260,000 takedown requests of AI deepfakes of their artists and the epidemic becoming “an uphill struggle.”

Unless Congress draws a line in the sand, more and more companies like OpenAI and Suno will determine that they can rip off the artists, authors and creators that they rely on to train their models. We cannot let the Trump Administration give permission for mass IP theft by the back door. America can lead the world in artificial intelligence without building it on theft.

Stolen Intelligence is not an achievement; it is a liability, and Congress should treat it as one.

Congresswoman Chellie Pingree (D-Maine), the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Interior, Environment, and Related Agencies, is demanding answers from National Endowment for the Humanities (NEH) Chairman Michael McDonald about a recent NEH-sponsored conference in Rome, Italy.

The two-day, taxpayer-funded event at a Roman palazzo—which featured several controversial right-wing academics, including one with close ties to former Hungarian dictator Viktor Orbán—was not publicized by NEH in advance and recordings of the panels were only available on an Italian government website.

“The fact that NEH has not highlighted this conference itself raises even more questions about whether you would prefer this event was kept under the radar,” Pingree wrote. “But such a seemingly exorbitant trip requires transparency and accountability to the American taxpayer and justification for its purpose.”

Pingree, who is set to take the gavel of the powerful Appropriations Subcommittee that oversees the NEH, also criticized the agency’s decision to dismantle longstanding programs that served veterans, educators, and communities across the country, while funneling tens of millions of dollars to President Trump’s pet projects.

“I find it inexplicable that you would convene a conference—which has resulted in no specific policy or program—in a Roman palazzo while simultaneously eroding the reach and capacity of the Endowment to support everyday Americans,” Pingree said.

Pingree requested additional information about the two-day conference—as well as NEH’s travel budget and expenses—including documentation relating to travel costs and accommodations, the source of the funding within NEH’s budget for such a trip, a list of attendees, and a breakdown of NEH’s travel budget for fiscal years 2026 and 2027.

The full letter is available here and is copied below.

Last year, Pingree sounded the alarm over the Trump Administration’s unprecedented and legally dubious grantmaking practices, and called the integrity of the NEH into question.

+++

Dear Chairman McDonald:

I am writing to seek information regarding the concerning use of taxpayer funds for a National Endowment for the Humanities (NEH)-sponsored junket called “Classical Foundations and Moral Authority" at the Palazzo San Macuto in Rome, Italy.

According to The New York Times, the two-day conference featured nearly a dozen Anglophone academics, most of them conservative critics of universities, modern secular liberal democracy, or both. Speakers also included the president of a Budapest think tank closely aligned with former Hungarian President Viktor Orbán. Recordings of the panels were posted on an Italian government website, yet NEH chose not to publicize the conference in advance or while it was happening.

The fact that NEH has not highlighted this conference itself raises even more questions about whether you would prefer this event was kept under the radar. But such a seemingly exorbitant trip requires transparency and accountability to the American taxpayer and justification for its purpose.

Historically, NEH funding has reached thousands of towns and communities, supporting local organizations and providing access to humanities for all Americans. During your tenure, NEH has gutted funding for public programming in favor of large dollar sole-source grants. You have also canceled or significantly rolled back all programming for veterans, Humanities Perspectives on Artificial Intelligence, and educator professional development, among other topics.

Even more disturbingly, you are siphoning off tens of millions of dollars towards President Trump’s vanity projects, including his proposed Triumphal Arch, the Garden of Heroes, and other so-called beautification efforts in the District of Columbia.

Under your leadership, NEH has laid off more than 100 employees and unlawfully terminated more than 1,400 grants to support scholars, research institutions, and humanities organizations. I find it inexplicable that you would convene a conference—which has resulted in no specific policy or program—in a Roman palazzo while simultaneously eroding the reach and capacity of the Endowment to support everyday Americans.

Please provide a response to these questions and the requested information by December 17, 2026.

Provide all documentation related to this conference, including the purpose and a breakdown of costs, including airfare, lodging, per diems, honoraria, etc.

Provide the source of the funding within NEH’s budget that was used to support these expenses.

In your opening remarks at the conference, you express “profound gratitude” to the Wilson Center and its President, Natasha Jacome. Specifically, what support did the Wilson Center provide? Was it financial, and if so, provide a complete accounting of the funds.

Provide a list of attendees of the conference and the justification for each person whose attendance was covered by NEH or Wilson Center funding.

Provide a breakdown of the NEH’s travel budget for fiscal years 2026 and 2027.

Do you intend for this conference to be a one-time event, or recurring?

Sincerely,

###

WASHINGTON, DC – U.S. Representatives Nellie Pou (D-NJ-09), Marc Veasey (D-TX-33), August Pfluger (R-TX-11) and Zach Nunn (R-IA-3) introduced the Cybersecurity Clinics Grant Program Act. This bill would require the Department of Homeland Security, through the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, to establish a grant program to fund higher education-based cybersecurity clinics at community colleges and minority-serving institutions.

“Cybersecurity threats are growing more sophisticated every day. We need to make sure our communities have the tools and trained professionals to meet them,” said Congresswoman Pou. “I am proud to co-lead the Cybersecurity Clinics Grant Program Act which will help give the next generation of diverse graduates at community colleges, Hispanic-serving institutions, and other minority-serving colleges hands-on experience while strengthening our nation’s cyber defenses through these new cybersecurity clinics. This legislation represents a smart investment in our national security and in the next generation of cybersecurity professionals.”

“I am proud to work alongside Representatives Pfluger, Pou, and Nunn to help grow and diversify the next generation of young Americans in the cybersecurity workforce,” said Congressman Veasey. “The Cybersecurity Clinics Grant Program Act will help do that by ensuring that institutions of higher education, including community colleges and colleges minority-serving institutions, can have the proper tools they need to educate their students in this growing field.”

“Developing a robust cyber workforce is critical to our national and economic security. AI has become an incredible tool for identifying vulnerabilities, but it is also making attacks faster and harder to detect. We cannot defend the homeland without talented professionals who have the skills and know-how to recognize, understand, and stop these threats. Angelo State University, now an NSA National Center of Academic Excellence in Cyber Defense, is training students who protect West Texas cities, schools, and hospitals in real time through its Regional Security Operations Center. I’m proud to co-lead this bipartisan bill to expand on this model and build the cyber workforce that our national and economic security depend on,” said Congressman Pfluger.

“Cyberattacks are an increasingly serious threat to our national security, economy, and the small businesses that power communities across Iowa,” said Congressman Nunn. “As a former White House Cybersecurity Director, I know we need to train the next generation of cyber professionals today to stay ahead of tomorrow’s threats. Our bipartisan bill will help community colleges establish cybersecurity clinics that give students hands-on training and real-world experience while equipping small businesses and local governments with the tools to defend against cybercriminals. We’re strengthening America’s cyber workforce and putting those skills to work protecting the communities that need them most.”

This bipartisan legislation will help create the framework for a robust and strategic model that can help the U.S. shore up national security defenses domestically and globally.

matches.text:
At East Boston Town Hall, Congresswoman Calls for Medicare for All, Abolishing ICE, Reparations, Reproductive Freedom, Housing Affordability, and More

Pressley Has Called on Democrats to Meet the Moment by Delivering Bold, Transformative Policy in 120th Congress

Video (YouTube)

BOSTON –At a town hall in East Boston, Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley (MA-07) laid out her vision and priorities for the Democratic majority in the 120th Congress and solicited feedback from constituents about what policies she should fight for in a “People’s Agenda.” Congresswoman Pressley, who has always sought to model “cooperative governing,” was joined at the town hall by State Senator Lydia Edwards.

Congresswoman Pressley has consistently called on Democrats to meet the moment and use their new majority to pursue bold, transformative policies and aggressively pursue accountability for the corruption, cruelty, and harm inflicted by the Trump administration over the past two years.

In her remarks at the town hall, the Congresswoman outlined several policy fights Democrats should take on in the 120th Congress, including but not limited to:

Medicare for All and Healthcare Justice: Passing Medicare for All so no person or family goes bankrupt because they get sick, restoring funding for Medicaid, and renewing the Affordable Care Act tax credits Republicans let expire.

Housing Affordability: Building on the success of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act by further expanding affordable housing and investing in homeownership to ensure working families can afford to remain in the communities they call home.

Abolishing ICE and Immigrant Justice: Abolishing ICE, ending qualified immunity for ICE agents, and extending Temporary Protected Status for Haitian, Venezuelan, Salvadoran, and other immigrant communities.

Reproductive Freedom: Overturning the horrific Dobbs decision, passing the EACH Act to end the discriminatory Hyde Amendment, and expanding access to the full suite of reproductive healthcare, including IVF and contraception.

Racial and Economic Justice: Advancing reparations for Black America by passing H.R. 40 to address the harmful legacy of slavery and establish a federal commission to develop reparations proposals.

Affordability and Economic Justice: Passing universal childcare and paid leave, raising wages, investing in workforce development, and addressing the crisis of Black unemployment.

Peace and Human Rights: Ending Trump’s illegal war with Iran and passing the Block the Bombs Act to stop U.S. tax dollars from funding the Israeli government’s genocide in Gaza.

AI Regulation and Stopping Data Centers: Enacting a federal moratorium on data centers until comprehensive federal AI legislation and stringent environmental protections are in place, including the AI Civil Rights Act.

Rooting Out Corruption and Pursuing Accountability: Conducting aggressive oversight and pursuing accountability for the cruelty, callousness, and corruption of the past two years, including the economic harm done to families across our country.

A transcript of excerpts from the Congresswoman’s opening remarks at the town hall is available below and the video is available here.

Transcript: Pressley Lays Out Vision for Democratic Majority, Solicits Community Feedback on “People’s Agenda”

November 16, 202

East Boston, MA

…

Look, I believe that the election outcome was truly a cease-and-desist letter sent at the ballot. It was a condemnation. It was a condemnation and rejection of an anti-freedom agenda, a fascist administration that wants to control your body, that wants to control the books you read, that wants to attack the free press, that wants to criminalize free speech, that wants to disenfranchise you at the ballot box–that is an anti-freedom agenda.

So what happened on Election Day was a condemnation and a rejection of that anti-freedom agenda. It was not an affirmation of the Democratic Party, in my opinion.

And so the job is not finished because it was never a compelling enough argument for Democrats to simply say “we are not them.” We now have a responsibility to affirm who are we, and we have to move with boldness and with urgency because it is about keeping not only the trust of the people, it is about, again, advancing a people’s mandate and agenda in the People’s House.

And moreover, in my opinion, we’ve got to move quickly because I want us to get to the work of a trifecta in getting that executive. I’m excited about what we have, having that gavel back in the House and the Senate, but we have so much work to do.

And East Boston is not afraid of hard work. You know, I just want to say thank you, East Boston, for how you stand up every day for your neighbors. Everybody deserves places of safety and belonging and joy. And thank you for how you show up for one another. You have one of the most inspiring blueprints for what radical mutual aid really looks like. The infrastructure that you have stood up as a community and as a people, and so let’s just you know clap for the nonprofit and community-based organizations, the everyday people taking care of one another.

And so again as I think about this mandate for justice, a mandate for compassion, a mandate for progress, as I consider this powerful rejection of cruelty, callousness, and corruption by the people, as I think about the subpoenas will issue from the oversight committee on which I serve.

You know my priorities and what is top of mind for me in this moment is that we not operate from a place of incrementalism. I think the first thing we have to focus on is repair. So when you think about Medicaid cuts and SNAP and vouchers and all those things, so we have to do the work of repair and restoration.

And true enough, the Big Betrayal of a Bill, the Big Ugly Bill, the impacts of that will not really be felt until January 1, and they’ve done that on purpose because they knew the Democrats would likely be the governing majority, and they wanted us to wear that bill. We have to continue to remind people who are the architects of that bill, and we have to actively do the work of mitigating those acute harms, and that means working with boldness and urgency to do repair and restoration.

But in my opinion, yes, we can address affordability and accountability, and we can ensure, and we can ensure that we do not default to an unjust status quo.

…

Now, before I turn it over to Senator Edwards and your questions, again, I’m just going to take a few minutes to outline my priorities for this majority, so in no particular order:

Medicare for All. So we’ve already spoken a bit about healthcare and the cuts to Medicaid and Obamacare subsidies [that] have made coverage simply unaffordable for too many people. This is a top priority for me. As I said, I represent a district that’s deeply unequal, that has disparate outcomes across all issues, but including and especially when it comes to health. You know, people are tired of me saying the statistic, but I’ll keep saying it until it changes. From Cambridge to Roxbury, life expectancy drops by 23 years.

Okay, and because of the nefarious work that is private equity, I’ve lost Carney Hospital, St. Elizabeth’s, and other healthcare assets in my district, and so this is quite literally a matter of people’s lives. So the goal is Medicare for All, so that no person and no family has to go bankrupt because they get sick in the richest country in the world.

…

No one should be rationing, in the richest country in the world, rationing asthma inhalers and insulin, but that is exactly what is happening.

So, in this majority, my message is: don’t tell me what a majority is. Show me what a majority is. So don’t just talk about healthcare justice. Pass Medicare for All. Healthcare is a human right, and our policies should reflect that.

Secondly, housing. Housing is our most important infrastructure. It is a determinant for health. It is social and economic mobility. I serve on the Financial Services Committee. We have got to make housing more affordable. You all know people should not be spending more than 30 percent of their income on rents, and home ownership is farther, increasingly so, farther and farther out of reach. People are spending upwards of 80 percent of their income on rents. So housing costs remain one of the most urgent burdens facing working families. I know that is true in East Boston, certainly throughout the Massachusetts 7th. Rent is too high. Homeownership is out of reach. Too many families, quite literally, are one emergency away from eviction or homelessness, one illness, one death, one divorce, one layoff, one disruptive life event away. The majority of people in this country do not even have $400 saved for an emergency.

So this crisis impacts everyone: young people who dream of home ownership and seniors who want to remain in the community that they help build. It affects working families who are doing everything right and still finding that the cost of housing is becoming impossible to manage.

…

[W]e have to be exhaustive in our efforts to ensure that families can afford to live in the communities they call home. And Washington should be acting with urgency, and I will continue to advocate.

Okay, so Medicare for All, housing. Third, abolish ICE.

Now, as the kids would say, I’m not new to this, I’m true to this. While in 2026, it has taken the harm and the injury and the murder for many to understand that this racist, rogue, lawless agency cannot be reformed. I have been calling for ICE to be abolished since I ran for Congress in 2018. It is beyond reform, and you have experienced it here on the front lines. They terrorize our communities, kidnap our neighbors, kill people on the street with impunity. There is no reforming this lawless agency and Congress should not be funding their campaign of cruelty.

They are quite literally profiting off of people’s pain, and I have to say that this is two sides of the same evil for-profit coin. If you give a damn about mass incarceration locking up low-income and Black and Brown folks, the same corporations like GEO and CoreCivic that are incentivized to lock folks up in that way, are the same people financially profiting and incentivized to lawlessly disappear people, our neighbors from community to detain and to deport them. So those issues are closely connected.

So we must abolish ICE, and we have to end qualified immunity for ICE agents.

Okay, Medicare for All, housing, abolish ICE, and abortion access.

I will be co-chairing the Reproductive Freedom Caucus in the 120th Congress. We have to both restore, protect, and expand abortion access. Fight for full rights and freedoms is not completed, that does not include the fundamental right to reproductive freedom and bodily autonomy. Abortion care is healthcare, a fundamental human right. So we need to restore abortion protections and we need to expand them.

And this is what I mean about a reimagining, because even when Roe was the law of the land, because of racist and discriminatory policies like the Hyde Amendment, there were still many people that could not access health care. It prevented folks on Medicaid and other government-sponsored health plans from having abortion coverage. And so, not only do we need to restore Roe, we also need to repeal the Hyde Amendment. We also need to enshrine the right to contraception, IVF treatment, and ensure folks have access to the full suite of reproductive health care.

So I have a north star bill, which I think is actually very attainable if we have the political will and courage. And I have a mandate of the people behind me to get it done to advance my Abortion Justice Act, which would speak to all of these tenets. So again, very proud to serve as co-chair of the Reproductive Freedom Caucus.

Okay, making sure y’all are keeping up. We’re rounding out here, I promise. Okay, the good senator here already spoke about my commitment to extending Temporary Protected Status.

For those of you unaware, I do represent the third largest Haitian diaspora in the country. That is certainly a source of pride for me. In Congress, I do chair the House Haiti Caucus, and as was shared, because I love to do the work of consensus building, we built a broad coalition and used a rare procedural maneuver. And the House ultimately did pass my bill with bipartisan support: 10 Republicans and one independent. Because I will appeal to any person of conscience that is serious about doing this work, and that is how we were able to get that bill done.

So I will continue to champion this priority. Hundreds of thousands of lives are at stake here, including not just our Haitian neighbors, but our Salvadorian neighbors, right, Senator, Venezuelan, Syrian, Honduran, and also our Nepalese families. TPS holders are essential. They’ve built their lives here, strengthened our economy, and deepened the fabric of our communities. So let me say this clearly: the fight is not over. We will not abandon our friends to be sent back to countries that are quite literally a death sentence.

Okay, and then the last two tenets. Before turning it over to you, I’m just going to name them and just list them off.

Okay, child care and paid leave. The care economy is not a nice to have; it is a must have.

We have to end the war in Iran. The American people spoke loud and clear. They do not want this war to continue, so we have to heed their calls and end it once and for all.

Also, we need to block the bombs. Okay? Now look, the headlines have faded, but the Israeli government is still carrying out a genocide in Gaza. Starvation, targeting, the murdering of Palestinians is still happening in broad daylight, despite the so-called ceasefire in the region. So we have to continue to push to save lives, and for a true, just, and lasting peace, we can start by passing the Block the Bombs Act to stop our tax dollars from funding this genocide.

All right, y’all. I promise you, I’m rounding out, Senator. It’s just a robust agenda. It’s a robust agenda.

Okay, reparations. HR 40. It is one of the honors of my life. You may be unaware of this history, but an ancestor, may he rest in peace and power, the first black state senator in the state legislature, Bill Owens, was the first member of a state legislature to introduce a bill for reparations. That bill became foundational for legislation authored by the great John Conyers, a congressman from Detroit, who carried that mantle. He’s an ancestor. That mantle was then passed on to Congresswoman Sheila Jackson Lee of Texas. She is an ancestor, and when the congresswoman transitioned, they asked if I would pick that mantle up as a part of this broad coalition. It has been 40 years since that legislation, HR 40, was introduced, and it is high time we have a floor vote on that. There is momentum around the country for reparations to begin the process of reparative justice for Black America, and this bill would create a pathway toward truth, reconciliation, and accountability. It is even more important after two years of anti-Blackness on steroids by this administration, attacks on DEI, rising Black unemployment, especially among our federal workforce.

So black folks, especially black women, delivered this historic Democratic majority, and it’s time Democrats deliver for Black America reparations now.

Okay, and the last edict, I promise, is we have to stop the data centers. The groundswell has been loud and clear. It’s been incredible as I’ve traveled the country in places like Tennessee to see rural and urban folks coming together, coalescing around this issue. Now, look, I just have the honor of presenting on the main stage at Afro Tech. I am very clear that AI is here, but we need to create sensible guardrails and stringent environmental protections in place.

A community like East Boston knows what it looks like when that doesn’t happen. So, in my opinion, we should push for a moratorium on data centers until we can pass comprehensive federal and human-first AI legislation to regulate them and ensure that no town or city is bearing the environmental, economic, or health burden for the billionaire CEOs.

So I know that was a long list, but these are the fights that I’m prepared, the righteous fights, I’m prepared to take on, that have been informed and shaped by my being, you know, daily in conversation and in community, actively listening to all of you. And I’m eager to hear what else is on your mind.

matches.text:
Demands action as NYSEG, Central Hudson, and National Grid fail state audits four years in a row.

WASHINGTON, DC — Representative Josh Riley (NY-19) introduced the Utility Accountability Actto hold utility monopolies accountable for safety failures, frequent, prolonged outages, and poor customer service. Under Riley’s bill, an investor-owned utility that fails a state audit of its performance, reliability, or safety standards would owe each of its residential customers a $100 credit towards their bill.

The legislation follows the New York State Public Service Commission’s latest audit, which found that NYSEG, Central Hudson, and National Grid failed to meet minimum customer service standards for the fourth consecutive year, resulting in nearly $35 million in penalties for 2025 alone.

Those findings are consistent with what Upstate New Yorkers reported in a survey conducted as part of Riley’s investigation into local utilities. Of the more than 5,000 NY-19 residents who responded, 38% reported unexpected increases in their utility bills, 16% reported poor customer service, and 7% reported problems with their smart meters. And when residents turned to their utilities for help, two-thirds of those who reported a problem said the company never fixed it.

“Upstate New Yorkers are being forced to pay through the nose for electricity each month – but instead of using our money to improve service and upgrade the grid, the utility monopolies are sending record profits overseas. I’ve heard from folks struggling with blackouts, broken smart meters, bills that make no sense, and hours on hold. And more often than not, when they report a problem, it never gets fixed,” said Riley. “Enough is enough. If these monopolies can’t meet basic standards of service, they should pay Upstate New Yorkers back out of their own pockets.”

Under the Utility Accountability Act, state utility regulators would conduct annual audits certifying whether investor-owned electric utilities meet state performance, reliability, and safety standards. If a utility fails, it would be required to issue direct bill credits to residential customers starting at $100 in the first year and increasing by $100 for each consecutive year of failure ($100 in year one, $200 in year two, $300 in year three…).

To protect taxpayers and ratepayers, the bill explicitly prohibits utilities from passing the cost of the credits back onto residential customers — forcing corporate investors to absorb the full cost — and authorizes the Secretary of Energy to withhold federal assistance from state regulatory authorities that fail to enforce the bill credit orders.

You can read the text of the billHERE.

The Utility Accountability Act builds on Riley’s ongoing work to take on utility monopolies and lower energy costs for Upstate New York families. Riley has:

Joined the NYSEG and Central Hudson rate cases to fight their rate hikes directly, going head-to-head with the companies on behalf of Upstate ratepayers.

Introduced the Weatherization Enhancement and Readiness Act (H.R. 1355) to help families weatherize their homes, use less energy, and lower their monthly bills.

Introduced the Keep the Lights Local Act (H.R. 5487) to end foreign ownership of American utilities.

Introduced the No Bonuses for Utility Executives Act (H.R. 6590) to ban utility executives from cashing in on bonuses while they jack up rates faster than inflation.

Introduced the No Taxes on Utility Bills Act (H.R. 8350) so families can deduct the taxes and state surcharges tacked onto their gas and electric bills.

Introduced the Lowering Utility Bills Act (H.R. 8568) to stop utility companies from overcharging customers.

Introduced the FAIR Data Act (H.R. 9655) to make sure Big Tech’s data centers pay their own way instead of sticking Upstate families and small businesses with higher energy bills.

Introduced the Smart Meter Data Privacy Protection Act (H.R. 10284) to stop utility companies from selling your personal data collected through smart meters.

WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Representatives Suhas Subramanyam (VA-10) and Vince Fong (CA-20) have introduced the Promoting High-skilled Doctoral Talent (PHD Talent) Act, bipartisan legislation to speed up the process for students to obtain a Ph.D. in critical and emerging technology fields. This legislation will propel more American scientists and engineers into the domestic workforce, ensuring the United States remains a global technological leader that delivers life-changing breakthroughs.

The bill creates a five-year Department of Energy (DOE) pilot program that brings universities, National Laboratories, and private industry together. Students in these programs would get hands-on research experience, mentorship, and workforce training while earning an advanced degree in less time.

Congressman Subramanyam issued the following statement on the bill:

“Our country faces a critical shortage of scientists, engineers, and mathematicians. This bill shores up and strengthens our pipeline of researchers. This will in turn help the next generation of students make breakthrough discoveries in science, health, and technology, solidifying our country's leadership in these fields.”

Congressman Fong issued the following statement:

“America’s economy and national security depends on us having a deep bench of skilled, capable, and credentialed American workers. Whether it’s cybersecurity, advanced manufacturing, defense research, advanced energy systems, medical innovations, or other emerging technologies, we need more homegrown talent. The PHD Talent Act gives students in the Central Valley and across the country a faster, clearer path to the advanced degrees these fields demand.”

Specifically, the bill:

Establishes a five-year DOE pilot program, with Ph.D. fellowships, for accelerated bachelor’s-to-Ph.D. pathways in critical and emerging technology fields, including artificial intelligence, quantum science, semiconductors, cybersecurity, and advanced manufacturing, among others.

Supports partnerships among universities, National Laboratories, and industry for accelerated hands-on research and training.

Shortens the time it takes to earn a STEM Ph.D. while maintaining robust academic standards.

Directs funding to fields where DOE identifies a need for more domestic doctoral talent.

Ensures taxpayer-funded student support is reserved for U.S. citizens, U.S. nationals, and lawful permanent residents.

matches.text:
Armstrong Urges Senate to Pass Bipartisan Permitting Reform to Lower Energy Costs and Get America Building Again

SENATOR HIGHLIGHTS HISTORIC COALITION BEHIND LEGISLATION TO UNLOCK INFRASTRUCTURE INVESTMENT, PROTECT CONSUMERS, AND STRENGTHEN AMERICAN COMPETITIVENESS

WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Senator Alan Armstrong (R-OK) took to the Senate floor today to urge passage of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), highlighting the legislation’s potential to lower energy costs, unlock private investment, and modernize America’s infrastructure without new taxpayer subsidies or weakening environmental protections.

Drawing on his decades of experience building energy infrastructure in the private sector, Armstrong emphasized that America’s rising utility costs are driven in part by the nation’s inability to build the infrastructure needed to connect abundant domestic energy resources to growing consumer demand.

“Everyone in Washington talks endlessly about affordability. Permitting reform is one of the very few practical solutions that delivers real cost relief to consumers and unlock investment without requiring a major new federal spending program,” Armstrong said.

Armstrong praised the bipartisan work of Senators Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Mike Lee (R-UT), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), and Martin Heinrich (D-NM), whose leadership helped bring together years of legislative work into a comprehensive permitting reform agreement.

The Senator emphasized three central benefits of the legislation:

Lower energy costs for American families. Streamlining infrastructure development would help connect affordable, reliable energy to consumers while requiring new data centers to bear the costs of grid upgrades associated with their facilities, protecting existing utility customers from those expenses.

More investment without new taxpayer subsidies. The legislation would reduce regulatory delays and litigation uncertainty, encouraging private capital investment in energy, manufacturing, mining, and other critical infrastructure while maintaining existing environmental protections.

A stronger, more competitive America. Modernizing the nation’s permitting system would help keep investment in artificial intelligence, critical minerals, energy production, and advanced manufacturing in the United States rather than driving those opportunities overseas.

Armstrong underscored the extraordinary breadth of the coalition supporting the legislation, bringing together traditional and renewable energy industries, labor unions, manufacturers, infrastructure developers, and other stakeholders that have historically disagreed over federal energy policy.

“We have accomplished something truly unprecedented: we’ve gotten the renewables industry, the fossil fuel industry, hydropower, and mining to all stick together and support this legislation,” Armstrong said.

“This broad alignment has held together because this bill does not pick winners and losers, it does not grant subsidies, and it does not compromise our environmental protections,” he continued.

The Senator also warned that failing to enact meaningful permitting reform would threaten American leadership in emerging technologies and push major investment opportunities to foreign competitors.

“If we fail to get this bill passed, the immediate reality is that we are going to start shipping our most critical economic opportunities overseas,” Armstrong said.

Closing his remarks, Armstrong called on his Senate colleagues to seize a rare opportunity to deliver lasting reform.

“After ten years of endless debate, we finally have industry, labor, and a broad bipartisan coalition aligned; if we don’t seize this moment now, I frankly don’t know when anyone will ever have the momentum or appetite to fix permitting in this country again.”

WASHINGTON — U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, highlighted his Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), legislation to lower energy bills, hold data centers accountable, reduce emissions, and create good-paying jobs, during an interview with The Hill’s Alex Bolton.

“We can make a big difference in people's energy costs — particularly their electric bill. And there's a real desire by the American people just for us to do our jobs and produce actual results for them, and not be, you know, pulled around by the extreme voices in, in any debate,” said Heinrich.

U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, highlights his Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act during a sit-down interview with Alex Bolton, Senate congressional reporter for The Hill, November 17, 2026.

On BAAJA Lowering Energy Costs:

Alex Bolton: “I get the sense that there's real, you know, pent up demand to actually do something to pass legislation that makes an impact, and that's what we're seeing right now with these big votes.”

Senator Heinrich: “I think [there’s] just a desire to actually do things. You know, nothing's going to be perfect, but obviously the last election was prosecuted on the necessity of giving people some relief from the inflation and the higher prices that are just driving the conversation with normal Americans everywhere in the country. And this is one of the places where we can make a difference. We can make a big difference in people's energy costs, and particularly their electric bill. And there's a real desire by the American people just for us to do our jobs and produce actual results for them, and not be, you know, pulled around by the extreme voices in, in any debate.”

Bolton: “The Rhodium Group estimates the bill will reduce household electricity bills by $50 to $70 a month by the year 2040. Are you looking at that assessment? How big of an impact do you think this will have on families' energy bills over the next five to 10 years? Can you put a number on it?”

Heinrich: “I think their estimate is as good as any [estimate] I've seen. I think the principle here is that we need to put more cheap electrons onto the grid a whole lot faster, and right now we have literally almost 2,000 gigawatts of generation sitting in interconnection queues for an average of over six years, just waiting in line. That's not the permitting side of things. That's just the waiting in line to plug into the grid side of things, so we make that much faster and easier in this legislation. We make permitting faster, and so we're going to be able to put more cheap, clean electrons onto the grid, and that is the only way we're going to reverse this trend of electricity just getting more and more and more expensive.”

On Potential Amendments to BAAJA:

Bolton: “I understand there are negotiations on amendments. You're working on a manager's amendment...What changes do you think will be included in the manager's amendment? I know this requires consensus, but what do you think is most likely to be included in that amendment, or what other amendments do you think are likely to get votes before the end of the week?”

Heinrich: “There are a number of amendments around the Tribal provisions in the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA). I think those are helpful. You know, we'll release something as soon as we can. But as you can imagine, in terms of a manager's amendment, it requires four corners agreement. And those changes will be relatively modest because it requires the chairs and ranking members of both committees.

On Heinrich's Work to Codify Tribal Consultation in BAAJA:

Heinrich: “I think one of the things that's important to recognize with the Tribal provisions in the NHPA is what our actual choices are, because this administration was moving forward on a process that would have effectively replaced Tribal consultation with a 30-day comment period. And I can't overstate how problematic that would be, because what works in consultation, having been through a lot of projects in my state that require Tribal consultation, is when an agency sits down with a Tribe, and there is an actual conversation, and that deconflicts a project away from places that are problematic, places that we want to protect historic and cultural sites and landscapes. And so, we need that to be a robust process. And one of the things I like about this legislation is that we were actually able to incorporate in the manager's package a statutory requirement for the agencies to consult at each of the steps in the NHPA, and so that's actually a big step forward. But because of where we started with the administration and the Tribes, I don't think that has fully been recognized yet. Like, what an improvement to the process that will be for Tribal governments.”

On BAAJA Expediting the Approval of Clean Energy Projects:

Bolton: “You've talked about and written about the SunZia project, the largest clean energy infrastructure project in the Western Hemisphere, in New Mexico. More than 900 wind turbines. It took 17 years to permit and build. If BAAJA becomes law, what kind of impact would it have on a project like that – in terms of how long it takes?”

Heinrich: “My guess is that project could have probably been completed in five or six years as opposed to seventeen. That's a big, big difference, and, you know, that's a project that I would argue was one of the best-designed projects because the developers actually listened. They avoided the places I warned them were, you know, were to be avoided for other values. We are a big public land state. People love their wilderness and their wilderness study areas, their refuges, and so they were very smart about how they designed the transmission route. It was a clean energy project. They came in and they actually protected a bunch of habitat in order to compensate for the impacts that building has. And yet, if you have all the boxes checked, like this is one of the best-designed projects that I've had to engage with, and it still took 17 years. You know, something's wrong. And biggest project labor agreement in the history of the Southwest, $20 billion worth of economic impact to the states of New Mexico and Arizona. We should be able to get to yes for a good project in a reasonable amount of time. We should be able to get to no for a poorly designed project. And if you're going to get to no, let's fail fast and then move on to a better project.”

On Heinrich’s Priorities as the Incoming Chairman of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee:

Bolton: “With a new Democratic majority coming in, what changes do you want to further empower committees? Because I think the lesson from this is that when you empower the committees and you empower the Chairman, there's bipartisanship and things get done. How do you take that lesson going forward into the next Congress?

Heinrich: “I think we do better work when committees are empowered, and so one of the things I want from leadership on both sides is to let their Chairman negotiate and get to actual good legislation. I think the more power that is pushed down to the committees, who have the most knowledge of how to come up with a good product, the more that benefits our ability to produce a better product.”

“We should hold AI to the same standard we have held other dangerous technologies: the more dangerous it is, the tighter the controls.”

Today, Arizona Senator Mark Kelly unveiled A Safety and Security Framework for Frontier AI, a plan to protect Americans from risks posed by the most advanced AI models. The framework draws on decades of experience and isbased on how America already treats risks like nuclear materials and weapons systems. It would establish clear safety standards for powerful AI models, deploy independent examiners to assess national security risks and evaluate companies’ safeguards as models are developed, and require rigorous testing and accountability for AI used in military operations.

“I’ve spent my career around powerful technology: fighter jets, spacecraft, weapons systems. The rule has always been simple: the more dangerous it is, the more carefully you check it. AI should be no different. This framework makes sure the companies building the most powerful AI systems are held to the same standards we expect everywhere else when national security is on the line,” saidKelly.

Kelly’s framework comes as whistleblowers from top frontier AI companies warn of the risks of unchecked acceleration of AI technology and following the Hugging Face attack where a powerful OpenAI model broke out of its controlled environment, exploited security vulnerabilities, and hacked into a separate AI company without being instructed to do so. He warns of the risks of advanced AI models being misused for cyberattacks or the development of weapons, all of which could harm Americans.

The framework points to three problems: there is no common measuring stick for when a model becomes dangerous, companies oversee themselves with outside review only after the fact, and AI models used by the military lack standardized acquisition and deployment requirements.

In the framework, Kelly lays out why the governmenthas tostep in: “The same advanced AI models that could help cure deadly diseases can also help someone develop biological weapons or launch devastating cyberattacks. Yet today, companies are deciding for themselves which models are dangerous and how much protection is enough. Too often companies act in the best interest of their bottom line, not the safety of the American people […] We can’t wait until Americans are harmed to act.”

The framework answers with three pieces that build on each other: a rulebook, a referee, and accountability. Standards define the safeguards needed to address AI risks, independent examiners identify national security threats as models are developed, and new defense acquisition rules require rigorous safety testing and hold contractors accountable for hiding or neglecting known risks.

Kelly also pushes back on the idea that the federal governmentshouldn’tstep in to protect Americans: “Some will believe that the federal government can’t — or shouldn’t — take on this problem. They seem to have lost faith that we can do hard things. Looking at how we have handled other dangerous, rapid innovations in the past, one thing is clear: It’s not a question of if we have the power to do big, hard things and protect the American people — it’s if we have the courage.”

Kelly’s framework draws on his experience as a Navy pilot and astronaut, and his national security oversight on the Senate Armed Services and Select Intelligence Committees. It also builds on Kelly’s leadership in AI.

Last year, Kelly released AI for America, a roadmap outlining principles to make AI work for all Americans—not just large companies. In September, Kelly introduced the Make AI Work for Americans Act to require the companies benefitingmost from AI to pay into a federal fund that invests in American workers. Kelly has also introduced bills to improve research on how AI is changing the workforce, secure America’s AI systems from foreign adversaries, preserve human judgment and accountability as the military integrates AI with two bills included in this year’s Senate NDAA, study how AI affects older Americans, and protect seniors from deceptive AI chatbots.

Washington, D.C. — U.S. Senators Adam Schiff, Alex Padilla (both D-Calif.), Ron Wyden, Jeff Merkley (both D-Ore.), Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), and Ed Markey (D-Mass.) launched an inquiry into the Trump Administration’s politically motivated campaign against state Medicaid programs, after the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) withheld billions of dollars from Democratic-led states while dismantling the federal infrastructure designed to detect and prevent fraud.

In their letter to CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, the Senators explained that CMS attacks on state Medicaid programs have undermined fraud-prevention infrastructure within the federal government and targeted Democratic-led states.

“The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services is running the most aggressive public enforcement campaign against state Medicaid programs in the agency’s history, while accelerating the systematic dismantling of the federal infrastructure Congress funded to prevent Medicaid fraud in the first place,” the lawmakers wrote. “That is not program integrity. That is political theater layered over a decade of neglect, with states across the country, and in particular, an overwhelming number of Democratic-led states that have become the Trump administration’s targets, left to answer for both.”

The letter comes as the Trump Administration has threatened state health programs with severe funding cuts based on flawed data. CMS recently moved to withhold billions in funding from California and Minnesota without providing any evidence of wrongdoing to the states. At the same time, the Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General (HHS OIG) decertified state Medicaid Fraud Control Units (MFCUs) in Hawaii and New York. Public reporting, including an investigation by the Associated Press, revealed that the Administration’s fraud claims against New York relied on a basic math error, while other withholding actions have sparked lawsuits from states like Minnesota.

Rather than working with states to fix issues, CMS has replaced on-site reviews and dedicated oversight staff with a public relations “War Room” and artificial intelligence pilots. The letter points out that the Administration is violating federal law by failing to maintain the minimum required funding and staffing levels for the Medicaid Integrity Program, which was created by Congress to help states fight fraud.

Full text of the letter is available here and below:

Administrator Oz:

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) is running the most aggressive public enforcement campaign against state Medicaid programs in the agency’s history, while accelerating the systematic dismantling of the federal infrastructure Congress funded to prevent Medicaid fraud in the first place. That is not program integrity. That is political theater layered over a decade of neglect, with states across the country, and in particular, an overwhelming number of Democratic-led states that have become the Trump administration’s targets, left to answer for both.

Since you were confirmed as Administrator, you sent all 50 governors letters demanding provider revalidation on a ten-business-day clock. You moved to withhold more than $2 billion annually in federal Medicaid funds from Minnesota without providing the State any details on its alleged noncompliance, and then issued successive deferral actions in February, April, and July 2026 totaling more than $500 million in additional federal Medicaid funds. In successive deferral actions in May, July, and October 2026, you also withheld more than $3.4 billion in federal Medicaid funds tied to California’s In-Home Supportive Services program and personal care services, citing nothing more than California’s growth rate relative to other states, with no specific evidence of wrongdoing.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General (HHS OIG) has decertified Hawaii and New York’s Medicaid Fraud Control Units and placed all 53 Medicaid Fraud Control Units (MFCUs) under review. Though most MFCUs are housed within state Attorneys General offices, all serve as the primary mechanism for prosecuting Medicaid provider fraud; consequently, decertifying them in the name of fighting fraud is self-defeating. Moreover, while statutory oversight of MFCUs rests with HHS OIG, the CMS Center for Program Integrity (CPI), whose statutory role is to serve as the federal bridge to state MFCUs so that state Medicaid program integrity units work in partnership with and refer cases to their respective MFCUs, has provided no visible support to states navigating this review. During New York’s decertification, it appears that CPI provided no technical assistance or support to the program integrity unit, leaving state investigators without a functioning federal pathway. Instead, you have launched a Medicaid Fraud “War Room” that your Deputy Administrator publicly calls “what modern program integrity looks like.” Modern program integrity should start with meeting the mandates Congress already wrote into law.

Medicaid program integrity has been under-resourced across administrations. That is precisely why Congress established the Medicaid Integrity Program (MIP) in the Deficit Reduction Act of 2005 and imposed a statutory floor of no less than $75 million and no fewer than 100 full-time employees (FTEs) dedicated annually to working collaboratively with states to fight Medicaid provider fraud and abuse. At the same time, Congress enacted mandatory federal technical assistance, on-site state reviews, and analytical support to states. Those obligations are not discretionary, and CMS cannot treat dedicated funding as optional funding or repurpose it at will.

The Trump administration and CMS under your leadership are not meeting these binding statutory obligations. Instead, you are hollowing out MIP under the guise of enforcement and compounding institutional failures:

The Division of Fraud Research and Detection, the only CMS division dedicated exclusively to Medicaid analytics, which maintained direct data feeds from approximately sixteen states’ Medicaid Management Information Systems (MMIS), was eliminated in the 2015 CPI reorganization. The defining failure of the current era is that these vital tools were never rebuilt, allowing what was once a temporary reorganization to harden into a permanent blind spot.

Comprehensive on-site State Program Integrity Reviews have been replaced with remote “Focused Reviews” issuing non-binding “Observations.” CMS no longer tells states what to fix; it tells states what to consider. Until this administration, even as the MIP infrastructure weakened, CMS and states maintained a working collaborative relationship on program integrity – sharing data, issuing joint fraud alerts with HHS OIG, and working through disallowances backed by evidence. That collaborative posture has been replaced by performative enforcement.

The Medicaid Integrity Institute’s residential training at the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) Ernest F. Hollings National Advocacy Center (NAC), CMS’s flagship in-person training for state program integrity staff, has been eliminated in favor of an all-virtual calendar. State program integrity directors have asked, in every available forum, for the in-person peer-led instruction to return, and CMS has refused. Public reporting and CMS’s own training calendars indicate the Institute has been reduced to a handful of virtual webinars per year and a few regional in-person listening sessions with State Medicaid Agencies and MFCUs between July and November 2026.

Publicly reported accounts indicate the federal workforce dedicated exclusively to Medicaid program integrity has fallen dramatically below the 100-FTE floor Congress set.

CMS state liaisons, fraud alerts issued jointly with HHS OIG, State Medicaid Director letters on program integrity, and the Annual Summary Report of Program Integrity Reviews have all been eliminated or discontinued.

An enforcement campaign built on gutted infrastructure produces shoddy results. On April 10, 2026, news reports revealed that CMS acknowledged its fraud probe of New York Medicaid rested on a figure that was off by a factor of ten – a basic mathematical error in calculating annual unique beneficiaries that independent analysts traced to a fundamental misunderstanding of how Medicaid data is counted. The administration publicly shared whatever figures served its political purposes, and the resulting mistake was then used to threaten a state. California has faced a separate but equally troubling pattern: CMS has imposed federal payment deferrals that have now accumulated to more than $3.4 billion, with California’s Medicaid director publicly rejecting the validity of CMS’s claims and stating that CMS has provided no evidence supporting the deferrals. Minnesota has gone further and filed suit against CMS, HHS, you, and Secretary Kennedy over the attempted withholding of $243 million in Medicaid payments, alleging that CMS imposed the withholding, without informing the state, despite it asking repeatedly, how it was noncompliant or what corrective steps were required.

CMS is putting on theatrics about going after states to “crush fraud” without any legitimate data to back up their claims, all the while starving the federal office Congress created to help states prevent those failures. A fake war room is not a substitute for a Medicaid integrity program that meets its statutory obligations. Contracting Medicaid analytics out to General Dynamics Information Technology (GDIT), the current Trusted Third Party for the Healthcare Fraud Prevention Partnership (HFPP), a multi-payer public-private partnership, is also not incompliance with a statute that requires Medicaid-dedicated federal capacity.

On October 15, 2026, your Deputy Administrator announced at an industry conference that CMS is piloting artificial intelligence to flag suspicious Medicaid billing patterns “in near real-time before Medicaid payments are made,” with the stated goal of scaling the pilots into a “national, standardized, continuously improving platform.” CMS does not, however, operate the claims systems that generate the underlying data. In fee-for-service Medicaid, state agencies adjudicateclaims; in managed care, Medicaid Managed Care Organizations do. CMS receives Medicaid claims and encounter data on a lag, and the federal pre-payment analytical capacity that could plausibly support such a platform is precisely the capacity CMS dismantled. Congress is entitled to understand what data CMS actually has, how it is obtaining it, and under what legal authority, before any such platform is scaled nationally.

Therefore, to assess CPI’s current compliance with Section 1936 of the Social Security Act (the Act) and the fiscal accounting of the MIP appropriation, I request the following documents and information by November 27, 2026:

For each fiscal year from FY 2015 through the present, please provide the number of filled federal FTE coded exclusively to the MIP appropriation, reconciled to the 100-FTE statutory floor under Section 1936 of the Act. To the extent the workforce has fallen below the statutory floor in any fiscal year, please provide CMS’s legal justification for its noncompliance.

Please provide SF-133 quarterly budget execution reports for the MIP Treasury Account Symbol for FY 2020 through FY 2025, including unobligated balances brought forward each fiscal year.

Please identify any MIP-appropriated funds obligated since FY 2015 for Medicare activities, shared CMS overhead, non-Medicaid purposes, or Medicaid beneficiary eligibility verification (as distinct from the statutorily specified provider fraud and abuse purpose), together with CMS’s legal justification for those obligations under the Purpose Statute, the Anti-Deficiency Act, and the Miscellaneous Receipts Act, given that MIP is a mandatory appropriation with a specific statutory purpose.

Please provide the methodology for, and actual allocation of, Unified Program Integrity Contractor costs between the MIP appropriation and Medicare appropriations from FY 2020 through the present, with Medicaid-specific deliverables identified for each fiscal year.

Please provide, for each fiscal year from FY 2015 through the present, (a) MIP funds obligated to the Medicaid Integrity Institute residential training program housed at the DOJ NAC, including all deobligations and modifications of the CMS-DOJ interagency agreement, (b) actual institute expenditures by fiscal year, with a breakdown of in-person training expenditures, virtual training expenditures, and non-training expenditures (including per-class costs and number of classes offered) and (c) documentation of how funds no longer obligated for in-person training have been reallocated.

Please identify any current, planned, or forecasted contract action, modification, or statement of work moving Medicaid Integrity Institute functions, including training logistics, curriculum development, state travel administration, or data analytics, to a contractor, including but not limited to GDIT. For any such action, please provide (a) the proposed and executed contract value compared to historical institute operating costs under the DOJ interagency agreement; (b) the methodology for allocating contractor labor hours and overhead between MIP-funded Medicaid-exclusive activities and HFPP funded multi-payer activities; (c) CMS’s legal analysis under the Purpose Statute, the Anti-Deficiency Act, and the Miscellaneous Receipts Act of using MIP’s Medicaid restricted mandatory appropriation to fund any multi-payer or non-Medicaid-exclusive activity; and (d) the current status of the CY 2027 MII training calendar, including whether its publication is dependent on the execution of any HFPP-related contract action.

Please identify the appropriation account, funding source, staffing plan, contractor support, and Medicaid-specific deliverables of the Medicaid Fraud War Room. Please state whether any Fraud War Room resources, including, but not limited to, personnel, contract, or overhead, are drawn from the MIP appropriation, and provide the legal basis for any such allocation. Please also provide the underlying data documentation for the $203 million and 50-provider figures announced on July 28, 2026, and a breakdown of amounts actually recovered versus payments flagged, together with the underlying data documentation for the updated $342 million and 124 notices-of-intent-to-exclude figures referenced in your Deputy Administrator’s October 15, 2026 ADAPT conference presentation, and an explanation reconciling the two sets of public figures.

Please describe the artificial intelligence and machine learning pilots referenced by your Deputy Administrator at the ADAPT conference on October 15, 2026, including: (a) the data sources, data flows, and legal authorities under which CMS is obtaining Medicaid claims or encounter data on a pre-payment basis in fee-for-service and managed care Medicaid; (b) the states participating in each pilot and the terms of their participation, including the Indiana-Oracle pilot and the five additional state pilots referenced; (c) the contractor(s) supporting each pilot and the acquisition vehicle(s) under which they were engaged; (d) the appropriation account(s) funding each pilot, including whether any MIP appropriated funds are being used; (e) the privacy, data security, and HIPAA frameworks governing CMS’s collection and use of pre-payment Medicaid claims and encounter data; and (f) the relationship, if any, between the pilots’ data architecture and the direct state MMIS data feeds maintained by the Division of Fraud Research and Detection prior to its elimination.

Please explain how the President’s FY 2027 Budget submission treats the MIP appropriation, the Medicaid Integrity Institute, and the Section 1936 workforce, training, and technical assistance mandates, and state CMS’s position on statutory compliance in the current and coming fiscal years.

Please provide all internal analyses, contractor deliverables, and data sources supporting (a) the 5 million people with personal care services figure cited in your April 2026 letter to New York Governor Kathy Hochul, (b) the alleged noncompliance related to the withholding action against Minnesota including the analytical and evidentiary basis, (c) all federal payment deferrals imposed against Minnesota, including the analytical and evidentiary basis for each deferral, (d) all federal payment deferrals imposed against California, including the analytical and evidentiary basis for each deferral, and (e) CPI’s role, if any, in supporting the HHS OIG process leading to the decertification of Hawaii and New York’s respective MFCUs.

I also request a staff-level briefing within two weeks on CPI’s current compliance with Section 1936 of the Act and the operational and fiscal relationship among the MIP, the Medicaid Fraud War Room, and the Healthcare Fraud Prevention Partnership.

Medicaid serves more than 73 million Americans. Program integrity in a program of that scale demands sustained investment, deep expertise, and genuine partnership with states. Congress created and funded the infrastructure to do this work, and the administration and CMS are required by law to carry out those mandates. CMS is not free to redirect the funding, redefine the mission, or replace true program integrity with a flashy, politicized rebrand.

###
