WASHINGTON — U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) today delivered the following remarks on the Senate floor:

Thune’s remarks below (as delivered):

“Mr. President, one of our priorities this Congress has been finding ways to make life easier for hardworking Americans.

“And one of the ways we’ve gone about that is by eliminating some of the red tape that drives up prices and causes headaches for consumers, businessowners, and builders.

“We’ve rescinded costly regulations through the Congressional Review Act that would have driven up prices for a host of items.

“In fact, we have voted [on] 25 different CRA – Congressional Review Act – resolutions of disapproval to undo burdensome Biden-era … regulations.

“Twenty-five times here, the Senate has voted on those, Mr. President, in an attempt to try and lessen the cost and the red tape of doing business and creating jobs in this country, and ultimately of driving up costs for consumers, which is what all that red tape, in the end, does.

“We passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which cuts some of the red tape that has driven up the price of housing by making it difficult to build new homes.

“And we’re continuing those efforts this week with the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act – a major permitting reform bill to help America build again.

“Mr. President, the federal permitting process is broken.

“Too often, projects are bogged down in bureaucratic delays for months, and often years, at a time.

“Delays cause project budgets to balloon, which then leads to higher costs for American consumers.

“And it’s not just the dollars-and-cents cost, Mr. President.

“Project delays have serious opportunity costs as well:

“Jobs put on hold because a new factory won’t open on time.

“Communities without internet access because broadband infrastructure is delayed.

“And Americans driving on bad roads and rickety bridges while plans for improvements are stuck in an office in Washington.

“Mr. President, it’s not that construction projects shouldn’t undergo a thorough review of their impacts on communities and the environment.

“Input from the local community, from state and local governments, and from other stakeholders is a critical part of determining whether and how to execute a project.

“But the federal permitting process has unfortunately gone far beyond these reasonable expectations.

“And that’s due in large part to senseless delays caused by cascading litigation from environmental groups and by agencies determined to study a project to death.

“We’ve seen those delays happen to everything from water projects to broadband deployment to affordable energy and improving roads and bridges.

“Mr. President, last week I mentioned the Potomac Interceptor, which burst earlier this year and sent nearly 250 million gallons of raw sewage spewing into the Potomac River.

“The local water company identified vulnerabilities in this 60-year-old sewer pipe a full seven years before it burst.

“But proposed repairs languished in the federal permitting process year after year after year.

“And the project was still undergoing an environmental review when the pipe burst and caused an environmental disaster.

“And that was just to replace something that had been there for decades.

“Mr. President, for Americans wondering why important projects aren’t making progress, the answer is too often federal permitting delays.

“It takes four and a half years on average for federal agencies to approve an environmental impact statement.

“Add another 15 months to that for a new bridge.

“And if a NEPA lawsuit is filed over a proposed project, it takes almost two years to resolve it.

“Mr. President, if we want better roads and bridges, if we want to strengthen American manufacturing, if we want to be energy independent, we need permitting reform.

“And I’m grateful to Chairs Shelley Moore Capito and Mike Lee for working with their Democrat counterparts to put forward a bipartisan permitting reform bill that I hope we will complete this week.

“This bill would streamline the review process, putting federal bureaucrats on the clock to give a yes or no answer to a project.

“This would make a huge difference on energy projects.

“As I said, projects are often stuck in limbo for years as they work their way through government approvals.

“That adds costs to the project, delays construction, and ultimately leaves American families paying higher utility bills.

“But by streamlining those processes, the Council of Economic Advisers estimates that provisions in this bill could save a typical household hundreds of dollars on energy bills and other expenses every single year.

“Importantly, this bill also provides much-needed certainty and clarity to a variety of stakeholders, including farmers and ranchers.

“For one, it extends Clean Water Act permits from five to 10 years, giving farmers more time to complete projects before having to renew their permits.

“It shortens reviews under the Endangered Species Act, allowing grazing-related projects – like a new fence on a ranch – to move along faster.

“And it ensures that local governments and landowners will continue to have a say in projects that affect them.

“Mr. President, for a lot of Americans, the type of project that most concerns them these days is a data center coming to their community.

“And I’m pleased to report that the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would enact new protections for local communities when it comes to data centers.

“That starts with requiring – requiring – data centers to shoulder their own energy costs – whether that’s their operating and construction costs or the cost of grid improvements needed to accommodate them.

“This legislation ensures those costs don’t show up on household utility bills.

“It would also provide assistance to communities to help them understand and explore the impact a proposed data center would have on their locality – everything from the economic impact to the energy costs and infrastructure requirements that would be associated with the project.

“Mr. President, well-intentioned rules and regulations can quickly turn into death by a thousand cuts.

“Or, as is too often the case, death by delay.

“The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act restores the balanced approach to permitting that’s needed.

“It ensures local stakeholders have a say in projects in their community.

“And it provides accountability to ensure that bureaucrats in Washington don’t prevent needed projects from moving forward.

“A closed bridge.

“A burst sewer pipe.

“A factory built overseas.

“Bureaucratic delays, Mr. President, have real consequences.

“We need to get permitting reform done to get things built in this country and to make life more affordable for American families.”

WASHINGTON – U.S. Sen. Mark R. Warner (D-VA), Vice Chairman of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence and co-chair of the Senate Cybersecurity Caucus, released the following statement:

“I understand why Americans are concerned about the widespread outages we’ve seen in recent days, affecting everything from banks and major technology companies to critical government systems. At this point, there is no indication that these incidents are the result of a cyberattack, foreign interference, or some coordinated effort. What appears to be happening instead is a consequence of how quickly artificial intelligence is changing the cybersecurity landscape. AI is making it possible to identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change. While we still need to get to the bottom of these incidents, the evidence so far points toward legitimate efforts to secure our systems, not malicious activity.

“Still, these disruptions should serve as a wake-up call. It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences. This is exactly why I’ve been pushing for commonsense guardrails on AI and stronger cybersecurity protections. Unfortunately, President Trump has shown little interest in confronting these challenges, his administration has repeatedly undermined its own credibility, and its cuts to CISA have weakened the very expertise we need to navigate moments like this. Americans deserve clear, reliable information and a government that is prepared to respond. I’m going to keep digging into these incidents, pressing for answers, and making sure we’re doing everything possible to protect our critical systems. But based on what we know today, there is good reason to believe these disruptions are the unintended consequences of efforts to make our systems safer, not evidence of a broader attack.”

Sen. Warner has been a leading voice in Congress on the national security, economic, and societal implications of artificial intelligence. Earlier this year, he unveiled A Framework for America’s AI Future, a comprehensive legislative agenda focused on AI safety and competition, national security, workforce disruption, and the infrastructure needed to power the technology. Most recently, Warner introduced the Artificial Intelligence Risk Management and Security Act of 2026 with Sens. Brian Schatz (D-HI) and Andy Kim (D-NJ), legislation that would establish enforceable safety and security standards for the most advanced AI systems, including pre-deployment testing, stronger cybersecurity requirements, and mandatory reporting of serious AI safety and security incidents. Warner and his colleagues took to the Senate floor this week to seek unanimous consent to pass the legislation.

###

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Reps. Pete Aguilar (CA-33) and Jay Obernolte (CA-23) introduced a bipartisan resolution designating November 18, 2026, as National Geographic Information System (GIS) Day. The resolution recognizes GIS as an essential, rapidly growing technology and encourages students, educators and professionals across the country to use it to learn, solve problems and grow the economy.

GIS collects, analyzes and maps location data so users can better visualize and make sense of geospatial information, patterns and the relationships of our world. Government agencies, businesses, nonprofits, schools and the public use it for things like urban planning, emergency response and disaster management, supply chain logistics, farming, utilities and infrastructure and scientific research.

“From wildfire preparedness to neighborhood zoning, GIS shapes our lives in countless ways most people never see,” said Rep. Pete Aguilar. “GIS users in the Inland Empire and across the world are innovators who drive economic growth and keep our communities safe and well-connected. I’m proud to recognize their work and the importance of this technology with a bipartisan resolution designating National GIS Day.”

“Geographic Information Systems have become indispensable to everything from emergency preparedness and infrastructure development to economic growth,” said Rep. Jay Obernolte. “Here in California’s 23rd District, Esri continues to demonstrate how American innovation can address real-world challenges while supporting high-quality jobs and technological advancement. I’m pleased to recognize National GIS Day and the dedicated professionals, educators, and students who continue to advance this important technology.”

“I want to commend Representatives Aguilar and Obernolte for their bipartisan collaboration in introducing the House resolution honoring GIS Day 2026,” said Jack Dangermond, President, Esri. “This annual event celebrates geographic information systems and the dedicated GIS technologists who are having an ever-increasing impact on all sectors. These tools play a crucial role in operations at every level of government and help nonprofits, educational institutions, and the private sector with geospatial analysis of a wide range of questions and issues. GIS systems are driving significant economic growth and are integrating with AI-enabled tools to better help us solve problems. Happy GIS Day to all!”

“On behalf of the National Society of Professional Surveyors (NSPS), I thank Representatives Aguilar and Obernolte for once again recognizing National GIS Day,” said Tim Murphy, PLS, NSPS President. “Every map, model, and spatial analysis depends on knowing precisely where things are. Land surveyors and GIS professionals share responsibility for that foundation. As advances in high-accuracy positioning and the modernization of the National Spatial Reference System change how we measure our nation, the partnership between surveying and GIS has never been more important. GIS Day is an opportunity to honor the work of the geospatial community and to inspire the next generation to join it.”

“On behalf of the Subsurface Utility Engineering Association (SUEA), we commend the bipartisan leadership of Representatives Pete Aguilar and Jay Obernolte for sponsoring the GIS Day resolution,” said Nicholas Zembillas, SUEA President. “The value and practice of subsurface utility engineering is enhanced by leveraging GIS technology to help identify, designate, and locate underground utilities using records research, geophysical methods, and non-destructive excavation to reduce project risk. When used accurately and combined with the best practices and standards in SUE, GIS technology enables SUE professionals and professional firms conducting SUE to best serve their clients and help protect the public.”

“New and exciting applications of geospatial data, services, and technology portrayed, visualized, and accessed in Geographic Information Systems (GIS) are brought to the market for the benefit of individual citizens, government at all levels, and private enterprise every day,” said John “JB” Byrd, Policy Coordinator, U.S. Geospatial Executives Organization (U.S. GEO). “And Congress is increasingly recognizing the value of ‘where’ in legislation. GIS Day is a time to recognize how billions of dollars in business activity, the creation and support of tens of thousands of jobs, economic growth and development, protection of the environment, and many other important activities are supported by GIS. U.S. GEO commends Representatives Aguilar and Obernolte for introducing the GIS Day resolution in the U.S. House of Representatives.”

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Congressmen Vince Fong (CA-20) and Josh Gottheimer (NJ-05) introduced H.R. 11055, the Bridging Resources for Innovative Defense and Government Expertise in Artificial Intelligence (BRIDGE AI) Act. This bipartisan legislation would authorize the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to collaborate with experienced private-sector artificial intelligence (AI) professionals to better defend U.S. critical infrastructure.

“Communities and critical industries across the country are trying to keep up with the surge in AI-driven cyberattacks that steal sensitive data and disrupt operations,” said Congressman Fong. “In the Central Valley, cyberattacks have increasingly targeted schools, hospitals, and water systems, threatening the critical services our communities depend on. These attacks are becoming more frequent and sophisticated. These threats are real, and they aren’t waiting for the government to catch up. By bringing in AI and emerging technology specialists from the private sector, the BRIDGE AI Act ensures our nation’s cybersecurity experts receive the additional tools and expertise needed to modernize our systems, address vulnerabilities, and protect the essential services Americans rely on.”

“Our adversaries are using AI to attack our networks faster than ever, and CISA, the agency on the front lines of defending them, doesn’t have enough capacity to keep pace,” said Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5). “The BRIDGE AI Act is a commonsense, bipartisan fix that gives CISA a fast way to bring in the best AI and tech minds to hunt down intruders, patch vulnerabilities, and stress-test AI tools before they are exploited. Protecting our families, our water systems, and our national security shouldn’t be a partisan issue, and I’m proud to partner with Congressman Fong to get this done.”

Specifically, the bill:

Creates a mission-focused pilot program for 75 - 125 private-sector professionals to serve within CISA.

Supports structured knowledge transfer so that career CISA employees gain advanced AI expertise.

Ensures rigorous ethics and conflict of interest safeguards.

Requires a semiannual report to Congress on program status, participation, and recommendations for improvement.

Background

CISA leads national efforts to defend against emerging cyber threats by working with federal agencies, state, local, tribal, and territorial governments, and private-sector partners to protect America’s 16 critical infrastructure sectors.

In April, Congressman Fong hosted a cybersecurity roundtable with Homeland Security Committee Chairman Andrew Garbarino, CISA, regional military installations, local officials, and infrastructure sectors. The discussion focused on current, existing, and future cybersecurity challenges facing the Central Valley, developing a local workforce ready to combat cybersecurity threats, and protecting utility providers, local governments, and their infrastructure from cyberattacks. You can learn more about the roundtable here.

Recent examples highlighting how the cyber threat environment is escalating include:

February 2026: A ransomware attack on the University of Mississippi Medical Center (UMMC) forced the closure of all 35 clinic locations statewide and the cancellation of scheduled appointments and elective surgeries. The attack took down UMMC's IT network, including its EPIC electronic medical records system.

May 2026: Instructure, the provider of the popular Canvas education system, suffered a massive data breach orchestrated by the ShinyHunters cybercriminal group. The historic breach exposed student names, IDs, and private communications, ultimately forcing Instructure to pay a ransom to prevent a catastrophic data leak.

July 2026: A suspected Iran-linked cyber group, CyberAv3ngers, executed a wave of cyberattacks that disrupted municipal water operations across at least 12 states, targeting more than 30 municipal water systems in Minnesota alone.

October 2026: a cyberattack on the University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center forced New Mexico’s only Level I trauma center to divert ambulances and halted outpatient surgeries and appointments, disrupting access to emergency care.

Just this week, a cyberattack compromised 178 of the world’s most visited websites, including those belonging to Zoom, HSBC, Equifax, CNN, Salesforce, and IKEA, in an effort to steal cryptocurrency and infect iPhones.

AI is fundamentally reshaping the cyber battlefield, identifying weaknesses, analyzing systems, and accelerating cyber operations at a speed that was unimaginable just a few years ago. As our adversaries gain access to these capabilities, we must ensure federal agencies like CISA have the most advanced tools available to protect our critical infrastructure. By partnering our nation’s cyber defense agency with AI experts from the private sector, CISA can help communities strengthen their defenses, stay ahead of emerging risks, and keep our critical infrastructure secure and resilient.

Today, Rep. Fong and Rep. Gottheimer hosted a press conference to announce the introduction of the legislation. Click here to watch.

Text of the BRIDGE AI Act can be found here.

WASHINGTON, DC — Today, Wednesday, November 18, 2026, on the heels of last week’s attacks, Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5) and Congressman Vince Fong (CA-20) announced the bipartisan BRIDGE AI Act, new federal legislation to help the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) bring in additional AI expertise to secure American critical infrastructure.

Watch Gottheimer’s remarks here.

“Our adversaries are using AI to attack our networks faster than ever, and CISA, the agency on the front lines of defending them, doesn’t have enough capacity to keep pace,” said Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5). “The BRIDGE AI Act is a commonsense, bipartisan fix that gives CISA a fast way to bring in the best AI and tech minds to hunt down intruders, patch vulnerabilities, and stress-test AI tools before they are exploited. Protecting our families, our water systems, and our national security shouldn’t be a partisan issue, and I’m proud to partner with Congressman Fong to get this done.”

“Communities and critical industries across the country are trying to keep up with the surge in AI-driven cyberattacks that steal sensitive data and disrupt operations,” said Congressman Fong (CA-20). “In the Central Valley, cyberattacks have increasingly targeted schools, hospitals, and water systems, threatening the critical services our communities depend on. These attacks are becoming more frequent and sophisticated. These threats are real, and they aren’t waiting for the government to catch up. By bringing in AI and emerging technology specialists from the private sector, the BRIDGE AI Act ensures our nation’s cybersecurity experts receive the additional tools and expertise needed to modernize our systems, address vulnerabilities, and protect the essential services Americans rely on.”

Investing in the people securing our critical infrastructure will directly protect American families and our national security. Foreign adversaries, including China, Iran, and Russia, are using AI to find and exploit weaknesses in U.S. networks faster than ever. CISA is the agency responsible for defending federal networks and helping protect critical infrastructure, but it doesn’t have enough in-house AI expertise to keep up, and the Trump administration has repeatedly slashed the agency to the bone. Recent software outages of critical services, including the government’s classified systems, paired with this summer’s cyber attacks on municipal water systems in at least a dozen states underscore this urgent need.

The BRIDGE AI Act creates a pilot program that lets experienced tech professionals serve inside CISA and speeds up onboarding, so experts can start helping bolster U.S. cybersecurity sooner. These new hires would work on specific projects with clear goals, including:

Hunting for intruders in federal networks;

Fixing known vulnerabilities faster;

Testing AI tools for security flaws.

The BRIDGE AI Act builds on Congressman Gottheimer’s role as Co-Chair of the House AI Commission, where he has worked to develop policies that protect American systems and critical infrastructure from the growing cybersecurity threat AI poses:

The bipartisan AI Cyber Defense Act gives America’s critical infrastructure operators free access to the most powerful, cyber-capable AI models.

The bipartisan Securing Our Critical Infrastructure Act creates a dedicated rapid-response and threat notification service at CISA, built specifically for small and medium water and electric utilities.

Washington, D.C. – U.S. Representative Jim Himes (D-CT), Ranking Member of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, today released the following statement:

“Over the past week, I have heard from many concerned Americans about the series of high profile and disruptive computer network outages, including Microsoft Outlook, an Air Traffic Control system, JP Morgan Chase, and an internal National Security Agency system. I want to be clear that as Ranking Member of the House Intelligence Committee, I have seen no evidence to suggest any of these outages were the result of a malicious actor. To the contrary, the owners of these systems have acknowledged publicly that the outages were caused by internal actions, not by an outside attacker.

“Stepping back, the risk of disruptive or even damaging cyberattacks is very real, and we need to do more to harden our critical infrastructure against attack. The rapid advent of highly cyber capable AI models, including open-weight models, has accelerated the ability of both attackers and defenders to discover vulnerabilities and create exploits, necessitating even greater urgency to patch systems regularly. It is possible that the increased pace of vulnerability discovery and patching could cause more frequent outages, but the breakneck pace of patching we have seen in recent months is vital to shore up the security of all IT infrastructure. Disruptions in networks, whether through internal errors or outside attack, are a fact of life, but we can do much more to be prepared and resilient.”

Washington, D.C. — Today, Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (CA-37), Ranking Member of the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on South and Central Asia with jurisdiction over export controls; Rep. Jamie Raskin (MD-8), Ranking Member of the House Judiciary Committee; and Rep. Gregory Meeks (NY-5), Ranking Member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, sent a letter to Cantor Fitzgerald Chairman Brandon Lutnick demanding records to determine whether his father, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, blocked efforts to stop the suspected smuggling of advanced NVIDIA chips to China while his family’s firm held hundreds of millions of dollars in NVIDIA stock.

The letter comes days after NVIDIA announced that its CEO, Jensen Huang, had resigned amid revelations of an alleged Chinese intelligence operation tied to the suspected smuggling of billions of dollars in restricted chips.

“[T]he American people deserve to know: Did the Secretary of Commerce seriously and perhaps irreversibly compromise U.S. national security interests to make money for his adult children and Cantor Fitzgerald?” wrote the lawmakers.

From September 2025 to March 2026, White House and U.S. intelligence officials examined whether a Chinese intelligence operation had targeted NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang to help smuggle restricted AI chips to China. China’s Ministry of State Security reportedly recruited Alice Huang, the former chief executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based NVIDIA customer, to compromise him. Jensen Huang resigned after admitting that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including with the alleged Chinese asset.

As U.S. officials pressed to cut off Megaspeed’s access to advanced NVIDIA chips, Secretary Lutnick reportedly resisted. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said four federal agencies had backed blacklisting Megaspeed for months while Lutnick’s Commerce Department, which controls the blacklist, held out.

Before Lutnick became Commerce Secretary, Cantor Fitzgerald had disclosed holding more than 3.5 million NVIDIA shares. After his confirmation, Lutnick agreed to transfer ownership of the firm to trusts benefiting his adult children. While U.S. officials were scrutinizing Megaspeed, Cantor Fitzgerald cut its reported NVIDIA shareholdings by nearly half. The firm still held roughly $310 million in NVIDIA shares at the end of March 2026.

Secretary Lutnick’s push to weaken proposed chip export restrictions raises another question about whether Cantor Fitzgerald’s business interests influenced his decisions. The New York Times reported that Secretary Lutnick pushed to narrow proposed restrictions on overseas data centers that use advanced NVIDIA chips to serve Chinese customers. One project that could be affected is a Malaysian data center run by a Cantor Fitzgerald client.

The lawmakers are demanding records identifying every NVIDIA trade Cantor Fitzgerald has made since January 2024, along with an accounting of the firm’s business dealings in China and Southeast Asia. They are also seeking internal and client communications about U.S. export controls and suspected chip smuggling, communications with the Commerce Department about NVIDIA, Megaspeed, and Asian data center projects, and records concerning President Trump’s reported NVIDIA investments.

The lawmakers also called on Cantor Fitzgerald to immediately preserve all relevant records, including encrypted messages and business communications on personal devices, and to confirm in writing by December 1 that it has done so.

Click here to read the letter.

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Congressmembers Sam Liccardo (CA-16), Nick Begich (AK-AL), Scott Peters (CA-50), and Erin Houchin (IN-09) introduced the bipartisan Data Center Community Empowerment Act of 2026. Senators John Curtis (R-UT) and Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-DE) previously introduced companion legislation in the Senate.

As data center developers look to build data centers across the country, local communities face difficult decisions about energy costs, infrastructure demands, and potential economic benefits. Yet many local governments lack the technical expertise needed to assess these projects and negotiate on equal footing with developers. This bipartisan legislation would give communities access to independent technical expertise supported by the Department of Energy, arming local leaders with the facts they need to make informed decisions.

“Local communities should decide whether hyperscalers build in their backyards. But when we pit small towns against hyperscalers, we set them up to get steamrolled,” said Rep. Liccardo. “Every data center proposal shouldn't become a David and Goliath battle. This bill gives communities a fighting chance to make the decisions that best serve their residents.”

“When local leaders have good information about what a knowledge infrastructure project means for power bills, water supplies, and local roads and services, they can make decisions in the best interest of those they represent. This bill makes sure no community is left out of these important conversations,” said Rep. Begich.

“Data centers have left communities across the country worried about their utility bills, the quality of their neighborhoods, and the environment,” Rep. Peters said. “San Diegans already pay some of the highest utility rates in the nation, and they deserve to know what’s coming before decisions are made. We should provide communities with resources and the technical knowledge to understand the real impacts of data centers, so they can make informed decisions. I’m glad to be part of the solution and to lead this bipartisan, bicameral bill that gets Americans the answers they need and helps them advocate for their best interests.”

“Local communities deserve a meaningful say in what gets built in their own backyards. That’s why I’m proud to join Congressman Liccardo on this bill to provide the information and tools needed to make informed decisions about data center development. As our nation’s demand for critical infrastructure grows, we must respect local control and ensure that economic growth and technological innovation do not come at the expense of local priorities,” said Rep. Houchin.

“Data centers need to benefit their host communities, but local officials often lack the resources to negotiate on equal footing with hyperscalers, who have the funds and expertise to tip deals in their favor,” said Brad Carson, President of Americans for Responsible Innovation. “Giving officials the expertise and information they need will help them secure fair deals with real benefits for their constituents. We shouldn’t leave local communities outmatched at the negotiating table.”

The Data Center Community Empowerment Act of 2026 would give communities access to technical expertise to better understand the potential benefits, costs, and infrastructure impacts of proposed data center development-while leaving decisions about whether and how to accommodate that development in the hands of local communities.

The bill would establish a program at the Department of Energy (DOE) to:

Provide technical assistance to State, local, and Tribal governments on the potential energy, water, infrastructure, economic, and other community impacts associated with data center development;

Develop a Data Center Community Toolkit with easy-to-understand information and resources specifically designed for nontechnical local officials;

Provide independent project analysis at a community's request, including an assessment of information voluntarily provided by a data center developer and the reliability of its data and reasonableness of its assumptions, projections, and conclusions; and

Preserve local decision-making by requiring DOE to remain neutral on individual data center projects and prohibiting the Department from recommending whether a particular project should be approved or rejected.

WASHINGTON – U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib (MI-12) introduced the No Secret Deals Act, which would prohibit government agencies and public officials from entering into private non-disclosure agreements with corporations. NDAs have been increasingly used to accelerate contracts and projects like AI data centers and water utility privatization, hiding potential environmental and public health harms, details of tax break packages, and shielding government from accountability to the people.

In Michigan, NDAs have been abused by state and local governments to hide key details of tax giveaways to corporations. A 2023 report found that 1 in 5 Michigan lawmakers had signed an NDA with a state agency to shield business incentive details from the public. As the Detroit City Council debates a $548 million tax incentive package for billionaire Dan Gilbert’s Renaissance Center redevelopment, key details of the project are hidden by an NDA.

“Our government is making secret deals with greedy corporations that we know don’t have our best interests in mind. They know these projects like AI data centers are unpopular, so they’d rather make these business arrangements in the dark and cut out public opinion entirely,” said Rep. Tlaib. “My bill stops the secret deals and brings them into the light so people can see how their tax dollars are being spent. We deserve to have a say in projects that use our tax dollars and public land, that affect our health and environment.”

Even after data centers are built, NDAs help hide and obscure their energy effects. A research team from Harvard University relied on satellite imagery and carbon footprints to determine that 403 data centers in the US used more electricity than both New York City and Los Angeles combined and emitted 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide. Data centers are also not required to publicly disclose their electricity use and emissions.

The No Secret Deals Act would unveil critical details of agreements and business dealings between government agencies and corporations, protecting the public’s right to be informed. Read the full bill text here.

The bill is cosponsored by U.S. Reps. Maxwell Frost (FL-10) and Adelita Grijalva (AZ-07).

“No private company should be allowed to enter into an NDA with public officials – whether a data center, meat packers, a private water utility or any other profit-driven company. NDAs seek to keep critical information from voters and impacted communities. They are used to subvert democracy,” said Mitch Jones, Managing Director of Policy and Litigation at Food & Water Watch. “We thank Reps. Tlaib, Frost and Grijalva for introducing the No Secret Deals Act of 2026. By banning these NDAs, communities will at least have a clear picture of what these aggressive corporations are angling for, and where their local leaders stand.”

“For generations, communities of color and low-income have been excluded from critical permitting decisions that have adverse consequences for their health, local economies, and overall quality of life,” said Yosef Robele Federal Policy Manager at WE ACT for Environmental Justice. “Communities have a right to know what potentially harmful projects are being built in their backyards. The industry practice of using NDAs allows polluting projects such as data centers, warehouses, and other facilities to be built with little transparency and accountability. We need legislation like the No Secret Deals Act to stop this antidemocratic practice and protect the rights of environmental justice communities.”

“The No Secret Deals Act is exactly the kind of sound legislation we need to reign in an out of control tech industry that puts billionaires over people and the planet. The data center buildout has been opaque from the start, with corporations hiding environmental and public health impacts of their facilities while making us subsidize the harms and costs,” said Mar Zepeda Salazar, legislative director at Climate Justice Alliance. “Banning nondisclosure agreements imposed by corporations on local governments is a great first step to ensure communities have all the information they need to make informed decisions about what is built in their backyards. We applaud the members of Congress who are spearheading this direly needed legislation.”

WASHINGTON, D.C. –– As the use of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) grows, Rep. Van Epps (R-TN) introduced the Improving Nonhuman-Agent Security, Identification, Governance, Handling, and Traceability Act, or AI INSIGHT Act. This legislation would establish a framework for securing AI agents operating on federal civilian information systems, with CISA providing operational support, guidance, and technical assistance.

Rep. Van Epps stated, “We need commonsense AI safeguards. Agentic AI can help streamline workflows and automate cybersecurity tasks in both the public and private sectors. However, oversight and transparency measures are essential to ensure agents are properly managed and secured as they interact with systems and data. Every agent with access to a federal network presents a new opportunity to harness efficiencies, but also a new potential target for adversaries.”

“The AI INSIGHT Act would build on existing cybersecurity programs and controls to help agencies identify which agents are operating on their networks, limit their access to what their tasks require, monitor their activity, and suspend or revoke access when necessary. This legislation is an important step to ensure federal agencies can take advantage of this cutting-edge technology to deliver services to the American people without opening new doors for adversaries,” he continued.

Background: Rep. Van Epps introduced this legislation as part of a coordinated legislative push from the Homeland Security Committee to strengthen and modernize DHS’ cybersecurity mission, especially as AI drastically reshapes the threat landscape.

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Congressman Eugene Vindman (Va.-07) introduced a package of four bills aimed at lowering electricity costs, strengthening oversight of utility companies, and protecting Virginia families and small businesses from bearing the costs of unnecessary utility company projects.

As electricity demand continues to grow and utility companies invest billions in expanding and modernizing the electric grid, consumers must not be forced to shoulder costs that could be avoided or fairly assigned back to utility companies.

“Virginians are already struggling with rising electricity bills, and they shouldn’t have to pay even more for utility companies’ poor investments and lack of accountability,” said Vindman. “As energy demand grows, we need to modernize our grid, make sure large energy users like data centers pay their fair share, and protect families and small businesses from being saddled with unnecessary costs. The bottom line is simple: hardworking Virginians shouldn’t be footing the bill for utility companies and massive corporations to protect their bottom lines.”

As we face the rapid expansion of energy-intensive data centers, outdated transmission infrastructure, and unnecessary utility spending, Virginians deserve a grid that is reliable, affordable, and built with ratepayers in mind. This package would promote smarter investments, reduce unnecessary costs, and hold utility companies accountable for putting consumers first.

The following bills are included in this package:

The Make Data Centers Pay Act would protect Virginians from rising utility bills by requiring medium and large data centers to pay the full cost of the power generation, transmission lines, and grid upgrades needed to serve them.

The Lower Electricity Bills Act wouldforce utilities to use low-cost modern technologies whenever they build or upgrade transmission lines, and to deploy them wherever the benefits outweigh the costs. Companies that fail to make these improvements will face penalties from federal regulators.

The Smart Transmission Line Placement Act would cut unnecessary red tape by exempting transmission line upgrades within existing right-of-way corridors from lengthy federal reviews. This policy improvement would make it easier for utility companies to boost grid capacity by modernizing infrastructure already in place rather than building new projects.

The Local Transmission Accountability Act would strengthen oversight of utility companies’ local transmission projects to help prevent unnecessary infrastructure spending from driving up electricity bills for consumers. Utility companies that start projects that harm local ratepayers will face steep fines.

BACKGROUND

Vindman has long been a champion for holding data centers and electric utilities accountable.

He introduced the Make Data Centers Pay Act to protect hardworking Virginia families and small businesses from being forced to shoulder the rising electricity costs associated with the growing electricity demands of data centers.

He also introduced the Smart Data Center Policy Act to prevent data center development near neighborhoods, schools, and parks.

Vindman introduced the Home Energy Affordability Act to limit how often utilities can change residential utility rates and change prices for everyday Virginians, as well as the Utility Hikes Transparency Act, which would create the first comprehensive, machine-readable federal database of retail utility rate changes in the United States.

He has also fought against corruption in the energy sector by championing the Energy Utility Lobbying Ban Act, which would bar former government officials from lobbying on behalf of the companies they used to regulate.

What’s more, Vindman was the first member of Virginia’s congressional delegation to publicly oppose the proposed merger between NextEra and Dominion Energy, raising concerns about its potential impact on electricity rates and Virginia consumers.

He delivered remarks at a Virginia State Corporation Commission (SCC) public hearing on the proposed merger, urging regulators to reject the proposal and put the interests of ratepayers ahead of corporate profits. Vindman submitted official public comments to the SCC urging them to block the NextEra-Dominion merger.

matches.text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Senator Katie Britt (R-Ala.) yesterday attended a Senate Judiciary Crime and Counterterrorism Subcommittee hearing on how the online gaming platform, Roblox, is endangering America’s children.

This week, Senators Britt and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) introduced the Ending Forced Arbitration of Children Online Act. During the hearing, Senator Britt used her time to question witnesses about Roblox’s attempt to use forced arbitration as a shield against accountability in cases of child exploitation and grooming. Witnesses included Michael Schlep and Woody Doe, both survivor and online safety advocates; Khari James, Senior Legal Counsel at the National Center on Sexual Exploitation; and Professor Myriam Gilles of the Northwestern Pritzker School of Law.

Senator Britt began by thanking witnesses for telling their story and calling for commonsense protections: “Thank you for telling your story … The things we’re talking about today are absolutely commonsense, right? There is no way an eight-year-old … could read those terms and then sign away their right to a moment in court, effectively silencing themselves, dealing with the trauma that they endured online and then the trauma of not being able to use their voice and tell their story. And as a result of that, more and more children become victims. And at what point is this body not going to stand up and do the right thing?”

Senator Britt highlighted several of her legislative priorities to protect children from Big Tech companies: “I am hopeful that we will all stand with Senator Blumenthal and Senator Blackburn and get the Kids Online Safety Act, get that passed before the end of this Congress. We cannot allow Big Tech to continue to put their profits ahead of people, ahead of precious children, stealing innocence and in the most just damning circumstances, stealing lives … I was so honored to stand next to Senator Blumenthal and introduce yesterday the Ending Forced Arbitration of Children Online Act. The time to pass this is now. This bill would invalidate the pre-dispute arbitration agreements in cases in which a minor has suffered harm on a platform, including physical injury, mental or psychological harm, a violation of privacy or a misuse of personal data. Platforms covered by this bill of Senator Blumenthal’s and mine include social media platforms and gaming platforms like Roblox. I believe arbitration does have a place in our judicial system, but I do not believe that platforms like Roblox should be able to use arbitration as a shield against accountability for the harms they have caused to minors allowing them to become repeat offenders over and over and over again.”

Professor Gilles explained what parents should know about Roblox: “Well, first of all, they are completely aware that the design choices they’ve made are basically delivering these children to predators, and they’re doing nothing about it. And when families and victims sue them, trying to get change, trying to get some reform, they force those cases into secret arbitration. Let’s be clear, arbitration has a place in the system … If a family or a victim would like to go into arbitration, we should let them do that … But forcing a child as a precondition to playing a game, which we’ve heard is a game that they want to play, forcing them to sign away rights they don’t even understand, that’s not fair. That’s not that’s not real … Now, this is all happening in secret, and I think children are going to continue to be abused and harmed unless this body does something.”

Senator Britt asked Mr. Schlep to detail Roblox’s conscious decision to deemphasize moderators on the platform: “In fact, Roblox bragged to investors in a shareholder announcement that they were decreasing their spending on moderation while their player base was exploding. What context does that even make sense for Roblox to decrease their moderation while their users are going up? Hindenburg found that Roblox has one of the lowest moderator-to-user ratios than any other social media website … [T]he current leadership at the company has truly shown that they are putting profits ahead of safety. And that’s not me giving my opinion, that is their own employees saying that.”

Senator Britt continued, asking the witnesses, “What is the one thing you feel like this body needs to know or could do that would make a difference in what we’re seeing on kids’ online safety in general? I think it is absolutely reprehensible and feckless that Congress has done nothing. The most vulnerable and our most precious asset is the next generation, and we continue to kick the can down the road instead of do the right thing.”

Professor Gilles responded, highlighting Senator Britt’s legislation, “As we’re looking at what we do towards the end of the year, there are some wonderful bills. You and Senator Blumenthal have a bill, Senators Hawley and Durbin have a bill. Pass one of these bills and just get rid of forced arbitration. You will be amazed by how quickly the company will change its behavior once it is sued in public court.”

Ms. James agreed that online gaming platforms like Roblox need to be held liable in order to enact change: “I agree with my colleague here that there needs to be a consequence, and the consequence is being held liable, and how we can make that happen is through passing legislation, whether it’s Stop CSAM, KOSA, the Forced Arbitration Act, something has to be done.”

Mr. Doe noted, “They’re protecting themselves from their investors through this forced arbitration. All their dirty laundry is hidden. The minute that goes out the window, they’re really going to feel the repercussions of their actions. All I can ask is please get on those bills.”

Finally, Mr. Schlep called for better moderation from Roblox: “I fundamentally believe that Roblox needs better moderation … And some of the stuff that they’ve released, like age estimation and all this other stuff, is clearly not working. And at the end of the day, their overreliance on stuff like AI moderation, when they should be doing stuff in-house here in the United States, is something that I really think Roblox needs to do more of.”

Washington, D.C. – During a U.S. Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources hearing today, Senator Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.) grilled Dennis Kirk, Department of Interior Inspector General nominee, about his plans to investigate conflicts of interest in the approval of AI data center construction on public lands.

“On September 18, The Washington Sun reported that the Trump Administration is preparing to develop AI data centers and related infrastructure on nearly 18,000 acres of public land across six Western states, including Oregon, Wyoming, Idaho, Nevada, Utah and Arizona,” began Cortez Masto.

“At the same time, it was reported that hundreds of political appointees in the Trump Administration hold stocks or have other financial connections to Nvidia, Google, Meta – all of whom have plans to build data centers or would benefit from creating more data centers. This includes Steve Pearce, the director of the [Bureau of Land Management],” she continued.

“Would it be your obligation to open an investigation into whether employees of the Interior Department are financially benefitting from investments they have in these data management companies?” she asked.

Kirk refused to commit to investigating these conflicts of interest. When Cortez Masto asked if he’d be willing to look into the Trump Administration’s potential misuse of taxpayer dollars for personal gain, Kirk did not respond.

In addition to these conflict of interest concerns, Cortez Masto pressed Kirk to commit to investigating the Trump Administration’s reallocation of funds intended for critical maintenance projects on public lands across the United States, including for Great Basin National Park and Lake Mead Recreation Area, to vanity projects in Washington, D.C. Kirk also refused to commit to investigating this misuse of Congressionally appropriated taxpayer dollars.

Senator Cortez Masto has worked to ensure that regulations concerning AI innovation and use take privacy, national security, and environmental considerations into account. She voted against a Republican bill that claimed to regulate AI data centers but was entirely voluntary and instead pushed for legislation with real teeth. Cortez Masto is the cosponsor of legislation led by Senator Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) to demand more transparency from data centers by requiring them to clearly disclose their energy and water usage. She also recently demanded answers from Mark Zuckerburg about its use of billions in federal research and development tax credits to fund its rapid buildout of AI data centers.

WASHINGTON — A new official Government Accountability Office investigation requested by U.S. Senator Maggie Hassan (D-NH), incoming Chair of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, found that four of the most-used AI platforms — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok — all provided terrorist attack plans in a real-world test to determine AI safety risks. The results raise serious alarm bells about the need for Congress to take up and pass safety legislation, which incoming Chair Hassan announced today will be an early priority of the Committee.

“A terrorist can log onto an AI platform and in less than 12 hours walk away with a concrete playbook for how to carry out a deadly attack. Today’s new report makes it clear that the AI public safety threat is no longer theoretical. If Congress does not act, it is a question of when – not if – a bad actor will use AI to plan and carry out a major attack,” said incoming Chair of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, Senator Maggie Hassan. “Congress must quickly take up and pass legislation to address AI safety threats. To that end, in the new Congress, one of the first hearings of the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee will focus on the risk that AI poses to our homeland security and critical infrastructure, and our committee will prioritize developing legislation to address these threats.”

During an independent government audit, AI platforms were asked to provide plans to conduct either a mass casualty event by developing an improvised explosive device (IED) or to maximize economic harm through an attack on electrical infrastructure in major cities. All four AI platforms provided terrorist attack plans in less than 12 hours, including dates, times, guides to maximize damage, maps, diagrams, and more depending on the platform. While the platforms initially avoided providing the requested information or deleted information after it was provided, all of these safeguards were easily bypassed. Independent experts also confirmed that the details provided by the platforms would, in fact, have detonated explosives or caused harm. For safety reasons, the report withholds the exact prompts used to bypass the safeguards and which platform provided what level of information.

In response to the findings, incoming Chair Hassan announced that she will work to address the threat that AI platforms can pose to public safety and our critical infrastructure, and that one of the Committee’s first hearings in the new year will focus on AI safety. Incoming Chair Hassan is exploring various solutions to address this safety threat, including requiring more rigorous safety testing before AI platforms publicly release models.

WASHINGTON – Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) today delivered a farewell speech on the Senate floor, reflecting on his time serving Ohioans throughout his more than 25 years of public service and the accomplishments he delivered on their behalf.

Husted got four bills signed into law, returned millions of dollars to Ohioans through constituent casework and local infrastructure projects and advanced policies to make life more affordable for Ohio families and help the workforce and economy grow through his time in the Senate.

Husted also reflected on the importance of building on that progress and continuing to keep Ohio and America moving forward.

Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and Sens. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) and Bill Cassidy (R-La.) also spoke on the Senate floor to honor Husted’s service to Ohioans.

Thune remarks

Wicker remarks

“Since 2001, I have had the honor of serving in the Ohio State House as Speaker of the House, as Secretary of State, Lieutenant Governor, and now serving Ohio as its U.S. Senator.”

. . .

“I remember having two main goals.

“It was education and jobs.”

. . .

“In 2010, Ohio had a 9% unemployment rate and $0.89 left in our rainy-day fund.

“We were broke, and CNBC had ranked Ohio the 34th worst state in the country to do business.”

. . .

“16 years later, it is a new day with the rising sun.

“As of this year, in 2026, Ohio hit the lowest unemployment rate in our state’s history at 3.3%.

“And CNBC ranked Ohio the number-one state in the country to do business.”

. . .

“I’m not going to go through all of what it takes to do this, but you don’t go from 34th to 1st by accident.

“I know what it takes.

“I was part of most of it, and I led much of it.”

“I often say you can’t do Made-in-America without Made-in-Ohio because from the food you eat, to the cars you drive, to the trucks that deliver, to the airplanes that fly, to the steel, to the energy, to space exploration.

“And yes, even your AI and online life depends on the Ohio supply chain.

. . .

“This is what makes public service worth the sacrifice.

“When you go get to meet people who you’ve actually done something to change their future, it makes it all worth it.”

. . .

“I hope you will see that in all these things that I am most proud of, they had nothing to do with politics, political ideology, or labels.

“They’re just about solving people’s problems and making their lives better.

“That’s been my passion.”

. . .

“If you step into the Capitol Rotunda and you look up the stories painted on the dome, you’re reminded of an enduring pattern.

“Americans built our nation through personal sacrifice, often at a steep human cost.”

. . .

“A nation that once rallied around sacrifice, in war, in rebuilding, in laying foundations for the future, however, has seemingly given away to a new cultural mood.”

. . .

“In 1967, the year I was born, the national debt stood at $330 billion.

“Today, it’s over $40 trillion.

“And a child born today inherits $121,000 as their share of that burden.”

. . .

“We only sacrifice for the things we love.

“If we truly love our country and our children and our grandchildren, we should stop taking from them and make sacrifices for them.”

. . .

“We need to prove that we love our children by ending the generational theft that has occurred over the past 50 years.

“And I know that’s tough. So tough.

“I’m not preaching here, I’m praying.

“I’m not trying to tell people I know the right way, because I know you all know the right way.

“But it’s hard, it’s hard to overcome the politics of our time.”

. . .

“But I’ll still pray that you find a way.”

. . .

“Serving Ohioans from the state house to the upper chamber of the people’s house been a great honor and a privilege.

“It really is one for which I will always be grateful.”

. . .

“To the people of the great state of Ohio.

“Whether you voted for me or you’ve never voted for me, thank you for the honor of representing and serving you.”

. . .

“Public service has given me a daily purpose in life.

WASHINGTON – U.S. Senators Roger Wicker, R-Miss., and Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., today introduced the Stealth Bot Prohibition Act to confront the illegal and deceptive use of internet bots that threaten Americans’ intellectual property.

In light of the rise of artificial intelligence (AI), automated web crawlers are now roaming across the internet. While many have legitimate uses, bad actors have exploited the technology to wreak havoc on online producers, including local newspapers and journalists. Many of these advanced bots evade paywalls, scrape information, and overwhelm websites. “Stealth bots” are a particular class of disguised web crawlers that America’s adversaries deploy to steal protected online content and use it to train their own AI models.

The Stealth Bot Prohibition Act would enact transparency standards to combat these unauthorized practices. If passed, this legislation would provide a new tool for publishers to combat deceptive operators by requiring the disclosure of identities and purposes of bots when accessing websites without banning legitimate research and other beneficial automated material.

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) would be in charge of the enforcement of the bill’s provisions and would empower state attorneys general to take legal action to protect residents from violators.

“The Chinese Communist Party is notorious for stealing Americans’ intellectual property by any means possible. Now, it is weaponizing artificial intelligence and deploying droves of malicious bots against online publishers,” said Senator Wicker. “Our legislation recognizes these threats and offers a solution to insulate digital producers from bad actors.”

“AI is advancing rapidly, creating new challenges and threats for the American people. Congress must act immediately to ensure transparency and accountability for those who misuse this technology,” said Senator Luján. “That’s why I’m joining my colleagues in introducing the Stealth Bot Prohibition Act to crack down on bad actors and protect creatives, small businesses, and local news. No one should profit by stealing others’ hard work, ideas, or livelihoods.”

“News publishers of all sizes are drowning in bot traffic, hurting their ability to provide high-quality content to the American public. The Stealth Bot Prohibition Act is a common-sense, bipartisan solution to the problem of bad bots. It offers straightforward transparency requirements and enforcement mechanisms that uncover bad actors while leaving responsible uses of bots unaffected. The News/Media Alliance thanks Senators Wicker and Luján for their leadership on this issue, and their commitment to protecting American content creators, websites, and consumers, from a flood of bad bots. We look forward to working with them and their colleagues in Congress to pass this critical piece of legislation and offer American businesses and the American people the relief they deserve,” said Danielle Coffey, President and CEO of the News/Media Alliance.

Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senators Ron Wyden, D-Ore., Edward J. Markey, D-Mass., and Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., today questioned Big Tech companies over the widespread availability of so-called ‘nudify’ apps in app stores, nearly a year after the senators raised concerns about X and Grok remaining available despite enabling mass-generation of nonconsensual sexual images of women and children.

Although Apple and Google ban nudify apps in their terms of service, researchers recently revealed that apps marketed on Meta ads as nonconsensual sexual image generators are widely available in app stores, and generated over $100 million in revenue. One common tactic is for apps to be updated after passing review to add nudification tools.

“These findings raise questions not only about individual failures of app review, but also about [Google and Apple’s] ability to identify repeat offenders, disrupt coordinated networks, and monitor apps after approval,” the senators wrote.

Today U.S. Representatives Don Beyer (D-VA), Sara Jacobs (D-CA), and Celeste Maloy (R-UT) released an outline containing details of the Safe and Accountable Federal Evaluations of Artificial Intelligence (SAFE AI) Act, forthcoming bipartisan legislation that would create federal safety requirements for frontier artificial intelligence.

The broad, ambitious legislation would mandate safety frameworks, incident reporting, and increased transparency from frontier labs with strong government oversight and due process. The outline is available here.

“This outline is a roadmap towards a safer AI future for the country and the world.” said Rep. Don Beyer. “Recent AI incidents and the growing chorus of warnings from experts underscore the urgency of the task before us. It is vitally important that Congress tackle AI safety swiftly, and that we get it right. At this moment we are continuing to seek input on our forthcoming legislative text from experts and safety leaders, in coordination with committees of jurisdiction. We are sharing this blueprint today to show the direction our work is taking and to encourage further constructive feedback and discussion on what we believe should be a priority for Congress. I thank Reps. Jacobs and Maloy for the leadership and partnership on this bill, which I hope will move the ball forward on AI safety so we can usher in an age of responsible AI innovation."

“No industry gets to police itself, and AI shouldn’t be the exception,” said Rep. Sara Jacobs. “Right now, the companies write their own rules while their own models break out of test environments and hack other companies’ systems. Americans are rightly concerned about unchecked AI threatening public safety, critical infrastructure, national security, and the systems we all depend on. That’s why the bipartisan SAFE AI Act puts real guardrails on frontier models, with civil penalties for violations and targeted emergency authority to stop dangerous models when they pose a serious and immediate danger. Our proposal is a floor – not a ceiling, empowering states to adopt stronger protections for their communities. And it is built to adapt as the technology changes, so Americans’ safety never depends on a company’s promise.”

"The companies building the most powerful AI systems ought to be able to show they’ve done their homework before those systems go into wide use,” said Rep. Celeste Maloy. “This bill gives them clear rules, brings in an outside set of eyes to check their work, and leaves room for Utah and other states to set safeguards of their own."

Rep. Don Beyer (D-VA) serves as co-Chair of the Congressional Artificial Intelligence Caucus, and previously served on the bipartisan Task Force On Artificial Intelligence, convened by Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries and Speaker Mike Johnson. He is the author of the AI Foundation Model Transparency Act and a lead cosponsor of the CREATE AI Act, the Federal Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Act, and the Artificial Intelligence Environmental Impacts Act. Beyer is currently attending George Mason University as a part time student pursuing a master’s degree in machine learning, to help inform his work on AI in Congress.

Today, Reps. Don Beyer (D-VA), George Whitesides (D-CA), and Nathaniel Moran (R-TX), announced the launch of the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, the first congressional caucus focused specifically on addressing AI safety and security risks posed by increasingly advanced AI systems while ensuring the United States remains a global leader in innovative AI technologies.

As AI capabilities accelerate, so do the potential consequences of catastrophic misuse, loss of control over advanced systems, and threats to national security. In July, an experimental OpenAI agent escaped its testing environment and breached the external platform Hugging Face to cheat on an evaluation, without any human directing it to. Anthropic also disclosed three separate incidents in which its AI models escaped testing environments and gained unauthorized access to external organizations during cybersecurity evaluations. These recent security incidents have underscored the need for Congress to better understand these risks and develop policy solutions to prevent these incidents before emerging threats become larger problems. By addressing these challenges proactively, Congress can help create the conditions for continued American innovation and ensure the public can confidently benefit from advances in AI.

“AI has immense potential to improve our lives and strengthen American innovation, but that progress can’t come at the expense of our national security or public safety,” said Rep. Don Beyer. “Recent cyberattacks involving AI agents and growing warnings from leaders and researchers at the companies developing these technologies make clear that the risks are real and growing. We can’t afford to wait for a major catastrophe before putting meaningful safeguards in place. I’m proud to join the AI Safety Caucus and work with my colleagues to advance responsible legislation that strengthens oversight, security, and transparency while ensuring AI is developed and deployed safely and responsibly.”

“AI is advancing faster than ever before, and Congress needs to move just as quickly,” said Rep. George Whitesides. “Now is the time to build bipartisan consensus and advance commonsense guardrails we know will reduce the most serious risks. Americans are rightly concerned about where this technology is heading, but too often the debate in Washington is framed as a choice between doing nothing and banning AI altogether. That’s a false choice. We have an opportunity to pursue smart, targeted solutions that protect the public while allowing American innovation to thrive. I co-founded this caucus with Reps. Moran and Beyer to fight for that balance, because safe, secure, and controllable AI is the only path to unlocking its full promise for humanity.”

“We don’t have to choose between innovation and safety,” said Rep. Nathaniel Moran. “We can, and we should, do both. Artificial intelligence affects every American, and it should not be a partisan issue. This caucus gives us a place to find the areas of consensus, set partisanship aside, and put smart, targeted policies in place so we can innovate while we keep people safe. Congress needs to be prepared, and I’m proud to be one of the co-chairs leading that work.”

Specifically, the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus will:

Champion AI safety legislation: Develop legislative proposals and endorse existing bipartisan bills that establish thoughtful, targeted guardrails against the most serious AI risks while supporting continued innovation and American technological leadership.

Rapidly respond to AI incidents: Convene AI developers, technical experts, and government officials to brief Members and staff when significant AI safety incidents or developments occur and identify potential policy responses.

Equip congressional offices: Keep Members and staff informed about emerging AI developments, connect them with outside experts, and provide resources to navigate complex AI policy decisions.

Elevate AI safety publicly: Raise public awareness and make AI safety a national priority through public statements, op-eds, and press events.

Shape Congress’ AI agenda: Help develop federal AI safety policy and provide Members outside the committees of jurisdiction with an avenue to contribute to the conversation and legislative process.

By quickly addressing emerging threats, the AI Safety and Innovation caucus will ensure AI can continue to make key improvements in the fields of American science, medicine, productivity, and national security. This new bipartisan caucus will advance thoughtful, targeted guardrails, engaging technical experts and industry leaders, and equip Congress to respond quickly to emerging risks and significant AI incidents while ensuring America continues to lead in AI innovation.

The House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus launched with Reps. George Whitesides (D-CA), Nathaniel Moran (R-TX), and Don Beyer (D-VA) serving as co-chairs. Founding members include Reps. Greg Casar (D-TX); Yvette Clarke (D-NY); Ben Cline (R-VA); Mike Flood (R-NE); Bill Foster (D-IL); Valerie Foushee (D-NC); Pat Harrigan (R-NC); Jim Himes (D-CT); Sara Jacobs (D-CA); Mike Kennedy (R-UT); Ro Khanna (D-CA); Sam Liccardo (D-CA); Ted Lieu (D-CA); Zoe Lofgren (D-CA); Doris Matsui (D-CA); April McClain Delaney (D-MD); Blake Moore (R-UT); Jay Obernolte (R-CA); Scott Peters (D-CA); Brad Sherman (D-CA); Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA); Ritchie Torres (D-NY); Lori Trahan (D-MA).

matches.text:
WASHINGTON, DC (November 19, 2026) — Today, the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology is holding a Space Subcommittee hearing titled, “Weathering the Solar Storm: Advancing America’s Space Weather Capabilities".

Space and Aeronautics Subcommittee Ranking Member Valerie Foushee (D-NC)'s opening statement is below as prepared for the record:

Good morning. Thank you, Chairman Babin, for hosting this committee hearing to review our national efforts to research, forecast, and mitigate the effects of space weather. I thank our two witnesses, from NASA and NOAA, for attending today as well.

We live in an increasingly technologically dependent society. If we did not realize this already, I think that all of us who had our e-mail communications disrupted, planes grounded and delayed, and bank accounts made inaccessible just in the last week have been reminded of it. And through my work on advancing responsible AI policy, I have emphasized the importance of ensuring that emerging technologies and the critical infrastructure we increasingly depend on are safe, secure, and reliable for the American public.

None of those disruptions were due to space weather phenomena, of course. But, as it turns out, they are all examples of the kinds of disruptions that can occur if a severe space storm hit Earth; such an event could degrade our power grid, aircraft radio communications, GPS satellites, and other critical infrastructure, with implications across our society. It has become important for operators across sectors as diverse as finance, transportation, agriculture, defense, cybersecurity, and communications to monitor space weather forecasts and know how to respond when an extreme event is predicted, just as they do for potential extreme terrestrial weather events, such as those we have experienced in my district and across North Carolina. And although they share the term “weather,” terrestrial and space weather are fundamentally different, and each requires specialized observations, models, and advanced forecasting capabilities to provide accurate predictions and protect lives, property, and critical infrastructure.

NASA and NOAA, who we will hear from today, as well as NSF, lead and support essential components of a robust space weather ecosystem, including the scientific foundation, observation systems, and the development of operational forecasts and predictions. These essential efforts require a considerable amount of coordination and collaboration across the federal government beyond these core agencies, as well as the necessary funding to sustain these critical activities.

The Science Committee—which many of us often fondly refer to as the Committee of the Future—has been on the case. In 2020, after many years of effort, Congress passed the Science Committee’s Promoting Research and Observations of Space Weather to Improve the Forecasting of Tomorrow Act, or the PROSWIFT Act, which codified the roles and responsibilities of many of the key agencies involved. The law also directed new activities to improve coordination across the federal government, the research community, and the end user community, while ensuring the advancement of basic research and the continuity of critical space weather observing systems.

This hearing provides an opportunity to assess progress in implementing PROSWIFT, and to identify any remaining challenges and potential opportunities moving forward.

I am concerned that much of the momentum for federal space weather activities that had been maintained under multiple Administrations and supported by Congress on a bipartisan basis may be stalled, as activity seems to have slowed, or even halted altogether, under the second Trump Administration.

I think we all know that we simply cannot afford to slow down here. Again, I thank our witnesses for appearing today, and I look forward to their testimony.

With that, I thank you, Mr. Chairman, and I yield back.

Washington, D.C. – This week, Congresswomen Laurel Lee (FL-15) and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (NY-14) joined Paris Hilton, fellow House members, and advocates at the U.S. Capitol for a press conference urging the passage of the Disrupt Explicit Forged Images and Non-Consensual Edits Act (DEFIANCE Act), bipartisan legislation that would grant survivors the right to take civil action against individuals who knowingly produce, distribute, solicit, receive, or possess with the intent to distribute nonconsensual sexually explicit digital forgeries.

Congresswoman Lee, Congresswoman Ocasio-Cortez, Paris Hilton, and advocates previously gathered in January to urge the passage of the DEFIANCE Act. The renewed bipartisan effort today emphasizes the importance of strengthening protections for women and children targeted by sexually explicit deepfakes and ensure victims have the legal recourse they deserve.

“The images may be fake, but the victims are real, their suffering is real, and their right to seek justice should be real, too,”said Congresswoman Laurel Lee.“As artificial intelligence continues to advance, we must ensure our laws keep pace with emerging threats and protect women and children from online sexual exploitation. The bipartisan DEFIANCE Act gives victims meaningful legal tools to seek justice and hold perpetrators accountable. I am pleased to work alongside Congresswoman Ocasio-Cortez, Paris Hilton, and the courageous survivors and advocates who have brought national attention to this issue. Protecting victims and holding perpetrators accountable should never be a partisan issue, and I urge my colleagues to come together and support this critical legislation.”

“Every single day that the DEFIANCE Act does not pass is a day that more children, women, and people are victimized with no recourse and that there is no accountability for abusers and predators. And so what it means is that thousands of people in this country, if not tens of thousands and eventually millions, could be subject to sexual abuse on our watch just due to complacency.”said Representative Ocasio-Cortez.“I am grateful for the support of my co-lead Representative Laurel Lee, Paris Hilton and the Democratic and Republican Women’s Caucuses in pushing this critical legislation across the finish line.”

“The Defiance Act would give survivors a civil path to hold people accountable for creating and distributing non-consensual, sexually explicit deep fakes. The Senate understood the urgency and passed this legislation unanimously in January. Now the House must act too,”said Paris Hilton.“Why wait another day? If they don't pass this bill before the end of the year, all of our progress will be lost and we will have to start all over again.”

Stefan Turkheimer, RAINN VP of Public Policy: "RAINN is grateful to Congresswomen Ocasio-Cortez and Lee for their bipartisan leadership in fighting for the DEFIANCE Act. Deepfake sexual abuse causes real harm, and survivors deserve a path to justice. The Senate has acted. Now it’s the House’s turn to stand for survivors and give them their day in court."

The DEFIANCE Act would establish a federal civil right of action for victims of nonconsensual sexually explicit digital forgeries, allowing survivors to seek damages and hold perpetrators accountable. The legislation builds on progress made through the TAKE IT DOWN Act, signed into law in May 2025, by providing victims with a legal avenue to seek justice for the damage caused by exploitation.

In January 2026, the Senate passed the DEFIANCE Act by unanimous consent, demonstrating broad bipartisan support for addressing digital sexual exploitation. Congresswoman Lee, Congresswoman Ocasio-Cortez, and advocates are continuing their efforts to secure passage in the House and send the legislation to the President’s desk.
