matches.text:
Congresswoman Chellie Pingree (D-Maine), co-chair of the Congressional Arts Caucus, along with Congresswomen Becca Balint (D-Vt.) and Deborah Ross (D-N.C.), are demanding answers from Attorney General Todd Blanche about the Justice Department’s decision to intervene in a major copyright case involving OpenAI and Microsoft. The case could shape whether AI companies must seek permission to use copyrighted work to train their models, with consequences for artists and creators who rely on licensing income, among other sources, to make a living.

In their letter to Blanche, the lawmakers ask why DOJ reportedly bypassed the U.S. Copyright Office and the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office before filing its September 1 statement of interest—and whether any outside companies or organizations helped influence the filing.

The case, brought by The New York Times and other plaintiffs, could have ramifications well beyond newsrooms. Musicians, photographers, illustrators, and authors can earn income by licensing their work. A ruling on whether AI training qualifies as fair use could affect their ability to negotiate how their work is used and whether they’re paid for that use. Those decisions are especially important to independent creators and small publishers, whose work can help train tools that produce content competing with their own.

“In re: OpenAI, Inc. Copyright Infringement Litigation will likely be one of the most consequential intellectual property cases of the decade. The ruling will undoubtedly have ripple effects through the creative sector, which was estimated to contribute over $2 trillion or 7.66% to U.S. GDP,” Pingree and the lawmakers wrote. “There are nearly 150 copyright lawsuits involving an AI system, model, training pipeline, or output currently pending that hinge on the resolution of many of the legal questions this case raises.”

DOJ argued that restricting the use of copyrighted material to train generative AI could harm U.S. national security. The lawmakers questioned how broadly DOJ applied that argument to AI tools with widely different uses. They also asked how the filing squares with the Trump Administration’s stated support for letting courts resolve whether AI training on copyrighted material constitutes fair use.

“The DOJ’s apparent decision to forego consultation with USCO and USPTO and its efforts to justify intervening in this case altogether raise serious questions about potential bias,” the lawmakers wrote. “This SOI stands to undermine public trust in the impartiality of the DOJ and its ability to represent the best interests of the nation.”

The lawmakers are asking DOJ to provide the following by November 30:

Its procedures for reviewing and approving statements of interest in intellectual property cases, including who approved the September 1 filing.

Confirmation of whether DOJ consulted either federal office and an explanation for any decision to proceed without its input.

All internal drafts and supporting documents used to develop the filing, along with the names of any outside companies or organizations that provided legal analysis, briefing materials, or other communications related to it.

Representatives Suzanne Bonamici (D-Ore.), Greg Casar (D-Texas), Judy Chu (D-Calif.), Valerie Foushee (D-N.C.), Maxwell Frost (D-Fla.), Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-Calif.), Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), and Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-Ill.) joined Pingree, Balint, and Ross in signing the letter.

The letter is available here.

WASHINGTON, DC — The U.S. House of Representatives has passed the Dismantle Foreign Scam Syndicates Act (H.R. 5490) – legislation cosponsored by Representative Josh Riley (NY-19) to protect Upstate New Yorkers from online scams. This bipartisan bill creates a first-of-its-kind interagency task force to shut down the foreign criminal networks behind mass online scams targeting Americans.

As AI and other technological developments have fueled a wave of increasingly sophisticated online scams, New Yorkers are among the hardest hit. The Consumer Federation of America estimates that New Yorkers lose $8.7 billion a year to online scams and fraud. In 2025, 45,255 New Yorkers reported cybercrimes to the FBI – one of the highest rates in the country.

“Folks shouldn’t have to wonder whether that call, text, or email from their grandchild or friend is real or a con,” said Riley. “Scammers go after seniors on fixed incomes and working families who’ve spent their whole lives saving, and they hide overseas, thinking nobody will come after them – but we are. This bill shuts down their operations, sanctions the corrupt officials who protect them, and makes clear that if you rob Americans, you’re going to pay for it.”

Since 2021, Chinese criminal organizations active in Southeast Asia have increasingly targeted Americans with elaborate investment schemes. Run by so-called “scam centers,” they often operate as joint ventures between the Chinese criminal groups and autocratic governments in Burma, Laos, and Cambodia. They have robbed thousands of people of their life savings while making transnational criminal syndicates and corrupt leaders richer and more entrenched.

In addition to creating a task force to take on these scam centers, the Dismantle Foreign Scam Syndicates Act authorizes sanctions on corrupt officials who enable and profit from these networks. It will also strengthen international law enforcement by helping trusted foreign partners investigate financial crimes, shut down scam compounds, combat money laundering, and protect trafficking victims.

You can read the text of the Dismantle Foreign Scam Syndicates Act HERE.

Today U.S. Representatives Sara Jacobs (D-CA), Celeste Maloy (R-UT), and Don Beyer (D-VA) released an outline containing details of the Safe and Accountable Federal Evaluations of Artificial Intelligence (SAFE AI) Act, forthcoming bipartisan legislation that would create federal safety requirements for frontier artificial intelligence.

The broad, ambitious legislation would mandate safety frameworks, incident reporting, and increased transparency from frontier labs with strong government oversight and due process. The outline is available here.

“No industry gets to police itself, and AI shouldn’t be the exception,” said Rep. Sara Jacobs. “Right now, the companies write their own rules while their own models break out of test environments and hack other companies’ systems. Americans are rightly concerned about unchecked AI threatening public safety, critical infrastructure, national security, and the systems we all depend on. That’s why the bipartisan SAFE AI Act puts real guardrails on frontier models, with civil penalties for violations and targeted emergency authority to stop dangerous models when they pose a serious and immediate danger. Our proposal is a floor – not a ceiling, empowering states to adopt stronger protections for their communities. And it is built to adapt as the technology changes, so Americans’ safety never depends on a company’s promise.”

“The companies building the most powerful AI systems ought to be able to show they’ve done their homework before those systems go into wide use,” said Rep. Celeste Maloy. “This bill gives them clear rules, brings in an outside set of eyes to check their work, and leaves room for Utah and other states to set safeguards of their own.”

“This outline is a roadmap towards a safer AI future for the country and the world,” said Rep. Don Beyer. “Recent AI incidents and the growing chorus of warnings from experts underscore the urgency of the task before us. It is vitally important that Congress tackle AI safety swiftly, and that we get it right. At this moment we are continuing to seek input on our forthcoming legislative text from experts and safety leaders, in coordination with committees of jurisdiction. We are sharing this blueprint today to show the direction our work is taking and to encourage further constructive feedback and discussion on what we believe should be a priority for Congress. I thank Reps. Jacobs and Maloy for the leadership and partnership on this bill, which I hope will move the ball forward on AI safety so we can usher in an age of responsible AI innovation.”

Washington, D.C. — Today, U.S. Representative Scott Peters (CA-50) released the following statement after the Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). Central components of the package draw on Rep. Peters’ priorities to unleash clean energy, fast-track transmission, and lower utility costs.

“BAAJA lowers costs and lowers emissions. It’s that simple. It’s unimaginable that after this month’s election, when the entire country demanded lower costs, we would whiff on the opportunity right in front of us.

“Senate Democrats and Republicans just came together to pass the largest permitting reform package in history. Unfortunately two Senators, at the last minute, opposed bipartisan amendments to make a good bill better for tribal partners. We should make sure this bill gets across the finish line to lower costs and emissions and then continue our work to make the progress they opposed, and more.

“An environmental movement in 2026 that doesn’t prioritize greenhouse gas emissions doesn’t make any sense. Climate change is the biggest threat to our environment and underserved communities. We call it a crisis for a reason. But we will never mitigate this challenge unless we build things quickly and resolve challenges fairly and faster. We must transition to renewable energy at scale, and reduce emissions, now. BAAJA’s transmission and process reforms are our only chance to do that. All reputable analyses agree it would reduce our carbon footprint.

“There will be no better deal on the table. With Donald Trump in the White House and 60 required votes in the Senate, bipartisanship is unavoidable, whether it’s this Congress or next.

“The status quo isn’t working. House leadership should bring this package to the floor as soon as possible so we can get it to the President’s desk and signed into law before this Congress ends.”

Background:

Since coming to Congress, Rep. Peters has been an outspoken advocate for faster energy and permitting reform. As a member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, he has long argued that excessive process requirements slow the clean energy buildout and has pushed for transmission to be included in any permitting reform legislation.

Rep. Peters has authored major bipartisan bills including the SPEED and Reliability Act to streamline the buildout of electric transmission lines to lower costs for consumers, the CERTAIN Act to accelerate energy and infrastructure projects by enforcing strict application timelines and stop administrations from canceling permits that were already legally approved, the CLEAR Act to give developers and local stakeholders the certainty to plan and build large energy infrastructure and transmission projects, the BIG WIRES Act to direct FERC to better coordinate construction of an interregional transmission system, and the ePermit Act to digitize the U.S. permitting process.

These bills are all included in BAAJA, and most of the package is built on bipartisan legislation from Rep. Peters' colleagues on the Energy and Commerce committee.

After BAAJA was unveiled in the Senate, he highlighted BAAJA’s inclusion of several bills he’s championed over multiple sessions of Congress and encouraged further discussions and input on the bill. He also hosted a press conference in San Diego with leaders from the renewable energy and labor sectors to discuss local and federal efforts to hold data centers accountable, increase clean energy production, lower costs, and create jobs.

See a full breakdown by Rep. Peters on the need to pass BAAJA here.

Today, Congresswoman Lori Trahan (MA-03), a member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, released a section-by-section summary of her updated Frontier Risk Oversight, National Transparency, Independent Evaluation, and Reporting (FRONTIER) Act. Full bill text will follow in the coming weeks.

“The American people are fed up with the biggest AI companies writing their own rules and grading their own homework. That approach failed on social media, and we can’t let it happen again with an even more powerful technology,” said Congresswoman Trahan. “We can’t wait until January to start building strong, durable guardrails that can pass both chambers of Congress and be signed into law. Building the coalition to get there starts now.”

Trahan is working to update the legislation to reflect months of feedback from a broad coalition of stakeholders. Key changes include:

Floor preemption: State laws more protective than the legislation are preserved. States with weaker or no standards are preempted to create a federal floor.

Embedded, independent verification. Prescriptive language to guarantee embedded access for independent verification organizations (IVOs) and mechanisms for government assignment of IVOs to avoid a race-to-the-bottom.

Addressing recursive self-improvement. Automated AI research and development, including recursive self improvement, is its own category of catastrophic risk. Each of the bill’s obligations apply to it, including frameworks, reporting, and IVO assessments.

Enforceable corrective orders. When frontier developers fail to adequately mitigate risk, the federal government can require specific corrective action, backed by civil penalties and injunctive relief. IVOs have a duty to recommend corrective actions to developers.

Penalties and reporting requirements for near misses. Penalizes frontier developers for near misses to incentivize precautions before a catastrophe materializes. Also mandates that developers report these incidents to the government.

Office of AI Security. Formally establishes a new office within the U.S. Department of Commerce to administer the regulatory regime, led by a Senate-confirmed Assistant Secretary for AI Security. The bill authorizes significant appropriations for this office and grants it special hiring authorities.

Broader incident reporting. Reportable incidents now include near misses, models deceiving their developers, and incidents affecting critical infrastructure. Also includes a broader knowledge standard, requiring developers who “should have known” about an incident to report it.

Outcome-based standard. Frontier developers’ published safety frameworks must be reasonably designed to adequately mitigate catastrophic risk. Commerce must publish guidance for companies on best practices, standards, and methods to meet the standard.

A copy of the section-by-section released today can be accessed HERE.

Today, the House Homeland Security Committee held a hearing titled “Worldwide Threats to the Homeland: 25 Years After 9/11.” Witnesses included Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin; Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton; and Deputy Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation Christopher Raia.

Click here to watch Rep. Van Epps’ Remarks and Questions

Rep. Van Epps gave the following opening statement:

“Thank you, Chairman Garbarino, for continuing to hold these hearings, and thank you, Secretary Mullin, Deputy Director Raia, and Director Clayton, for joining us today. I am deeply grateful for the services you provide to this country.

It is an honor to serve on this committee dedicated to stewarding this country's security. We know that the threats facing us today are more varied and complex than ever before [as] the cyber domain grows increasingly competitive and difficult to defend; our critical infrastructure is vulnerable to attacks from the other side of the planet; our young people are being radicalized online, [and] biological, technological, and ideological threats evolve faster every day.

During last year’s Worldwide Threats hearing, I discussed emerging AI threats. Today, that threat is still a priority. Foreign cyber actors continue to use AI tools to threaten our cyber infrastructure. Part of our responsibility is to ensure the federal government safeguards our critical systems from these threats while also clearly delineating how AI can be used across our systems to make them stronger and more efficient.”

Rep. Van Epps was also able to ask the following questions:

Rep. Van Epps asked:

“Director Clayton, leading American AI developers have activated heightened safeguards on their most capable models because they cannot rule out that those models could meaningfully help a novice build a biological weapon. In September, Anthropic disclosed five cases since December in which users tried to get around its safeguards on dual-use biology, involving highly pathogenic avian influenza, orthopoxviruses, and toxins. Open-weight models offer no such protections once downloaded. Does ODNI assess [that] terrorist groups or other non-traditional actors are actively seeking to use AI to acquire chemical or biological weapons capabilities, and how has the intelligence community adjusted its collection to detect it?”

Director Clayton responded:

“Thank you, and I commend you for the context in which you placed that question. American frontier model developers are at the forefront; that capability is very important to national security for many of the reasons that you just mentioned. That is not isolated work. They are ahead; they are working with us, seeking to develop this capability in what I would say is a responsible and controlled environment. That does not mean people around the world are following those same rules. It is one of those reasons why we need to be out in front… of those who would seek to develop similar technology, seek to have similar compute, and not use it for good. The United States has demonstrated through every technological development that our leadership is good for the world. We need to keep doing that.”

Rep. Van Epps then asked:

“Deputy Director Raia, the terror threat landscape in the U.S. is increasingly shaped by emerging Nihilistic Violent Extremism, or NVE. These decentralized online groups are primarily run by minors who promote cycles of victimization and coercion, including self-harm, extortion, and mass attacks. I am very concerned about what this is doing to our youth. At the federal level, how has the FBI approached investigations and prosecutions tied to NVE groups since most are minors with prosecutorial limitations?”

Deputy Director Raia responded:

“Thank you for that question, Congressman. I, as yourself, [am] very concerned about that threat, and the FBI is concerned about that threat. That is a threat that we have pushed a lot of resources into. It encompasses, obviously, for us, it is considered a domestic terrorism threat. Groups like 764, the Com, which I know you are familiar with. But it also has a crimes against children aspect to it. Because it is targeting one of our most vulnerable populations, our children. So what we have done at the FBI is create the NVE fusion cell, and we have taken experts from our domestic terrorism folks and experts from our crimes against children folks, and we put them in one room in order to create that synergy to investigate those cases. So we have seen a lot of wins in that space recently. But as you have said, a lot of these are minors, and as you know, the federal system is not set up for minors, so we rely a lot on our state and local partners in not only disrupting those individuals but also in getting some type of jail time in making sure they are held accountable. In extreme circumstances, with some of our older children, we can go to the Attorney General and prosecute on a federal law. But that is something that does not happen that often. That is something we continue to work on, we’re going to continue to push a lot of energy into, and we’re going to continue to keep our children safe because that is a priority of this administration and of our director.”

Congressman Van Epps asked if Deputy Director Raia had any additional comments on UAS systems.

Deputy Director Raia responded:

"We have made a lot of space in [the] last 21 months, and we are much better postured now combating as a country, state, local, and federal… combating that threat than we were just 21 months ago."

Watch Rep. Van Epps talk about the hearing on Washington Watch here.

Bipartisan congressional caucus will champion AI safety legislation, address emerging security threats, and help Congress respond more quickly to AI safety incidents

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Reps. George Whitesides (D-CA), Nathaniel Moran (R-TX), and Don Beyer (D-VA), announced the launch of the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, the first congressional caucus focused specifically on addressing AI safety and security risks posed by increasingly advanced AI systems while ensuring the United States remains a global leader in innovative AI technologies.

As AI capabilities accelerate, so do the potential consequences of catastrophic misuse, loss of control over advanced systems, and threats to national security. In July, an experimental OpenAI agent escaped its testing environment and breached the external platform Hugging Face to cheat on an evaluation, without any human directing it to. Anthropic also disclosed three separate incidents in which its AI models escaped testing environments and gained unauthorized access to external organizations during cybersecurity evaluations. These recent security incidents have underscored the need for Congress to better understand these risks and develop policy solutions to prevent these incidents before emerging threats become larger problems. By addressing these challenges proactively, Congress can help create the conditions for continued American innovation and ensure the public can confidently benefit from advances in AI.

“AI is advancing faster than ever before, and Congress needs to move just as quickly,” said Rep. George Whitesides. “Now is the time to build bipartisan consensus and advance commonsense guardrails we know will reduce the most serious risks. Americans are rightly concerned about where this technology is heading, but too often the debate in Washington is framed as a choice between doing nothing and banning AI altogether. That’s a false choice. We have an opportunity to pursue smart, targeted solutions that protect the public while allowing American innovation to thrive. I co-founded this caucus with Reps. Moran and Beyer to fight for that balance, because safe, secure, and controllable AI is the only path to unlocking its full promise for humanity.”

“We don’t have to choose between innovation and safety,” said Rep. Nathaniel Moran. “We can, and we should, do both. Artificial intelligence affects every American, and it should not be a partisan issue. This caucus gives us a place to find the areas of consensus, set partisanship aside, and put smart, targeted policies in place so we can innovate while we keep people safe. Congress needs to be prepared, and I’m proud to be one of the co-chairs leading that work.”

“AI has immense potential to improve our lives and strengthen American innovation, but that progress can’t come at the expense of our national security or public safety,” said Rep. Don Beyer. “Recent cyberattacks involving AI agents and growing warnings from leaders and researchers at the companies developing these technologies make clear that the risks are real and growing. We can’t afford to wait for a major catastrophe before putting meaningful safeguards in place. I’m proud to join the AI Safety Caucus and work with my colleagues to advance responsible legislation that strengthens oversight, security, and transparency while ensuring AI is developed and deployed safely and responsibly.”

Specifically, the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus will:

Champion AI safety legislation: Develop legislative proposals and endorse existing bipartisan bills that establish thoughtful, targeted guardrails against the most serious AI risks while supporting continued innovation and American technological leadership.

Rapidly respond to AI incidents: Convene AI developers, technical experts, and government officials to brief Members and staff when significant AI safety incidents or developments occur and identify potential policy responses.

Equip congressional offices: Keep Members and staff informed about emerging AI developments, connect them with outside experts, and provide resources to navigate complex AI policy decisions.

Elevate AI safety publicly: Raise public awareness and make AI safety a national priority through public statements, op-eds, and press events.

Shape Congress’ AI agenda: Help develop federal AI safety policy and provide Members outside the committees of jurisdiction with an avenue to contribute to the conversation and legislative process.

By quickly addressing emerging threats, the AI Safety and Innovation caucus will ensure AI can continue to make key improvements in the fields of American science, medicine, productivity, and national security. This new bipartisan caucus will advance thoughtful, targeted guardrails, engaging technical experts and industry leaders, and equip Congress to respond quickly to emerging risks and significant AI incidents while ensuring America continues to lead in AI innovation.

The House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus launched with Reps. George Whitesides (D-CA), Nathaniel Moran (R-TX), and Don Beyer (D-VA) serving as co-chairs. Founding members include Reps. Yassamin Ansari (D-AZ); Greg Casar (D-TX); Yvette Clarke (D-NY); Ben Cline (R-VA); Mike Flood (R-NE); Bill Foster (D-IL); Valerie Foushee (D-NC); Josh Gottheimer (D-NJ); Pat Harrigan (R-NC); Jim Himes (D-CT); Sara Jacobs (D-CA); Mike Kennedy (R-UT); Ro Khanna (D-CA); Sam Liccardo (D-CA); Ted Lieu (D-CA); Zoe Lofgren (D-CA); Celeste Maloy (R-UT); Doris Matsui (D-CA); April McClain Delaney (D-MD); Blake Moore (R-UT); Jay Obernolte (R-CA); Scott Peters (D-CA); Brad Sherman (D-CA); Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA); Ritchie Torres (D-NY); Lori Trahan (D-MA).

A one-pager on the caucus can be found here.

WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senator Katie Britt (R-Ala.) celebrated passage of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA), legislation that overhauls the federal permitting process to speed the construction of energy and infrastructure projects and lower costs for American families. “Alabama families and small businesses are paying too much to keep the lights on, and Washington’s broken permitting system is one of the primary culprits,” said Senator Britt. “Projects that would create good-paying jobs and deliver affordable, reliable energy have been stuck behind red tape for years and are often suffocated by endless litigation. This bill sets firm deadlines on process reviews and puts an end to frivolous lawfare. These provisions, among others in the bill, still retain crucial environmental and preservation standards while accelerating the approval of critical infrastructure projects. Under Republican leadership, the Senate worked across the aisle and with President Trump to get done what Washington has talked about for decades. Lowering costs is the top priority for Alabamians, and the House should send this bill to the President’s desk without delay.”

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 codifies the Ratepayer Protection Act, of which Senator Britt is a proud cosponsor. Senator Britt has long called to codify President Trump’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge to lower energy prices for Alabamians and ensure families and small businesses aren’t left paying for the energy infrastructure needed to support new data centers.

Federal agencies take an average of 4.5 years to complete an environmental impact statement, according to a White House Council on Environmental Quality analysis of reviews from 2013 to 2018. Data from the National Association of Manufacturers shows that permitting delays are costing America’s manufacturers $12.1 billion every year, including $363 million in additional costs in Alabama alone. According to data from McKinsey, $1.8 trillion of investments are locked up in the federal permitting system right now, including $20.6 billion of sidelined investments in Alabama.

Senator Britt has been a consistent champion for meaningful permitting reform. In August, she joined Senator Alan Armstrong (R-OK) in introducing the American Energy and Mineral Infrastructure Act. matches.text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Coal miners, homebuilders, oil and gas producers, manufacturers, labor workers, and construction firms applauded the passage of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act in the U.S. Senate. The legislation delivers lower energy prices, upgraded infrastructure, and economic growth to the American people.

The legislation, passed today by a bipartisan vote of 62 to 33, accelerates project approvals, limits frivolous litigation, and provides businesses with greater investment certainty. Endorsed by President Donald Trump, the bill now heads to the House of Representatives for consideration.

U.S. Senator Kevin Cramer (R-ND), chair of the Senate Environment and Public Works Subcommittee on Transportation and Infrastructure, has spent much of the last year building bipartisan support for the legislation and applauded its passage.

In recognition of the bill’s passage, Cramer delivered a speech on the Senate floor, saying, “For decades, the process of approving the building of the infrastructure necessary to meet the demands of a growing and dynamic economy have been mired in partisan politics, and an out-of-control bureaucracy, which limits our nation's potential, our prosperity, and stifles our global competitiveness. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is an opportunity for us to turn that corner. […] Whether it's transmission lines to load centers, or pipelines to refineries, steel mills, or drone factories, or family housing, we must secure durable changes to the federal permitting reform process or continue to fall behind our global competitors.”

For energy-producing states like North Dakota, timely federal permitting is essential to responsibly developing natural resources. Pipelines, electric transmission lines, processing facilities, roads, and other infrastructure often depend on federal permits. Delays mean deferred investment, which leads to inefficient supply chains, cost increases, and fewer opportunities for workers.

“It took uncommon leadership, and I'm grateful for my colleagues who worked tirelessly, mostly cheerfully, for the last year to get us to this point,” said Cramer in his floor speech. “Most importantly, I thank you, Environment and Public Works Chair Shelley Moore Capito and Ranking Member Sheldon Whitehouse. […] And thank you, Energy and Natural Resources Chair Mike Lee and Ranking Member Martin Heinrich, for hanging in there. […] The work of these four leaders and a host of others is what results in the law that is as durable as it is balanced. A special thank you also goes to the president's team at the White House. […] Now, let’s get the job done. […] Because today, our country depends on us.”

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is historic permitting reform legislation which updates key federal laws to grow the economy, reduce costs, strengthen national security, and improve quality of life—all while maintaining the nation’s worldwide standard of environmental protection.

The bill incorporates U.S. Senator John Hoeven (R-ND) and Cramer’s BLM Mineral Spacing Act to eliminate certain federal oil and gas drilling permit requirements on nonfederal lands where the federal government owns less than 50% of the mineral estate. It also reforms the laws governing federal environmental reviews and permitting, including the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, National Historic Preservation Act, and federal land management authorities to establish clearer timelines, improve project certainty, and limit judicial review.

Judicial Reforms

The legislation streamlines judicial review of federal permitting decisions by setting tighter deadlines for lawsuits, limiting who can sue, and giving federal agencies greater deference. These changes are intended to prevent prolonged litigation from delaying linear infrastructure projects and allow them to continue while agencies and developers correct potential legal deficiencies instead of courts halting construction.

NEPA: Lawsuits challenging NEPA reviews must be filed within 150 days—down from six years—by individuals who participated in the public comment process and can demonstrate direct harm. Cases would go directly to federal courts of appeals rather than district courts. The only remedy courts could impose would be a procedure known as remand without vacatur or an injunction, during which time agencies and developers would have 180 days to make necessary corrections.

Clean Water Act: Challenges to Section 404 permits, state-assumed programs, and general-permit verifications must be filed within 150 days. Only parties that participated in the public comment period to raise their relevant legal concerns can challenge. Courts cannot vacate or enjoin permits unless there is an “imminent and substantial danger,” and remands are limited to 180 days.

Modernizing NEPA

The bill represents the most significant NEPA reforms in decades. The reforms reinforce the Supreme Court’s Seven Counties decision which limited the scope of NEPA to the immediate impacts of a project and clarify NEPA establishes a procedural framework rather than mandating a particular project outcome. It exempts projects from NEPA review when the federal government’s only involvement consists of a loan or loan guarantee. The bill narrows the definition of major federal actions by excluding transmission and pipeline repairs, retrofits, upgrades, and modifications within existing rights-of-way which do not increase capacity by more than 20%.

The bill empowers states and tribes to satisfy NEPA requirements through their own environmental review processes when those processes serve a similar function. It also requires the lead agency to issue a record of decision within 45 days of a published review and outstanding federal authorization within 90 days for agencies participating in the review and 120 days for those that didn’t.

Clean Water Act Reforms

This provision maintains the ability of states to enforce Section 401 water quality certifications and compliance while limiting states’ ability to use the process to simply block or delay projects. States may deny certification only when they present clear and convincing evidence no reasonable conditions could address their concerns and must act within one year. For gas pipelines and transmission lines, the reforms limit reviews to direct point-source discharges and impose a nine-month deadline.

The legislation extends key Clean Water Act permit terms from five to ten years, including Section 402 National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System permits and Section 404 nationwide permits. It also bars the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency from retroactively vetoing Section 404 permits.

Transmission Provisions

The legislation reforms the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (FERC) federal backstop transmission siting authority and eliminates the existing U.S. Department of Energy’s National Interest Electric Transmission Corridor framework. FERC may site interstate transmission lines of 230 kV or greater when a state lacks siting authority, fails to act within one year of an application, or denies a certificate. It requires transmission costs to align roughly with the benefits received, while exempting public power entities and electric cooperatives.

The bill strengthens ratepayer protections against data center-related costs. It prohibits grid operators from shifting incremental costs associated with data centers to other customers, regardless of the facility’s size. Separately, it creates a new oversight mechanism allowing state public utility commissions to refer local transmission projects they believe conflict with local transmission needs to FERC’s Office of Enforcement.

Project Certainty

The bill prohibits federal agencies from rescinding or suspending a permit, halting construction, or stopping the operation of a project unless a court has ordered the action, the permit was violated, the permittee committed fraud, or to prevent immediate harm to life, property, or national security. The bill allows permit holders to seek an expedited court review if they believe the federal actions to cancel or suspend a permit were not justified and entitles them topursue attorneys’ fees, costs related to the delay, and economic damages.

It establishes a one-year deadline for authorizations which do not go through NEPA and allows applicants to seek injunctive orders to force agency action within 60 days and requires the court to act within 120 days.

matches.text:
WASHINGTON – Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) today voted to advance a major piece of bipartisan legislation that would overhaul the country’s broken federal environmental review and permitting system, which is currently holding up $16.8 billion worth of projects in Iowa. By reducing project delays and giving businesses more certainty to invest and build in America, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) will help lower energy costs for American families, create good-paying jobs and accelerate economic growth. The Senate approved the legislation by a vote of 62-33. The bill now heads to the House of Representatives.

“Too many critical infrastructure projects are stuck in limbo because of red tape and endless delays. This leads to lost jobs, missed economic opportunities and higher utility costs for families. Today, I voted to fix our broken permitting system so Iowans can get building without bureaucrats standing in the way,” Grassley said. “The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will keep our country competitive for decades to come by strengthening our infrastructure, producing affordable energy and lowering costs for Iowans.”

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act also includes the Ratepayer Protection Act, which protects Iowans from paying for the rising energy costs of large electricity users, such as data centers. Specifically, the provision creates a national standard that makes data centers pay their own way for transmission lines and other infrastructure instead of forcing American consumers to face increased costs through rising utility bills. Iowa is currently home to some of the cheapest, most predictable and cleanest energy sources in the country, in part thanks to the long standing and renewed partnership between Iowa’s utility companies and data centers.

The following are the impacts of permitting delays in Iowa:

$16.8 billion: total value of Iowa projects stuck in the federal permitting process right now.

$280 million: total cost of federal permitting delays to Iowa manufacturers annually.

$29.1 billion: total economic impact on hold due to the current federal permitting holdup in Iowa (including jobs, in-state spending, tax revenue and more).

3.6%: The total economic impact of Iowa projects entering the federal permitting process annually is equivalent to 3.6% of Iowa’s total GDP.

This week, Grassley spoke on the Senate floor in support of the legislation, highlighting how delays have impacted communities across the country. In his remarks, Grassley cited a road in Colorado that took 13 years to build, a wind project in Wyoming that waited 12 years for federal approval and a mine in Minnesota that took 12 years for its environmental review. Grassley also highlighted Iowans’ support for the legislation, including Joe Murphy of the Iowa Business Council who said, “This bipartisan legislation will bring greater certainty and predictability to the federal permitting process, establish clear timelines for reviews and decisions and make important changes to the way major energy and infrastructure projects are approved.”

Background:

Currently, it takes an average of 4.5 years for federal agencies to approve environmental impact statements. Each year, manufacturers incur $12.1 billion in costs due to permitting delays, and $1.1 to $1.5 trillion in investments are currently locked up in the federal permitting system.

Without regulatory certainty, companies delay meaningful investments in communities across America, holding up roads, bridges, energy infrastructure, manufacturing facilities and other investments that create jobs and strengthen local economies.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act overhauls the federal environmental review and permitting system by establishing deadlines for environmental reviews, providing greater certainty for projects that have already received federal permits and reducing unnecessary delays and litigation. The bill is designed to help projects of all types, not adjust processes for some types of projects but not others. Projects like coal mines, windmills, gas pipelines, solar farms, and steel mills will all benefit from this legislation.

It’s estimated that this legislation could result in an $82 billion to $164 billion increase in economic output every year. The bill is also expected to increase real wages and reduce electric bills for the average household.

WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, released the following statement after the Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), bipartisan legislation to lower energy bills, hold data centers accountable, reduce emissions, and create good-paying jobs.

“In June, SunZia — the largest clean energy infrastructure project in the Western Hemisphere — came online in New Mexico after nearly two decades. The actual construction took just two years. That's how badly our permitting system is holding America back.

“Americans sent Congress a clear message in this historic election: lower costs. They're tired of watching their electricity bills go up while some of the wealthiest corporations in the world get a free ride. We don't have to wait another year to deliver relief. We can act right now.

“The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will get more affordable energy onto the grid faster, make data centers pay their fair share of electricity and grid costs, and create more than 100,000 good-paying American jobs — all while maintaining important environmental protections and strengthening Tribal consultation.

“This was a hard-fought bipartisan agreement, and it wasn't easy. But we proved that Democrats and Republicans can put politics aside and deliver meaningful results for the American people.

“I'm proud of what we've accomplished. Now let's get this bill across the finish line and signed into law.”

Independent analyses project that the legislation will:

Now that the legislation has passed the Senate, it must also pass the House of Representatives before heading to the President's desk to be signed into law.

Heinrich, along with U.S. Senators Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, Shelley More Capito (R-W. Va.), Chairman of the U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and Mike Lee (R-Utah), Chairman of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act in September.

Since introducing the legislation, Heinrich has led an extensive effort to build bipartisan support, engage stakeholders, and make the case for why permitting reform is essential to lowering energy costs and building America's energy future. He has held press conferences in Washington, D.C., and New Mexico; met with labor leaders, energy developers, Tribal representatives, and community stakeholders; and secured important improvements to the legislation through negotiations and amendments.

In a recent op-ed for The Economist, Heinrich made the case that America's permitting system has become one of the country's most expensive economic bottlenecks — and explained how BAAJA can help the country build more energy infrastructure while protecting communities and holding data centers accountable.

Earlier this month, Heinrich released a Substitute Amendment to BAAJA. The Substitute Amendment included clarifying, conforming, and technical edits to reflect feedback received since the bill’s introduction in September.

WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator John Hickenlooper sent a letter to Leader Schumer and Senator Van Hollen pushing the candidates to commit to an agenda that prioritizes AI safety alongside affordability and accountability.

“With the presidential election two years away, we have a two-year audition to show Americans we can deliver on three priorities: affordability, accountability, and AI safety,” Hickenlooper wrote.

“Ensuring this technology benefits all Americans, not just those building this technology will not be easy. It will take a leadership team with the right agenda and determination. That starts with an open discussion within our caucus.”

In the letter, Hickenlooper set clear expectations for the next Majority Leader on AI:

“…The next Majority Leader should have a day-one plan for responsible regulation. That should include policies that support a robust third-party evaluation ecosystem, mitigate national security challenges like cyber and biorisk, and establish clear rules of the road to hold AI companies accountable,” he wrote.

“…Meeting this moment requires more than just legislation,” he added.“We should consider a Select Committee on AI that has the power and resources to help the Senate keep pace with this rapidly evolving technology.”

Senator Hickenlooper is the ranking member of the Senate Commerce subcommittee on Consumer Protection, Technology, and Data Privacy, and previously called on the committee to lead responsible AI regulation.

Hickenlooper has long called for responsible AI regulation and outlined a framework for it in 2024. He’s introduced bipartisan legislation to responsibly regulate AI, including the VET AI Act, which directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to develop standards and guidelines for independent third-party evaluations of AI systems.

Full text of the letter is available HERE and below:

Leader Schumer and Senator Van Hollen,

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is threatening to upend every part of American life. And the U.S. Senate is acting too slowly. That’s why the race for Senate Majority Leader is so important.

Thanks to the leadership of Leader Schumer, Democrats could hold as many as 56 seats. We just won in places like Kansas, Mississippi, and Texas, where Democrats haven’t won Senate races in decades. With the presidential election two years away, we have a two-year audition to show Americans we can deliver on three priorities: affordability, accountability, and AI safety.

Following two years of unchecked chaos, Americans are desperately looking to Washington for leadership — especially on AI. Young people are wondering how they’ll ever get their footing when AI is removing the first rung of the traditional career ladder. Families are worried about their energy bills climbing. Farmers are concerned about data centers draining their already limited water resources. Meanwhile, AI experts are warning that as model capabilities grow, the risks that a catastrophic incident will occur in the short term become even greater.

AI has the potential to help us solve our greatest challenges and unlock scientific breakthroughs in medicine, agriculture, and more. But we should also be deeply worried about what AI means for our future. The potential for even more massive concentrations of wealth and extreme inequality, the risks of war, blackouts, and acts of terror should concern us all. Every day the Senate fails to act moves us closer to these potential dangers.

The next Senate Majority Leader will play an outsized role in championing the tools we need to protect against consequences that are both profound and irreversible.

The next Majority Leader should have a day-one plan for responsible regulation. That should include policies that support a robust third-party evaluation ecosystem, mitigate national security challenges like cyber and biorisk, and establish clear rules of the road to hold AI companies accountable. We also need to examine how best to promote competition and open-source innovation and consider banning Recursive Self-Improvement to prevent AI systems from autonomously advancing beyond our ability to control them.

Meeting this moment requires more than just legislation. We should consider a Select Committee on AI that has the power and resources to help the Senate keep pace with this rapidly evolving technology. This Committee could complement the work of our other relevant committees while shining an even brighter, constant spotlight on AI, positioning Democrats as the party Americans trust to act in their best interests.

Ensuring this technology benefits all Americans, not just those building this technology will not be easy. It will take a leadership team with the right agenda and determination. That starts with an open discussion within our caucus.

The next Majority Leader must be prepared to deliver on affordability, accountability, and AI safety. I look forward to hearing more about your plans and working with our next leadership team to make these issues a top priority.

Sincerely,

###

WASHINGTON – Senator John Hoeven, a member of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, today joined his Senate colleagues in voting to pass bipartisan legislation to reform the federal environmental review and permitting processes. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026:

Provides certainty that permitted energy and infrastructure projects will retain their permits, except for extraordinary circumstances, violations of law or court order.

Makes targeted reforms to ensure energy projects are reviewed in a fair and timely manner.

The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) Mineral Spacing Act to streamline and improve the permitting process for energy development, remove duplicative regulations and better respect the rights of private mineral holders. Less than half of the subsurface minerals within a drilling spacing unit are owned by the federal government; and

The federal government does not own or lease any surface rights within the impacted area.

The Harnessing Energy at Thermal Sources (HEATS) Act to support the expanded development of geothermal energy. The bill eliminates duplicative federal permitting and ensures majority holders of a geothermal estate located on non-federal lands can exercise their property rights in developing these resources. Hoeven’s legislation would remove the federal permitting requirement for geothermal operations in instances when:

Less than half of the subsurface geothermal estate is owned by the federal government.

Geothermal exploration and production activities are conducted on non-federal surface acres.

The operator has received a state permit.

“Across the country, there are $1.1 trillion worth of projects that are held up by regulation, and this bill will help get those projects going. WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Angus King (I-ME) shared the following statement after the Senate passed bipartisan legislation to lower home utility bills and increase access to renewable energy sources. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA), which passed the Senate in a 62-33 vote, is an important step forward in unlocking the bureaucratic process for transmission lines that would bring renewable energy sources like solar and wind to homes across the country.

According to energy distribution modeling, it is likely that with a level regulatory playing field that BAAJA provides, clean energy sources will prove cheaper and improve carbon emissions nationwide. It now heads to the House of Representatives for consideration.

“Today we saw the passage of the Permitting Reform Bill, and I want to share some thoughts about it. First, and foremost, it deals with two of the most pressing challenges facing America today. One immediate, and one in the longer term. The immediate one is affordability; this bill will bring down electric prices. Not right away, not next week, or next month, but in the reasonably foreseeable future. By making the grid more efficient, and by lowering and bringing on cheaper sources, I’m going to talk about that in a minute.

“The other thing that is important about the bill, and certainly important to me, it’s a major step forward in the fight against climate change. It will allow us to electrify more of America, to bring fossil fuels down as a source of energy, and to really strengthen the role that renewables play in the electric source. Which then, as we electrify transportation and home heat through heat pumps will basically reduce the carbon footprint of this country substantially.

“Now, is it a perfect bill? No, there’s some things in it that that I don’t like. If I had written it myself, it may have said some other things. But it’s the bill that we can get right now, and there is no clear alternative to it, either now or even in the next Congress. And that’s why I ended up voting ‘yes.’

“It wasn’t an easy choice. I listened to my environmental friends in Maine, many of whom were opposed to the bill, I talked to people in the energy field, particularly in the renewable field, and decided that on balance this bill is a lot better than the status quo.

“Let me talk about electricity costs for a minute: the cheapest form of energy today is solar and wind, it’s about half the cost of natural gas. If you add storage, it’s still competitive with natural gas, and then it becomes baseload power. This bill unlocks an enormous amount of renewable energy, that is now basically unable to get to the market because of a lack of transmission.

“The other piece of the bill that I really like is it requires the transmission buildout that’s inevitable, that’s going to happen, to be done in the most economic way possible and the most efficient way possible. It also specifically shifts about $35 billion worth of grid construction costs onto data centers, by making it absolutely clear that they have to pay any costs that they’re imposing on the grid.

“The bill has a lot of very important provisions, and yes, it makes it easier to permit all kinds of energy facilities, and transportation facilities like highways and bridges. But I don’t think it really compromises environmental standards. What it focuses on is the process, how long it takes to get things done. And there’s an enormous growth in energy demand in this country, and it’s going to be met one way or the other. I want it to be met by renewables. This bill is essential to unlocking those renewables, which are often far from the markets that they need to serve.

“So those are some of the reasons I came to the conclusion, as I said, this bill is a lot better than the status quo. I think it’s a one-time opportunity, I don’t think we’re going to have this opportunity in the new Congress, and it’s an opportunity for us to make our country safer, our country more affordable, and to deal with the challenge of climate change, which is bearing down on us more seriously every day.”

matches.text:
Washington, D.C. – This week, U.S. Senators Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) and Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) introduced the bipartisan Stealth Bot Prohibition Act to confront the illegal and deceptive use of internet bots that threaten Americans’ intellectual property.

In light of the rise of artificial intelligence (AI), automated web crawlers are now roaming across the internet. While many have legitimate uses, bad actors have exploited the technology to wreak havoc on online producers, including local newspapers and journalists. Many of these advanced bots evade paywalls, scrape information, and overwhelm websites. “Stealth bots” are a particular class of disguised web crawlers that America’s adversaries deploy to steal protected online content and use it to train their own AI models.

The Stealth Bot Prohibition Act would enact transparency standards to combat these unauthorized practices. If passed, this legislation would provide a new tool for publishers to combat deceptive operators by requiring the disclosure of identities and purposes of bots when accessing websites without banning legitimate research and other beneficial automated material. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) would be in charge of the enforcement of the bill’s provisions and would empower state attorneys general to take legal action to protect residents from violators.

“AI is advancing rapidly, creating new challenges and threats for the American people. Congress must act immediately to ensure transparency and accountability for those who misuse this technology,” said Senator Luján. “That’s why I’m joining Senator Wicker in introducing the Stealth Bot Prohibition Act to crack down on bad actors and protect creatives, small businesses, and local news. No one should profit by stealing others’ hard work, ideas, or livelihoods.”

“The Chinese Communist Party is notorious for stealing Americans’ intellectual property by any means possible. Now, it is weaponizing artificial intelligence and deploying droves of malicious bots against online publishers,” said Senator Wicker. “Our legislation recognizes these threats and offers a solution to insulate digital producers from bad actors.”

“We are immensely grateful to Senator Ben Ray Luján for his leadership in co-sponsoring the Stealth Bot Prohibition Act. By bringing critical transparency to online bot activity, this common-sense legislation takes a vital step toward protecting American businesses and securing a healthy digital marketplace for news and content. With automated internet traffic now exceeding human traffic and bot and AI scraping activity growing exponentially, this has caused increased costs and slowdowns of our websites. We must have greater transparency to give website owners the choice and ability to block stealth bots and nefarious actors while allowing proper use of their sites and content,” said Patrick Dorsey, Publisher of The Santa Fe New Mexican and Board Chair, America’s Newspapers.

“We thank Senator Luján for his commitment to New Mexico’s journalism industry, and for his commitment to protect American content creators, websites, and consumers, from a flood of bad bots. News publishers of all sizes are drowning in bot traffic, hurting their ability to provide high-quality content to the American public. The Stealth Bot Prohibition Act is a common-sense, bipartisan solution to the problem of bad bots,” said Belinda Mills, President & CEO of the New Mexico Press Association.

“News publishers of all sizes are drowning in bot traffic, hurting their ability to provide high-quality content to the American public. The Stealth Bot Prohibition Act is a common-sense, bipartisan solution to the problem of bad bots. It offers straightforward transparency requirements and enforcement mechanisms that uncover bad actors while leaving responsible uses of bots unaffected. The News/Media Alliance thanks Senators Wicker and Luján for their leadership on this issue, and their commitment to protecting American content creators, websites, and consumers, from a flood of bad bots. We look forward to working with them and their colleagues in Congress to pass this critical piece of legislation and offer American businesses and the American people the relief they deserve,” said Danielle Coffey, President and CEO of the News/Media Alliance.

“As AI bots continue to pose an increasing threat across the creative landscape, the Stealth Bot Prohibition Act will be a critical tool in ensuring that the constitutional copyright protections of creators can continue to be upheld and respected, especially across online platforms. AAP thanks Senators Roger Wicker and Ben Ray Luján and Representatives Laurel Lee, Valerie Foushee, and Gus Bilirakis for introducing this important legislation to help defend the integrity of human innovation,” said Maria A. Pallante, President and CEO, Association of American Publishers (AAP).

To read the full text of the bill, click here.

Senators Write Meta, Google and Apple Following Reports That Nonconsensual Image Generating Apps Are Evading Bans by App Stores and Meta Ads

Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senators Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.), Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), and Edward J. Markey (D-Mass.) questioned Big Tech companies over the widespread availability of so-called ‘nudify’ apps in app stores, nearly a year after the senators raised concerns about X and Grok remaining available despite enabling mass-generation of nonconsensual sexual images of women and children.

Although Apple and Google ban nudify apps in their terms of service, researchers recently revealed that apps marketed on Meta ads as nonconsensual sexual image generators are widely available in app stores, and generated over $100 million in revenue. One common tactic is for apps to be updated after passing review to add nudification tools.

“These findings raise questions not only about individual failures of app review, but also about [Google and Apple’s] ability to identify repeat offenders, disrupt coordinated networks, and monitor apps after approval,” the senators wrote.

The senators also questioned Meta over its continued role in advertising apps marketed as generating nonconsensual intimate images of women and children.

“Despite Meta’s stated prohibition on these ads, independent investigations have documented extensive ad campaigns on Facebook and Instagram directing customers to apps capable of digitally undressing people in photographs or placing their likeness into sexually explicit content without their consent,” the senators wrote.

AI tools have supercharged the spread of nonconsensual sexual imagery online, creating real harm to women and children in particular. A 2024 survey by the Center for Democracy & Technology found that 15% of U.S. public high school students knew of AI-generated nonconsensual intimate imagery (NCII) depicting someone at their school. A separate 2025 Thorn survey found that 6% of young people reported having been targeted by AI-generated NCII.

NCII is frequently weaponized against female journalists, human rights defenders, politicians, and other prominent women – not simply to humiliate them, but to discredit, intimidate, and silence their work and advocacy. Research by the American Sunlight Project revealed that one in six female Members of Congress were targeted by sexually explicit deepfakes and a 2025 New America investigation documented 100 cases involving public officials across 14 countries, 97 of them involving women.

Permitting reform legislation builds on Senator McCormick’s longstanding efforts to cut red tape, lower energy costs, unlock American economic growth

WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator Dave McCormick (R-PA) today applauded the U.S. Senate passage of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA), landmark legislation to modernize federal permitting processes, accelerate critical infrastructure projects, lower energy costs, and create good-paying American jobs. Senator McCormick thanked U.S. Senators Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Mike Lee (R-UT), and Martin Heinrich (D-NM) for their leadership in delivering this win. This fulfills one of Senator McCormick’s key campaign promises to overhaul our permitting process to lower costs and make Pennsylvania a better place to invest.

In April, Senator McCormick introduced the Unlock American Energy and Jobs Act of 2026, legislation targeting four major federal permitting chokepoints that have delayed energy infrastructure projects: the abuse of onerous water permitting rules, baseless lawsuits brought by environmental groups, outdated nuclear licensing, and federal barriers to LNG exports. BAAJA addresses two of them, streamlining water permitting and shutting down frivolous lawsuits aimed at delaying projects.

“Pennsylvania has the energy resources, skilled workforce, and innovative companies to power America’s future, but burdensome regulations and permitting delays have held us back,” said Senator McCormick. “This was a day one promise of mine when I entered the Senate, and today’s bipartisan passage is a major step toward delivering American energy dominance. I’ll keep pushing next Congress to cut red tape in areas this bill doesn’t address.”

BAAJA reforms the federal environmental review and permitting process, providing greater regulatory certainty for approved projects. It also requires data centers to cover their own transmission costs instead of shifting those expenses onto American ratepayers.

As Pennsylvania continues to attract growing investment in energy, manufacturing, and emerging technologies, modernizing the nation’s permitting system is essential to turning those commitments into real projects, economic growth, and good-paying jobs across the Commonwealth.

The bipartisan legislation now heads to the U.S. House of Representatives for consideration.

Washington, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) penned an op-ed in the Wall Street Journal highlighting concerns that if an AI industry bubble bursts it has the potential to destabilize the economy. The Senator says that Congress must make clear that American taxpayers will not act as a fail-safe to bail out the industry or its investors.

Schiff notes: “This may be the biggest economic gamble in American history, and policymakers should make clear that Congress and American taxpayers won’t act as its fail-safe should this industry falter under its own immense weight… If these enormous bets fail, Big Tech and Wall Street billionaires will no doubt turn to Washington for emergency rescue, a path unfortunately well-trodden by corporate giants before them. But the risk should be borne by these companies and their investors, not working families.”

In the op-ed, Schiff points to AI’s explosive buildout being financed by opaque debt structures and special-purpose vehicles, as companies are borrowing capital from an increasingly consolidated group of investors and lenders while free cash flow is declining.

Schiff says: “The billionaire investors may be taking this gamble with the assumption that as in 2008, they will be bailed out for failed investments and corporate risk-taking. Congressional majorities should be clear: We won’t bail them out.”

Read the full op-ed below:

Wall Street Journal Op-Ed: No AI Company Is Too Big to Fail

By Adam B. Schiff

Our nation is in the midst of what will be one of the largest economic transformations in human history, driven by rapid advances in artificial intelligence and the corporations fueling their growth.

This technology has boundless potential to enhance our lives and expand our individual and collective capacity. But as the turmoil around Nvidia reminds us, this swift and massive investment also carries significant risk that an industry downturn or a bubble could destabilize the American economy. In the first six days of the scandal involving Nvidia and its former CEO, the sector lost $500 billion in value.

Given the risks to our economy and investors, Congress must make sure that industry understands this: No company is too big to fail, and in the event of a financial collapse of the tech sector, there will be no taxpayer-funded bailout.

The AI industry, after less than five years of market power, is already estimated to represent 3.6% of our nation’s economy. But much of its explosive build-out is financed by an opaque debt structure and expectations of increasing profitability. This may be the biggest economic gamble in American history, and policymakers should make clear that Congress and American taxpayers won’t act as its fail-safe should this industry falter under its own immense weight.

This year alone, AI will see nearly $1 trillion invested in its continued expansion. If these enormous bets fail, Big Tech and Wall Street billionaires will no doubt turn to Washington for emergency rescue, a path unfortunately well-trodden by corporate giants before them. But the risk should be borne by these companies and their investors, not working families.

We have seen this movie before. In the early 2000s, there were warning signs that the housing market had taken on immense systemic risk, which had the potential to drag down our entire economy. The American people and Congress were told by top bank and mortgage lending executives, as well as the Treasury secretary and Federal Reserve chairman, that the subprime mortgage market was contained from the rest of the financial system and that the economy was healthy.

That was catastrophically wrong. In 2008 those same officials begged Congress to forgive their error and pass an industry-wide bailout, while our nation was on the brink of a financial calamity.

The result, reluctantly approved by Democrats and Republicans in Congress amid the crisis, gave executives who gambled with America’s economy billions of dollars to forgive their gambling debt while the American people were plunged into the worst economic recession since the Great Depression. No executives were charged with criminal wrongdoing.

The average American family saw its wealth decline by a third from 2007 to 2010, with 1 in 4 households losing 75 cents of every dollar in its savings, home equity and net worth. Even as the economy began to stabilize, middle-class wealth remained stagnant and wages flat while the wealthiest Americans quickly made up what they had lost in the worst years.

This must not happen again. As venture-capital firms and trillion-dollar companies are increasingly taking on more debt to build out AI without the financial certainty that it will pay off—and with the added danger that AI companies will be held liable for the damage their agents do in the wild—they should do so understanding that this risk won’t be borne by others.

Now is the time to right-size the risk and debt, before a crisis. This is true not only of the big banks and investment houses, but also of the regional banks and pension funds. The collapse of Silicon Valley Bank demonstrated the fragility of the system when the financial liquidity of even midsize firms is threatened. Regulators should take precautions now, not after the fact.

Big Tech hyperscaling companies used to be able to finance their data-center infrastructure build-outs from the profits of their existing businesses. But as they race to invest massive sums they don’t have on hand to project confidence in their businesses, these companies are borrowing capital from an increasingly consolidated group of investors and lenders while their free cash flow is declining.

Smaller infrastructure companies are even more leveraged, borrowing billions against GPUs, data centers and anticipated future lease payments. Banks, private credit funds, insurers and pension funds are also financing this expansion, often through complicated corporate structures and special-purpose vehicles that obscure who ultimately holds the risk.

The billionaire investors may be taking this gamble with the assumption that as in 2008, they will be bailed out for failed investments and corporate risk-taking. Congressional majorities should be clear: We won’t bail them out.

On Election Day the American people rejected the corruption and special treatment that exists in our current politics across party lines, under which billionaires and industry giants get sweetheart deals at the expense of everyone else. We should listen to the message voters sent us.

Mr. Schiff, a Democrat, is a U.S. senator from California.

###

matches.text:
Legislation Lowers Energy Costs for Missouri Families, Holds Data Centers Accountable for Costs They Create

WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senator Eric Schmitt (R-MO) celebrated Senate passage of the “Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA),” landmark legislation to boost American energy production and drive down energy costs for Missouri families. The bill also requires data centers to shoulder the costs they inflict upon the grid, ensuring Missourians do not foot the bill for their increased energy demand.

“Tonight, I voted for landmark legislation on permitting reform that, for the first time forces data centers to pay their own way. No more fleecing ratepayers. It also unleashes American energy production by cutting leftist red tape and lowering costs, and it makes it easier to build in America again. More jobs! The reindustrialization of America is on. It’s past time we protect our communities and rebuild this country,” said Senator Schmitt.

BAAJA protects Missouri consumers from paying for data center development costs:

Requires new data centers to pay the costs they create by requiring utilities to recover the costs of serving data centers—including their electricity usage, power supply impact, and the grid upgrades necessary to meet them—from those companies.

Mandates that a customer’s share of new federally approved transmission costs must be in line with the benefits they receive by preventing customers from being forced to pay when those projects provide them with no meaningful benefit.

Ends a federal restriction on charging data centers for both the existing transmission grid and the additional upgrades needed to serve them by requiring utilities’ transmission rates to collect both charges from data centers.

Creates new reporting requirements for data centers’ electricity use to provide a clearer picture of their contribution to increasing energy demand.

Helps local government officials understand a proposed data center’s impacts before making decisions by creating a program that provides fact-based information and technical assistance upon request about its energy, water, economic, and community impacts.

Explicitly recognizes a state’s ability to charge data centers more than their costs and uses the extra revenue from data centers to lower electricity rates for homes and small businesses.

Last night, U.S. Senator Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) released the following video on the latest developments on Artificial Intelligence, calling for the Senate to immediately address the urgent threats posed to working Americans by AI. To watch the video, click here. A transcript of the video is provided below:

The last 24 hours and the next 24 hours show us how urgent it is to address the risks posed by AI.

We just had OpenAI release their latest model, which creates more risks. We have Anthropic going public tomorrow, which will be great for the billionaires, but we need to act urgently to address the threats to the rest of us.

We need to protect our workforce and our workers. We need to make sure that all of you aren't paying higher electric bills for data centers built by the biggest and richest corporations on the planet. We need to deal with issues of privacy.

There's one issue that is immediately pressing, and that is the issue of AI safety. And Congress and the Senate better have a day-one plan for how we're going to deal with this.

So, we need mandatory and independent third-party evaluation of these companies.

Number two, we need to make sure that companies are held accountable, liable, and responsible for any harm they do, like if these agents escape containment and get onto the internet. And there should be penalties also for putting people at risk.

We also need to deal with the very urgent matter of bioweapons and cyberattacks.

And finally, given how rapidly this is evolving, we need to consider banning recursive self-improvement. In other words, the fact that AI begins to train AI and get beyond human capacity to intervene.

That could put us all at risk, and we need to move quickly to address that big threat to all of us.
