WASHINGTON— U.S. Sens. Mark R. Warner (D-VA), a senior member of the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs and one of Congress’s leading voices on artificial intelligence policy, Sen. John Kennedy (R-LA), Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-MD), and Sen. Mike Rounds (R-SD) introduced the Advancing Uniform Disclosure of Investments and Transparency of Artificial Intelligence (AUDIT AI) Act, legislation to increase transparency around how publicly traded companies are investing in, deploying, and managing AI.

The legislation comes amid growing concerns about the unprecedented scale of AI investment and the increasingly complex financing arrangements underpinning the industry’s rapid expansion. As companies pour trillions of dollars into AI infrastructure, investors and regulators often lack a clear picture of the financing exposure, governance practices, and potential risks associated with these investments.

“AI has enormous potential to transform our economy, but the trillions of dollars pouring into this technology come with real financial risks,” said Sen. Warner. “Investors and policymakers deserve to know where that money is going, how these deals are being financed, and what risks are involved. We can’t afford to have massive financial exposure building up behind the scenes, only to discover it when something goes wrong. This bipartisan legislation would bring much-needed transparency and accountability to AI investments and help ensure we’re not setting ourselves up for the next financial crisis.”

“AI is the future, but investing in it shouldn’t be a guessing game. Companies are spending trillions of dollars on this technology, and investors deserve to know where that money is going and what risks they’re taking. Our bill will help make sure these companies put all their cards on the table,” said Sen. Kennedy.

“AI is no longer a far-off technology; it is already shaping how people work, learn, and receive health care. It is also reshaping our financial system, requiring clear guardrails from Congress to protect investors and consumers. Our bipartisan bill takes responsible steps to increase transparency around AI funding and protect our financial system. I will keep fighting to ensure AI expands opportunity, protects workers and consumers, strengthens American competitiveness, and builds public trust,” said Sen. Alsobrooks.

“Economic growth in the United States has been driven in large part by investment in the development of artificial intelligence capabilities,” said Sen. Rounds. “As AI continues to advance, it’s important that public companies disclose material information about how they oversee AI capabilities internally and where they invest their resources in outside AI capabilities. Our legislation would create transparent disclosure guidelines for public companies regarding their implementation of AI capabilities.”

The rapid expansion of AI is fueling an unprecedented wave of investment in data centers, semiconductors, energy infrastructure, and other critical resources. A recent report published by the Brookings Institution estimates that building out AI infrastructure could require $10.3 trillion in investment from 2025 to 2032, equivalent to approximately 3.6 percent of U.S. GDP each year. The scale of this investment could surpass historic American infrastructure booms, including the expansion of railroads, highways, electrification, canals, and telecommunications.

Slowdown in the buildout could ignite shockwaves throughout the U.S. economy and have far-reaching consequences for the financial sector. These risks are compounded by complex financing arrangements, including joint ventures, special purpose vehicles, and other debt structures, that can make it difficult for investors and policymakers to fully assess companies’ financial exposure. The AUDIT AI Act would help close these transparency gaps by strengthening corporate disclosures, improving oversight, and giving investors a clearer picture of the risks associated with these investments. Greater transparency will help policymakers and regulators better understand how these investments are connected to the broader financial system and where vulnerabilities could emerge.

Specifically, the AUDIT AI Act would:

Strengthen AI governance by requiring public companies to disclose whether they have an AI governance policy and a dedicated board committee focused on AI, and explain why if they do not. Companies with an AI governance policy would be required to make it publicly available.

Shed light on AI infrastructure financing by requiring non-financial public companies to disclose AI-related joint ventures, special purpose vehicles, variable interest entities, and other major debt arrangements in SEC filings and at the SEC’s discretion.

Standardize AI risk disclosure by requiring companies with significant AI exposure to provide standardized disclosure of material risks, including dependence on third-party models, compute concentration, costs, and data liabilities.

Examine whether financial reporting is keeping pace with AI by directing the SEC to study how companies account for AI research and development, revenues, and capital expenditures and make recommendations for future policymaking or standard setting.

Monitor AI’s impact on financial markets by requiring the SEC to report annually on how automated investment strategies are affecting price discovery, market efficiency, and potential herding behavior.

“Both the enormous potential and unprecedented risks of AI are top of mind in most American boardrooms. This bill will give investors critical insight on whether, and how, corporate leaders are overseeing the technology that will define our future. And it will shine crucial light on how enormous and opaque AI investments are actually being funded. Ordinary investors deserve to know who is behind the systemic shifts that AI will soon bring—and how they’re paying for it,” said Robert J. Jackson, Jr., Former Commissioner of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.

“I strongly support greater transparency in the financing of the AI buildout. Investors and policymakers need a clear picture of the debt, lease commitments, and guarantees supporting this investment–and who ultimately bears the risks. As financing spreads across joint ventures, private credit, and off-balance-sheet vehicles, conventional corporate accounts reveal only part of the story. Better disclosure is essential to support informed investment, strengthen accountability, and identify financial vulnerabilities while this rapidly growing industry is still taking shape,” said Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, the Earl Kazis and Benjamin Schore Professor of Real Estate at Columbia Business School.

“Governance and effective control over AI development and applications are critical aspects of a company’s effective and appropriate use of AI tools. Investors need greater transparency and visibility into companies’ governance and oversight process over development and use of AI applications that are important to a company’s ongoing operations,” said Paul Munter, Former Chief Accountant of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.

Read the full bill here and a section-by-section explainer of the bill here.

WASHINGTON D.C. — U.S. Senator Peter Welch (D-Vt.) today voted against the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), the Senate’s permitting reform legislative package, after the Senate failed to adopt amendments that would have improved the bill while preserving its historic gains in transmission and clean energy development—including ensuring states can enforce their own drinking water laws, and preventing developers from abusing the courtsand securing excessive damages at taxpayers’ expense, among others.

“We need to build things faster and more efficiently in Vermont and across the country. Permitting reform is especially important as we work to transition to the affordable, clean energy infrastructure we need to address climate change and lower utility bills for families. I am all for getting to yes or no faster. Unfortunately, the Senate failed to address several outstanding issues in the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, including provisions that could open the government up to unprecedented financial liability and changes that undercut states’ ability to protect their clean water resources,” said Senator Welch. “I offered fixes and amendments to this bill and am disappointed the Senate failed to consider these important changes to protect our communities.”

Senator Welch’s amendments to BAAJA included provisions to:

Prevent Project Developers from Abusing the Courts

Welch filed an amendment to eliminate the excessive damages in the permitting certainty sections of BAAJA, preventing project developers from receiving between 25-100% of project costs as settlements in certain cases where a permit is revoked or denied.

Mitigate Harms from BAAJA’s Changes to the Clean Water Act

Welch filed amendments to protect states’ authority to consider a range of project impacts that may harm clean water resources. The amendments would also prevent states from having to meet an unreachable burden of proof to protect clean water resources in court.

Protect Judicial Remedies Under the National Environment Policy Act (NEPA)

This amendment would maintain the courts’ authority to stop projects from moving forward with construction if they find a major NEPA violation.

Exclude Data Centers from Benefitting from the Bill

Welch filed an amendment to exclude data centers from BAAJA’s permitting certainty provisions, preventing data center approvals from being locked in by the current administration and protecting taxpayer dollars from potentially being awarded in settlements to Big Tech companies.

Better Support Local Communities That Host Transmission Projects

Welch filed an amendment to add his Energizing Our Communities Act to the bill. This legislation aims to support national transmission build-out by ensuring communities see the benefits of transmission at the ground level by investing revenue from certain Department of Energy loan programs back into communities, including tribal governments, that host transmission infrastructure.

Harness Energy Efficiency to Reduce Electricity Bills

Welch filed an amendment to ensure that energy efficiency and demand response resources are eligible tocompete in wholesale markets as distributed energy resources under the bill. It would add key components of Senator Welch’s E-Access Act to guarantee ratepayers have access to their energy consumption data in order toparticipate in these programs.

Contact: Lexi Kranich (814) 380-4408

WASHINGTON, D.C.—Today, Congressman Pat Harrigan (NC-10) introduced the Digital Infrastructure Security Act of 2026 to stop Chinese telecommunications companies from maintaining access to American data centers after losing their licenses over national security concerns. The bill would help protect the systems Americans rely on for banking, healthcare, business, and national defense.

“China has spent years stealing American technology and targeting our communications networks, and we know they're not going to stop,” said Congressman Harrigan. “What concerns me is that we've already identified these companies as national security threats, revoked their licenses, and somehow still allowed them to keep a foothold in our data centers. My bill would prohibit them from operating data centers here or doing business with Americans through cloud services. And they wouldn't be able to get around those restrictions by using a subsidiary or another company to do it for them. When we're talking about the systems that handle Americans' financial information, medical records, and sensitive military data, I think that's a pretty reasonable safeguard.”

“I’m proud to sponsor this legislation that will shore up the safety and national security of our telecommunications systems,” said Congressman Dave Min. “By banning companies that we know are national security threats from owning or operating data centers or cloud services in the United States, we are shoring up the security of this increasingly important critical infrastructure and protecting ourselves from bad actors and foreign adversaries.”

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) previously revoked or denied licenses for China Telecom Americas, China Unicom Americas, and China Mobile USA over national security concerns. But those actions didn't automatically remove their equipment and connections from American data centers. Investigations identified more than 108,000 incidents involving Chinese-linked networks redirecting internet traffic between 2018 and 2025, raising concerns about the potential for foreign interference and the exposure of sensitive information.

The legislation would extend existing telecommunications restrictions to data centers and cloud services, including certain affiliated companies and business partners. The FCC would enforce the law, with fines of up to $1 million per violation or per day for ongoing violations. Existing operations and contracts would have 180 days to comply after enactment, and the bill will now be referred to the appropriate House committee for consideration.

“I am deeply concerned about the so-called Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), and I cannot support this bill if it comes before the House of Representatives without significant improvements.

WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) issued the following statement after the Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026. The bill reforms federal permitting laws to advance critical energy and infrastructure projects.

Sen. Cruz said, “Burdensome regulations and unnecessary permitting delays have made it harder and more expensive to build critical energy infrastructure in America. The Senate’s passage of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is an important step toward removing these obstacles, expanding domestic energy production and mineral development, lowering costs, and creating American jobs. I urge the House to swiftly advance this legislation to President Trump’s desk.”

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 includes the following permitting reforms:

National Environmental Policy Act: Limits the scope of environmental reviews, expands categorical exclusions for certain projects, establishes a 150-day statute of limitations for legal challenges to environmental documents, and directs courts to remand deficient environmental documents to federal agencies rather than vacating permits or authorizations.

Clean Water Act: Limits certification reviews to compliance with water quality requirements, prohibits states from denying permits for reasons not related to water quality, and establishes a 150-day statute of limitations for challenges to Section 404 permits and permit verifications.

Endangered Species Act: Reduces statutory timelines for Section 7 consultations, establishes a state primacy program under specified conditions, and requires legal challenges to biological opinions to be filed within 150 days of publication.

Data Centers and Large Loads: Requires large data centers to cover specified electricity infrastructure costs rather than shifting those costs to residential and small-business customers.

National Historic Preservation Act: Restricts the range of impacts considered during historic preservation reviews, establishes new consultation deadlines, requires reviews to be completed within applicable NEPA timelines, and sets a 150-day statute of limitations for most challenges. The legislation also generally requires courts to remand deficient reviews rather than vacate approvals, and it restricts judicial review of programmatic agreements and historic preservation determinations.

On Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang:

Public reporting, including an investigation by the Associated Press, revealed that the actual figure was about 450,000, or 6-7% of enrollees.

Rather than working with states to fix issues, CMS has replaced on-site reviews and dedicated oversight staff with a public relations “War Room” and artificial intelligence pilots. The letter points out that the administration is violating federal law by failing to maintain the minimum required funding and staffing levels for the Medicaid Integrity Program, which was created by Congress to help states fight fraud.

Senator Gillibrand has long fought to protect Medicaid for New Yorkers. In March, she joined Senate colleagues to challenge the Trump administration over its threat to cut New York State’s Medicaid funding. As ranking member of the Senate Aging Committee, she also led colleagues in demanding answers from the administration on how its Medicaid cuts could cause states to scale back services under Medicaid for seniors and people with disabilities.

In addition to Senator Gillibrand, the letter is signed by Senators Adam Schiff (D-CA), Alex Padilla (D-CA), Ron Wyden (D-OR), Jeff Merkley (D-OR), and Ed Markey (D-MA).

WASHINGTON – Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) voted to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), a bill that would reform the nation’s permitting and environmental review processes, accelerate critical infrastructure projects and help lower energy costs for American families.

The package passed the Senate on November 19, 2026, by a vote of 62-33.

“Permitting reform is affordability. This package will help us build more energy, lower costs, create jobs and strengthen America’s energy supply chain. It cuts unnecessary red tape, establishes reasonable timelines for critical projects and gives businesses the certainty they need to invest and grow. I’m especially proud this package includes language I secured to protect Ohio families, farmers and small businesses from footing the bill for data center energy costs. This has been a priority of mine in the Senate, and I’m glad we were able to work across the aisle to get this done,” said Husted.

As a member of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, Husted has been actively involved in efforts to modernize the nation’s permitting system. The bill would:

Establish a clear, efficient federal environmental review process to give infrastructure and energy projects greater predictability.

Create a defined legal process for developers, the public and other stakeholders to resolve disputes without years of costly delays.

Provide greater certainty for approved projects by limiting the circumstances under which federal agencies can rescind or suspend issued permits.

BAAJA also includes language Husted negotiated, similar to provisions in his Ratepayer Protection Act, to protect consumers from footing the bill for data center energy and infrastructure costs.

Currently $45.1 billion of Ohio projects are stuck in the federal permitting process right now, and federal permitting delays cost Ohio manufacturers $669 billion annually. BAAJA would reform the process to be quicker and lower costs.

Specifically, the legislation would:

Set deadlines for environmental reviews, requiring environmental assessments within one year and full environmental impact statements within two years.

Limit lawsuits by requiring claims under the National Environmental Policy Act to be filed within 150 days.

Protect issued permits by limiting the circumstances under which federal agencies can rescind or suspend valid permits.

Preserve Ohio’s authority over transmission line siting and data center electricity rates.

WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator Todd Young (R-Ind.) voted for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, bipartisan legislation to reform our nation’s permitting and environmental review processes and make life more affordable for American families. The bill passed the Senate last night by a vote of 62-33.

“It costs too much and takes too long to build things in our country,” said Senator Young. “Indiana has billions of dollars in potential investment tied up in the federal permitting process. The simple reforms in this bill will help cut unnecessary red tape, move critical infrastructure projects forward, and create more opportunities for Hoosier workers and businesses. It’s long past time to modernize our permitting process, and I am pleased the Senate passed this bipartisan bill.”

Major infrastructure projects, including Interstate 69 and the I-69 Ohio River Crossing, have faced permitting challenges that contributed to delays and increased costs.

WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senator Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) released the following statement after voting in support of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on the Senate floor.

“Last Thursday, I voted for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. This bipartisan bill has both strengths and shortcomings, as with nearly every bill. I am grateful to the Michiganders who have reached out to share their concerns and perspectives, on this issue — both for and against.

“The central problem this Congress must face is the existential threat to America’s middle class. Michiganders of all political persuasions are demanding we do something to lower their costs. And we cannot meaningfully lower utility costs without legislation that reforms federal permitting laws. This bill does just that. Current laws mean it can often take four years to get permission to build or upgrade projects — which drives up the cost of these projects, particularly projects to bring cheaper and cleaner energy online.

“This bill will help decrease monthly utility costs for Michiganders by cutting the red tape around building new energy projects and allowing supply to keep up with demand. Importantly, this bill also puts in place the first federal guardrails on data centers to prevent them from passing on electrical costs to Michigan ratepayers, providing an estimated tens of billions of dollars in new revenue that can be used to lower energy bills for Michigan residents.

“Voting yes wasn’t simple. I pushed for amendments to address concerns about the bill’s impact on the Clean Water Act and its impact on tribal sovereignty. I am disappointed that fellow Democrats killed consideration of those amendments to try and tank the entire bill. I remain committed to addressing those concerns moving forward.

“Michigan families have been feeling the burden of their monthly utility costs, and we cannot delay easing that pressure. That is the bottom line, and it’s why I voted to pass this bill.”

Today, U.S. Senators Tim Kaine (D-VA), Mike Rounds (R-SD), Chris Coons (D-DE), Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), and Andy Kim (D-NJ) concluded a series of bilateral meetings and panels at the 18th annual Halifax International Security Forum in Halifax, Canada to discuss American security priorities and opportunities to strengthen strategic cooperation with U.S. allies and partners.

Kaine, Rounds, and Gillibrand are members of the Senate Armed Services Committee. Kaine and Coons are members of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

“I’m proud to have led this year’s bipartisan congressional delegation to the Halifax International Security Forum because the U.S.-Canada relationship matters deeply to Congress, and because it’s an important opportunity to meet with our allies to talk about our shared security challenges,” said Kaine. “We covered a lot of ground, including how interwoven America and Canada’s economies and security are, the United States’ commitment to NATO, the need to support Ukraine in the fight against Putin’s brutal invasion, and more. Strong relationships and open channels of communication alone don’t ensure success, but the absence of dialogue with democracies around the world guarantees failure. And when it comes to our national security, failure isn’t an option.”

“As the United States finds itself in one of the most complex threat environments in our nation’s history, the Halifax International Security Forum continues to be an important assembly of partners from around the world,” said Rounds. “The forum offers us the opportunity to have candid discussions about security challenges, defense resourcing and burden sharing to address some of the most pressing concerns facing the United States and our allies. Thank you to everyone who participated in this year’s forum.”

“Canada is an essential U.S. ally. We have to do more to win back and deserve their trust,” said Coons. “I was grateful to be back in Halifax this weekend at the annual security conference along with a bipartisan group of Senators to reinforce our congressional commitment to rebuilding trust with Canada and so many other allies represented here.”

“From ongoing wars in Europe and the Middle East to authoritarian threats and the rapid rise of AI, global security is at a critical crossroads,” said Gillibrand. “I was honored to join my bipartisan colleagues at the Halifax International Security Forum to reaffirm our commitment to Canada and our allies. Now, we must continue the work to make our democratic alliances stronger than ever.”

“As technology rapidly advances and the threats from rogue AI, cyber-attacks, and drones become more common, it is vital we lean into our alliances and partnerships to ensure our shared security,” said Kim. “I leave this year’s Halifax International Security Forum confident that Congress can deliver a foreign policy that provides economic opportunity and security for Americans by working with our global counterparts.”

The members emphasized the importance of the U.S.-Canada bilateral relationship and defense partnership with Canadian Minister for National Defense David McGuinty and Shadow Minister for National Defense James Bezan.

The delegation also hosted meetings with delegations from Germany, Latvia, and Norway to discuss continued defense collaboration to support Ukraine. Those discussions included Germany’s Deputy Minister of Defense Dr. Nils Schmid, Deputy Chief of Defense Dr. Nicole Schilling, the Federal Foreign Office’s Head of Cabinet Ambassador Henning Speck, Ambassador to Canada Ambassador Matthias Lüttenberg; Latvia’s Minister for Defense Raivis Melnis; and Norway’s Minister of Foreign Affairs Espen Barth Eide and Ambassador to Canada Hanne Ulrichsen.

Additionally, lawmakers from the delegation highlighted the United States’ shared commitment to a free Indo-Pacific and strong trade relations with Taiwan’s Deputy Foreign Minister Dr. Chen Ming-Chi, Taipei Economic and Cultural Office (TECO) in Canada Representative Dr. Harry Ho-Jen Tseng, and Director General at the Department of North American Affairs at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs Liang-Rudy Ke.

Lastly, members of the delegation spoke with David Smolansky and met virtually with María Corina Machado to discuss the status of Venezuelan democracy and the need for elections in 2027.

The senators also participated in various panel discussions regarding the future of NATO and other critical alliances, immigration and combating antisemitism, and AI technology.

WASHINGTON, D.C. – This weekend, Senator Andy Kim (D-N.J.) joined a bipartisan Congressional delegation at the Halifax International Security Forum where he underlined the essential role of the United States’ allies and partners in ensuring our shared security. Senator Kim emphasized that by leaning into strategic partnerships around the world, we create economic opportunity and security for Americans at home.

“There are so many different problems out there, especially when it comes to the rise of artificial intelligence, new technologies, new warfare that we’re seeing happening in Ukraine and elsewhere. This is not a time for us to linger on our disagreements, but instead to find new partnerships,” said Senator Kim during the forum.

WATCH SENATOR KIM’S PLENARY SESSION

While at the conference, Senator Kim spoke on a panel focused on what allies can learn from each other and highlighted how Americans directly benefit when the United States works with allies and partners to tackle global challenges like rogue AI, cyber defense, the future of warfare, and more. The Senator cited key areas of opportunity for collaboration, including shipbuilding and “Mythos proofing” AI systems.

Senator Kim shared: “I think in the United States we have to get over the idea that ‘America first’, translated on the international level, was very much read as ‘America only’ or ‘America alone’. We have to figure out how to be able to build together, in part because we can’t do it all on ourselves.”

As Americans continue to be directly impacted by global challenges and demand the end of the war in Iran as costs rise, the Senator encouraged leaders to “widen the circle of what national security means” to better understand how American policies abroad shape the lives of the American people at home.

Additionally, the Senator participated in bilateral conversations with world leaders, including David McGuinty, the Canadian Minister of National Defense; Mark Wiseman, the Canadian Ambassador to the U.S.; and other Canadian officials. The Senator directly reiterated his commitment to Canada and the United States’ allies and the incredible importance of the U.S.-Canada relationship. He also spoke with a delegation from Taiwan about their economic resilience and trade relations and affirmed bipartisan commitment to the U.S.-Taiwan relationship.

matches.text:
Washington, D.C.—Today, Rep. Mike Levin (CA-49) announced that he cannot support the Senate-passed energy permitting bill, known as BAAJA, as currently written. While the legislation includes important reforms to modernize the electric grid and accelerate clean energy deployment, Rep. Levin raised concerns about its impacts on the environment, Tribal sovereignty, and future fossil fuel development. He urged House and Senate leaders to negotiate changes that address these concerns before the bill moves forward in the House. Rep. Levin released the following statement:

“I can’t support the energy permitting bill the Senate just sent to the House, known as BAAJA, at least not as it's written today. Here’s why:

“I’ve spent my career as a clean energy advocate and an environmental attorney. I want us to build clean energy, and to build it far faster than we do now. So I’ve measured this bill against three questions. Will it lower costs for families? Will it protect our clean air and water? Will it help clean energy grow?

“There’s real promise on costs and clean energy deployment. The bill would modernize a power grid that too often can’t carry affordable clean energy to the homes that need it, and it would require data centers to pay for their own grid upgrades instead of passing the cost on to families. Many of those reforms are similar to legislation I wrote with Sean Casten and Kathy Castor, and I want to see them become law. I believe the emissions reductions and cost savings may be smaller and less certain than supporters suggest, however.

“Other parts of the bill raise concerns. The bill would limit California’s ability to protect its own water, weaken the science behind endangered species decisions, and keep courts from halting a project even when an agency skips the review the law requires. It would also make this administration’s fossil fuel approvals, offshore leases included, extremely hard for a future president or a judge to undo. For those of us who have spent years fighting to keep new oil rigs off the California coast, that’s a serious threat.

“Tribal nations have warned that the bill’s changes to historic preservation law could endanger sacred sites and undercut Tribal sovereignty, and they deserved a far bigger voice in writing it.

“Those harms would be permanent, while the clean energy gains would rise or fall with whoever happens to be carrying out the law.

“I’ve thought hard about the old saying that a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush. These grid reforms are real, and there’s no guarantee a better bill comes along that can actually become law soon. That risk is significant. But in the end, taking the current deal would mean giving up protections we may never win back in exchange for gains that aren’t guaranteed either.

“Since the Senate released the bill, I’ve worked with my colleagues in the House Sustainable Energy and Environment Coalition on targeted fixes to permitting certainty, clean water, endangered species, judicial review, and historic and Tribal protections. None of our major concerns have been addressed. I’ve also heard from hundreds of people across our district, and they oppose this bill by roughly two to one.

“Senators Sheldon Whitehouse and Martin Heinrich, who helped write this bill, are my friends and have long been champions of climate action. Many allies I deeply respect support it, and I know they want the same future I do.

“There’s still time to get this right. If House and Senate leaders from both parties sit down together and negotiate sufficient changes, I’ll be ready to vote yes.

“We can and we must find a better balance that protects communities and the clean air and water they rely on. I believe this is possible this Congress and I urge my colleagues to be responsive to the concerns of Americans across the country and fix this bill before it becomes law.”

Rebuilding trust and showing that the U.S. can be a reliable partner in addressing climate change going forward was top of mind for a group of House Democrats who attended a United Nations climate conference in Turkey last weekend, Rep. Dave Min, D-Irvine, said.

And though the delegation focused on exploring ways the U.S. could strengthen relationships to address climate issues, Min said they also felt some skepticism from others in attendance. Min said there is some worry that the U.S. cannot commit to climate issues long-term, because of how the political winds of the federal government can change quickly.

“You could feel the lack of trust they have in the United States these days, and that trust is going to take a long time to earn back,” Min said.

“That being said, I think everyone also agrees that the future is here,” he continued. “We can catch up. People still believe in the innovation economy of the United States. They believe we can catch up, but right now we’re way behind.”

Min said the delegation was met with “legitimate excitement” when they arrived because the U.S., under President Donald Trump, has not sent an official delegation to the conference in previous years.

Min said he and other members of Congress were set to attend last year’s conference in Brazil, but their trip was canceled amid the 43-day federal government shutdown.

One of the big issues Min said he is motivated to address once the 120th Congress convenes at the beginning of next year is to cut carbon emissions in the U.S., and even before the new Congress is sworn in, the House may be voting on new legislation that aims to speed up review processes for energy infrastructure.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which the Senate passed Thursday, would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects, like building power plants and other infrastructure, while also forcing data centers to pay for their own energy costs.

The bill was set to receive a vote from the House this week, but a lack of House Republican attendance delayed any action, Min said.

Though in principle, Min is in favor of the bill, he said he will ultimately be a no-vote when the time comes. Min argued that if enacted, the law would strip localities of control over their own backyard and limit their ability to prevent major infrastructure, like data centers, from being built, he said.

“This is a topic we discussed extensively at (the conference). When you’re talking about data centers, it’s not just the energy costs, although that’s a big part of it. It’s also the other ways in which they impact local communities — noise and heat, water usage — that should be part of any package we’re talking about,” Min said. ” At the end of the day, localities should be the ones deciding whether or not they want to put up a data center … with that being said, we should be pushing forward with permitting reform, for all of the above.”

matches.text:
Cyber Resilience for Critical Infrastructure Act would help utilities, hospitals, and water systems patch vulnerabilities faster and wall off systems that can’t be patched quickly

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Reps. George Whitesides (D-CA) and Josh Gottheimer (D-NJ) introduced the Cyber Resilience for Critical Infrastructure Act, legislation to help critical infrastructure operators fix security vulnerabilities faster, modernize outdated systems, and defend against increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks.

Recent outages that grounded flights nationwide and locked customers out of their bank accounts have shown how fragile the systems Americans rely on every day have become. Some disruptions come from cyberattacks, which AI is making faster and easier to launch. Others come from aging systems that fail under heavy network loads or break during routine updates.

As AI accelerates cyber threats, the window to respond is shrinking. Attackers can exploit security flaws in hours, while the utilities, hospitals, and water systems Americans rely on often take months to deploy fixes, leaving small, rural, and municipal operators especially vulnerable.

The legislation closes that gap by establishing sector-specific cybersecurity benchmarks and authorizes $250 million in competitive grants to help operators patch vulnerabilities, replace outdated equipment, and protect systems that cannot be quickly updated, without imposing new regulatory mandates.

“AI is changing the cybersecurity landscape faster than our critical infrastructure can keep up. Attackers can now turn a newly disclosed flaw into a working exploit in days, while the systems that keep our lights on and our water clean can stay exposed for months,” said Rep. Whitesides. “This bill gives operators, especially the small, rural, and municipal utilities that serve communities like ours in the Antelope and Santa Clarita Valleys, the tools to patch faster and protect systems that can’t be patched quickly. We should not wait for a major attack on a hospital or water system before we act.”

“Our hospitals, water systems, and power grids can’t keep a 21st-century cyber threat at bay with a 20th-century patching process. AI is helping hackers work faster and more effectively. Our critical infrastructure needs the tools to keep up,” said Rep. Gottheimer. “This bill helps operators conduct automated patching or contain systems that can’t be fixed quickly, so a software flaw doesn’t become a blackout, a contaminated water supply, or an outage at a local hospital. I’m proud to partner with Congressman Whitesides on this commonsense, practical bill to protect families in North Jersey and across the country.”

“AI cyber capabilities have reached an inflection point, and America’s critical infrastructure needs support,” said Mike Sexton, Senior Policy Advisor for AI, Third Way. “Congress should pass the Cyber Resilience for Critical Infrastructure Act—an urgent step to getting our national security back on track.”

The Cyber Resilience for Critical Infrastructure Act would:

Accelerate fixes for critical security vulnerabilities: Direct NIST to establish clear, voluntary, sector-specific benchmarks for how quickly operators should address vulnerabilities, accounting for safety risks and operational challenges.

Invest $250 million to strengthen critical infrastructure: Provide CISA grants to help operators deploy security updates faster, replace outdated equipment, and protect vulnerable systems from cyberattacks.

Prioritize small, rural, and municipal operators: Cover 100 percent of eligible project costs for smaller operators and state, local, Tribal, and territorial governments, while reserving 30 percent of grant funding for small, rural, and municipal operators.

Strengthen accountability without new mandates: Track whether grant recipients are fixing vulnerabilities faster while protecting sensitive security information and avoiding new regulatory penalties.

Rep. Whitesides has been a leader in Congress addressing the national security risks of advanced AI, and previously introduced bipartisan legislation to counter AI distillation and other attacks on national security and to monitor self-improving AI systems. Reps. Whitesides and Gottheimer are members of the bipartisan AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, which is focused on addressing emerging AI safety and security risks while advancing American innovation and ensuring the United States remains a global leader in artificial intelligence.

A one-pager on the bill can be found here.

The full bill text can be found here.

Washington, D.C. – As new reporting shows Thanksgiving prices soaring across the country, U.S. Senator Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.) joined legislation led by Senators Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) and Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) to ban corporations from using AI and other new technologies to increase grocery prices for Americans. The Stop Price Gouging in Grocery Stores Act prohibits the use of surveillance pricing in grocery stores.

Big corporations collect and purchase Americans’ personal information to create a detailed profile of consumers. This data, coupled with mobile apps, facial recognition, and other biometric technology allows companies to charge different people different prices for the same item. Many of the largest grocery chains are poised to implement the widespread use of electronic shelf labels, a technology that allows stores to change the price of an item in a matter of seconds, whether it’s online or in-person, from a remote location.

“As Nevadans get ready to celebrate the holidays, big corporations are investing in new tools – including AI – that they can use to inflate prices on everything from turkey to cranberry sauce,” said Senator Cortez Masto. “Price gouging hardworking families trying to put food on the table is unacceptable. That’s why I’m fighting to put a stop to this corrupt practice.”

Specifically, the Stop Price Gouging in Grocery Stores Act addresses the ability of corporations to leverage new technologies against consumers by:

Prohibiting surveillance pricing in grocery stores;

Requiring grocery stores to disclose the use of facial recognition technology;

Banning electronic shelf labels in large grocery stores; and

Establishing an enforcement mechanism to hold corporations accountable.

For years, Senator Cortez Masto has been fighting to make life more affordable for working families. After the Trump Administration began the Iran war, raising gas prices across the country, she introduced legislation to prevent big oil companies from colluding to artificially raise energy prices. Cortez Masto helped pass the most comprehensive legislative package to lower housing costs in decades. She introduced legislation to help everyday Americans lower their energy costs by putting money back into their pockets if they make their homes more energy efficient. Cortez Masto introduced the No Tax on Tips Act to exempt tipped wages from federal income tax and has been fighting to ensure the Trump Administration properly implements its No Tax on Tips policy.

Today, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, member of the Senate Intelligence and Armed Services Committees, released the following statement in response to Jensen Huang being reinstated as president, CEO, and board director of Nvidia:

“A boardroom vote does not resolve a national security risk. Nvidia’s board may answer to shareholders, but Jensen Huang must answer to the American people about his proximity to a suspected Chinese intelligence operative and the whereabouts of billions in advanced AI chips.

“Mr. Huang and Nvidia’s directors must testify to Congress publicly and under oath. I will continue to advocate bipartisan legislation to keep America’s most critical technology out of the CCP’s hands.”

matches.text:
Background

Ranking Member Huffman outlined five critical fixes in the jurisdiction of the Natural Resources Committee needed to earn his support for the Senate-passed permitting bill:

Respect Tribal sovereignty. Preserve Tribal consultation obligations, treaty rights, and the ability to enforce those rights in court.

Protect communities’ access to justice. Ensure people can challenge illegally approved projects and judges can stop damaging construction before the harm is done.

Close “forever permit” loopholes. Preserve future administrations’ ability to address illegal approvals and adopt health and environmental safeguards without forcing taxpayers to compensate corporations.

Protect endangered wildlife. Ensure decisions about endangered species follow the best available science.

Protect public lands and sacred places. Preserve protections for America’s special places like the Boundary Waters, Chaco Canyon, and America’s Arctic, and block giant AI data centers on public lands.

Full video transcript below:

"Let’s talk about where things stand in the final three weeks of this Congress on BAAJA, a huge 500-page permitting reform bill that passed the Senate last week. I want to be clear on exactly what is in this bill, why I oppose it in its current form, and how we can fix it – either now, if the bill’s supporters will negotiate reasonable changes, or six weeks from now, when Democrats hold the gavels in the next Congress.

Like most members of Congress, I support responsible permitting reform. I want our government’s approval processes for all types of projects to be faster and better for everyone involved – for companies who build things, workers who need jobs, and communities who deserve a say in projects that impact them. And I’m willing to support significant changes to make that happen.

But there’s a lot more going on in BAAJA than just streamlining the permitting system. As drafted, this bill is the most sweeping rollback of environmental laws we’ve ever seen – dramatically weakening protections for public lands, clean air and water, endangered wildlife, and sacred tribal sites.

The bill fundamentally changes federal reviews and approvals for all types of projects – not just power lines, but everything from data centers to pipelines and LNG terminals, uranium mines, ICE detention centers, and even President Trump’s vanity projects.

And it dramatically curtails the ability of impacted communities to engage in the review process – including native American tribes, sportsmen who hunt, fish and recreate on public lands, and conservation groups. And when they do, it makes it virtually impossible to force changes or to stop harmful projects in court, even when laws are broken.

Now, in a normal legislative process, especially for a huge complex bill like this, you would see public hearings with testimony from experts and careful deliberation. And legislators would have a chance to vote on amendments to fix major problems. But the Senate didn’t allow any of that with BAAJA – which is why two-thirds of Senate Democrats voted No.

And Republicans now want to rush it through the House and get it to President Trump’s desk before the end of the year.

I stand with a growing majority of Democrats who are drawing a principled line and refusing to be jammed – we will not support BAAJA unless there are fixes to the most glaring problems. We support responsible permitting reform – and there’s just too much at stake here for a rush job, just to get a deal done before the next Congress takes over.

Some have suggested that Democrats are just opposed to reaching ANY deal with Republicans and the Trump administration. And that’s not true – certainly not on this issue.

So let’s be specific. The most controversial and problematic parts of BAAJA fall under the jurisdiction of the Natural Resources Committee, which I hope to be chairing when the new Congress convenes a few weeks from now. I will tell you the specific changes that would remove my opposition and get me, and I believe many other Democrats, to “yes” as soon as next week.

Respecting Tribal Nations comes first. When a project threatens a Tribe’s water, treaty rights, or sacred sites, the federal government has obligations it must honor. The changes to the NHPA and CWA in BAAJA strip tribal nations of their seat at the table and their rights in court. That has to change.

The same goes for other impacted communities who deserve a fair chance to voice concerns about projects that could be harmful to them and – if the government breaks the law in approving a data center, mine, a pipeline or other project – to sometimes challenge that decision in court. BAAJA not only makes it much harder for impacted communities to bring a case, it blocks judges from issuing orders to change or stop a project even if it’s found to be illegal. That must change.

BAAJA also has loopholes that create “forever permits.” In other words, the permits the Trump administration hands out to their buddies over the next two years – even if they are found to be destructive or illegal – could be locked in for good. The extreme, unpopular policies and corruption we’ve seen from this administration are going to end when Donald Trump leaves the White House two years from now. But on energy and environmental policy, BAAJA essentially legislates a third term for Trump by tying the hands of future administrations regarding Trump’s decisions and putting taxpayers on the hook for massive damages if new health or environmental safeguards are placed on polluting projects.

BAAJA includes a radical rollback of the Endangered Species Act that goes far beyond anything that could be justified in the name of permit streamlining. The ESA is our most important safeguard for protecting America’s wildlife and habitat endangered species need to survive. BAAJA provisions that undermine the independence and quality of the science to skew ESA decisions against protection of wildlife must be removed.

Finally, data centers on public lands. I don't think there should ever be data centers on public land, but it's a real threat. This administration is pushing over a dozen giveaways of public land for huge data centers. At a minimum, if Donald Trump is going to propose data centers on our public lands that belong to all of us, there has to be a full and complete environmental review with a chance for everyone to participate in that process, and for those who may be impacted by it to challenge it in court.

The changes I’ve outlined won’t solve every problem with the bill. But we deserve at least this much to protect the basic interests of our environment, tribes, and communities all over the country.

We have specific legislative text ready to go to make these changes happen, and that is being shared with the sponsors of BAAJA. If the bill’s backers are open to compromise and will work with us on these changes – we can still pass the bill in this Congress, despite the terrible process that brought us to this point.

But if they continue the “take it or leave it” ultimatum approach, I’ll do everything I can to stop this bad deal. And six weeks from now, when Democrats are in charge, we will get to work on a strong, responsible permitting reform that everyone can get behind.

The American people, including the people’s House, deserve a say in this bill, and House Democrats – especially after the recent election – are going to insist on that.

So, for those who want to pass BAAJA now, I’ve told you how to fix it and I’m ready to work with you to make that happen. But if it can’t happen in the remaining three weeks of this Congress, that’s not the end of the story. Because if BAAJA doesn’t pass, I guarantee you House Democrats will keep working on this and we’ll deliver a much better deal – responsible permitting reform that helps build the things we need faster and more affordably without throwing tribes, local communities and the environment under the bus.”

Dear Mr. Roussel:

We write regarding highly concerning reports that over one hundred million Americans may have had personally identifying information (PII) stolen and sold on the dark web. While the Federal Bureau of Investigation is currently investigating the source of the data, this breach’s scale warrants additional attention to the data-handling practices of companies like yours.

In September, cybersecurity researchers discovered “Nexus,” an identity theft service on the dark web. Nexus sold illegally obtained PII, including over 150 million American drivers licenses, nearly 600,000 medical cards, and other forms of PII such as employment authorizations, Common Access Cards, and travel documents at a large scale. Nexus also offered PII of high-ranking American military and intelligence officials, and reports indicate other government employees were impacted. According to reports, the data was "continuously” exfiltrated from a breach at a “major identity verification company,” for months. While reports indicate Nexus has since disappeared offline, the consequences of this theft may be widespread and persistent.

Remedying this kind of breach is extremely difficult, underscoring the importance of strong data security practices to prevent any such breach. If the reported extent of the breach is true, tens of millions of Americans' data have been exposed and are at risk of identity theft. This risk is further heightened by Nexus allegedly selling ultraviolet, infrared, and other detailed license images. Criminals can combine such PII with commercially available data to commit fraud or other crimes. And foreign adversaries are likewise increasingly able to infer Americans’ behavior though commercial data linked to government credentials. Given the difficulty of tracking these credentials and data sales, remedying this breach will pose substantial challenges even where no further crime is committed.

The Nexus breach is only one of numerous incidents that place Americans’ privacy at risk and hurt the economy. Your duty to safeguard data is critical in light of AI-driven cyberattack capabilities, which may be utilized by cybercriminals for zero-day exploits. Companies like yours should reduce these risks by employing zero-trust architectures, proactively examining vulnerabilities in their systems, and minimizing overall data exposure through limited retention, collection, and sharing of PII where possible.

To better understand existing data-handling practices and risks around ID-verification, we respectfully request responses to the following questions by January 5, 2027.

Does your company adopt the following privacy principles for Americans whose identities are verified by your service? If so, what specific actions are taken to ensure these principles are followed?

Data minimization;

Use limitations;

End-to-end security; and

Consumer notice and transparency.

Do you sell or share any PII associated with identity verification to third-party organizations?

If so, please identify which third-parties, including any parties in which you contact with, as well as the purpose of the transfer and/or sale.

If so, what data associated with identity verification can third-party organizations access?

In what circumstances, if any, are biometrics, genetics, or other sensitive documents retained by third-party organizations using your service?

If applicable, is it made clear to screened individuals what PII is being shared with third-party organizations?

Please outline your retention schedule for individuals’ PII.

If any PII is retained, are consumers able to request deletion in a timely manner?

Is any PII from users stored in the cloud or a central location within your company or a third-party organization?

If applicable, when using in-person scanners for IDs, is any PII sent off-device?

What insight, if any, do you have into how third-party organizations that use your service protect data of screened individuals?

Do you impose data use restrictions on third-party organizations?

Do you provide PII handling guidance to third-party organizations? If so, could you estimate the rate of compliance with this guidance?

What cybersecurity practices does your company adopt to protect sensitive PII?

Are you participating in any partnerships to use AI technologies to identify cybersecurity vulnerabilities?

Has your company experienced a data breach related to government issued IDs in the past year?

Have you or a third-party organization unintentionally exposed PII associated with verification attempts?

If applicable, what was the source and size of the security incident?

If applicable, did you report to CISA, Ic3, or other relevant government entities?

If applicable, what steps did you take to aid and inform victims or third-party organizations?

If you use physical ID scanners, how often are software or firmware updates provided, on average? Are there security audits for scanners?

We look forward to receiving your response. Thank you for your attention to this matter.

Sincerely,

###
